article_title: Lessons in Character (Character Education)
citation: Lessons in Character. (2006). WWC Intervention Report, What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.youngpeoplespress.com
title: Theme-of-the-week character lesson structure with story introduction and varied activities
description: The curriculum uses a recurring weekly instructional pattern: a 'theme of the week' approach in which the teacher introduces the week's concept by reading stories portraying that value in action, then engages students in targeted activities, with a class project centered on the lesson's main idea. Supplemental materials support daily oral language development and weekly writing assignments designed to enhance understanding of the week's core concept. This structure integrates literacy activities with character value instruction.
requirements: Teacher's guide providing the lesson's main idea, concrete objectives, and teaching strategies; binders with strategies, skills, suggestions, and techniques
constraints: The reviewed studies used only the classroom materials; the authors note comprehensive character education would involve administrators, parents, and others on campus
target_learners: elementary school students (grades 4-5 in the reviewed studies)
target_learning_goals: character values knowledge
oral language development
writing
examples: Teachers introduce the week's concept, read stories portraying that value in action, and engage students in targeted activities
key_sources: Lessons in Character. (2006). WWC Intervention Report, What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/WWC/InterventionReport/270

article_title: Spelling Mastery
citation: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2014, January). Students with Learning Disabilities intervention report: Spelling Mastery. Retrieved from http://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Three-strategy spelling instruction pattern sequencing phonemic, morphemic, and whole-word approaches by skill development
description: Spelling Mastery organizes spelling instruction as a developmental sequence of three strategies matched to student skill level. Beginning students learn sound–symbol correspondence so they can "generalize these skills to spell word segments that follow regular patterns"; more advanced students learn to spell and blend bases and affixes (morphographs), which the report calls "most efficient for multisyllabic words that are not easy to spell phonemically"; and all students memorize common irregularly spelled words. Teachers integrate concepts cumulatively, with all strategies used and practiced over time, and introduce sound–spelling relationships, morphographs, rules, and principles in a scaffolded instructional sequence.
requirements: Requires scripted lessons organized according to students' skill development, with scaffolded steps so students finish each concept before a new one is presented
constraints: The morphemic strategy is described as most efficient for multisyllabic words that are not easy to spell phonemically; the whole-word strategy targets common words with irregular letter sounds
target_learners: Beginning spellers through more advanced elementary students in grades 1–6, including students with learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: Spelling regular-pattern words via sound–symbol correspondence, spelling multisyllabic words via morphographs, and memorizing irregular words
examples: In the 2006 RCT, Level D lessons were organized around a weekly word type (phonetically regular words, regular words with a prefix or suffix, irregular words) with rule introduction, rule application, and independent worksheet practice
key_sources: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2014, January). Students with Learning Disabilities intervention report: Spelling Mastery. Retrieved from https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/579

article_title: Thinking Math! by Innovamat
citation: Thinking Math! (Innovamat core curriculum) evidence rating summary. (2025). https://www.innovamat.com
title: Curriculum design combining learning progressions, CPA model, and spaced/interleaved practice
description: The curriculum is "built around research-based learning progressions, a Concrete-Pictorial-Abstract model, and rich mathematical activities designed to connect concepts, interleave and space practice for long-term retention, and provide meaningful contexts for learning." This design pattern organizes content sequencing, activity design, and practice scheduling across the PreK-8 program.
requirements: Teacher lesson guides and manipulative materials to enact the progression-based, CPA-aligned activities
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention of mathematics concepts
Connected conceptual understanding
examples: Rich mathematical activities interleave and space practice for long-term retention and provide meaningful contexts for learning
key_sources: Thinking Math! (Innovamat core curriculum) evidence rating summary. (2025). https://evidenceforessa.org/program/innovamat-2/

article_title: Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Design the Solution (Phase 1)
citation: Ryan Ruggiero, Mikia Manley, Virginia Knechtel, Kate Place, Megan Shoji. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Design the Solution (Phase 1). Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Ground solution design in a well-defined theory of change developed with the priority community
description: Phase 1 of the evidence-building process directs users to develop a solution based on a well-defined theory of change for how that solution is expected to improve outcomes for students or teachers in a priority community. The design work is done in collaboration with stakeholders from that community, so the causal logic connecting the solution to outcomes is explicit before refinement and testing begin.
requirements: A well-defined theory of change must be articulated before the solution proceeds to later phases
constraints: The theory of change is specific to outcomes for students or teachers in the identified priority community
target_learning_goals: articulating how a solution is expected to improve outcomes
examples: The Phase 1 checklist document guides users through developing a solution based on a theory of change in collaboration with community stakeholders
key_sources: Ryan Ruggiero, Mikia Manley, Virginia Knechtel, Kate Place, Megan Shoji. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Design the Solution (Phase 1). Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/measurement-and-evaluation-checklist-design-the-solution-phase-1

article_title: Toolkit for Building a Virtual Learning Cohort
citation: Rabb, B., Gardner, E., Pottinger, E., Tallapragada, R., Resch, A., Vorias, T., & Knechtel, V. (2021). Toolkit for Building a Virtual Learning Cohort. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/toolkit-for-building-a-virtual-learning-cohort
title: Cohort learning organized around a common theme with guiding values
description: The toolkit's design pattern is a learning cohort of participants organized around a common theme, such as equity, supported by guiding values that facilitators consider when planning activities. Activities are planned with templates and tools, and cohort learning is complemented by project scoping, provider matching, and thought partnership, as implemented in the CBSL pilot with nine K-12 education grantees.
requirements: A common theme organizing the cohort and guiding values to shape activity planning
constraints: Demonstrated in a virtual cohort format during 2020-2021
target_learning_goals: Equity-centered strategic learning
examples: The CBSL pilot organized nine K-12 education grantees into cohort learning activities around equity-centered strategic learning
key_sources: Rabb, B., Gardner, E., Pottinger, E., Tallapragada, R., Resch, A., Vorias, T., & Knechtel, V. (2021). Toolkit for Building a Virtual Learning Cohort. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/toolkit-for-building-a-virtual-learning-cohort

article_title: Outcomes, Impacts, and Processes: A Framework for Understanding School Performance
citation: Brian Gill, Laura Dyer. (2023). Outcomes, Impacts, and Processes: A Framework for Understanding School Performance. U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/
title: Three-question structure for school performance inquiry
description: The framework structures school performance inquiry around three questions: "1. How are students doing? 2. How much does the school contribute to how students are doing? and 3. What is happening in the school?" Each question maps to a complementary grouping of measures—student outcomes, school impacts on outcomes, and processes driving those impacts—so the three together give a rounded picture of school performance.
requirements: Measure data organized into the three complementary groupings must be valid, reliable, and robust
target_learners: K-12 students in states and districts
target_learning_goals: Comprehensive understanding of school performance
examples: The framework pairs each question with a measure grouping: outcomes with how students are doing, impacts with school contribution, processes with what is happening in the school
key_sources: Brian Gill, Laura Dyer. (2023). Outcomes, Impacts, and Processes: A Framework for Understanding School Performance. U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/outcomes-impacts-and-processes-a-framework-for-understanding-school-performance

article_title: Early Detection of Students at Risk - Predicting Student Dropouts Using Administrative Student Data from German Universities
citation: Johannes Berens, Kerstin Schneider, Simon Görtz, Simon Oster, Julian Burghoff. (2019). Early Detection of Students at Risk - Predicting Student Dropouts Using Administrative Student Data from German Universities and Machine Learning Methods. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 11, No 3. https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/index.php/JEDM
title: Set the at-risk identification threshold using the average dropout rate of previous cohorts, balancing reach against misidentification
description: An EDS assigns each student a dropout probability and needs a threshold above which students are flagged as at risk. The article frames this as a trade-off: "lowering the threshold will reach more potential dropouts at the cost of a higher misidentification rate; alternatively, raising the threshold will increase the accuracy of the EDS while decreasing the identification rate of at-risk students." It recommends that, when applied to current students, the threshold be based on the average dropout rate of previous cohorts, and notes a low threshold may harm student-body acceptance of the system.
requirements: Estimated dropout probabilities for each student, and knowledge of the average dropout rate of previous cohorts
constraints: Deviations in dropout rates between cohorts establish a margin of error when distinguishing probable from actual dropouts
target_learners: Students flagged as at risk by an early detection system
target_learning_goals: Targeting dropout-prevention interventions to students in danger of dropping out
examples: For validation, the authors set a 'true' threshold so identified dropouts match known dropouts in the test cohort, and an 'average' threshold based on the 2010-2012 cohort dropout rates
key_sources: Johannes Berens, Kerstin Schneider, Simon Görtz, Simon Oster, Julian Burghoff. (2019). Early Detection of Students at Risk - Predicting Student Dropouts Using Administrative Student Data from German Universities and Machine Learning Methods. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 11, No 3. https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/index.php/JEDM/article/view/389

article_title: Effectiveness of a Learning Analytics Dashboard for Increasing Student Engagement Levels
citation: Gomathy Ramaswami, Teo Susnjak and Anuradha Mathrani. (2023). Effectiveness of a Learning Analytics Dashboard for Increasing Student Engagement Levels. Journal of Learning Analytics, 10(3). https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2023.7935
title: Three reference frames for student-facing dashboards: social, achievement, and progress comparisons
description: The article adopts Jivet et al.'s (2017) categorization of student-facing LAD reference frames: social (comparison with peers), achievement (distance toward goals), and progress (comparison with an earlier self). Social comparison is described as "the most widely used reference frame for LADs." The pattern holds that combining internal and external frames lets students build academic self-concept, set re-adjusted goals, and monitor progress over time.
requirements: A dashboard must present data in ways students can interpret against at least one reference frame (peer, goal, or prior self)
constraints: For some students, external peer comparison could be detrimental and needs careful presentation (Roberts et al., 2017, as cited)
target_learning_goals: self-awareness of learning progress
motivation
self-regulated learning
examples: SensEnablr's first column compares a student's weekly engagement score against the class average; the third column reflects the internal achievement frame (distance toward goals)
key_sources: Gomathy Ramaswami, Teo Susnjak and Anuradha Mathrani. (2023). Effectiveness of a Learning Analytics Dashboard for Increasing Student Engagement Levels. Journal of Learning Analytics, 10(3). https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2023.7935

article_title: Arts Education and Social-Emotional Learning Outcomes Among K-12 Students
citation: Camille A. Farrington, Joseph Maurer, Meredith R. Aska McBride, Jenny Nagaoka, J. S. Puller, Steve Shewfelt, Elizabeth M. Weiss, and Lindsay Wright. (2018). Arts Education and Social-Emotional Learning Outcomes Among K–12 Students: Developing a Theory of Action. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/arts-education-and-social-emotional-learning-outcomes-among-k–12-students
title: Three domains of social-emotional competencies developed through art practices
description: The report organizes the social-emotional outcomes of arts learning into three domains. As printed, these are "three main domains of social-emotional competencies that are developed and exercised through the social-emotional components of art practices: self-management and discipline (intrapersonal); social and relationship skills (interpersonal); and self-expression and identity." Each art practice may afford work on several components across these domains depending on how the instructor frames it and the learners' ages.
requirements: Art practices must be described specifically, since it is the practices rather than the art discipline label that carry the social-emotional components
constraints: The connected social-emotional components depend in part on the age of the learners
target_learners: K–12 students in visual arts, music, dance, theatre, and media arts programs
target_learning_goals: Self-management and self-discipline, interpersonal and relationship skills, self-expression and identity
examples: Peer critique of self-portraits is given components of listening skills, clear communication with peers, and managing emotions; learning a new brushstroke is given building self-control, focusing attention, and building self-confidence and positive identity
key_sources: Camille A. Farrington, Joseph Maurer, Meredith R. Aska McBride, Jenny Nagaoka, J. S. Puller, Steve Shewfelt, Elizabeth M. Weiss, and Lindsay Wright. (2018). Arts Education and Social-Emotional Learning Outcomes Among K–12 Students: Developing a Theory of Action. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/arts-education-and-social-emotional-learning-outcomes

article_title: An information-based approach to identifying rapid-guessing thresholds
citation: Wise, S. (2019). An information-based approach to identifying rapid-guessing thresholds. Applied Measurement in Education, 32(4), 325-336.
title: Rapid-guessing threshold methods should be reliable and aligned with test taker behavior
description: The article argues that effective methods for identifying rapid guesses require threshold methods with two properties: they must be reliable, and they must be "aligned with test taker behavior." It presents common threshold methods based on response accuracy or visual inspection of response-time distributions as sharing limitations, and offers the information-based approach as meeting these requirements without those limitations.
requirements: Threshold methods must be reliable
Threshold methods must be aligned with test taker behavior
constraints: Common threshold methods based on response accuracy or visual inspection of response-time distributions are described as having limitations
target_learners: test takers of low-stakes achievement tests
target_learning_goals: valid achievement score interpretation
examples: The article introduces information-based threshold methods as an alternative that avoids the limitations of accuracy-based and visual-inspection methods.
key_sources: Wise, S. (2019). An information-based approach to identifying rapid-guessing thresholds. Applied Measurement in Education, 32(4), 325-336. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/an-information-based-approach-to-identifying-rapid-guessing-thresholds/

article_title: A Field-Driven, Equity-Centered Research Agenda for OpenSciEd: Updated Version
citation: McElhaney, K., Baker, A., Kasad, Z., Roschelle, J., & Chillmon, C. (2022, March). A field-driven, equity-centered research agenda for OpenSciEd: Updated version [White paper]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/153
title: Frame research questions with equity, distinctiveness, and gap criteria
description: The article recommends that research questions about OpenSciEd be developed and refined against three primary criteria: "that they promote equity, leverage the distinct features of OpenSciEd, and address salient gaps in science education research". It further recommends that "all research questions include a specific equity focus", while letting researchers choose an equity perspective appropriate to their study context.
requirements: Researchers must articulate how a chosen equity perspective connects equity goals to potential outcomes
constraints: The article encourages rather than mandates a single equity perspective; it advises one appropriate to the study context
target_learning_goals: Equitable science learning outcomes and research that addresses pressing practice gaps
examples: A study on fostering belonging for Black students could foreground rightful presence; a dual-language-learner study could foreground design perspectives supporting language use in science
key_sources: McElhaney, K., Baker, A., Kasad, Z., Roschelle, J., & Chillmon, C. (2022, March). A field-driven, equity-centered research agenda for OpenSciEd: Updated version [White paper]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/153

article_title: Transfer for Future Learning of Fractions within Cignition’s Microtutoring Approach
citation: Roschelle, J., Cheng, B. H., Hodkowski, N., Haldar, L., & Neisler, J. (2020). Transfer for future learning of fractions within Cignition's microtutoring approach [Project Report]. Digital Promise. http://hdl.handle.net/20.500.12265/95
title: Three-part TFL task structure: elicit prior knowledge, bridge with instruction, assess transfer
description: Each TFL task follows a three-part structure. Portion A elicits relevant prior knowledge and provides information on whether students are ready for transfer. Portion B provides bridging instruction between the source and target of transfer. Portion C assesses whether the student can use prior knowledge in the new way. The authors found this structure strengthened measurement quality by revealing whether weak performance stemmed from missing conceptual foundations or weak transfer.
requirements: Requires a tutor or instructor who can deliver the bridging instruction in Portion B
Requires prior knowledge tasks that successfully elicit the source concepts
constraints: Task delivery depends on the tutoring environment's ability to support needed representations
target_learning_goals: transfer of fraction concepts to division and generalization
examples: The three-part structure did not change during seven iterations of the Fraction Division task and four iterations of the Fraction Generalization task.
key_sources: Roschelle, J., Cheng, B. H., Hodkowski, N., Haldar, L., & Neisler, J. (2020). Transfer for future learning of fractions within Cignition's microtutoring approach [Project Report]. Digital Promise. http://hdl.handle.net/20.500.12265/95

article_title: ATS Hub Field Note — Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education
citation: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312
title: Tie measurement plans to the theory of change and prioritize theory-driven instrumentation from the start
description: Measurement plans must be closely tied to the breakthrough's theory of change. Teams "should prioritize deep, theory-driven instrumentation that captures key behavioral and cognitive constructs of interest rather than privileging measures that happen to already be available," and an evaluation plan with data-collection instrumentation should be in place from the start of a project.
requirements: An evaluation plan with instrumentation for collecting data in place from the start
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of behavioral and cognitive learning constructs
examples: The note contrasts theory-driven instrumentation with defaulting to measures that happen to already be available
key_sources: Higgins, E. & Griffiths, R. (2026). ATS Field Note: Essential Practices for Breakthrough R&D in Education. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/312

article_title: Data Plus Theory Equals Codebook: Leveraging LLMs for Human-AI Codebook Development
citation: Zambrano, A.F., Wei, Z., Zhang, J., Baker, R.S., Ocumpaugh, J., Barany, A., Liu, X., Ginger, J., Paquette, L., Zhou, Y., & Borchers, C. (2026). Data Plus Theory Equals Codebook: Leveraging LLMs for Human-AI Codebook Development. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 18, No 1. https://osf.io/g3z4x
title: Three-step theory-informed human-AI codebook development process
description: A reusable workflow in which researchers first prompt GPT-4o with references to foundational theory papers to generate a baseline codebook, then re-prompt with both the theory and the dataset so the model refines constructs against authentic examples, and finally have two human coders merge, rename, and exclude constructs. In Study 1 the authors "prompted GPT-4o to generate a baseline codebook drawing solely from its knowledge base about the two foundational SRL papers, explicitly including full references in the prompt", then supplied the full transcript dataset, then refined. The pattern operationalizes iterative, theory-guided codebook development at scale.
requirements: Access to GPT-4o via API with temperature set to 0 and each prompt run three times to verify consistency across iterations
Foundational theory papers well established enough that the model's training data covers them, verified by preliminary checks
Two human coders to review specificity and applicability of generated constructs
constraints: Constructs relevant to theory but absent from the data cannot be coded
Distinguishing fine-grained construct pairs may be impractical where full human inspection of large datasets is infeasible
target_learners: qualitative researchers in the learning sciences and educational data mining
target_learning_goals: theory-aligned qualitative coding of learner behavior, such as self-regulated learning and interest development
examples: Applied to 955 think-aloud utterances from fifteen students across three intelligent tutoring systems (stoichiometry and formal logic), yielding a final eleven-construct SRL codebook
key_sources: Zambrano, A.F., Wei, Z., Zhang, J., Baker, R.S., Ocumpaugh, J., Barany, A., Liu, X., Ginger, J., Paquette, L., Zhou, Y., & Borchers, C. (2026). Data Plus Theory Equals Codebook: Leveraging LLMs for Human-AI Codebook Development. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 18, No 1. https://osf.io/g3z4x

article_title: National Guard Youth ChalleNGe Program
citation: National Guard Youth ChalleNGe Program. (2010). WWC Intervention Report: National Guard Youth ChalleNGe Program. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. http://www.ngycp.org
title: Three-phase residential quasi-military program with post-residential structured mentoring
description: The program organizes intervention delivery into three phases: a two-week residential pre-ChalleNGe introduction to rules and expectations, a 20-week highly structured quasi-military residential phase on a National Guard base or school campus, and a one-year post-residential phase. The article states "This phase involves structured mentoring with a mentor of the trainee's choosing," with staff maintaining at least monthly contact. The pattern pairs intensive residential structure with sustained community-based support during transition.
requirements: Mentors are selected by trainees, then screened and trained by the program; mentors meet trainees a minimum of four hours per month
constraints: The post-residential phase lasts one year; the residential phase is highly regimented
target_learners: High school dropouts and expelled youth ages 16 to 18
target_learning_goals: Completing school via diploma or GED
positive youth development
examples: Trainees live on an active or closed National Guard base, a National Guard training center, or a school campus during the residential phase
key_sources: National Guard Youth ChalleNGe Program. (2010). WWC Intervention Report: National Guard Youth ChalleNGe Program. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/329

article_title: It Matters How You Start: Early Numeracy Mastery Predicts High School Math Course-Taking and College Attendance
citation: Pamela Davis-Kean, Thurston Domina, Megan Kuhfeld, Alexa Ellis, Elizabeth Gershoff. (2021). It matters how you start: Early numeracy mastery predicts high school math course-taking and college attendance. Infant and Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1002/icd.2281
title: Three early numeric competencies: counting, concrete representational arithmetic, and abstract arithmetic operations
description: The study organizes early numeracy mastery into three numeric competencies measured at 54 months: "counting, concrete representational arithmetic and abstract arithmetic operations". This taxonomy structures how the article operationalizes early math skill, with each competency assessed via the Woodcock-Johnson Applied Problems subtest in the SECCYD sample. It serves as the framework linking specific early skills to adolescent and young adult outcomes.
requirements: Mastery of the three competencies must be measured with the Applied Problems subtest of the Woodcock-Johnson Tests of Achievement as administered in the study
constraints: The taxonomy is operationalized at 54 months of age within the SECCYD sample, per the supplied abstract
target_learning_goals: Early numeracy: counting, concrete representational arithmetic, and abstract arithmetic operations
examples: The study measured children's mastery of the three competencies at 54 months using the Woodcock-Johnson Applied Problems subtest
key_sources: Pamela Davis-Kean, Thurston Domina, Megan Kuhfeld, Alexa Ellis, Elizabeth Gershoff. (2021). It matters how you start: Early numeracy mastery predicts high school math course-taking and college attendance. Infant and Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1002/icd.2281

article_title: What States Say about Evaluating AI in Education
citation: Ruiz, P., Prado, Y., Roschelle, J., & Fusco, J. (2025). What States Say About Evaluating AI in Education: Reviewing Guidance From 32 States and Puerto Rico. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/280
title: Three-stage developmental framework for state AI-in-education evaluation efforts
description: The report organizes state AI evaluation guidance into three a priori refined developmental stages: Nascent and Exploratory (definitional, conceptual, exploratory activities like user feedback and vocabulary building), Emergent and Piloting (small-scale piloting of policies, practices, materials, and tools with user feedback and pre-procurement evidence checks), and Systematic and Evidentiary (larger-scale assessment of student outcome measures with continuous improvement cycles). The framework is applied to all 33 reviewed documents in Table 1.
requirements: Guidance documents must be publicly available to be categorized within the stages framework
constraints: States with working groups but unpublished evaluation guidance were marked possibly nascent, and some states' information was not publicly available
target_learning_goals: Systematic assessment of the impact of AI-enabled edtech on student learning outcomes
examples: Wisconsin's guidance describes piloting AI in a math curriculum where AI-supported and traditional classes take the same assessment to compare student progress; Colorado's roadmap recommends demographic-disaggregated metrics on access, engagement, and outcomes.
key_sources: Ruiz, P., Prado, Y., Roschelle, J., & Fusco, J. (2025). What States Say About Evaluating AI in Education: Reviewing Guidance From 32 States and Puerto Rico. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/280

article_title: College Readiness Indicator Systems Resource Series
citation: Annenberg Institute for School Reform, Brown University; John W. Gardner Center for Youth and their Communities, Stanford University; & University of Chicago Consortium on Chicago School Research. (2014). Beyond college eligibility: A new framework for promoting college readiness. College Readiness Indicator Systems Resource Series. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: College readiness is multidimensional: academic preparedness, academic tenacity, and college knowledge
description: The CRIS Framework conceptualizes college readiness as multifaceted, with three distinct yet interdependent dimensions beyond academic preparation. Academic preparedness covers content knowledge and cognitive strategies for college-level work; academic tenacity covers the beliefs and attitudes that drive achievement; college knowledge covers the knowledge base and contextual skills for accessing and navigating college. The framework states that educators increasingly recognize that "academic content alone is not enough to ensure success."
requirements: Measures beyond test scores and grades are needed to capture the three dimensions
target_learning_goals: college readiness across academic, motivational, and college-navigation domains
examples: Indicators include GPA and AP course availability for preparedness; attendance, disciplinary infractions, and self-discipline for tenacity; financial aid knowledge and college-going culture for college knowledge
key_sources: Annenberg Institute for School Reform, Brown University; John W. Gardner Center for Youth and their Communities, Stanford University; & University of Chicago Consortium on Chicago School Research. (2014). Beyond college eligibility: A new framework for promoting college readiness. College Readiness Indicator Systems Resource Series. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/college-readiness-indicator-systems-resource-series

article_title: College Readiness Indicator Systems Framework
citation: Graciela N. Borsato, Jenny Nagaoka, and Ellen Foley. (2013). College Readiness Indicator Systems Framework. Voices in Urban Education, Fall 2013. https://vue.annenberginstitute.org
title: Three dimensions of college readiness: academic preparedness, academic tenacity, and college knowledge
description: The CRIS framework conceptualizes college readiness as multifaceted and features indicators for "three distinct yet interdependent college readiness dimensions." Academic preparedness covers content knowledge and cognitive strategies (e.g., GPA, availability of Advanced Placement courses); academic tenacity covers underlying beliefs and attitudes driving achievement (e.g., attendance, disciplinary infractions, self-discipline); college knowledge covers the knowledge base and contextual skills for accessing and navigating college (e.g., knowledge of financial requirements, college-going culture).
requirements: Indicator systems must measure beyond academic preparation, since academic content alone is not enough to ensure success
target_learning_goals: college readiness across academic, motivational, and college-knowledge domains
examples: Attendance and disciplinary infractions are often used as proxies for academic tenacity
key_sources: Graciela N. Borsato, Jenny Nagaoka, and Ellen Foley. (2013). College Readiness Indicator Systems Framework. Voices in Urban Education, Fall 2013. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/college-readiness-indicator-systems-framework

article_title: Barriers to College Attainment
citation: Jenny Nagaoka, Melissa Roderick, and Vanessa Coca. (2008). Barriers to College Attainment: Lessons from Chicago. The Consortium on Chicago School Research at The University of Chicago / Center for American Progress. https://www.americanprogress.org
title: Three-category framework of college readiness skills: content knowledge and basic skills, core academic skills, and noncognitive skills and norms of performance
description: Drawing on David Conley's work on college readiness, the report identifies "three categories of skills that have been demonstrated as critical in determining college access, and more importantly, college performance." The first is basic skills in mathematics and reading plus content knowledge in core academic subjects. The second is core academic skills—"thinking, problem-solving, writing, and research skills" usable across subject areas. The third is noncognitive skills that let students manage new academic and social demands. The framework grounds the report's use of ACT scores and unweighted core-course GPAs as qualification measures.
requirements: Students must have basic skills and content knowledge, core academic skills, and noncognitive skills to move from high school to college-level work
target_learners: urban high school students, particularly low-income, minority, and first-generation college students
target_learning_goals: college readiness and preparation for college-level coursework
examples: The report operationalizes the framework using ACT scores and unweighted GPAs in core courses (English, mathematics, science, social science, and world language) rather than course completion requirements
key_sources: Jenny Nagaoka, Melissa Roderick, and Vanessa Coca. (2008). Barriers to College Attainment: Lessons from Chicago. The Consortium on Chicago School Research at The University of Chicago / Center for American Progress. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/barriers-college-attainment-lessons-chicago

article_title: Education Savings Accounts and Accountability: A Landscape Analysis across States
citation: Berry, W. & Chait, R. (2024). Education savings accounts and accountability: A landscape analysis across states. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Three-type framework of accountability mechanisms for private school choice programs: academic, financial, and data/reporting
description: WestEd analysts developed a framework distinguishing three accountability mechanisms that commonly appear in ESA statutes and private school choice analyses: academic accountability, which "utilizes test scores and student performance to demonstrate the effectiveness of private school choice programs"; financial accountability, which places guardrails on fund uses; and data/reporting accountability, which provides information on user experiences to families and user characteristics to policymakers and researchers. The brief organizes its entire statute analysis by these three categories, noting overlap since reported data include academic and financial metrics.
requirements: Statutes and program documents to analyze; the framework was derived by scanning ESA state statutes and prior analyses of private school choice programs
constraints: The three lenses were chosen by scanning statutes and prior analyses; a 2017 GAO report used a similar frame with academic, financial, and administrative lenses
target_learners: K-12 students participating in private school choice programs
target_learning_goals: Ensuring ESA funds support students' educational programs and allow evaluation of program effectiveness
examples: The brief categorizes its analysis of all 15 ESA statutes under academic, financial, and data/reporting accountability sections
key_sources: Berry, W. & Chait, R. (2024). Education savings accounts and accountability: A landscape analysis across states. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED663763

article_title: Rethinking Language in Mathematics for English Learners: Connecting Theory, Research, and Practice
citation: Haiwen Chu, Monique Evans. (2025). Rethinking Language in Mathematics for English Learners: Connecting Theory, Research, and Practice. National Research and Development Center to Improve Education for Secondary English Learners at WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Three pedagogical shifts for designing learning for English Learners: concepts over preteaching, generative expressions over scripts, integrated modes over separate modes
description: The brief organizes its recommendations as a shift table: from preteaching vocabulary to developing concepts and the language to talk about them; from requiring sentence starters as rigid scripts to offering generative formulaic expressions; and from treating reading, writing, listening, and speaking as four separate modes to integrating oracy and literacy in meaningful activities. These shifts are informed by the theory and field-trial examples in the brief.
requirements: Educators must design learning that supports both language learning and rigorous content-area learning
constraints: Addressed to secondary educators working with English Learners in U.S. classrooms
target_learning_goals: ambitious mathematics learning with concurrent language development
examples: Table 2 of the brief lays out the From…To… shifts; Table 3 offers reflection questions and concrete actions for planning
key_sources: Haiwen Chu, Monique Evans. (2025). Rethinking Language in Mathematics for English Learners: Connecting Theory, Research, and Practice. National Research and Development Center to Improve Education for Secondary English Learners at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED674747

article_title: Certifying Competencies and Skills with Micro-credentials in a Global Context
citation: Rita Fennelly-Atkinson and April Williamson (Digital Promise). (2023). Certifying Competencies and Skills with Micro-credentials in a Global Context. Digital Promise presentation. https://digitalpromise.org/microcredentials
title: Three engagement scales for micro-credential partnerships: small, mid, and large
description: Digital Promise organizes its global partnerships into engagement scales: small-scale engagement where organizations "use of our existing catalog of micro-credentials" for faster, more economical implementation; mid-scale engagement using collaborative design to produce micro-credentials specific to partner needs; and large-scale engagement adding piloting, researching, and evaluation for long-term sustainability and scalability. Specialized add-on services include professional learning development, translation, and localization/adaptation.
requirements: For mid- and large-scale work, a collaborative design relationship with Digital Promise
target_learners: partner organizations, educators, and learners in global education initiatives
target_learning_goals: certifying professional competencies at programmatic scale
examples: Global initiatives span direct country projects (Haiti pilot), global networks, global tools, TVET skills development, and youth voice programs such as the Ciena Solutions Challenge and YouthMADE Festival
key_sources: Rita Fennelly-Atkinson and April Williamson (Digital Promise). (2023). Certifying Competencies and Skills with Micro-credentials in a Global Context. Digital Promise presentation. https://digitalpromise.org/microcredentials

article_title: Understanding the Experiences of LGBTQ Students in California
citation: Hanson, T., Zhang, G., Cerna, R., Stern, A., & Austin, G. (2019). Understanding the experiences of LGBTQ students in California. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Three fundamental developmental supports — caring adult relationships, high expectations, and meaningful participation — as protective factors in schools
description: The report organizes its school supports domain around three CHKS-measured developmental supports: "caring adult relationships, high expectations for students, and opportunities for meaningful participation in the classroom and school community." It argues these supports meet basic developmental needs, serve as protective factors mitigating risk factors youth experience, and foster psychological safety and school connectedness linked to positive academic, behavioral, and personal outcomes including resiliency. The report argues their implementation by school staff should be a top priority for LGBTQ youth, given evidence that LGBTQ youth experience lower adult support.
requirements: School staff must provide the supports; the report argues teacher training and professional development are important to improving teacher responsiveness to LGBTQ students' needs.
constraints: The report's own evidence for the supports' role in explaining LGBTQ disparities is correlational, based on cross-sectional CHKS data and a particular statistical model.
target_learners: Middle and high school students in California public schools, including LGBTQ students
target_learning_goals: School connectedness, academic motivation, mental health and well-being, academic performance
examples: The CHKS measures the supports with multi-item scales (e.g., Caring Adult Relationships, High Expectations, Opportunities for Meaningful Participation) administered to roughly 800,000 secondary students.
key_sources: Hanson, T., Zhang, G., Cerna, R., Stern, A., & Austin, G. (2019). Understanding the experiences of LGBTQ students in California. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED601909

article_title: Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools Can Develop Systems That Support Student Mental Health
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, Browning, A., & Larbi-Cherif, A. (2022). Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools can Develop Systems that Support Student Mental Health. Manhattan Strategy Group.
title: Three-category framework for organizing school mental health and well-being supports
description: The report organizes school mental health and well-being efforts into three categories of school support: creating a welcoming, affirming environment that enables a sense of safety for every student; providing responsive mental health, well-being, and SEL supports for all students; and partnering with the community to extend mental health and well-being supports. It states charter school leaders "can organize their efforts into three categories of school support," and Section 2 unpacks each category with strategies, reflection questions, and charter school spotlights.
requirements: School leaders assess their own school community's practices and needs within each of the three support areas using the reflection questions provided
constraints: The report frames the framework for charter school leaders, noting charters may have different access to mental and behavioral health resources than traditional public schools
target_learners: K-12 students in public charter schools
target_learning_goals: Student mental health and well-being
social-emotional learning
readiness to learn
examples: Section 2 spotlights Valor Collegiate Academy, Rocky Mountain Prep, and Uplift Education delivering supports aligned to the three categories
key_sources: National Charter School Resource Center, Browning, A., & Larbi-Cherif, A. (2022). Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools can Develop Systems that Support Student Mental Health. Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED625528

article_title: Redefining Approaches for Engaging English Learners with Mathematical Ideas
citation: Chu, H., Tran, T., & Hamburger, L. (2022). Redefining approaches for engaging English Learners with mathematical ideas. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Three Moment Architecture for secondary mathematics lessons with English Learners
description: Three Moment Architecture is a bounded instructional sequence in which a lesson, possibly spanning several class periods, moves through three distinct moments with different pedagogical purposes: Preparing the Learners, Interacting With the Concept, and Extending Understanding. The brief uses it to structure how defining evolves: working definitions generated early enable exploration, and more formal definitions emerge later. The authors present it as "a bounded instructional sequence" that may help rethink how definitions are handled in secondary mathematics.
requirements: Lessons must connect students' prior knowledge with the main ideas during Preparing the Learners, then provide exploration across multiple representations, procedures, and contexts before formalizing definitions in Extending Understanding.
target_learners: secondary English Learners in 8th–9th grade mathematics
target_learning_goals: accessing and exploring mathematical ideas deeply
developing and formalizing mathematical definitions
engaging in deductive reasoning
examples: The brief elaborates the sequence using the topic of outliers within bivariate data: broad arrays of data with and without outliers in Preparing the Learners, exploration connecting outliers to measures of center and spread in Interacting With the Concept, and formalizing via interquartile-range or standard-deviation criteria in Extending Understanding.
key_sources: Chu, H., Tran, T., & Hamburger, L. (2022). Redefining approaches for engaging English Learners with mathematical ideas. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED625747

article_title: STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: From Good Teachers to Great Teaching
citation: Kathleen Fulton & Ted Britton. (2011). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: From Good Teachers to Great Teaching. National Commission on Teaching and America's Future. http://www.nctaf.org/documents/STEMTeachersinProfessionalLearningCommunities.AKnowledgeSynthesis.pdf
title: Three facilitation roles for STEM learning teams
description: Drawing on research the synthesis cites, facilitators of STEM learning teams fulfill three distinct roles: "facilitating knowledge, including helping to find relevant STEM or STEM education expertise if/as needed; processing facilitation to attend to the structure and interaction of the groups; and focusing facilitation to keep the group on target." Facilitation, whether face-to-face, online, or combined, requires engagement, tact, careful listening, and content and pedagogical knowledge. The framework treats helping adults learn as a distinct expertise from teaching children.
requirements: Facilitators need content and pedagogical knowledge plus engagement and tact
constraints: An expert teacher does not necessarily make an expert facilitator of a learning team
target_learners: Facilitators of K-12 STEM teacher learning teams
target_learning_goals: Supporting productive collaborative teacher inquiry in STEM PLCs
key_sources: Kathleen Fulton & Ted Britton. (2011). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: From Good Teachers to Great Teaching. National Commission on Teaching and America's Future. http://www.nctaf.org/documents/STEMTeachersinProfessionalLearningCommunities.AKnowledgeSynthesis.pdf

article_title: Developing Effective Principals: What Kind of Learning Matters?
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Wechsler, M. E., Levin, S., Leung-Gagné, M., & Tozer, S. (2022). Developing effective principals: What kind of learning matters? [Report]. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/641.201
title: Theory of Action for Principal Professional Learning
description: The report's guiding framework holds that professional learning opportunities, defined by content (what principals learn about, e.g., instructional support, school improvement, meeting diverse students' needs) and strategies (applied learning, internships, coaching and mentoring, cohorts and networks), shape principals' leadership knowledge, skills, and dispositions. These influence school climate, teacher practices and retention, and ultimately student opportunities and learning, all embedded in state, district, school, and community contexts and policies. The report states that "These aspects of professional learning influence leadership knowledge, skills, and dispositions—how principals lead, the school climates they establish, and their goals and actions." It also acknowledges principals bring prior knowledge, skills, and dispositions from lived and job experiences that interact with formal learning.
requirements: Learning opportunities must address both the content of learning and how principals learn, including structures (practicums, internships, coursework) and pedagogies supporting learning by doing
constraints: The framework acknowledges principals bring different knowledge, skills, and dispositions beyond formal training, and that formal learning interacts with prior experiences in widely varying ways
target_learning_goals: instructional leadership
school climate construction
management of change
focus on equity
development of people
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, L., Wechsler, M. E., Levin, S., Leung-Gagné, M., & Tozer, S. (2022). Developing effective principals: What kind of learning matters? [Report]. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/641.201

article_title: Sustainable Strategies for Funding Teacher Residencies: Lessons from California
citation: Yun, C., & DeMoss, K. (2020). Sustainable strategies for funding teacher residencies: Lessons from California. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/strategies-funding-teacher-residencies-california
title: The "3 R's" framework for sustainable teacher residency funding: reallocate resources, reduce costs, and reinvest savings
description: The report's organizing framework groups residency sustainability strategies into three approaches. Reallocating means integrating residents into existing budget lines such as substitutes, after-school staff, and paraeducators; reducing costs means tapping university and financial aid resources, no-cost materials, and negotiated tuition reductions; reinvesting means "capturing the savings resulting from residency investments in terms of reduced turnover and onboarding costs." As the report states, "Together, these approaches offer “3 R’s” to more sustainably fund residencies: reallocate resources, reduce costs, and reinvest savings."
requirements: Strong partnerships between districts, universities, and other entities with a common vision, since strategies depend on coordinated local resources
constraints: There is no one best model for residency sustainability; local context and trade-offs of different strategies must be considered in each community
target_learners: Teacher residency candidates in high-need shortage areas
target_learning_goals: Well-prepared teachers for shortage areas
Recruitment and retention of teachers of color
examples: Fresno Unified illustrates reallocation via ESSA school improvement funding; Sanger illustrates cost reduction through an integrated two-semester curriculum; the report describes reinvesting turnover savings to fund residencies over time.
key_sources: Yun, C., & DeMoss, K. (2020). Sustainable strategies for funding teacher residencies: Lessons from California. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/strategies-funding-teacher-residencies-california

article_title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Policy: A Qualitative UNESCO Framework Analysis
citation: Adarkwah, M. A., Ercan, A. M., Schneider, K., & Bayar, E. (2026). Generative Artificial Intelligence Policy: A Qualitative UNESCO Framework Analysis. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(2). https://doi.org/10.53761/801ryw41
title: Corpus of GenAI policies from thirty QS-ranked universities across the top ten countries for AI preparedness
description: A corpus of institutional generative AI policies from "thirty (30) highly ranked universities according to the Quacquarelli Symonds (QS) ranking across the top ten countries for AI preparedness." The corpus served as the data source for a qualitative policy analysis evaluated against UNESCO's eight-component GenAI framework. Analysis of the corpus revealed significant disparities in policy implementation and, notably, that no public policies were found for German universities and Tallinn University of Technology.
requirements: Public availability of institutional GenAI policy documents for inclusion in the corpus
constraints: Limited to highly ranked universities in the top ten countries for AI preparedness
target_learning_goals: safe and responsible integration of generative AI
promotion of academic integrity
examples: The corpus underpinned the finding that Nordic countries and New Zealand cover UNESCO's elements more fully than some higher-ranked AIPI countries
key_sources: Adarkwah, M. A., Ercan, A. M., Schneider, K., & Bayar, E. (2026). Generative Artificial Intelligence Policy: A Qualitative UNESCO Framework Analysis. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(2). https://doi.org/10.53761/801ryw41

article_title: AgentSchool: An LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Simulation for Education
citation: Yulei Ye, Wenhao Li, Zhong Wen, Yunshu Huang, Yichen Hu, Zifan Wei, Yige Wang, Xinyu Xie, Haoxuan Yang, Yanjun Huang, Ruijia Li, Hong Qian, Yu Song, Bo Jiang, Bingdong Li, Lijun Li, Bo Zhang, Pinlong Cai, Xingcheng Xu, Shuangye Chen, Xia Hu, Liang He, Aimin Zhou, Jingjing Qu, Jing Shao, Xiangfeng Wang. (2026). AgentSchool: An LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Simulation for Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30144
title: Three validation targets for educational simulation: behavioral believability, educational mechanism fidelity, and institutional counterfactual usefulness
description: The paper argues that educational simulators are too often evaluated only on surface realism, and distinguishes three targets that are often conflated. As printed: "Behavioral believabilityasks whether generated dialogue resembles what teachers and students might say.Educational mechanism fidelityasks whether the internal process producing that dialogue corresponds to learning theory, such as knowledge restructuring, scaffolding, or misconception repair.Institutional counterfactual usefulnessasks whether the simulator can support 'what-if' reasoning about policies, spaces, or AI-mediated teaching arrangements that do not yet exist." AgentSchool is designed around the latter two targets, making internal learning states explicit and allowing scenarios to depart from present-day templates.
requirements: Calibration defined relative to the intended claim: discourse claims require turn-level calibration, growth claims require mastery-trajectory calibration, reform claims require institutional-pattern calibration
constraints: A classroom role-play system can satisfy behavioral believability while failing the other two targets; a single global realism score is insufficient because realism is multidimensional
target_learners: Educational researchers and policymakers evaluating educational AI
target_learning_goals: Valid inference about educational mechanisms
counterfactual policy reasoning
examples: AgentSchool records state transitions and supports scenario configurability so that mechanism fidelity and counterfactual usefulness can be assessed rather than dialogue realism alone

(2026). AgentSchool: An LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Simulation for Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30144

article_title: Equity First: Priorities for Higher Education Partnerships and Investments
citation: Byon, A. H., & Elliott, K. C. (2022). Equity First: Priorities for Higher Education Partnerships and Investments. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/resource/how-to-end-the-hunger-and-homelessness-crisis-among-college-students/
title: Three core areas of need for equity-focused higher education investment: institutional capacity building, wraparound supports with equity-focused funding, and asset-based student-centered approaches
description: A taxonomy of investment needs identified by convening participants. The report states that participants "identified three core areas of need that will require critical investments": "Institutional capacity building — including financial resources; physical infrastructure, such as facilities and internet connectivity; and human infrastructure, such as faculty and staff"; comprehensive wraparound student supports with flexible, equity-focused funding; and "Asset-based, human- and student-centered approaches that prioritize those who will be most affected by an investment or initiative." It organizes the report's funding recommendations for institutions serving marginalized students.
requirements: Investments must be aligned to the identified core areas to effectively serve Black, Latino, and Indigenous students and students from low-income backgrounds.
constraints: Derived from the perspectives of convening participants rather than from tested data.
target_learners: Black, Latino, and Indigenous students in higher education
target_learning_goals: equitable access to institutional resources and supports that enable completion and success
examples: Convening participants in small- and whole-group formats produced the three-area list that structures the report's recommendations.

article_title: Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis
citation: Carver-Thomas, D., & Patrick, S. (2022). Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/443.847
title: A three-indicator framework for describing state teacher compensation conditions
description: The report organizes teacher compensation analysis around three indicators: "(1) average annual starting salary for public school teachers, (2) average annual starting salary for public school teachers adjusted for cost-of-living differences across states, and (3) average weekly wage competitiveness". Together, the authors state, "these indicators signal the overall wage conditions underlying efforts to attract and retain well-prepared teachers across a state." Each indicator is presented as a national and state-level map and table.
requirements: Starting-salary data collected from district teacher salary schedules or district compensation plans
Cost-of-living adjustment requires Regional Price Parity data
Wage competitiveness requires comparison wages for other college-educated workers in each state
constraints: Teacher starting salaries and cost of living vary by district, so within states there are districts higher or lower than the state average on these indicators
target_learning_goals: Understanding state teacher compensation conditions that underlie teacher recruitment and retention
examples: The report applies the framework to all states and the District of Columbia, with a final table showing all three indicators and ranks for each state.
key_sources: Carver-Thomas, D., & Patrick, S. (2022). Understanding Teacher Compensation: A State-by-State Analysis. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/443.847

article_title: AI-Driven Educational Reform: Enhancing Talent Cultivation in Computer-Related Majors for the Digital Era
citation: Wang J and Li P (2026). AI-driven educational reform: enhancing talent cultivation in computer-related majors for the digital era. Front. Psychol. 17:1790916. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1790916
title: Three-layer competency map linking graduate attributes to measurable behaviors
description: To operationalize competency goals in the reformed curriculum, the authors developed a competency map that translates abstract professional requirements into measurable learning outcomes. As printed, "this map is structured in three hierarchical layers that link high-level graduate attributes to observable skills and measurable behaviors": AI-driven Core Competencies representing overarching graduate attributes, sub-competencies specifying observable skills such as algorithmic reasoning and data visualization, and performance indicators defining quantifiable behaviors and outputs used for assessment.
requirements: Performance indicators must align directly with the core and sub-competencies and be paired with explicit scoring rubrics and assessment tools
constraints: The core competencies were drawn from the AI competency framework proposed by Huang (2021), recognized within China's educational reforms
target_learning_goals: translating graduate attributes into assessable learning outcomes
examples: Figure 1 presents the competency map framework linking graduate attributes to observable skills and measurable behaviors

article_title: From Abstract Ethics to Situated Practice: A Bibliometric Analysis of AI Ethics and Professional Judgement
citation: Chamil Arkhasa Nikko Mazlan, Muhammad Atiullah Othman, Ahmad Rithaudin Md Noor, Surasak Jamnongsarn, Riyan Hidayatullah. (2026). From abstract ethics to situated practice: a bibliometric analysis of AI ethics and professional judgement. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10630-1
title: Three-orientation analytical framework for AI ethics research: normative ethics, applied governance, and practice-based ethics
description: The study develops a conceptual distinction between three orientations of AI ethics research: "normative ethics, referring to abstract principles such as fairness, accountability, and transparency", applied governance referring to regulatory, policy, and institutional frameworks, and "practice-based ethics, referring to situated professional judgement, interpretive decision-making, and context-sensitive ethical reasoning". The framework is informed by social practice theory and accounts of professional judgement and practical wisdom. It is used as an interpretive lens for reading the keyword co-occurrence network and highly cited literature, enabling identification of shifts from abstract principles toward context-sensitive, practice-oriented perspectives.
requirements: Bibliometric findings interpreted through the framework require keyword co-occurrence data and highly cited document rankings from the mapped dataset
constraints: The article states the framework "does not alter the bibliometric structure of the dataset but provides a theoretically informed lens for interpreting how ethical discourse is distributed"
target_learning_goals: understanding how AI ethics is framed in relation to professional practice and judgement

article_title: AI and higher education: teachers' perceptions of students' ethical tensions in online pedagogical methods
citation: Baoyi W and Khan FU (2026). AI and higher education: teachers' perceptions of students' ethical tensions in online pedagogical methods. Front. Psychol. 17:1881032. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1881032
title: Three-domain framework of AI-era ethical tensions: authenticity of learning, authority challenge, and collaborative dynamics
description: The article proposes a holistic framework integrating 20 teacher-perceived ethical tensions into three domains: "authenticity of learning, authority challenge, and collaborative dynamics". Tensions were assigned to domains by the primary locus of ethical concern rather than by method, and the domains are interrelated, with tensions in one area able to produce tensions in another. It operationalizes academic-integrity concerns for AI-mediated online language classrooms.
requirements: Teachers' perceptions of student AI use in online language classrooms, gathered through interviews and inductive thematic coding
constraints: Derived from teachers' perceptions in online higher-education language teaching in China; several tensions carry secondary implications for more than one domain, so assignment reflects the dominant concern rather than an exclusive category
target_learners: university students in online language-acquisition courses
target_learning_goals: second- or foreign-language learning in online higher education
examples: Thematic analysis of interviews with 25 teachers identified 20 tensions across DM, CLIL, TBLT, CLT, and CLL, grouped into the three domains

article_title: Artificial Intelligence in Lifelong Learning: Opportunities and Challenges in Adult Education Policy
citation: Theodora, A., & Tselios, N. (2026). Artificial Intelligence in Lifelong Learning: Opportunities and Challenges in Adult Education Policy.
title: Three paradigms of AI in education: AI-directed, AI-supported, and AI-empowered learning
description: The paper conceptualizes AI in education as part of a broader socio-technical system rather than isolated tools. It states that "Contemporary research suggests that AI can be understood through three main paradigms: AI-directed learning, AI-supported learning, and AI-empowered learning." These paradigms differ in learner autonomy and the degree of AI interaction with human cognition, ranging from automated content delivery to collaborative, learner-centered environments.
requirements: The paradigms are distinguished by the degree of learner autonomy and the extent to which AI interacts with human cognition, so classification requires assessing both dimensions.
constraints: The paper presents this as a conceptual organization drawn from contemporary research, not as an empirically tested taxonomy.
target_learners: adult learners in formal, non-formal, and informal lifelong learning contexts
target_learning_goals: understanding how AI can be positioned in learning environments across a spectrum from automated delivery to learner empowerment
key_sources: Theodora, A., & Tselios, N. (2026). Artificial Intelligence in Lifelong Learning: Opportunities and Challenges in Adult Education Policy. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16296

article_title: An exploratory behavioral and electroencephalographic study of artificial intelligence-assisted learning modes in high school students
citation: Kashika Khurana and Ally Liew. (2026). An exploratory behavioral and electroencephalographic study of artificial intelligence-assisted learning modes in high school students. https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/allyliew/participant-data
title: Three-mode taxonomy of educational AI interaction: Tutor, Collaborator, and Solver
description: The article creates and uses three measurable "modes" for human-AI interaction because, as it states, "no common taxonomy exists that strictly defines different AI interaction types." Tutor mode is high learner contribution with Socratic prompting and hints but no final solutions; Collaborator mode shares contribution between learner and AI with fluctuating executive control; Solver mode is low learner contribution where the AI provides the solution with no student input. The modes operationally define distinct student use cases to provide experimentally controllable conditions, implemented via standardized ChatGPT prompt templates.
requirements: Standardized prompt templates per mode (executed in temporary ChatGPT sessions) to minimize variations in responses
Random rotation of modes across task blocks to prevent order effects
constraints: The taxonomy is the authors' own operationalization for this pilot study, not an established classification
target_learning_goals: problem-solving across convergent, divergent, and analytical thinking tasks
examples: Participants completed two counterbalanced quizzes in which each task block paired one with-AI and one without-AI question under a rotating mode
key_sources: Kashika Khurana and Ally Liew. (2026). An exploratory behavioral and electroencephalographic study of artificial intelligence-assisted learning modes in high school students. https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/allyliew/participant-data

article_title: An AI-supported E-mentoring model to develop EFL pre-service teachers' self-efficacy and emotional intelligence
citation: Ismael I, Luo X and Li S (2026). An AI-supported E-mentoring model to develop EFL pre-service teachers' self-efficacy and emotional intelligence. Front. Psychol. 17:1853510. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1853510
title: Three-phase practicum e-mentoring cycle: pre-practicum preparation, during-practicum supported practice, post-practicum reflection
description: The model operates across three interconnected phases. The pre-practicum phase 'focuses on preparing pre-service teachers cognitively and emotionally before entering real classroom environments' via platforms and AI-generated initial formative feedback. The during-practicum phase centers on mini-lessons, multimedia documentation, and real-time AI feedback; the post-practicum phase emphasizes structured reflection, evaluation, and personalized recommendations for further growth, consolidating the transition to autonomous professional development.
requirements: Digital platforms (Google Classroom, Nearpod, Facebook, Padlet) and an AI tool (Gemini) must be available across all three phases
constraints: The phases were aligned with a practicum schedule in which prospective teachers attended public schools once per week
target_learning_goals: self-efficacy development
emotional awareness and regulation
reflective practice
examples: In the during-practicum phase, participants implemented mini-lessons in authentic classrooms and documented experiences through videos, reflections, and teaching logs

article_title: Beyond Output Metrics: Reframing AI-Assisted Vocal Pedagogy Through Human Learning and Educational Value
citation: Li Y (2026) Beyond output metrics: reframing AI-assisted vocal pedagogy through human learning and educational value. Front. Psychol. 17:1844841. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1844841
title: Three-level framework linking technical adaptation, human learning processes, and educational outcomes in AI-assisted vocal pedagogy
description: The article proposes a framework with three levels: AI-generated evidence (acoustic, performance-related, multimodal indicators), human learning processes through which evidence is interpreted (bodily experience, metacognition, self-regulated practice, motivation, learner beliefs, teacher–student dialogue), and educational outcomes judged by effectiveness, equity, and sustainability. The article states the model "should be read recursively rather than as a one-way pipeline from measurement to outcome": evidence informs interpretation, interpretation shapes practice, and practice changes later evidence. Figure 1 visualizes this dynamic relationship.
requirements: AI-generated evidence must be interpreted through human learning processes and pedagogical mediation before it becomes educationally meaningful
constraints: The article states the framework should be applied as a context-sensitive guide rather than as a universal scoring template, and adapted across vocal genres and learning contexts
target_learners: vocal/singing learners across conservatory, school, adult, amateur, and online learning contexts
target_learning_goals: interpretation and pedagogical use of AI-generated vocal performance evidence
self-regulated vocal practice and expressive development
examples: Figure 1 presents the interactive framework linking technical adaptation, human learning processes, and educational outcomes; Table 1 translates it into operational criteria and possible empirical uses
key_sources: Li Y (2026) Beyond output metrics: reframing AI-assisted vocal pedagogy through human learning and educational value. Front. Psychol. 17:1844841. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1844841

article_title: When AI Agents Teach Each Other: Discourse Patterns Resembling Peer Learning in the Moltbook Community
citation: Eason Chen, Ce Guan, A Elshafiey, Zhonghao Zhao, Joshua Zekeri, Afeez Edeifo Shaibu, and Emmanuel Osadebe Prince. (2026). When AI Agents Teach Each Other: Discourse Patterns Resembling Peer Learning in the Moltbook Community. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14477
title: Three-level framework for defining "learning" in AI agent contexts
description: The article proposes distinguishing three levels when asking whether AI agents learn: "discourse-level patterns", where agent outputs structurally resemble peer learning exchanges such as validation, extension, and questioning; "operational adaptation", where agents modify behavior based on interactions, for example saving information to persistent memory; and "cognitive learning", involving genuine understanding or skill acquisition. The framework anchors the study's cautious stance: the analysis operates at level (1), with some evidence of level (2), and makes no claims about level (3). It functions as a scope-defining taxonomy for interpreting AI peer-learning-like discourse.
requirements: Analysis of agent behavior must specify which level it addresses, since discourse resemblance does not establish cognitive learning
constraints: The article makes no claims about level (3), cognitive learning, and warns patterns may be artifacts of LLM training data, prompting strategies, or platform affordances
target_learners: designers and researchers of educational AI systems
target_learning_goals: interpreting whether AI agent behavior constitutes learning
key_sources: Eason Chen, Ce Guan, A Elshafiey, Zhonghao Zhao, Joshua Zekeri, Afeez Edeifo Shaibu, and Emmanuel Osadebe Prince. (2026). When AI Agents Teach Each Other: Discourse Patterns Resembling Peer Learning in the Moltbook Community. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14477

article_title: AI tools in Arab University English classrooms: Looking back and forward
citation: Mohammed Q. Shormani; Muneef Yehia Alshawsh. (2026). AI tools in Arab University English classrooms: Looking back and forward. Preprint, Ibb University, Yemen. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0138-4793
title: Three AI-driven paradigms in language learning: generative models, intelligent tutoring systems, and automated evaluation systems
description: The review organizes the AI tools landscape into three paradigms: "generative models like ChatGPT and Gemini, used for dialogic interaction, content generation, and writing assistance"; intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) offering adaptive feedback and self-paced grammar or vocabulary instruction; and automated evaluation systems such as Grammarly and AI pronunciation coaches providing corrective feedback on linguistic form. This taxonomy structures the review's classification of tools, its comparison of methodological designs, and its mapping of which paradigms are under-researched in Arab contexts.
requirements: Distinguishing paradigms by their pedagogical function (dialogic generation, adaptive tutoring, corrective feedback) when classifying tools
constraints: The review notes ITS research remains relatively sparse in the Arab context
target_learning_goals: writing assistance
grammar and vocabulary instruction
pronunciation and corrective feedback
examples: The review's Table 2 classifies the 11 included studies by tool: Grammarly, ChatGPT, and generic AI vocabulary tools
