article_title: AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge
citation: Brady D. Lund and Zoë Abbie Teel. (2026). AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge. University of North Texas.
title: A three-part framework of AI literacy as epistemic agency: Contextual Use, Critical Interrogation, and Participatory Governance
description: The paper proposes a framework for AI literacy organized around three interlocking dimensions rather than sequential stages. The authors state: "we propose a framework for AI literacy that is organized around three interlocking dimensions: Contextual Use, Critical Interrogation, and Participatory Governance." Each dimension corresponds to a distinct relationship to AI knowledge production: situated user, critical interpreter, and civic participant. The dimensions are cumulative but not hierarchical, mutually reinforcing as a practice rather than a ladder.
requirements: Learners engage with AI as situated users, critical interpreters, and civic participants simultaneously, since the dimensions are mutually reinforcing rather than sequential
constraints: The authors state it is not a complete curriculum or policy prescription but a theoretical frame; considerable work remains to translate it into concrete pedagogical practice and assess its effectiveness
target_learners: Students and adult learners using generative AI systems
target_learning_goals: Epistemic agency: critically evaluating, resisting, and participating in the governance of AI knowledge production
examples: The paper illustrates Contextual Use with a student researching a policy question who accounts for the model's framing assumptions, and Participatory Governance with the EU AI Act public consultation and the Detroit Digital Justice Coalition's data sovereignty work
key_sources: Brady D. Lund and Zoë Abbie Teel. (2026). AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge. University of North Texas. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27547

article_title: Awareness of Technological Isomorphism: Integrating AI into Elementary Mathematics Teaching on Data and Prediction
citation: Li Li, Yu Cao. (2025). Awareness of Technological Isomorphism: Integrating AI into Elementary Mathematics Teaching on Data and Prediction, A Case Study of the Compound Line Graph.
title: Three-stage pedagogical pathway of Perceiving, Comprehending, and Creating AI mapped to black, grey, and white box progression
description: Drawing on the Beijing Normal University "Black Box, Grey Box, White Box" cognitive progression model, the article "constructs a three-stage pedagogical pathway: 'Perceiving, Comprehending, and Creating.'" Stage 1 (Grades 1-3) uses AI-powered graphing tools experientially; Stage 2 (Grades 4-5) is the activation phase built on dual-track comparative analysis and reflection on prediction failures; Stage 3 (Grades 5-6) has students experience the machine learning pipeline with graphical programming tools. Two guiding principles govern implementation: Mathematical Primacy and Cognitive Progression from using to understanding to creating with AI.
requirements: Activation of isomorphism awareness is built upon students' thorough and robust mastery of mathematical reasoning
constraints: The empirical case validation in this study focuses specifically on Stage 2; the final internalization stage is left open for further operational development
target_learning_goals: AI literacy
statistical reasoning and trend-based prediction
examples: The Grade 5 compound line graph lesson implemented Stage 2 across three timed segments
key_sources: Li Li, Yu Cao. (2025). Awareness of Technological Isomorphism: Integrating AI into Elementary Mathematics Teaching on Data and Prediction, A Case Study of the Compound Line Graph. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09598

article_title: The critical-thinking paradox in generative AI-integrated learning: distinguishing efficiency from cognitive depth — a differentiated framework and testable propositions
citation: Lin J and Al-Hada NM (2026) The critical-thinking paradox in generative AI-integrated learning: distinguishing efficiency from cognitive depth—a differentiated framework and testable propositions. Front. Psychol. 17:1906070. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1906070
title: Differentiated three-level framework mapping AI-integration strategies onto surface, intermediate, and deep cognitive processing
description: The article proposes "a differentiated three-level framework that maps AI-integration strategies onto surface, intermediate, and deep cognitive processing, with a priori classification rules, level-specific AI roles, risks, and boundary conditions". For each level it specifies the cognitive operations involved, the appropriate AI role, primary risks of uncritical use, testable predictions, and preregistered boundary conditions. Surface tasks delegate operations extraneous to the focal objective, so AI serves as an efficiency tool; intermediate tasks require AI as a guided scaffold with metacognitive scaffolds; deep tasks require AI as a dialog partner while cognitive work stays with the learner. Task level must be classified a priori relative to the preregistered learning objective, coded by blind independent raters.
requirements: Task level must be classified a priori in relation to the preregistered learning objective, with the classification rule and examples preregistered and coded by two independent raters blind to condition and predicted direction.
constraints: The framework is presented as a falsifiable interpretation of a heterogeneous literature, not an established pattern; genuine heterogeneity across tasks, populations, and tools remains a rival explanation.
target_learners: learners using generative AI across educational levels, from primary school through university
target_learning_goals: durable, transferable higher-order learning including analysis, evaluation, and critical thinking
examples: Table 1 assigns AI roles per level: efficiency tool for surface retrieval and formatting tasks, guided scaffold for intermediate application tasks, and dialog partner for deep analysis, evaluation, and creative synthesis tasks.
key_sources: Lin J and Al-Hada NM (2026) The critical-thinking paradox in generative AI-integrated learning: distinguishing efficiency from cognitive depth—a differentiated framework and testable propositions. Front. Psychol. 17:1906070. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1906070

article_title: 'Co-pilot won't teach you to be a nurse': nursing academics' perspectives on GenAI use in undergraduate education
citation: Dabkowski, Elissa; Missen, Karen; Allen, Louise; Whitehead, Dean; Worn, Ryan. (2026). 'Co-pilot won't teach you to be a nurse': nursing academics' perspectives on GenAI use in undergraduate education. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00220-2
title: Three-theme account of nursing academics' sense-making about GenAI: ambiguity, core-value threats, and ethical development
description: The study's organizing framework groups nursing academics' accounts of GenAI into three major themes with nine minor themes: (1) Navigating the Unknown: Ambiguity in GenAI Use, covering policy ambiguity, divergent attitudes and curriculum adaptation; (2) GenAI Challenging Nursing's Core Values, covering professional identity, overreliance, and misconduct risks; and (3) Developing Ethical Nurses in a Digital Age, covering curricular integration, safeguarding critical thinking, and embedding professional values. The framework positions GenAI as disrupting not only integrity processes but "the basis on which nursing educators judge students' readiness for safe practice".
requirements: Derived from reflexive thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with academics involved in undergraduate nursing education and academic integrity processes.
constraints: Purposive sampling via the Australasian Academic Integrity Network; findings may not reflect academics outside that network or in other countries, and reflect a particular point in time.
target_learning_goals: understanding educator responses to GenAI
guiding curriculum and assessment redesign
examples: The framework emerged from 22 interviews averaging 39.05 minutes, analysed by three researchers using Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis.
key_sources: Dabkowski, Elissa; Missen, Karen; Allen, Louise; Whitehead, Dean; Worn, Ryan. (2026). 'Co-pilot won't teach you to be a nurse': nursing academics' perspectives on GenAI use in undergraduate education. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00220-2

article_title: Inquiry-Based Learning in STEM Education: The Impact of Generative AI-Based Chatbots on Primary School Students' Problem Posing Ability in Science
citation: Dai, Z., Huang, F., Xiong, J., Yang, Y., Zhang, Q., & Peng, X. (2026). Inquiry-based learning in STEM education: the impact of generative AI-based Chatbots on primary school students’ problem posing ability in science. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00631-0
title: Three progressive thematic inquiry lessons sequenced to develop problem posing ability
description: The instructional pattern is a sequence of three problem-based inquiry lessons layered onto regular lessons: "Based on this content, we designed three progressive thematic inquiry lessons; the teaching content and objectives are presented in Table 1". The progression moves from understanding the characteristics of good questions, to constructing logically progressive question chains, to interdisciplinary questioning from scientist, engineer, mathematician, and artist roles in a wind-turbine context. Each lesson targets a distinct problem posing objective and draws on prerequisite knowledge built in preceding regular lessons.
requirements: Regular lessons preceding each inquiry lesson to construct prerequisite knowledge for the topic
A context derived from the scientific content of the preceding regular lessons for each inquiry lesson
constraints: The pattern was implemented within the Grade 3 'Air' unit in regular classroom teaching in a Chinese primary school
target_learning_goals: Understanding good questions, building question chains, and developing interdisciplinary and creative problem posing
examples: Topic 2 used a 'drawing a question necklace' task in which students linked related questions into a logically progressive chain

article_title: Culturally-Aware AI for Cross-Boundary Community Learning: Undergraduate Innovation at the Intersection of Computation
citation: Jiaojiao Zhao, Weisheng Zhang, Jiawen Cai, Haibin Gao, and Luyao Zhang. (2026). Culturally-Aware AI for Cross-Boundary Community Learning: Undergraduate Innovation at the Intersection of Computation and Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09041
title: Three boundary-spanning events linking field data to community impact (field co-design, collaborative alignment, mutual validation)
description: The CBL course is structured as three structured occasions traversing institutional interfaces: Week 3 field co-design generating museum digital assets, Week 4 collaborative alignment of proposals with four SDGs (4, 8, 11, 17), and Week 7 mutual validation where "validation criteria are negotiated between stakeholders." The pattern links museum field data through student-created materials to intended community outcomes, followed by co-dissemination via open-source release and student co-authorship.
requirements: A community partner selected for geographic proximity, mission alignment, and expressed need
Boundary-spanning events at planned weeks of the course
constraints: Validated in one 7-week course with two students and one museum
target_learners: Undergraduate students in community-based learning courses
target_learning_goals: Participatory design with community stakeholders
Aligning technical projects with sustainable development goals
examples: Week 3 museum fieldwork produced photos, sketches, and audio notes; Week 7 symposium presented prototypes to community partners, staff, and peers

article_title: Improving Capstone Team Outcomes through Dynamic Skill Matching and Preference Alignment
citation: Brandon Pardi, Garret Castro, Michael Pisman, Avash Adhikari, and Santosh Chandrasekhar. (2026). Improving Capstone Team Outcomes through Dynamic Skill Matching and Preference Alignment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15572
title: Three-stage methodology combining student surveys, LLM skill extraction, and dynamic preference-aware matching
description: The article proposes a data-driven team-formation framework with three stages: "student surveys to capture detailed and granular skill sets and project preferences; (2) LLM-driven extraction of essential project skills from sponsor-provided descriptions; and (3) a dynamic matching algorithm that iteratively prioritizes currently unfulfilled skills and integrates student preferences during team formation." It is positioned as combining bottom-up student agency with top-down project skill requirements in a single scalable pipeline, addressing gaps in tools like CATME Team-Maker that do not match skills to projects or dynamically integrate preferences.
requirements: Students complete skill and preference surveys at the start of the course, with project summary descriptions available beforehand
A skill list predetermined from prior and anticipated project requirements
LLM-generated skill ratings are manually reviewed before use
constraints: Relies on self-reported skills and preferences, leaving it vulnerable to misrepresentation
The preference weight parameter requires manual tuning
LLM-generated project skills still require manual verification
target_learning_goals: effective team formation for project-based learning
student motivation and agency through preference alignment
examples: Validated on UC Merced capstone data from Fall 2023 (16 projects, 68 students) and Spring 2024 (27 projects, 122 students)
key_sources: Brandon Pardi, Garret Castro, Michael Pisman, Avash Adhikari, and Santosh Chandrasekhar. (2026). Improving Capstone Team Outcomes through Dynamic Skill Matching and Preference Alignment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15572

article_title: Edustories: A Collection of Real-world Case Studies from Classroom Practices
citation: Michal Štefánik, Jan Nehyba, Jirina Karasova, Martin Fico, Lucie Škarková, Markéta Košatková, David Kosatka. (2026). Edustories: A Collection of Real-world Case Studies from Classroom Practices. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20484
title: Three-facet Behavior Management Framework decomposition used for expert evaluation
description: To assess interventions, five educational experts decomposed classroom behavior management into three facets drawn from Behavior Management Frameworks: "(1) Humanistic orientation, reflecting emphasis on empathy, dialogue, and student needs versus reinforced control; (2) Reactivity, capturing reactive (cf. preventive) strategies; and (3) Systematicity" distinguishing generalizable strategies from incident-specific actions. Experts rated each facet on a centered Likert scale (-2 to +2) and combined them into an overall Appropriateness score mapped to the dataset's outcome labels.
requirements: Ratings by trained education experts familiar with behavior management frameworks
A centered Likert scale with defined mapping to outcome categories
constraints: The mapping treats -1 and 0 ratings as partial or short-term success and +1/+2 as long-term success, preserving zero-centered semantics
target_learning_goals: evaluating the appropriateness of classroom behavior-management interventions
examples: Experts rated interventions on humanistic orientation, reactivity, and systematicity before constructing the overall Appropriateness judgment

article_title: A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers based on goals, models
citation: Finkelstein, N. (2026). A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers on action based on goals, models of human learning, and use of technologies. Draft manuscript, University of Colorado, Boulder.
title: Three broad classes of goals for educational systems: developing individuals, societal infrastructure, and workforce development
description: The article enumerates three broad classes of goals spanning why educational systems exist: "1) Developing individuals", "2) Societal infrastructure", and "3) Workforce development". It places them in the author's priority order, arguing that workforce goals are achieved by addressing the first two, and that being explicit about goals ought to guide technology use in creating educational environments.
requirements: Educators must prioritize among potentially multifaceted and contradictory goals before allocating technology responsibilities
constraints: The ordering is explicitly the author's own priority order, and the article acknowledges others may hold different goals for educational systems
target_learning_goals: individual development, citizenship and societal participation, career preparation
examples: The article cites AAC&U (2009) and Finley (2021) in arguing that workforce development and job training goals are achieved by developing learners and preparing them to engage in society

article_title: Exploring Students' Perceptions of Using Generative AI-Assisted Problem Posing
citation: Lindsay Dawson, N. Sanjay Rebello. (2026). Exploring Students' Perceptions of Using Generative AI-Assisted Problem Posing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12523
title: Three-phase Gen AI-assisted problem-posing activity with pre-training, training video, and post-training reflections
description: A self-study activity administered as an extra-credit assignment in which "The study design consisted of three phases completed over one week". In Phase 1 students posed a variation of a recitation problem with a Gen AI platform of their choosing and reflected on the interaction with six guided questions; in Phase 2 they watched a 15-minute training video on Gen AI and prompt engineering; in Phase 3 they repeated the task using what they learned and answered additional reflection questions on training and willingness to continue. Students submitted their Gen AI conversations as data.
requirements: access to a Gen AI platform of the student's choosing
completion of the training video before Phase 3
constraints: administered as an extra-credit assignment in an online summer course, which the authors note may have skewed participation toward more agreeable views
target_learners: prospective engineering majors in first-semester calculus-based physics
target_learning_goals: problem posing as a self-study technique
effective prompting of Gen AI
examples: Phase 1 reflections asked students to discuss similarities and differences between the original and posed problem and the quality of the Gen AI response

article_title: DraftTrace: A Multi-View Analytics Environment for AI-Integrated Writing
citation: Divyansh Chandarana, Sandipan De, Vivek Gupta. (2026). DRAFTTRACE: A Multi-View Analytics Environment for AI-Integrated Writing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36544
title: Three complementary views of AI-integrated writing: product, process, and interaction
description: The article argues that understanding student writing in AI-mediated settings requires three complementary views: the product view characterizes the final artifact, the process view captures how the artifact develops over time, and the interaction view captures how the student engages with the AI during that process. The authors state that "understanding of writing requires considering three complementary views" and argue existing tools treat these capabilities as separate signals rather than complementary views of the same writing activity. DRAFTTRACE operationalizes this framework by capturing and aligning all three.
requirements: Writing activity must be captured within an environment that records product, process, and interaction signals so they can be aligned and interpreted together
constraints: The captured signals do not capture every aspect of the writing process and cannot observe all external resources or activities that may contribute to a response
target_learning_goals: understanding how writing activity contributes to student learning in AI-integrated settings
characterizing how students produce written assignments
examples: DRAFTTRACE records document events with timestamps and input channels, replays events to rebuild the document with per-character provenance labels, and persists each student prompt to the integrated assistant.
key_sources: Divyansh Chandarana, Sandipan De, Vivek Gupta. (2026). DRAFTTRACE: A Multi-View Analytics Environment for AI-Integrated Writing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36544

article_title: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) in Teaching and Learning Processes at the K-12 Level: A Systematic Review
citation: Marzano, D. (2025). Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) in Teaching and Learning Processes at the K-12 Level: A Systematic Review. Technology, Knowledge and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10758-025-09853-7
title: Ouyang and Jiao's three paradigms of AI in Education: AI-Directed, AI-Supported, and AI-Enhanced Learning
description: A taxonomy the review adopts to organize how Artificial Intelligence is used in Education, synthesizing three paradigms. In AI-Directed Learning "the student is the direct recipient of the AI system, which provides opportunities for individualized learning and immediate feedback". AI-Supported Learning is cooperative learning involving interaction between student and AI system, and AI-Enhanced Learning treats AI in Education as a complex system involving students, teachers, stakeholders and AI techniques serving as a tool to enrich human intelligence. The review presents this as a synthesis of prior literature rather than an empirically tested model.
requirements: Requires distinguishing the role of the AI system relative to the student (recipient, interaction partner, or enrichment tool) when classifying an AI application
constraints: Presented in the review as a conceptual synthesis attributed to Ouyang and Jiao (2021), not tested empirically in this article
target_learners: K-12 primary and secondary school students
target_learning_goals: Understanding how AI systems can be positioned in teaching and learning processes
examples: The review uses the taxonomy in its overview of existing literature to characterize how AIEd research has been studied

article_title: Generative AI as a Design Variable: An Evidence-Centered Framework for Principled Governance in STEM Assessment
citation: Gao, Y., Chen, Z., Li, M., & Zhai, X. (2026). Generative AI as a Design Variable: An Evidence-Centered Framework for Principled Governance in STEM Assessment.
title: Choose Restrict, Scaffold, or Require GenAI governance from the construct targeted and whether redesign can restore the inferential chain
description: The article articulates three governance stances grounded in validity: "Restrict is warranted when GenAI would contaminate the inferential link between student work products and targeted unaided proficiency"; "Scaffold is warranted when bounded GenAI support can support peripheral demands without revealing the target construct"; and Require is warranted when the target construct is disciplinary AI interaction competency with tasks eliciting distinguishable process artifacts. The stances are sequential: Restrict applies only after scaffold options fail.
requirements: An explicit ECD analysis of the student, evidence, and task models for the specific assessment before selecting a stance
constraints: Restrict is a last resort, triggered only when neither leveraging GenAI's generative capacity nor guardrailing within a redesigned task can preserve construct validity
target_learners: STEM students in assessment contexts where GenAI is available
target_learning_goals: Preserving assessment validity for targeted disciplinary constructs while preparing students for AI-enabled workflows
examples: Scaffold condition three permits GenAI to retrieve formulas but prohibits generating or checking numerical solutions in a physics problem-solving task, analogous to permitting a calculator
key_sources: Gao, Y., Chen, Z., Li, M., & Zhai, X. (2026). Generative AI as a Design Variable: An Evidence-Centered Framework for Principled Governance in STEM Assessment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24837

article_title: Knowledge-Based Design Requirements for Generative Social Robots in Higher Education
citation: S. Vonschallen, D. Oberle, T. Schmiedel, and F. Eyssel. (2026). Knowledge-Based Design Requirements for Generative Social Robots in Higher Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12873
title: Three knowledge types (self-, user-, context-knowledge) as drivers of autonomous GSR behavior
description: The article adopts a knowledge-based design perspective in which a generative social robot's autonomous behavior is driven by three types of agent knowledge. Self-knowledge is "the robot's internal understanding of its role, personality, functionalities, and expected behaviors"; user-knowledge is information about the learner enabling personalized tutoring; context-knowledge comprises domain- and task-relevant information. The framework holds that because GSR behavior is non-deterministic, engineering what the robot knows can make desired behaviors more reliable.
requirements: The robot's knowledge base must be deliberately curated and aligned with user and expert perspectives, since configuration left solely to developers may misalign with privacy and educational norms.
constraints: The framework addresses informational prerequisites, not the robot's appearance, system reliability, or the integration process, which the authors state were not explored.
target_learning_goals: responsible and effective tutoring support for learning lecture content
examples: The interview guideline asked participants what role and personality the robot should have (self-knowledge), what student information would help it interact effectively (user-knowledge), and what course and environment knowledge it would require (context-knowledge).
key_sources: S. Vonschallen, D. Oberle, T. Schmiedel, and F. Eyssel. (2026). Knowledge-Based Design Requirements for Generative Social Robots in Higher Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12873

article_title: 'It Felt a Bit Eerie": Exploring Humanlike Interactions During Collaborative Writing with an Artificial Agent'
citation: Michael Yin, Angela Chiang, Samuel Rhys Cox, and Robert Xiao. (2026). "It Felt a Bit Eerie": Exploring Humanlike Interactions During Collaborative Writing with an Artificial Agent. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24729
title: Three-variant AI-assisted collaborative writing text editor
description: A custom web-based text editor in which an LLM-backed artificial agent acts as a peer editor offering replacement suggestions and comments in an Editing Pane. The authors "built three variants of an AI-assisted text editor along a spectrum of simulated humanlike interaction (synchronous and with a cursor) to machinelike interaction (asynchronous and without a cursor)". The suggestion suite was constant across variants; variants differed only in temporal and visual humanlikeness. It was built with React and ProseMirror on the front end and a Python Flask back end calling the OpenAI gpt-4o API.
requirements: An LLM backend (OpenAI gpt-4o API calls) generating replacement and comment suggestions from the chunked text and previous suggestions
constraints: Humanlike behaviour heuristics (suggestion timing, cursor motion, typing speed) were tweaked subjectively and based on averages; the authors note "there is no 'average' human"
target_learners: adult writers in a lab study (18+, fluent in English)
target_learning_goals: collaborative writing and revision with AI support
examples: Heuristics for humanlike behaviour were derived from a formative study with 8 HCI researchers acting as peer editors, plus literature-based typing-speed parameters
key_sources: Michael Yin, Angela Chiang, Samuel Rhys Cox, and Robert Xiao. (2026). "It Felt a Bit Eerie": Exploring Humanlike Interactions During Collaborative Writing with an Artificial Agent. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24729

article_title: Cognitive Episodes in LLM Reasoning Traces Enable Interpretable Human Item Difficulty Prediction
citation: Chenguang Wang, Ming Li, Xinyue Zeng, Zhuochun Li, Hong Jiao, Tianyi Zhou, Dawei Zhou. (2026). Cognitive Episodes in LLM Reasoning Traces Enable Interpretable Human Item Difficulty Prediction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28186
title: Sentence-level episode-labeling corpus and RoBERTa classifier trained on ThinkARM annotations
description: To support sentence-level episode profiling, the authors build a labeled corpus from ThinkARM reasoning-trace annotations of traces generated by five reasoning models on Omni-MATH. After cleaning, the corpus contains 231,913 labeled sentence–episode pairs for training and validation, with a human-verified gold set of 7,067 sentences reserved for testing. A RoBERTa-based classifier trained on this corpus performs eight-way episode prediction; "On the human-annotated gold test set, the classifier achieves an accuracy of0.799, a macro-F1 of0.761, and a micro-F1 of0.799", and is then used as the automatic episode labeler in Epi2Diff.
requirements: Sentence segmentation of reasoning traces and GPT-5 annotations plus a human-verified gold set for final testing
constraints: The corpus is drawn from Omni-MATH mathematical reasoning traces, and the article calls for testing process signatures across additional assessment domains, reasoning models, and item formats
target_learners: Assessment items across mathematical, verbal, reading-comprehension, and medical domains
target_learning_goals: Automatic labeling of reasoning-trace sentences with problem-solving episode categories for difficulty modeling

article_title: To Facilitate or not to Facilitate: Human and LLM Facilitator Tendencies in Online Discussions
citation: Dimitris Tsirmpas, Katerina Korre, John Pavlopoulos. (2026). To Facilitate or not to Facilitate: Human and LLM Facilitator Tendencies in Online Discussions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28643
title: Three definitions of facilitative intervention: escalation, professional facilitation, and human judgment
description: The article isolates a taxonomy of three definitions of what a facilitative intervention is, finding "three common definitions implicitly used in prior work; escalation, professional facilitation, and facilitative comments". Definition 1 (escalation) ties intervention to the point where a discussion would derail, offering an unambiguous ground truth but missing successful interventions and other facilitator duties. Definition 2 (professional facilitation) treats all comments by a facilitator as facilitative, which is simple but requires identifiable professional facilitators. Definition 3 (human judgment) asks whether the majority agree facilitation is necessary, giving fine-grained but subjective labels.
requirements: Def. 2 requires that professional facilitators exist and can be identified; Def. 1 requires an unambiguous platform signal that a discussion has escalated
constraints: Def. 1 is inherently restrictive, excluding duties like summarizing and managing participation; Def. 2 excludes most web-crawled datasets; Def. 3 leaves ambiguous cases
target_learners: NLP researchers and designers of automated facilitation systems
target_learning_goals: defining and labeling facilitative interventions for model training and evaluation
examples: Table 1 shows the same discussion annotated under D1–D3, where Marie's facilitator comments differ in label per definition

article_title: When Evaluators Cry Wolf: Lessons from Production LLM-as-Judge Evaluation in Educational AI
citation: Chris Rohlfs, Rodrigo Vergara Bosse, Priscilla Hopper, Keanon O'Keefe, Patrick J. Russell. (2026). When Evaluators Cry Wolf: Lessons from Production LLM-as-Judge Evaluation in Educational AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28478
title: Three-lever calibration recipe for LLM-as-judge suites: unanimous-fail panels, per-evaluator judge-model choice, and rubric softening (U/P/C)
description: The article's account of calibrating a production LLM-as-judge suite treats each evaluator as a configurable instrument set by three levers. Panels repeat one judge model k times under a unanimous-fail rule with short-circuiting on the first passing verdict; judge models are chosen per evaluator (Sonnet 4.5 for semantic judgments, GPT-5.4 for structural and mathematical verification, Haiku 4.5 for lower cost); and rubrics are softened via three standard blocks: "U, require unambiguity—if the violation is a judgment call, pass; P, require pervasiveness—a single local instance is not enough, the failure must dominate the response; and C, simplify checklists."
requirements: Each evaluator targets a single failure mode with a free-text rubric defining it
Rubric edits must pass internal-consistency and alignment checks and match stakeholder intuition of the failure mode
Panels capped at five judges for cost and latency
constraints: The deployed configurations do not isolate the marginal contribution of any single lever (no factorial ablation)
The unanimous-fail rule routes split-judge cases to a minority-report channel, which the article says would not be appropriate for front-line moderation
Deployed judge models are proprietary, reducing reproducibility
target_learners: K-12 teachers and students using the MagicSchool AI product suite
target_learning_goals: Monitoring educational AI outputs for student safety, tone and instructional role, pedagogical value, and structural output quality
examples: Simplify checklists was selected for 11 of 21 evaluators, require unambiguity for 10, and require pervasiveness for 6
The Sycophancy A4 trigger was re-cast so a praise-count threshold became a corroborating check under shared unambiguity and dominance gates

citation: LUO Lan, WANG Anqi, ZHOU Muzhi, ZHU Junhua, CAI Jie, YU Ao, and PAN Hui. (2024). ParaTutor: Coordinating Parent-Child Math Tutoring through Role-Separated LLM Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18030
title: Three-phase tutoring structure for math word problems: understanding, calculation, and summarization
description: The article identifies a three-phase structure organizing parent-child math word problem tutoring. The article states that "word problem solving was described as a process that embodies three recurrent phases, namely understanding, calculation, and summarization." Each phase establishes a temporary focus of attention and shared expectations about what counts as progress, regulating when reasoning advances and how instructional authority is distributed. Phase boundaries are actively enforced by parents rather than implicitly assumed, serving as an interactional script that guides instruction and regulates problem-solving behavior.
requirements: Parents must actively enforce phase boundaries and authorize transitions between phases for the structure to regulate tutoring interaction

Aligns with classical problem solving models according to the article
target_learning_goals: Mathematical word problem solving including interpretation, calculation, and reflection
examples: Parents asked children to restate problems in their own words before calculation (understanding phase)
Teachers instructed students to return to the question instead of correcting numbers blindly (calculation to understanding transition)
Parents prompted children to articulate underlying principles after solving (summarization phase)

article_title: ParaTutor: LLM Mediated Parent Child Tutoring through Role Separated Scaffolding Interface in Real Time
citation: LUO Lan, WANG Anqi, ZHOU Muzhi, ZHU Junhua, CAI Jie, YU Ao, and PAN Hui. (2024). ParaTutor: Coordinating Parent-Child Math Tutoring through Role-Separated LLM Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18030
title: Three-dimensional scaffolding design coordinating user roles, tutoring phases, and guidance strategies
description: ParaTutor organizes its support as a design that "coordinates user roles, tutoring phases, and guidance strategies during parent-child math tutoring." The role dimension differentiates support between parents (guidance for conducting tutoring) and children (visual grounding for interpreting problems). The phase dimension structures how support changes across understanding, calculation, and summarization. The strategy dimension translates tutoring goals into concrete parent-facing guidance including suggested actions, example language, and ways of using the child-facing visualization. Together these dimensions define ParaTutor as a scaffold for parent-led tutoring.

Phase transitions controlled by explicit rule-based conditions rather than LLM decisions
Two synchronized panels separating parent-facing and child-facing interfaces
constraints: Designed for parent-child dyads in home math word problem tutoring, not single-user learning
Visual grounding withholds procedural solution steps reserved for parent-facing scaffolding
target_learners: Parent-child dyads with children aged 10-12 in grades 4-6
target_learning_goals: Mathematical word problem solving with shared understanding and active reasoning
examples: In the understanding phase, agents prioritize segmentation and grounding prompts while withholding solution procedures
In the calculation phase, agents support error localization and guided questioning
In the summarization phase, agents support reflection, consolidation, and transfer prompts

citation: Hansol Lee. (2026). Teacher intervention in K-12 AI-based instruction: a systematic review of processes, strategies, and effects. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00461-1
title: Three teacher intervention strategies in AI-based instruction: pedagogical translation of AI outputs, design of learning support, and reconstruction of interaction structures
description: The review identifies three strategies teachers use to intervene in AI-based instruction. "First, the pedagogical translation of AI outputs refers to the strategy by which teachers transform AI-generated information according to students' levels and classroom contexts, select what should be addressed, and turn it into actionable pedagogical practice." The second strategy organizes cognitive, affective-motivational, and procedural/self-regulatory support; the third coordinates peer interaction and student-AI interaction structures. The strategies are not mutually exclusive and can operate together within a single intervention scene.
requirements: Teachers need time and authority to interpret and select AI information, and the information itself must be interpretable, for translation to occur smoothly
constraints: Pedagogical translation can become a burden and increase teachers' cognitive load when information is excessive, hard to interpret, or there is insufficient time to review it

citation: Binkowski, K. P., & Hopkins, A. (2026). The University AI Didn't Replace: Rethinking Universities in the AI Era. Macquarie University. https://www.mq.edu.au/
title: Three emerging assessment-redesign approaches for AI-rich environments: AI-supported independent work, process-oriented reflective assessment, and observed authentic performance
description: Across its case studies the article identifies "three emerging approaches: AI-supported independent work, process-oriented and reflective assessment, and observed or authentic performance-based tasks". In the first, AI use is explicitly permitted but bounded by student accountability for interpretation and synthesis; in the second, learning is demonstrated through development over time with portfolios, reflection, and viva voce; in the third, understanding is evaluated through live performance and questioning. The pattern is reusable at unit level for assessment design where AI is available to students.

citation: Heidi Taveter and Marina Lepp. (2026). From Idea to Classroom in Days: Using “Vibe Coding” to Create a Programming Process Visualizer from IDE Activity Logs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24757
title: Thonny Log Visualizer: a teacher-facing web application that turns Thonny IDE logs into interpretable programming-process views
description: Thonny Log Visualizer is a web application that analyzes log files generated by Thonny, an IDE for Python, and produces interpretable views of students' programming processes. Per-student dashboards include an interactive activity timeline, a compact session summary, a code-size graph, a programming-process replay with an event feed, a paste-events view, and integrity-related indicators; cohort-level views include a sortable 'All people' table and comparison views for pair typing patterns and first-run progress. Teachers can upload a single log, a ZIP archive, or a folder, and the system parses all logs, groups them by student, and supports student-by-student navigation.

formative feedback
academic-integrity clarification

citation: Rummel, N., Nachtigall, V., & Panadero, E. (2026). “With a Thermomix You Lose the Ability to Cook”: A Kitchen Machine Analogy for Applications of Generative AI in Education.
title: The Thermomix analogy as a conceptual lens for generative AI in education
description: The article's central contribution is an analogy between the Thermomix smart kitchen appliance and generative AI in education. Both tools integrate previously distributed functions into one interface, provoke enthusiasm and skill-loss critiques, and can be used in ways ranging from passive substitution to interactive redefinition. The authors offer this as "a conceptual lens that makes visible the spectrum of possible uses of generative AI", aiming to move debate beyond whether AI supports learning toward how use shapes learning processes, identity, agency, and evaluation.

constraints: The authors note media-comparison designs risk confounding numerous factors and yield limited insight; future research must disentangle the conditions under which generative AI fosters or hinders productive learning

article_title: Three Pathways of Student-AI Interaction: Constraint-First Design for Higher-Order Thinking
citation: Zahra, F. T. (2025). Three Pathways of Student-AI Interaction: Constraint-First Design for Higher-Order Thinking. Manuscript under blind review; framework first presented at EAAI-25, Philadelphia, PA.
title: Three Paths of Student-AI Interaction typology
description: A typological framework identifying three qualitatively distinct modes of student-AI engagement: Passive Review (student accepts AI output with minimal scrutiny, unidirectional, limited higher-order opportunity), Direct Question (transactional gap-filling with surface evaluation, moderate opportunity), and Strategic Dialogue (dialogic, recursive, critical, metacognitive engagement with AI as a thinking partner, substantial opportunity). The article states "The typology distinguishes three paths—Passive Review, Direct Question, and Strategic Dialogue" and links them to degrees of cognitive and epistemic agency, mapping onto a developmental trajectory of AI literacy from treating AI as authoritative to maintaining epistemic agency. Its core claim is that learning outcomes depend on which path students are on, not whether they use AI.
requirements: A codebook with labels mapped to paths, trained coders, and interaction logs of student-AI exchanges to classify
constraints: The article notes the Path 1/2 boundary is the most contested site of the coding scheme and the framework needs testing across larger samples, disciplines, and settings
target_learning_goals: higher-order thinking
critical thinking
AI literacy
examples: Composite personas ground each path: Aisha and Malik (Path 1), Kofi and Amara (Path 2), Carmen and Jamal (Path 3); Table 1 compares the paths across behavior, engagement mode, and opportunity for higher-order thinking.

citation: Wang H and Shan W (2026). The safety gap: restoring productive struggle through pedagogically aligned generative AI. Front. Educ. 11:1757622. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1757622
title: A three-architecture taxonomy of educational generative AI: Oracle, Socratic tutor, and adversarial agent
description: The article organizes the educational AI landscape into three interaction-design architectures. The Oracle category comprises generic chatbots optimized for immediacy, which the authors call the primary drivers of the Safety Gap; the Socratic tutor withholds direct answers and offers hints to support schema construction; the adversarial agent critiques student work or plants plausible errors to build epistemic vigilance. As the article states, it contrasts 'generic Oracle models that prioritize immediacy with education-speciﬁc architectures (Socratic and Adversarial) designed to induce productive struggle and mitigate the Safety Gap'.
requirements: Socratic and adversarial behavior requires deliberate configuration via system prompts or educational wrappers, since general-purpose models are trained to satisfy user requests immediately.
constraints: The taxonomy is the authors' own analytic categorization; the label Oracle is their own analytic term for answer-delivery systems, not terminology taken from any cited source.

target_learning_goals: productive struggle and schema construction
epistemic vigilance

citation: Craig Wright. (2026). Transcription is not generation: distinguishing non-generative AI tool use from academic misconduct in higher education assessment. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00234-w
title: Three-category typology of AI output functions: novel content production, error-correcting reconstruction, and format conversion
description: The paper proposes a typology distinguishing three functionally distinct categories of AI output that policy discussion frequently conflates. Category A is novel content production, where the machine creates content the student did not author; Category B is error-correcting reconstruction, where the system 'resolves ambiguity in the existing content' during recognition; Category C is format conversion, a clerical operation producing no intellectual content. The typology grounds the paper's argument that Category C falls outside the purpose of generative-AI prohibitions, while Category B is a grey zone requiring case-by-case assessment.
requirements: A precise definition of generation is necessary to draw the policy boundary clearly, per the paper's stated purpose for the typology
constraints: The paper does not claim that the Category B/C boundary can be identified bright-line in every case
The typology is a proposal that has not been empirically validated
target_learning_goals: academic integrity policy interpretation
assessment validity
examples: Scenario contrasts: prompting a platform to solve a system of ODEs is Category A; instructing it to transcribe handwriting into LaTeX exactly as written is Category C

AI revisions were produced by ChatGPT-4 using "the same standardized prompt" covering six writing criteria (organization, development, cohesion and coherence, sentence structure, vocabulary, mechanics), with each student's first draft revised rather than a new essay generated. article_title: Confirming Correct, Missing the Rest: LLM Tutoring Agents Struggle Where Feedback Matters Most
citation: Tahreem Yasir, Wenbo Li, Sam Gilson, Sutapa Dey Tithi, Xiaoyi Tian, Tiffany Barnes. (2026). Confirming Correct, Missing the Rest: LLM Tutoring Agents Struggle Where Feedback Matters Most. arXiv:2605.16207. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16207
title: Three-way KG-grounded diagnosis of student proof steps (optimal, valid-alternative, incorrect)
description: The article's organizing evaluation framework classifies each student next step into three pedagogically distinct categories using a knowledge graph encoding all valid inference paths for each problem. The article states that "Unlike prior benchmarks relying on binary correctness, our KG encodes all valid inference paths, enabling three-way diagnosis." A step is Optimal if it follows an expert-authored path and strictly reduces distance to the conclusion, Valid-alternative if it is a valid inference that does not reduce distance, and Incorrect if it is not derivable under any valid rule. Edge-level annotation of rules and parent statements enables verification of both what was derived and how the derivation is justified.
requirements: A knowledge graph exhaustively enumerating all reachable proof states via forward chaining under a closed rule set, which the article notes is feasible in propositional logic
Edge-level annotation of inference rule and parent statements so that symbolically valid but inferentially unjustified steps can be flagged
constraints: The article limits the framework to propositional logic, where exhaustive solution-space enumeration is tractable; findings may not generalize to domains where enumeration is not tractable or symbolic constraints are weaker
target_learners: undergraduate Discrete Mathematics students using a propositional logic tutoring system
target_learning_goals: step-level propositional logic proof reasoning and inference rule application
examples: The benchmark encodes 32 proof problems from a logic tutor's interaction logs as knowledge graphs and classifies 10,836 LLM-simulated next-step solutions against them

citation: Kaşarcı İsmail, Yurt Eyüp. (2026). Effectiveness of AI-Supported Game-Based Learning: A Systematic Review of Outcomes, Challenges, and Future Directions. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071050
title: Three-pathway model of AI-GBL effectiveness: cognitive load optimization, motivational scaffolding, and epistemic scaffolding
description: The review proposes that AI-GBL operates through three distinct theoretical pathways grounded in cognitive load theory, self-determination theory, and Vygotsky's zone of proximal development. As the review states, "AI-GBL operates through three distinct pathways: cognitive load optimization (calibrating task difficulty to individual capacity), motivational scaffolding (maintaining optimal challenge and timely feedback), and epistemic scaffolding (AI characters supporting contextually appropriate knowledge construction)". The model explains why AI-GBL achieves outcomes that neither AI tutoring nor conventional GBL achieves alone, and is supported in the review by adaptive difficulty research, LLM scaffolding studies, and AI NPC evidence.

constraints: The review notes the model is supported by thematic synthesis of heterogeneous studies, not quantitative meta-analysis

target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition
motivation
higher-order thinking
examples: The review cites adaptive difficulty research (Panjaburee et al., 2025), LLM scaffolding studies (Huang & Chen, 2025; Ngu et al., 2025), and AI NPC evidence (Chernbumroong et al., 2026) as supporting the three pathways
