title: Three commitments of community-based AI learning: epistemic fine tuning, redistribution of authority, and situated discernment
description: The framework rests on "three interrelated commitments": situated epistemic negotiation, redistribution of epistemic authority, and collective discernment and action. Together these processes "localize critical AI literacy by calibrating trust, foregrounding community knowledge, and supporting collective judgment about when to design with, interrogate, or reject AI." The commitments integrate constructionist making, community-based epistemologies, and critical AI literacy into a situated theory of learning.
requirements: AI outputs must be engaged as materials for interpretation and deliberation, not definitive conclusions
constraints: Criticality is not uniform across settings; it is shaped by geography, infrastructure, exposure to harm, and local histories of technological entanglement
target_learners: Learners in communities encountering AI-mediated knowledge systems
target_learning_goals: Calibrating trust in AI
Collective judgment about designing with, interrogating, or rejecting AI
key_sources: Santiago Ojeda-Ramirez, Symone Gyles and Kylie Peppler. 2026. Community-Based AI Learning: Redistributing Artificial Intelligence's Epistemic Authority in Education. In Proceedings of 2026 Conference for Research on Equitable and Sustained Participation in Engineering, Computing, and Technology (RESPECT 2026). https://doi.org/10.1145/3796496.3811760

article_title: Thinking Through AI: Advancing Cognitive and Collaborative Research for AI in Education
citation: Tzirides, Anastasia Olga (Olnancy), Galla, Michele, Cope, Bill, & Kalantzis, Mary. (2025). Thinking Through AI: Advancing Cognitive and Collaborative Research for AI in Education.
title: Thinking Through AI framework: three dimensions for studying and co-designing AI-mediated learning
description: The Thinking Through AI framework is a methodological approach integrating cyber-social research with cognitive labs and think-aloud protocols to create continuous feedback loops in AI tool development. It is structured around three core dimensions: students' cognitive engagement with AI, educators' instructional strategies embedding rubrics and knowledge repositories, and the collaborative design of AI tools and learning experiences via Learning Experience Research (LXR). The article states it is 'a methodological approach that integrates principles of cyber-social research with cognitive labs and think-aloud protocols to facilitate continuous feedback loops in the development and implementation of AI-driven educational tools.'
requirements: Sustained engagement of students, educators, and developers in iterative design cycles, with think-aloud sessions and post-course surveys providing user input
constraints: Its iterative nature demands significant time and resources, requiring sustained engagement from all stakeholders
target_learning_goals: writing instruction
cognitive engagement with AI systems
AI tool co-design
examples: The framework guided a case study of the CGScholar AI Helper at a rural Alaska middle school, where think-aloud sessions with a structured moderator guide captured student interactions with the AI writing tool.
key_sources: Tzirides, Anastasia Olga (Olnancy), Galla, Michele, Cope, Bill, & Kalantzis, Mary. (2025). Thinking Through AI: Advancing Cognitive and Collaborative Research for AI in Education. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/s8hqe_v1

article_title: Mapping the Scaffolding of Metacognition and Learning by AI Tools in STEM Classrooms: A Bibliometric-Systematic Review
citation: Tsakeni, Maria, Stephen C. Nwafor, Moeketsi Mosia, and Felix O. Egara. 2025. Mapping the Scaffolding of Metacognition and Learning by AI Tools in STEM Classrooms: A Bibliometric–Systematic Review Approach (2005–2025). Journal of Intelligence 13: 148. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence13110148
title: Three-framework lens: Flavell's metacognition theory, General Systems Theory, and human-centred versus posthumanist AI paradigms
description: The review interprets how AI tools scaffold metacognition through "three complementary frameworks: Flavell's Theory of Metacognition (1979), General Systems Theory (GST), and Human-Centred vs. Posthumanist AI paradigms." Flavell's model, with Nelson and Narens' object-level/meta-level distinction, interprets AI support for both task performance and strategic monitoring. GST conceptualises STEM classrooms as interconnected adaptive systems where students, teachers, technologies, and pedagogies interact dynamically. The human-centred paradigm regards AI as supporting human agency under ethical oversight, while the posthumanist paradigm conceptualises learning as co-regulated between humans and AI systems.
requirements: Application of the frameworks requires distinguishing whether AI is framed as a supportive tool or a co-agent in reflective processes
constraints: The review clarifies that what is shared is not metacognition itself but the regulation of learning experiences scaffolded by AI alongside human agency
target_learners: STEM learners across primary, secondary, and tertiary levels
target_learning_goals: metacognitive development and self-regulated learning in STEM
examples: The review applies the lens to interpret keyword shifts from reflection and teacher scaffolding toward system-level reflection and machine awareness
key_sources: Tsakeni, Maria, Stephen C. Nwafor, Moeketsi Mosia, and Felix O. Egara. 2025. Mapping the Scaffolding of Metacognition and Learning by AI Tools in STEM Classrooms: A Bibliometric–Systematic Review Approach (2005–2025). Journal of Intelligence 13: 148. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence13110148

article_title: Sustainable Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization: A Value-Critical Approach
citation: Adeeb Obaid Alsuhaymi and Fouad Ahmed Atallah. (2026). Sustainable Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization: A Value-Critical Approach. Sustainability 2026, 18, 1257. https://doi.org/10.3390/su18031257
title: Three-way distinction between sustainable education, sustainability in education, and education for sustainable development
description: The article adopts, as a heuristic entry point, the analytical distinction between three concepts. Sustainability in education emphasizes institutional durability, efficiency, and system continuity; education for sustainable development focuses on curricular and pedagogical alignment with sustainability-related goals; and sustainable education is "a value-based and human-centered educational orientation concerned with long-term intellectual, ethical, and social flourishing". The article argues that failing to maintain these distinctions has generated conceptual ambiguity, allowing technologization to be treated as a proxy for sustainability rather than as a means that must itself be critically evaluated. It uses sustainable education as its primary analytical lens while situating it in dialogue with human-centered educational theory, critical educational technology scholarship, and AI governance frameworks.
requirements: The distinctions must be maintained analytically to avoid conflating technological efficiency, institutional resilience, and policy compliance with educational sustainability
constraints: The article employs the distinctions as a heuristic and comparative reference, rather than as a self-validating or exhaustive framework
target_learners: learners across educational systems affected by AI-driven digitalization
target_learning_goals: clarifying what sustainability should mean in educational contexts; protecting formative, ethical, and democratic purposes of education
examples: The article's discussion distinguishes system sustainability from sustainable education, noting AI-enabled outcomes like administrative automation enhance operational sustainability without necessarily advancing sustainable education as a normative project
key_sources: Adeeb Obaid Alsuhaymi and Fouad Ahmed Atallah. (2026). Sustainable Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization: A Value-Critical Approach. Sustainability 2026, 18, 1257. https://doi.org/10.3390/su18031257

article_title: A mixed-methods analysis of AI scaffolding patterns and student inquiry profiles in a middle-school agriculture-STEM classroom
citation: Kilinc, S., Aldemir, T., Misiejuk, K., Kaliisa, R., Sabanwar, V., Bicer, A., Song, D., & Yalvac, B. (2026). A mixed-methods analysis of AI scaffolding patterns and student inquiry profiles in a middle-school agriculture-STEM classroom. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, 11, 100683. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100683
title: Three collaborative engagement patterns explaining group revision trajectories with AI support
description: The article conceptualizes collaborative engagement as how students jointly work with chatbot support in peer discussion as they interpret, evaluate, adapt, and attempt to use it. It distinguishes three patterns: "Model uptake occurs when students treat chatbot input as a resource for joint reasoning"; cognitive offloading occurs when students shift intellectual work to the chatbot by accepting revisions without evaluation; and collaborative impasse occurs when group work stalls because students cannot establish a shared interpretation of the chatbot's input. Together these show whether AI support became a resource for collective reasoning, a substitute for it, or a point of breakdown.
requirements: Peer discussion in which students encounter chatbot input as a group and decide together whether it is relevant and how it applies
constraints: The same AI response may lead to different revision trajectories depending on how groups make sense of or work around it
target_learners: middle school student groups engaged in collaborative inquiry
target_learning_goals: interpreting, evaluating, and taking up AI feedback during scientific inquiry
examples: The codebook for the peer-discussion analysis of eight low-initial-quality groups was informed by this three-pattern conceptualization
key_sources: Kilinc, S., Aldemir, T., Misiejuk, K., Kaliisa, R., Sabanwar, V., Bicer, A., Song, D., & Yalvac, B. (2026). A mixed-methods analysis of AI scaffolding patterns and student inquiry profiles in a middle-school agriculture-STEM classroom. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, 11, 100683. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100683

article_title: A Critical Review of Critical Thinking in HCI Research About AI
citation: Inie, N., Kristensen, A. M., Misfeldt, M., & Dalsgaard, P. (2026). A Critical Review of Critical Thinking in HCI Research About AI. International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2026.2722522
title: Three theoretical traditions for studying critical thinking: cognitive-psychological, philosophical, and educational
description: The review organizes critical thinking research into three traditions that differ in focus and methods: the cognitive-psychological tradition, the philosophical tradition, and the educational tradition. The authors describe "the theoretical backgrounds of critical thinking as it is viewed and studied in the cognitive-psychological tradition, the philosophical tradition, and the educational tradition", and use this tripartite framework both to code the 80 reviewed studies and to structure their proposed research agenda for future HCI work.
requirements: Researchers situating a study in a tradition must choose methods and evaluations appropriate to that tradition, as the review's agenda outlines
constraints: The traditions disagree on the role of dispositions, domain specificity, transferability, and the role of criteria, so no single definition spans them
target_learners: HCI researchers studying critical thinking with or about AI
target_learning_goals: Theory-grounded definition, measurement, and study design for critical thinking research
examples: The review's data extraction coded each included study by which theoretical tradition it situates itself in, based on cited theoretical sources or evaluation methods
key_sources: Inie, N., Kristensen, A. M., Misfeldt, M., & Dalsgaard, P. (2026). A Critical Review of Critical Thinking in HCI Research About AI. International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2026.2722522

article_title: A Framework for Evaluation of Large Language Models in Essay Assessment: Reliability, Alignment, and Causal Reasoning
citation: Tongxi Liu, Luyao Ye, Wei Yan. (2026). A framework for evaluation of large language models in essay assessment: Reliability, alignment, and causal reasoning. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100565
title: Three-layered assessment framework for evaluating LLMs in essay assessment
description: A framework the article operationalizes to evaluate LLM essay scoring along three layers: consistency and reliability evaluation, human-LLM alignment analysis, and causal discovery analysis. Consistency assesses whether a model "maintains stable relative rankings of essay quality across repeated runs using identical prompts", while reliability captures absolute agreement of numeric outputs across runs; alignment serves as a measure of external validity against expert judgments; and causal discovery identifies "causal relationships between linguistic features and predicted scores". The article applies it to five LLMs scoring 60 higher-education essays.
requirements: Repeated independent scoring runs under identical prompts to separate stochastic variation from systematic behavior
Expert human ratings on standardized rubrics as an external validity benchmark
Linguistic feature extraction with theoretically grounded domain classification for the causal layer
constraints: Developed and applied to long English essays by non-native speakers in higher education, scored on the IELTS Task 2 rubric
target_learners: Higher education students, specifically non-native English speakers whose long essays are assessed
target_learning_goals: Reliable, valid, and interpretable automated assessment of extended academic writing
examples: Applied to GPT-4.1, Llama 4 Maverick, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4, and DeepSeek R1 scoring 60 essays three times each against three calibrated expert raters
key_sources: Tongxi Liu, Luyao Ye, Wei Yan. (2026). A framework for evaluation of large language models in essay assessment: Reliability, alignment, and causal reasoning. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100565

article_title: RoboBlockly Studio: Conversational Block Programming With Embodied Robot Feedback for Computational Thinking
citation: Leyi Li, Chenyu Du, Jiafei Sun, Erick Purwanto, and Qing Zhang. (2026). RoboBlockly Studio: Conversational Block Programming with Embodied Robot Feedback for Computational Thinking. Designing Interactive Systems Conference (DIS '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3800645.3813071
title: Three-tier progressive CT task structure: complete missing blocks, fix incorrect blocks, translate natural-language problems
description: RoboBlockly Studio organizes tasks into "three progressive levels of difficulty" aligned to design goal DG2. Introductory tasks require students to complete partially provided programs by inserting missing blocks; intermediate tasks require analyzing programs with deliberate flaws and correcting them; advanced tasks present text-based problems that students translate into executable block programs. The tiered structure implements progressive reduction of instructional support so novices build skills stepwise, and the study found students experienced it as a structured learning trajectory supporting warm-up, engagement, and increasingly reflective problem solving.
requirements: Progressive reduction of instructional support through tiered scaffolding so novice learners build skills within a controlled and stepwise learning environment
constraints: Tasks are designed for short classroom sessions and must fit teachers' time constraints and lesson structures
target_learners: high school novices without prior programming experience
target_learning_goals: abstraction, decomposition, debugging, and algorithmic design
examples: Introductory tasks have students add missing blocks so a robot traverses a grid; intermediate tasks include Minefield Exploration on a 5×5 grid; advanced tasks include the Wolf, Sheep, and Cabbage river-crossing puzzle and the Knight's Chessboard Challenge
key_sources: Leyi Li, Chenyu Du, Jiafei Sun, Erick Purwanto, and Qing Zhang. (2026). RoboBlockly Studio: Conversational Block Programming with Embodied Robot Feedback for Computational Thinking. Designing Interactive Systems Conference (DIS '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3800645.3813071

article_title: Understanding Student Dependency on AI: The Role of AI Literacy, Academic Self-Efficacy, and Resource Management Strategies
citation: Hilit Maizel, Maya Kalman Halevi, Miri Sarid, and Rony Tutian. (2026). Understanding Student Dependency on AI: The Role of AI Literacy, Academic Self-Efficacy, and Resource Management Strategies. Educ. Sci. 2026, 16, 1123. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci16071123
title: Integrative three-mechanism model of AI dependency: enabling capacity, compensatory motivation, and self-regulatory function
description: The article proposes that AI dependency "emerges from the interplay of three theoretically distinct mechanisms: an enabling capacity, a compensatory motivation, and a self-regulatory function". Skill-based AI literacy enables offloading by lowering the effort of delegating tasks; self-efficacy beliefs (academic and AI-specific) operate as a unified compensatory mechanism reducing motivational pressure to over-rely; and resource management strategies translate motivational tendencies into action, with effort regulation buffering and help seeking potentially channeling dependency. The model generates directional hypotheses tested via regression and motivates a person-centered cluster analysis.
requirements: Measures distinguishing skill-based from belief-based dimensions of AI literacy (e.g., the MAILS subscales used here)
constraints: Developed and tested with cross-sectional self-report data; the regression coefficients do not establish causal effects
target_learning_goals: balanced and intentional AI engagement in academic work
examples: The model's hypotheses were tested with a multiple regression on 478 Israeli higher education students and complemented by a K-means cluster analysis of literacy-dependency profiles
key_sources: Hilit Maizel, Maya Kalman Halevi, Miri Sarid, and Rony Tutian. (2026). Understanding Student Dependency on AI: The Role of AI Literacy, Academic Self-Efficacy, and Resource Management Strategies. Educ. Sci. 2026, 16, 1123. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci16071123

article_title: Transfer of test-enhanced learning: Meta-analytic review and synthesis.
citation: Steven C. Pan and Timothy C. Rickard. (2018). Transfer of Test-Enhanced Learning: Meta-Analytic Review and Synthesis. Psychological Bulletin. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/bul0000151
title: Three-factor framework for transfer of test-enhanced learning
description: The review's synthesis motivates a three-factor framework for transfer of test-enhanced learning, organized around the factors the meta-analysis identified as governing positive transfer: response congruency between initial and final tests, elaborated retrieval practice, and initial test performance. The authors state that "our results motivate a three-factor framework for transfer of test-enhanced learning and have practical implications for the effective use of practice testing in educational and other training contexts." The framework integrates the category-level findings with the moderator analyses and the publication-bias results.
requirements: Positive transfer depends on the presence of the identified moderators; the intercept analyses often indicated no positive transfer when none of the moderators are present
constraints: Developed from studies using the three-phase test-enhanced learning paradigm with a nontesting reexposure control, mostly with young adult university samples
target_learners: Learners in educational and other training contexts, primarily university students in the underlying studies
target_learning_goals: Flexible, transferable learning rather than retention of identical test items
examples: The framework is motivated by the meta-analysis of 192 transfer effect sizes spanning six major transfer categories from near to far transfer
key_sources: Steven C. Pan and Timothy C. Rickard. (2018). Transfer of Test-Enhanced Learning: Meta-Analytic Review and Synthesis. Psychological Bulletin. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/bul0000151

article_title: Prequestioning and Pretesting Effects: a Review of Empirical Research, Theoretical Perspectives, and Implications for Educational Practice
citation: Steven C. Pan, Shana K. Carpenter. (2023). Prequestioning and Pretesting Effects: a Review of Empirical Research, Theoretical Perspectives, and Implications for Educational Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09814-5
title: Three-stage framework of prequestioning and pretesting effects
description: The review proposes that the cognitive mechanisms underlying prequestioning and pretesting effects "can be represented by a three-stage framework" in which test-induced changes in subsequent learning behaviors, and possibly other processes, explain the benefits. It organizes how pre-instruction testing alters learners' engagement with subsequent study of correct answers, offering a structure for interpreting effects across materials and settings. The framework is presented as a synthesis of current theoretical perspectives rather than a tested model.
requirements: An opportunity to study the correct answers after the initial test, as the review states benefits occur "if there is an opportunity to study the correct answers afterwards"
constraints: The review states the underlying cognitive mechanisms only "appear to involve" test-induced changes and possibly other processes, and that further research is needed to clarify theoretical issues
target_learners: Undergraduate students and similar-aged learners, as in most reviewed studies
K-12 and medical students in the classroom and clinical studies reviewed
target_learning_goals: Retention of directly tested content
Transfer to untested materials, inferences, and classification of new exemplars
examples: The review uses the framework to interpret findings across text, video, word-pair, and trivia-fact studies, and to motivate future research on moderating factors
key_sources: Steven C. Pan, Shana K. Carpenter. (2023). Prequestioning and Pretesting Effects: a Review of Empirical Research, Theoretical Perspectives, and Implications for Educational Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09814-5

article_title: The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect.
citation: Rowland, C. A. (2014, August 25). The Effect of Testing Versus Restudy on Retention: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Testing Effect. Psychological Bulletin. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0037559
title: The bifurcation model of the testing effect
description: The bifurcation model (Kornell, Bjork, & Garcia, 2011) explains testing effects in terms of final test difficulty rather than initial test conditions. In the article's words, "study (and restudy) provides a modest increase to memory strength, whereas testing provides a more substantial increase, but only to those items successfully retrieved." Because testing strengthens only retrieved items, the model predicts testing effects are more likely, and larger, when the final test is more difficult. The article treats it as a viable framework for characterizing patterns across the literature.
requirements: Applies to designs comparing testing with restudy where item-level retrieval success at the intervening phase can bifurcate the tested items
constraints: The framework makes no assumptions about the impact of initial test conditions in dictating the degree of strength increment
target_learners: Adult laboratory participants learning verbal materials
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention of studied information
examples: The article cites the frequently observed finding that testing effects increase with longer retention intervals as base support for the role of final test difficulty.
key_sources: Rowland, C. A. (2014, August 25). The Effect of Testing Versus Restudy on Retention: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Testing Effect. Psychological Bulletin. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0037559

article_title: The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect.
citation: Rowland, C. A. (2014, August 25). The Effect of Testing Versus Restudy on Retention: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Testing Effect. Psychological Bulletin. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0037559
title: Transfer appropriate processing (TAP) theory of the testing effect
description: TAP theory, drawing from Morris, Bransford, and Franks (1977), explains the testing effect via overlap in processing between initial and final tests. The article states that "TAP theory states that an initial test during learning, compared with restudy (or no test), induces a greater similarity with the type of processing that occurs at the final test." Its clear prediction is that the larger the overlap in processing required for initial and final testing, the larger the benefit of the initial test. The article notes it remains influential despite mixed empirical support.
requirements: Prediction requires variation or classification of initial and final test formats to assess processing overlap
constraints: The article reports results problematic for the theory, including studies where matching initial and final test characteristics yielded no benefit or suboptimal performance
target_learners: Adult laboratory participants learning verbal or multimedia materials
target_learning_goals: Retention and transfer of studied material
examples: Johnson and Mayer (2009) found a crossover interaction between practice test type and final test type, with performance highest when initial and final test types matched.
key_sources: Rowland, C. A. (2014, August 25). The Effect of Testing Versus Restudy on Retention: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Testing Effect. Psychological Bulletin. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0037559

article_title: The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect.
citation: Rowland, C. A. (2014, August 25). The Effect of Testing Versus Restudy on Retention: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Testing Effect. Psychological Bulletin. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0037559
title: The elaborative retrieval hypothesis of the testing effect
description: The elaborative retrieval hypothesis (Carpenter, 2009; Carpenter & DeLosh, 2006) holds that testing benefits retention because retrieval elaborates the memory trace. Carpenter (2009) "proposed a mechanism for such elaboration, whereby engaging in a retrieval attempt produces an elaboration of the target of the memory search through the activation of semantic associates of the target." Generated erroneous candidates may later serve as retrieval cues for the target. The hypothesis predicts larger testing effects for weakly associated cue-target pairs and for more difficult initial tests.
requirements: Cue-target materials with semantic content that affords activation of semantic associates during retrieval
constraints: The meta-analysis found only limited support for semantic elaboration accounts of the testing effect
target_learners: Adult laboratory participants learning paired associates
target_learning_goals: Retention of cue-target pairs
examples: Carpenter (2009) demonstrated that weakly associated cue-target pairs generate larger testing effects than strongly associated pairs, attributed to greater elaboration potential.
key_sources: Rowland, C. A. (2014, August 25). The Effect of Testing Versus Restudy on Retention: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Testing Effect. Psychological Bulletin. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0037559

article_title: Interaction in Distance Education and Online Learning: Using Evidence and Theory to Improve Practice
citation: Abrami, P.C., Bernard, R.M., Bures, E.M., Borokhovski, E., Tamim, R.M. (2012). Interaction in Distance Education and Online Learning: Using Evidence and Theory to Improve Practice. In: Moller, L., Huett, J. (eds) The Next Generation of Distance Education. Springer, Boston, MA. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-1785-9_4
title: Three-type interaction taxonomy for distance and online learning
description: The chapter organizes interaction in distance and online learning into three types: "among students, between the instructor and students, and between students and course content". This taxonomy, drawn from the interaction literature in distance education, serves as the organizing axis for the chapter's review of evidence and its recommendations for instructional improvement in the next generation of distance and online learning.
requirements: Instruction in distance and online learning settings should provide for all three interaction types when designing courses
target_learning_goals: achievement and engagement in distance and online learning
key_sources: Abrami, P.C., Bernard, R.M., Bures, E.M., Borokhovski, E., Tamim, R.M. (2012). Interaction in Distance Education and Online Learning: Using Evidence and Theory to Improve Practice. article_title: Audience Perspective in Young Writers’ Composing and Revising
citation: Holliway, D.R., McCutchen, D. (2004). Audience Perspective in Young Writers' Composing and Revising. In: Allal, L., Chanquoy, L., Largy, P. (eds) Revision Cognitive and Instructional Processes. Studies in Writing, vol 13. Springer, Dordrecht. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-007-1048-1_6
title: Three-condition revision design varying reader insight (feedback only, rating-as-the-reader, reading-as-the-reader)
description: An instructional comparison design for studying audience perspective in writing: three revision conditions that "varied in the amount of reader insight they offered." The feedback-only condition gives writer-directed feedback; rating-as-the-reader and reading-as-the-reader progressively increase the writer's experience of the reader's perspective. The design was used with 5th and 9th graders composing and revising descriptive essays.
requirements: Descriptive writing tasks and a way to operationalize differing levels of reader insight across conditions
constraints: Studied in the context of descriptive essay revision and drafting by 5th and 9th grade US students
target_learning_goals: Audience-aware revision of descriptive writing
examples: The study's conditions were a feedback only condition, a rating-as-the-reader condition, and a reading-as-the-reader condition
key_sources: Holliway, D.R., McCutchen, D. (2004). Audience Perspective in Young Writers' Composing and Revising. In: Allal, L., Chanquoy, L., Largy, P. (eds) Revision Cognitive and Instructional Processes. Studies in Writing, vol 13. Springer, Dordrecht. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-007-1048-1_6

article_title: Leveraging the Potential of Large Language Models in Education Through Playful and Game-Based Learning
citation: Huber, S. E., Kiili, K., Nebel, S., Ryan, R. M., Sailer, M., & Ninaus, M. (2024). Leveraging the Potential of Large Language Models in Education Through Playful and Game-Based Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09868-z
title: Three learning processes of expertise development through practice
description: The article describes a framework, drawing on Elvira et al. and Tynjälä, in which novices advancing from easier to more difficult problems engage in three learning processes: transforming conceptual into experiential knowledge, explicating experiential into conceptual knowledge, and reflecting on both to improve problem-solving strategies and metacognitive and self-regulatory skills. Continuous practice integrating these knowledge forms "utilizes already existing expertise and contributes to its further development." The article uses this framework to argue why outsourcing practice to LLMs threatens expertise.
requirements: Development and preservation of expertise require practicing domain-specific problem-solving capabilities.
constraints: Modern theories acknowledge that many factors besides practice contribute to expertise development.
target_learners: novices developing domain expertise in formal education
target_learning_goals: domain-specific problem-solving expertise
metacognitive and self-regulatory skills
examples: The article applies the framework to Papert's Logo approach, showing how playful experimentation nurtured all three learning processes.
key_sources: Huber, S. E., Kiili, K., Nebel, S., Ryan, R. M., Sailer, M., & Ninaus, M. (2024). Leveraging the Potential of Large Language Models in Education Through Playful and Game-Based Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09868-z

article_title: Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems
citation: Sadler, D. R. (1989). Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems. Instructional Science, 18, 119–144. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00117714
title: Effective feedback requires three conditions that enable students to act on information about the gap between their work and the standard
description: The article identifies "Three conditions for effective feedback" and discusses their implications. Grounded in its functional definition of feedback, the principle holds that feedback is effective only when students can appreciate what high quality is, evaluate their own work against it, and act to modify it — otherwise information about the quality gap cannot be used by the learner.
requirements: Feedback must be accompanied by conditions enabling students to recognize the quality standard, evaluate their own work against it, and modify their work accordingly
constraints: Less relevant for outcomes where responses are simply correct or incorrect
target_learners: students in subjects where response quality is judged on multiple criteria
target_learning_goals: closing the gap between current and intended quality of student work
key_sources: Sadler, D. R. (1989). Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems. Instructional Science, 18, 119–144. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00117714

article_title: The costs and benefits of providing feedback during learning
citation: Matthew Jensen Hays, Nate Kornell, and Robert A. Bjork. (2010). The costs and benefits of providing feedback during learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review. https://doi.org/10.3758/PBR.17.6.797
title: New theory of disuse: learning increments are inversely proportional to the accessibility of the to-be-learned information
description: The article invokes the new theory of disuse (Bjork & Bjork, 1992) as its explanatory framework for why feedback after successful retrieval adds little. In this framework, "the magnitude of a learning increment is inversely proportional to the accessibility of the to-be-learned information." It predicts that feedback following a successful retrieval should have virtually no effect on learning, a prediction borne out by prior studies and consistent with the present results. The framework also explains the two cases where feedback after a correct response helps: when information is not fully accessible (low-confidence correct answers, delayed feedback).
requirements: Applies to learning situations where the to-be-learned information's accessibility can vary across retrievals
constraints: The article cites the framework as background theory from Bjork and Bjork (1992), not as a model tested directly in this experiment
target_learners: all learners of verbal or factual material
target_learning_goals: long-term retention and transfer
examples: The authors apply the framework to explain why immediate feedback after correct responses yields no retention benefit in Pashler et al. (2005) and in the present experiment
key_sources: Matthew Jensen Hays, Nate Kornell, and Robert A. Bjork. (2010). The costs and benefits of providing feedback during learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review. https://doi.org/10.3758/PBR.17.6.797

article_title: Reliability in Content Analysis: Some Common Misconceptions and Recommendations
citation: Klaus Krippendorff. (2004). Reliability in Content Analysis: Some Common Misconceptions and Recommendations. Human Communication Research 30, 3: 411-433. https://astro.temple.edu/~lombard/carman.htm
title: Three conditions for an agreement coefficient to serve as an index of data reliability
description: The article proposes that agreement, which is what is measured, becomes an index of reliability, which is what is inferred, only when three conditions hold. The coefficient must (1) be applied to proper reliability data produced by duplicating the coding process with independent coders; (2) it must treat units as separately categorizable and coders as interchangeable, since it "treats units of analysis as separately describable or categorizable, without, however, presuming any knowledge about the correctness of their descriptions"; and (3) its values must correlate with the conditions under which one relies on imperfect data, with anchor values for perfect reliability and chance. The framework organizes the article's evaluation of seven coefficients.
requirements: Reliability data must be generated by widely available coders following the same explicit instructions, working independently on identical units
constraints: No single coefficient can determine that coders are available, instructed, independent, and coding identical units; researchers must ensure these preconditions themselves
target_learning_goals: inferring data reliability from intercoder agreement
examples: The article applies the three conditions to seven dichotomous two-coder coefficients, including %-agreement, Scott's pi, Cohen's kappa, Benini's beta, and Bennett et al.'s S
key_sources: Klaus Krippendorff. (2004). Reliability in Content Analysis: Some Common Misconceptions and Recommendations. Human Communication Research 30, 3: 411-433. https://astro.temple.edu/~lombard/carman.htm

article_title: Alternative assessment of strategy use with self-report instruments: a discussion
citation: Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2011). Alternative assessment of strategy use with self-report instruments: a discussion. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9080-x
title: Three levels of strategy use: availability deficiency, prompted use, and spontaneous production
description: The article distinguishes three levels of strategy use relevant to interpreting prompted assessments: "(1) inadequate strategy use due to an availability deficiency, (2) prompted use of available strategies that may otherwise suffer from a production deficiency, and (3) spontaneously produced strategies." Prompted assessment methods such as MC-question enactment can detect availability deficiencies but cannot separate prompted use from spontaneous use.
requirements: Distinguishing all three levels requires assessments conducted first without prompting and only then with prompting (Veenman et al. 2000, 2005)
constraints: Prompting strategy use prior or concurrent to task performance restricts the scope of assessments to availability deficiencies; confidence ratings may assess inadequate calibration but not spontaneous use of calibration strategies
target_learners: learners being assessed for reading strategy use
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of spontaneous versus prompted strategy use
examples: Cromley and Azevedo's prompted enactment method provides valuable information about level 1 but cannot distinguish levels 2 and 3
key_sources: Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2011). Alternative assessment of strategy use with self-report instruments: a discussion. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9080-x

article_title: Testing the Difference between School Level and Academic Mindset in the Classroom: Implications for Developing Student Psycho-Social Skills in Secondary School Classrooms
citation: Hanson, J. (2017). Testing the Difference between School Level and Academic Mindset in the Classroom: Implications for Developing Student Psycho-Social Skills in Secondary School Classrooms. Journal of Educational Issues, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.5296/jei.v3i1.10479
title: Three-level model of mindset survey variables: individual, group/classroom, and school
description: Figure 1 of the article presents a model comparing and contrasting variables on three levels of mindset scales: individual, group/classroom, and school. The individual mindset survey, the PERTS survey, and the What's My School Mindset Survey (WMSM) quantify participant self-reports of psycho-social variables found in the literature and reported to improve student engagement in learning. The group-level models are consistent with Bandura's social cognitive theory, explaining reciprocal influences of the group on individuals' beliefs, choices, and behaviors. Research cited suggests interventions at the individual level show less potential for improving outcomes than those at group and organizational levels.
requirements: Likert-style surveys to quantify self-reports of psycho-social variables at each level
constraints: The article notes research suggests the individual's mindset has little correlation with the group level mindset culture in schools
target_learning_goals: understanding psycho-social influences on student engagement
examples: Hanson, Ruff, and Bangert (2016) used the What's My School Mindset? instrument to quantify a school's growth mindset culture
key_sources: Hanson, J. (2017). Testing the Difference between School Level and Academic Mindset in the Classroom: Implications for Developing Student Psycho-Social Skills in Secondary School Classrooms. Journal of Educational Issues, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.5296/jei.v3i1.10479

article_title: Working Memory and Attention – A Conceptual Analysis and Review
citation: Oberauer, K. (2019). Working Memory and Attention – A Conceptual Analysis and Review. Journal of Cognition, 2(1): 36. https://doi.org/10.5334/joc.58
title: A three-level framework of selection in working memory: activated part of LTM, region of direct access, and focus of attention
description: The review proposes that selection in WM operates at three nested levels: selecting information into WM (the activated part of long-term memory), selecting a subset of the memory set (the region of direct access), and selecting a single item (the focus of attention). Behavioral evidence shows retro-cues can select subsets and then items within subsets, supporting "three levels of selection in WM". The framework has been computationally implemented (Oberauer et al., 2013).
requirements: The framework requires that selection at each level serves a functional purpose, such that selecting multiple items simultaneously is feasible only when doing so does not undercut the purpose of selection
constraints: The review notes it is currently not clear whether more than one WM representation is neurally active at the same time, so the neural characterization of the second versus third level remains open
target_learning_goals: understanding the architecture of selection within working memory
understanding how retro-cues and item-switch costs reveal levels of selection
examples: Retro-cue paradigms demonstrate that a cue presented one to several seconds into retention can guide attention to one item or a subset, improving memory for cued content at the expense of uncued content
key_sources: Oberauer, K. (2019). Working Memory and Attention – A Conceptual Analysis and Review. Journal of Cognition, 2(1): 36. https://doi.org/10.5334/joc.58

article_title: Think-Pair-Share and Roundtable: Two Cooperative Learning Structures to Enhance Critical Thinking Skills of 4th Graders
citation: Silva, H., Lopes, J., Dominguez, C., & Morais, E. (2022). Think-Pair-Share and Roundtable: Two Cooperative Learning Structures to Enhance Critical Thinking Skills of 4th Graders. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 15(1), 11-21. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2022.274
title: Think-Pair-Share three-phase discussion structure
description: Think-Pair-Share (TPS) is a cooperative learning technique that unfolds in three phases: Thinking, where students get "time to think individually" about a topic or problem; Pairing, where pairs within groups discuss to reach a common answer; and Share, where pairs share answers and one member reports the group's answer to the class. The article states TPS enables oral and written argumentation and increases response quality by increasing waiting time. It was used with similar frequency to RoundTable across 21 activities.
requirements: Heterogeneous groups of four students
A topic or problem stated by the teacher
Time allocated for individual thinking
target_learning_goals: Oral and written argumentation
Critical thinking through discussion of different perspectives
examples: Used in the experimental class across Language Arts, Environment Study and Mathematics on topics such as pollution, children's rights, and community life of bees and ants
key_sources: Silva, H., Lopes, J., Dominguez, C., & Morais, E. (2022). Think-Pair-Share and Roundtable: Two Cooperative Learning Structures to Enhance Critical Thinking Skills of 4th Graders. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 15(1), 11-21. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2022.274

article_title: The audience effect in adolescence depends on who's looking over your shoulder
citation: Wolf L.K., Bazargani N., Kilford E.J., Dumontheil I., Blakemore S.-J. (2015). The audience effect in adolescence depends on who's looking over your shoulder. Journal of Adolescence, 43, 5–14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.adolescence.2015.05.003
title: Three proposed mechanisms for adolescent peer audience effects: arousal, fear of social evaluation, and self-awareness
description: The article proposes three putative mechanisms underlying performance differences under evaluative observation: "changes in arousal in the presence of others"; increased "fear of social evaluation" leading adolescents to spend time mentalising about how peers judge their abilities, distracting them from the task; and increased self-awareness of discrepancies between current and ideal performance, which in complex tasks may cause excessive self-monitoring. These are offered as hypotheses for future study, not tested results.
requirements: Future studies are needed to test these mechanisms, as the article states the mechanisms are putative and untested.
constraints: The mechanisms are the authors' interpretation, not findings of the experiment; the article did not measure fear of social evaluation.
target_learning_goals: cognitive task performance (relational reasoning) under social observation
key_sources: Wolf L.K., Bazargani N., Kilford E.J., Dumontheil I., Blakemore S.-J. (2015). The audience effect in adolescence depends on who's looking over your shoulder. Journal of Adolescence, 43, 5–14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.adolescence.2015.05.003

article_title: Training English language student teachers to become reflective teachers
citation: Ali Al-Issa & Ali Al-Bulushi. (2010). Training English Language Student Teachers to Become Reflective Teachers. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, Vol 35, 4. https://ro.ecu.edu.au/ajtec/vol35/iss4/4/
title: Three levels of reflection-on-action: descriptive, dialogic/deliberate, and critical
description: The article organises reflective teaching around three forms or levels of reflection-on-action drawn from the literature (van Manen, Hall, Hatton & Smith, Schon). The first is "'random' and 'descriptive'", the lowest level, involving describing and reporting events and returning to experience; the second is "'deliberate' (Hall, 1997) or 'dialogic'", re-evaluating experience and critically analysing situations to generate alternative solutions; the third is "of a more 'critical' nature", locating ELT within wider social, political and cultural contexts and judging the value of the existing context. The levels complement and build on one another, and trainees moved gradually between them can analyse their whole context.
requirements: Student teachers should be trained to move gradually from one level to another
constraints: The article notes the descriptive level does not serve deep learning and students at that level most likely cannot apply understanding to different contexts
target_learning_goals: developing reflective teaching practice and critical evaluation of teaching contexts
examples: The article uses the three levels to frame why SQU trainees need training in reflective skills suited to the Omani ELT context
key_sources: Ali Al-Issa & Ali Al-Bulushi. (2010). Training English Language Student Teachers to Become Reflective Teachers. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, Vol 35, 4. https://ro.ecu.edu.au/ajtec/vol35/iss4/4/

article_title: Effects of games in STEM education: a meta-analysis on the moderating role of student background characteristics
citation: Michaela Arztmann, Lisette Hornstra, Johan Jeuring & Liesbeth Kester (2023). Effects of games in STEM education: a meta-analysis on the moderating role of student background characteristics. Studies in Science Education, 59:1, 109-145. https://doi.org/10.1080/03057267.2022.2057732
title: Three-category outcome framework for game-based learning research: cognitive, motivational, and behavioural outcomes
description: The article organises game-based learning outcomes into three categories, adapting Hainey et al.'s four categories by merging knowledge acquisition with perceptual and cognitive outcomes. Cognitive outcomes include "assessed learning outcomes, knowledge retention ... or conceptual knowledge"; motivational outcomes combine affect and motivation (intrinsic motivation, interest, self-efficacy, enjoyment); behavioural outcomes include "self-reported strategy use, behavioural engagement, or effort". The framework structures the three separate meta-analyses and the moderator analyses.
requirements: Studies must investigate at least one of the three defined outcome variables to fit the framework
constraints: The sociocultural perspective, focusing on game features such as individual versus collaborative play, is explicitly beyond the scope of this framework's application
target_learning_goals: STEM knowledge acquisition
STEM motivation
learning-related behaviour
examples: The meta-analysis coded each study's outcome measures into cognition, motivation, or behaviour and ran one random-effects meta-analysis per category.
key_sources: Michaela Arztmann, Lisette Hornstra, Johan Jeuring & Liesbeth Kester (2023). Effects of games in STEM education: a meta-analysis on the moderating role of student background characteristics. Studies in Science Education, 59:1, 109-145. https://doi.org/10.1080/03057267.2022.2057732

article_title: Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics
citation: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3
title: Three types of measures derivable from gameplay telemetry: overall game performance, in-game performance, and in-game strategies
description: The chapter proposes that "three types of measures can be derived from gameplay: (a) overall game performance, (b) in-game performance, and (c) in-game strategies," each with certain uses and selected according to the question being asked. In the case study, overall performance was the last level reached, in-game performance included addition errors, level resets, and player deaths, and in-game strategies were derived from sets or sequences of behaviors analyzed with methods such as cluster analysis.
requirements: Telemetry designed per the chapter's guidelines so events and context are uniquely identifiable
constraints: Measures based on discovery of interesting patterns are more tenuous, since identified patterns must be interpreted in light of the task and the player's presumed domain knowledge
target_learners: players of serious games, e.g., students learning rational-number concepts
target_learning_goals: measuring overall achievement, in-game use of cognitive demands, and player strategies
examples: In Save Patch, overall performance was the last level reached; in-game performance used incorrect rope placements; strategies were identified via cluster analysis
key_sources: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3

article_title: Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue
citation: Taylor Martin & Bruce Sherin. (2013). Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 22(4), 511–520. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.840466
title: Three fundamental assumptions of the learning sciences perspective on learning: ubiquitous, heterogeneous, and complex
description: The article articulates three assumptions it calls "critical for the selection of research methods": "1. Learning events are not rare events. 2. Learning is a heterogeneous phenomenon. 3. Learning is a complex process." Learning happens in all places and times, takes dramatically different forms from aha moments to incremental change, and involves wandering a complex space of possibilities rather than climbing a unidimensional stairway. These assumptions imply that methods must capture learning across contexts, in diverse forms, and as an unfolding process rather than only start and end points.
requirements: Methods must be "widely deployed to capture learning phenomena of many sorts, across multiple contexts and in diverse forms," and must yield process data, not just outcome data.
target_learning_goals: Framing research questions about learning in ways consistent with the field's core assumptions
examples: The article derives methodological implications directly from the assumptions: complexity of learning motivates collecting data on the process, not just its start and end points.
key_sources: Taylor Martin & Bruce Sherin. (2013). Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 22(4), 511–520. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.840466

article_title: Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach
citation: Mayer, Richard E. (2014). Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach. The MIT Press. http://direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/4028/bookpreview-pdf/2362507
title: Three-genre taxonomy of research on games for learning: value-added, cognitive consequences, and media comparison
description: The book organizes all research on games for learning into three research paradigms. The value-added approach compares a base game against the base game plus one added feature; the cognitive consequences approach compares pretest-to-posttest change for extended off-the-shelf game play versus no play; the media comparison approach compares learning from a game versus conventional media on the same material. The book states it "distinguishes among three genres of game research: the value-added approach, the cognitive consequences approach, and the media comparison approach" and systematizes the field by sorting experiments into these categories.
requirements: Each genre requires methodologically sound experimental comparisons: random assignment, matched treatment and control groups, and appropriate measures of learning outcome
constraints: The taxonomy applies to experimental comparisons meeting basic requirements of experimental methodology, not to speculative essays or methodologically flawed studies
target_learning_goals: academic learning outcomes and cognitive skills from computer games
examples: The book's meta-analysis chapters each address one genre: chapter 5 value-added, chapter 6 cognitive consequences, chapter 7 media comparison
key_sources: Mayer, Richard E. (2014). Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach. The MIT Press. http://direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/4028/bookpreview-pdf/2362507

article_title: Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach
citation: Mayer, Richard E. (2014). Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach. The MIT Press. http://direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/4028/bookpreview-pdf/2362507
title: Three kinds of cognitive processing during game learning: extraneous, essential, and generative
description: The book applies cognitive load theory to game learning by distinguishing three types of cognitive processing: "extraneous processing, which wastes precious cognitive capacity; essential processing, aimed at attending to and mentally representing the academic content; and generative processing, which involves deeper reflection on the academic content." Extraneous processing is caused by poor game design, essential processing by the inherent difficulty of the material, and generative processing by the player's motivation to engage in learning. The stated goal of effective game design is to reduce extraneous processing, manage essential processing, and foster generative processing.
requirements: Effective game design must manage limited cognitive capacity across the three processing types
target_learners: players of games for learning across K-12, college, and workplace settings
target_learning_goals: academic knowledge and skill acquisition from games
examples: Table 1.3 attributes extraneous processing to poor game design and generative processing to the player's motivation to engage in learning
key_sources: Mayer, Richard E. (2014). Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach. The MIT Press. http://direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/4028/bookpreview-pdf/2362507

article_title: Executive Function in Education: From Theory to Practice
citation: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive Function in Education: From Theory to Practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com
title: Denckla's three-level description linking ADHD, executive function dysfunction, and brain localization
description: Denckla's chapter argues that three levels of description must be connected: ADHD at the surface syndromic level, executive function dysfunction (EDF) at the intermediate cognitive analysis level, and frontal, striatal, and cerebellar localizations at the neurological level. She reports that heterogeneity characterized each level, most clearly at the neurological level, and that neuroimaging of disorders such as neurofibromatosis 1 showed ADHD-syndromic characteristics with subcortical abnormalities.
requirements: Assessment and diagnosis must specify which of the three levels is being described
constraints: Heterogeneity within ADHD, within the brains of those with ADHD, and within the EF domain complicates research replication
target_learning_goals: understanding neurodevelopmental bases of academic performance
key_sources: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive Function in Education: From Theory to Practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com

article_title: Rethinking Education in a Changing World
citation: UNESCO Secretariat. (2013). Rethinking Education in a Changing World. UNESCO Education Research and Foresight. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/
title: Three time-frames of education: short-term response, mid-term policy, and long-term transformation of mental structures
description: Drawing on Fernand Braudel's three time-frames of history, the report proposes thinking about education's role at three scales. As printed: 'the short-term that attempts to respond to more immediate and urgent concerns; the mid-term perspective that refers to policy, educational structures, pedagogical approaches; and the longer-term perspective that has do to with mentalities and a transformation of mental structures'. The report judges the longer-term transformation of worldviews the most challenging.
requirements: Education policy must be articulated across all three time horizons rather than only the short term
constraints: The report states the longer-term perspective, the transformation of worldviews, is the most challenging
target_learners: societies and education systems at local, national and global levels
target_learning_goals: global responsibility, human dignity and transformation of mental structures
examples: The report frames its guiding questions for education in the 21st century within these three time-frames
key_sources: UNESCO Secretariat. (2013). Rethinking Education in a Changing World. UNESCO Education Research and Foresight. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/

article_title: Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children
citation: Chen Y, Wang Y, Wang S, Zhang M and Wu N. (2021). Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children. Front. Psychol. 12:793000. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.793000
title: Three-component model of executive function (inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, working memory)
description: The article adopts the multidimensional conceptualization of executive function in which "It is often postulated in the literature that EF has three elementary components: inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility." Each component is measured by a separate task (Red-Blue Test, Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, Backward Digit Span), and the components are moderately associated but separable. The study's design treats each component's link with sleep separately, which the authors say previous research neglecting the multidimensionality tended to miss.
requirements: Separate tasks for each component; the article notes few studies have systematically investigated sleep against all components
constraints: The structure of EF develops with age; the article notes shifting was found mixed with inhibition in young children, so correlation patterns may differ across age groups
target_learners: typically developing children in early primary school
target_learning_goals: understanding how sleep relates to distinct executive function components underlying school performance
examples: Applied in the current study with one classic task per component, administered counterbalanced in about 20 min per child
key_sources: Chen Y, Wang Y, Wang S, Zhang M and Wu N. (2021). Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children. Front. Psychol. 12:793000. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.793000

article_title: Emergent Writing in Preschoolers: Preliminary Evidence for a Theoretical Framework
citation: Puranik, C. S., & Lonigan, C. J. (2014). Emergent Writing in Preschoolers: Preliminary Evidence for a Theoretical Framework. Reading Research Quarterly, 49(4). https://doi.org/10.1002/rrq.79
title: Three-domain organizational framework of emergent writing: Conceptual, Procedural, and Generative Knowledge
description: The framework organizes preschool emergent writing skills into three distinct but correlated domains. Conceptual Knowledge covers understanding of the purposes, conventions, and functions of writing; Procedural Knowledge covers code-related mechanics such as alphabet knowledge, letter writing, name writing, and spelling; Generative Knowledge covers composing beyond the word level. The authors hypothesized that "three distinct but correlated dimensions would account for children’s emergent writing skills," deliberately excluding sociocultural factors because the focus was on the skills children demonstrate while writing. The framework parallels the transcription/text-generation distinction in models of older children's writing.
requirements: Assessment tasks designed to index each of the three domains, as in this study's battery of conceptual, procedural, and generative subtests
constraints: The framework did not include sociocultural factors; it concerns the skills young children demonstrate while writing, not the reasons or contexts for writing use
Cross-sectional data cannot address causal relations between the dimensions
target_learning_goals: Emergent writing skills, including print concepts, letter and word transcription, and early composition
examples: CFA of 372 preschoolers' performance on writing tasks indexing the three domains supported the framework over one- and two-factor alternatives
key_sources: Puranik, C. S., & Lonigan, C. J. (2014). Emergent Writing in Preschoolers: Preliminary Evidence for a Theoretical Framework. Reading Research Quarterly, 49(4). https://doi.org/10.1002/rrq.79

article_title: The increasing role of metacognitive skills in math: a cross-sectional study from a developmental perspective
citation: Van der Stel, M., Veenman, M. V. J., Deelen, K., & Haenen, J. (2010). The increasing role of metacognitive skills in math: a cross-sectional study from a developmental perspective. ZDM Mathematics Education, 42, 219–229. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-009-0224-2
title: Thinking-aloud protocol scoring system for math metacognitive skillfulness (four subscales, quantity and quality)
description: An observational coding system in which thinking-aloud protocols are analyzed for spontaneous metacognitive activities during math problem solving. "Metacognitive skillfulness was divided into four subscales: orientation (O), planning and systematical orderliness (P), evaluation (Ev), and elaboration (El)", with math-specific and general example activities for each (e.g., goal setting, making a sketch, checking an answer by recalculating). Scoring is two-step: utterances are coded per subscale for frequency, and each subscale receives a qualitative score on a five-point scale (0–4), with judges avoiding confounding scores with correctness of content. Interrater reliability was 0.95 and 0.98 for qualitative scores.
requirements: Thinking-aloud protocols collected during task performance; trained judges with criteria per subscale
constraints: Judges intentionally avoided confounding metacognition scores with the correctness or incorrectness of the content matter
target_learning_goals: metacognitive regulation of math problem solving
examples: Two judges independently rated six protocols of both years to establish interrater reliability
key_sources: Van der Stel, M., Veenman, M. V. J., Deelen, K., & Haenen, J. (2010). The increasing role of metacognitive skills in math: a cross-sectional study from a developmental perspective. ZDM Mathematics Education, 42, 219–229. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-009-0224-2

article_title: Components of executive control with advantages for bilingual children in two cultures
citation: Bialystok Ellen, Viswanathan Mythili. (2009). Components of Executive Control with Advantages for Bilingual Children in Two Cultures. Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2009.06.014
title: Three-component decomposition of executive control: response suppression, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility
description: The article treats executive control as a set of separable components, building on the widely accepted view that "the executive control system consists of three components: inhibition, updating (also called working memory), and shifting (also called cognitive flexibility)". It further distinguishes two processes conflated under the term inhibition: inhibitory control, resolving conflict "by selectively attending to a relevant stimulus cue and ignoring a competing cue", and response suppression, refraining from an automatically cued response. The faces task operationalizes each component as a specific RT cost, allowing the components to be tested separately in the same children.
requirements: A task that yields separable cost measures for each component in the same population, as the faces task does for children
constraints: The components emerge at different developmental times, so bilingualism may have different influences at different ages
target_learning_goals: Executive control processes: response suppression, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility
examples: The faces task assessed response suppression by the red-minus-green eye RT difference, inhibitory control by the gaze-shift-minus-straight-eye difference in mixed blocks, and switching by the mixed-minus-blocked difference.
key_sources: Bialystok Ellen, Viswanathan Mythili. (2009). Components of Executive Control with Advantages for Bilingual Children in Two Cultures. Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2009.06.014

article_title: Life-span changes to adults' language: Effects of memory and genre
citation: Kemper, S., Kynette, D., Rash, S., O'Brien, K., & Sprott, R. (1989). Life-span changes to adults' language: Effects of memory and genre. Applied Psycholinguistics, 10, 49-66. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716400008419
title: Three-sample language elicitation battery with WAIS vocabulary and digit-span tests
description: A measurement battery combining three language samples with cognitive tests. Samples were "an oral questionnaire eliciting information about the adults' background, education, and current health and activities; an oral statement describing the person they most admired; and a written statement recounting the most significant event in their lives," plus "the WAIS vocabulary and digit-span tests." It yields length, clause-structure, and fluency measures across genres.
requirements: Elicitation of comparable oral and written samples from each participant
Administration of vocabulary and digit-span measures for correlational analyses
target_learning_goals: measuring syntactic complexity, fluency, and clause structure in adult language
examples: Used with young adults 18-28 and elderly adults 60-92 to compare complexity across oral and written genres
key_sources: Kemper, S., Kynette, D., Rash, S., O'Brien, K., & Sprott, R. (1989). Life-span changes to adults' language: Effects of memory and genre. Applied Psycholinguistics, 10, 49-66. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716400008419

article_title: Creativity in Collaborative Learning across the Life Span
citation: Margarida Romero, Pirkko Hyvönen, Elena Barberà. (2012). Creativity in Collaborative Learning across the Life Span. Creative Education. https://doi.org/10.4236/ce.2012.34066
title: Three theoretical perspectives on late adulthood: normative crisis, successful aging, and specific or partial theories
description: The article distinguishes three theoretical perspectives on late adulthood. First, theories about normative crisis, which are "basically descriptive and rely on age-related sequences in the human life span structured by developmental phase", including Erikson's "eight ages", Piaget's "genetic epistemology" and Baltes's vital cycles. Second, theories about successful aging, which are "not based on developmental deficits" but "driven by a satisfactory construct of life", describing ways to arrive at high personal satisfaction by adapting to change. Third, specific or partial theories focused precisely on the period of older adulthood, dealing mainly with cognitive achievement and sensory functions, socio-emotional selectivity, and developmental contextualism. All these perspectives agree that late adulthood is a period of adaptation to new personal resources.
requirements: The perspectives are used to frame the specificities of the elderly target group and their creative capabilities
constraints: Older adults "have not been the subject of extensive study to date", per the article
target_learning_goals: understanding creative capabilities in late adulthood
adaptation to new personal resources
examples: The article uses these perspectives to explain the paradox that older adults experience progressive decline in activity yet are better able to adapt, supporting so-called practical intelligence or wisdom in decision-making
key_sources: Margarida Romero, Pirkko Hyvönen, Elena Barberà. (2012). Creativity in Collaborative Learning across the Life Span. Creative Education. https://doi.org/10.4236/ce.2012.34066

article_title: First Language and Second Language Writing: The Role of Linguistic Knowledge, Speed of Processing, and Metacognitive Knowledge
citation: R. Schoonen, A. van Gelderen, K. de Glopper, J. Hulstijn, A. Simis, P. Snellings, M. Stevenson. (2003). First language and second language writing: the role of linguistic knowledge, speed of processing, and metacognitive knowledge. Language Learning, 53(1), 165-202. https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9922.00213
title: Three-component model of writing proficiency: linguistic knowledge, accessibility/fluency, and metacognitive knowledge
description: The article organizes writing proficiency into three hypothesized components: linguistic knowledge (vocabulary, grammar), the fluency or accessibility of that knowledge (speed of processing), and metacognitive knowledge. Using structural equation modeling, the components' relative contributions to L1 (Dutch) and L2 (English) writing were estimated and compared. The model treats writing as drawing on both knowledge resources and the efficiency with which they can be retrieved, allowing cross-language comparison of component weights.
requirements: Measures of linguistic knowledge, processing speed/fluency, and metacognitive knowledge in both languages
Writing performance measures in both L1 and L2
Structural equation modeling to estimate relative component weights
constraints: Component weights estimated for grade 8 students learning English as L2 in a Dutch L1 context
Findings pertain to the measures and models used in this study
target_learning_goals: L1 and L2 writing proficiency
examples: SEM compared the three components' relative importance across L1 and L2 writing in 281 students
key_sources: R. Schoonen, A. van Gelderen, K. de Glopper, J. Hulstijn, A. Simis, P. Snellings, M. Stevenson. (2003). First language and second language writing: the role of linguistic knowledge, speed of processing, and metacognitive knowledge. Language Learning, 53(1), 165-202. https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9922.00213

article_title: How does mathematics anxiety impair mathematical abilities? Investigating the link between math anxiety, working memory, and number processing
citation: Skagerlund K, Östergren R, Västfjäll D, Träff U (2019) How does mathematics anxiety impair mathematical abilities? Investigating the link between math anxiety, working memory, and number processing. PLoS ONE 14(1): e0211283. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0211283
title: Three-pathway model of how math anxiety impairs mathematical performance
description: The article's organizing framework: MA impedes math performance through (1) an indirect pathway via working memory ability, supporting the 'affective drop' hypothesis in which negative emotions and self-referential worry drain WM resources needed for computation; (2) an indirect pathway via symbolic number processing, corroborating domain-specific mechanisms pertaining to number; and (3) a direct effect of MA on math performance, possibly due to distal avoidance behavior. The model was instantiated as two SEM path models (arithmetic and numeracy) and the pathways' relative strength varied by task type.
requirements: Measures of WM, symbolic number processing, MA, and the math outcome, modeled jointly (e.g., via SEM) to separate direct from indirect effects
constraints: Correlational SEM in adults; the authors state longitudinal and experimental manipulations are needed to make firm claims about directions of causality; BNT reliability (α = .41) limits the numeracy model
target_learners: adults (university students) with varying levels of math anxiety
target_learning_goals: arithmetic calculation ability
numeracy
examples: Two fitted path models: MA→WM→arithmetic (standardized -.15) and MA→WM→numeracy (standardized -.14) were significant, while MA→NP→numeracy was not
key_sources: Skagerlund K, Östergren R, Västfjäll D, Träff U (2019) How does mathematics anxiety impair mathematical abilities? Investigating the link between math anxiety, working memory, and number processing. PLoS ONE 14(1): e0211283. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0211283

article_title: Response to Intervention for Reading Difficulties in the Primary Grades
citation: Denton Carolyn A. (2012). Response to Intervention for Reading Difficulties in the Primary Grades: Some Answers and Lingering Questions. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219412442155
title: Three-tier RTI model for primary-grade reading: Tier 1 core instruction, Tier 2 supplemental intervention, Tier 3 intensive intervention
description: The article describes RTI for early reading as a schoolwide, multitiered prevention framework in which "students are provided with evidence-based classroom reading instruction and supplemental intervention when it is needed, and decisions related to intervention are based on student assessment data." Tier 1 is evidence-based core classroom instruction with universal screening; Tier 2 is supplemental intervention for at-risk students; Tier 3 is more intensive intervention for inadequate responders. Progress is monitored with repeated curriculum-based measures, and teacher professional development supports fidelity.
requirements: Student progress monitoring data, typically repeated curriculum-based measures, to inform tier placement decisions
Teacher professional development to ensure high-quality, faithfully delivered instruction at all tiers
constraints: The article focuses on a three-tiered model, noting some RTI systems use four or more tiers
target_learners: Primary-grade students at risk for reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: Early reading skills: phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension
key_sources: Denton Carolyn A. (2012). Response to Intervention for Reading Difficulties in the Primary Grades: Some Answers and Lingering Questions. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219412442155

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives
citation: Fred Paas, Tamara van Gog, John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 115-121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9133-8
title: Three categories of cognitive load: intrinsic, extraneous, and germane, with communicating-vessel dynamics
description: CLT identifies three categories of cognitive load: intrinsic load caused by the complexity of the materials, extraneous load caused by poorly designed instructional procedures that interfere with schema acquisition, and germane load, the working memory resources devoted to dealing with intrinsic load.
