The article states that "it is important to consider extraneous and germane cognitive load as communicating vessels", because reducing extraneous load frees resources for germane processing.
requirements: Extraneous load must first be eliminated; intrinsic load must be managed so that simultaneous processing of all interactive elements remains possible
constraints: When intrinsic cognitive load is high, decreasing extraneous load becomes especially important, otherwise the combination might exceed maximum cognitive capacity
target_learning_goals: schema acquisition
effective use of working memory resources
examples: Studying worked examples instead of solving conventional problems is described as an effective way of reducing extraneous load
key_sources: Fred Paas, Tamara van Gog, John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 115-121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9133-8

article_title: Breaking Bad Behaviors: A New Tool for Learning Classroom Management Using Virtual Reality
citation: Lugrin J-L, Latoschik ME, Habel M, Roth D, Seufert C and Grafe S (2016) Breaking Bad Behaviors: A New Tool for Learning Classroom Management Using Virtual Reality. Front. ICT 3:26. https://doi.org/10.3389/fict.2016.00026
title: Three elements of effective training: realistic exposure, fine control of stimuli, and fine performance feedback
description: The article proposes that effective training depends on three major elements: exposure to realistic training scenarios and stimuli, fine control over training stimuli and scenarios (including adjusting difficulty to the trainee's current competence and repeating identical stimuli), and fine performance feedback that is fine-grained, unambiguous, and timely. The authors note a compromise between realism and control in real classrooms, where "the unpredictability of a real classroom greatly diminishes any control over the exact nature and difficulty of training stimuli". They designed 3B to combine all three elements in an immersive VR simulation.
requirements: Control of stimuli and provision of feedback would ideally occur in a closed real-time loop between trainer and trainee
constraints: In real classrooms, feedback is largely restricted to deferred reviews decoupled from the actual situational context
target_learning_goals: Adjusting behavior to achieve better results through realistic practice with controlled stimuli and timely feedback
examples: The 3B system implements the three elements via a simulated classroom, instructor-controlled behavior levels, and synchronous and asynchronous feedback
key_sources: Lugrin J-L, Latoschik ME, Habel M, Roth D, Seufert C and Grafe S (2016) Breaking Bad Behaviors: A New Tool for Learning Classroom Management Using Virtual Reality. Front. ICT 3:26. https://doi.org/10.3389/fict.2016.00026

article_title: Developing Symbolic Interpretation Through Literary Argumentation
citation: Teresa Sosa, Allison H. Hall, and Susan R. Goldman; Carol D. Lee. (2015). Developing Symbolic Interpretation Through Literary Argumentation.
title: Three-phase progression for teaching symbolic interpretation with increasing text complexity
description: The module organized symbolic interpretation into a sequence the authors describe as "three phases that built on one another": first identifying symbols via associations, then making symbolic interpretive claims grounded in textual evidence connected to characters and their worlds, and finally making claims from patterns of evidence across extended texts. Texts increased in complexity in parallel, from everyday images and pop songs to a culturally less familiar lengthier text. Supporting worksheets accompanied each phase.
requirements: Worksheets scaffolding each phase
Class discussions providing practice and feedback on sensemaking and interpretive processes
constraints: The module was implemented in two ninth-grade sections in a suburban school program for students reading below the 30th percentile
target_learners: ninth-grade students in an integrated freshman support program
target_learning_goals: identifying symbols
making evidence-based symbolic interpretive claims
connecting symbols to characters and themes
examples: Days 4–5 used cultural data sets (flags, roses, pop songs); Days 11–14 used short texts with Worksheet 2; the final seven days centered on "Two Kinds" from The Joy Luck Club.
key_sources: Teresa Sosa, Allison H. Hall, and Susan R. Goldman; Carol D. Lee. (2015). Developing Symbolic Interpretation Through Literary Argumentation. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2015.1124040

article_title: Teacher–Student Dialogue During Classroom Teaching: Does It Really Impact on Student Outcomes?
citation: Howe, C., Hennessy, S., Mercer, N., Vrikki, M., & Wheatley, L. (2018). Teacher-Student Dialogue during Classroom Teaching: Does it Really Impact upon Student Outcomes? To appear in The Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://gtr.ukri.org/projects?ref=ES/M007103/1
title: Theoretically productive classroom dialogue framework: five recurring themes plus the cross-cutting theme of high student contribution
description: The article defines theoretically productive dialogue as classroom verbal interaction complying with five recurring themes: open questions, elaboration of previous contributions, reasoned discussion of competing viewpoints, linkage and coordination across contributions, and meta-cognitive engagement with dialogue, plus high student contribution. It states that amongst proposals about optimizing outcomes, "five themes recur", and uses the framework to code routine lessons and test whether the themes relate to student outcomes in teacher-student dialogue, not just small-group work.
requirements: All participants, teachers and students, should contribute fully to ensuring interaction complies with the themes, implying high levels of student involvement
constraints: Researchers differ over which themes they emphasize and over the labels used, especially the term dialogue
The themes emerged from decades of classroom observation and vary in how they are operationalized
target_learners: Primary school students aged 10-11 years (Year 6) in whole-class teacher-student dialogue
target_learning_goals: Curriculum mastery in mathematics, science and literacy
General reasoning
Educationally relevant attitudes
examples: The authors contrast open questions such as asking why Edinburgh became a major cultural centre with closed questions such as asking for the capital of Scotland
key_sources: Howe, C., Hennessy, S., Mercer, N., Vrikki, M., & Wheatley, L. (2018). Teacher-Student Dialogue during Classroom Teaching: Does it Really Impact upon Student Outcomes? To appear in The Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://gtr.ukri.org/projects?ref=ES/M007103/1

article_title: Theories of learning as theories of society: A contrapuntal approach to expanding disciplinary authenticity in computing
citation: Philip, T., & Sengupta, P. (2020). Theories of Learning as Theories of Society: A Contrapuntal Approach to Expanding Disciplinary Authenticity in Computing. Journal of the Learning Sciences. http://www.isls.org/
title: Theories of learning are implicit theories of society
description: The article's central framework holds that theories of learning emerge within researchers' sociopolitical contexts and co-construct the worlds they describe, so learning theory cannot be treated as politically neutral. The authors argue that "theories of learning are implicit theories of society" and that the field must attend to "the lens of imperialism" in analyzing learning. This reframes how designs and theories should be evaluated in the Learning Sciences.
requirements: Researchers must treat the sociopolitical context and consequences of learning theories as part of the theory itself, not as external background
constraints: The authors state the field cannot yet predict what will unfold from new theories and methods developed under this lens
target_learners: Learning Sciences researchers and graduate students
target_learning_goals: Understanding learning as political and situated in sociopolitical contexts
examples: The authors reread behaviorism, cognitivism, and sociocultural theory as theories of society, and read disciplinary authenticity in computing education contrapuntally against sociology of immigrant tech workers
key_sources: Philip, T., & Sengupta, P. (2020). Theories of Learning as Theories of Society: A Contrapuntal Approach to Expanding Disciplinary Authenticity in Computing. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2020.1828089

article_title: Classical dialogs in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Classical dialogs in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 4. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9071-y
title: Lonchamp's three-level integration of dialog, knowledge, and action analysis for dual-interaction CSCL environments
description: Jacques Lonchamp proposes a systematic integration of three analytic approaches, describing "three levels of analysis — dialog, knowledge, and action — which he claims fit together like semantics, syntax, and pragmatics to provide an integrated view of communication." He applies this within dual-interaction environments built using his generic and customizable Omega+ model.
requirements: Environments must support dual-interaction spaces; analysis requires coordinating the three levels
constraints: The editorial contrasts Lonchamp's designer perspective with Çakır et al.'s practice perspective on a comparable synchronous dual-interaction system
target_learners: Students collaborating in synchronous dual-interaction systems
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge construction in shared digital workspaces
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Classical dialogs in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 4. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9071-y

article_title: The effect of a script and a structured interface in grounding discussions
citation: Judith Schoonenboom. (2008). The effect of a script and a structured interface in grounding discussions. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-008-9042-8
title: Three-phased grounding script for distance student groups
description: A collaboration script that "provides a format for carrying out a grounding discussion among students who have to work together at a distance and who do not know each other". It divides grounding into an input phase, in which participants individually make their knowledge and objectives explicit; a discussion phase focused on differences and inconsistencies between members; and a consensus phase in which the group resolves differences and summarizes shared knowledge. Its theoretical rationale draws on small-group work, brainstorming, and CSCW research, on the idea that students should negotiate common goals and build detailed models of each other's knowledge, skills, and motivation.
requirements: Students who do not know each other and work together at a distance on a joint assignment
A discussion forum or comparable environment in which the scripted discussion can take place
constraints: The script pushes but does not force students to interact in a particular way, so unintended use is possible
Too much control in the dialogue can diminish motivation and endanger learner autonomy
target_learners: international distance-education students in small groups of three to six
target_learning_goals: establishing common ground about group members' knowledge, objectives, and qualities before collaborative work
examples: In the European Virtual Seminar, the script's input phase posed seven questions on participants' knowledge and objectives; the discussion phase asked members to identify differences and inconsistencies; the consensus phase asked the group to resolve them and summarize shared knowledge and remaining points of disagreement.
key_sources: Judith Schoonenboom. (2008). The effect of a script and a structured interface in grounding discussions. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-008-9042-8

article_title: Transactive discourse in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2013). Transactive discourse in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 8:145–147. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9171-6
title: Thick description as the analytic basis for understanding transactive discourse
description: Stahl draws on Austin and Geertz's notion of thick description: CSCL researchers understand transaction meanings because they share a community with their subjects. He contrasts "a thin description of someone's eye twitching vs. a thick description of someone winking" — a wink is a meaningful transaction requiring subtle cultural knowledge, unlike objective physiological description. Computers cannot formulate or understand thick descriptions of discourse moves.
requirements: The analyst must be a member of the same broad community as the subjects and possess subtle cultural knowledge
constraints: Computers cannot formulate or understand thick descriptions of discourse moves, so automated approaches must be indirect
target_learners: CSCL researchers and analysts of collaborative learning data
target_learning_goals: analysis and measurement of collaborative discourse
examples: Austin's twitch-versus-wink distinction illustrates why objective movement description cannot capture meaningful interaction
key_sources: Gerry Stahl. (2013). Transactive discourse in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 8:145–147. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9171-6

article_title: Traversing planes of learning
citation: Stahl, G. (2012). Traversing planes of learning. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 467–473. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9159-7
title: Three planes of learning in CSCL: individual, small-group, and community
description: The article names a tripartite unit-of-analysis framework for CSCL: "analyses of CSCL are often conducted on one of three levels: individual learning, small-group cognition or community knowledge building". The planes are actualized in classroom practice, where individual activities precede small-group work that culminates in whole-class sharing. The framework is grounded in CSCL practice and in Vygotsky's foundational role for intersubjective learning.
requirements: Analyses must select a unit of analysis; current analytic methodologies are designed for only one plane
constraints: The planes are intrinsically intertwined, and there is little theoretical understanding of how they are connected
target_learners: students in CSCL settings working individually, in small groups, and in whole-class community discussion
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge building and learning analyzed at multiple units of analysis
examples: Typical CSCL classrooms provide initial time for individual activities such as background reading or homework drill, followed by small-group work, then whole-class sharing of group findings
key_sources: Stahl, G. (2012). Traversing planes of learning. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 467–473. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9159-7

article_title: Beyond folk theories of CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). Beyond folk theories of CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9098-0
title: Three-type taxonomy of CSCL researchers by their relation to theory
description: The editorial organizes CSCL research practice into three kinds of researchers: those who "simply observe results of interventions" without theory, those who "follow a particular theory or theoretical framework that they accept as is", and those who "conduct CSCL research in order to investigate theoretical issues and refine theoretical perspectives specific to CSCL". The third group starts from a framework or commonsensical understanding but aims at pushing theories further and refining conceptualizations of collaborative learning; the issue's articles exemplify this approach.
requirements: Researchers must reflect on their theoretical footing rather than adopt common-sense assumptions unexamined
constraints: Imported frameworks not developed for CSCL "may fail to identify phenomena that are characteristic of CSCL"
target_learning_goals: Designing and interpreting research on computer-supported collaborative learning
examples: The editorial presents the four ijCSCL volume 5 case studies as exemplars of the third, theory-refining group.
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). Beyond folk theories of CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9098-0

article_title: Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation
citation: Gweon, G., Jain, M., McDonough, J., Raj, B., & Rosé, C. P. (2013). Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2013).
title: Ground the design of automated collaborative-process analysis models in theoretical constructs from social and cognitive psychology
description: The article recommends that computational models for automated collaborative-learning process analysis be structured using theories from social and cognitive psychology, so that models capture deep structure in the data and generalize better. The authors state that "The significance of this finding from a methodological standpoint is that it highlights the importance of considering the theoretical foundation for a construct when setting up a machine learning model to use for automated assessment." Theory informed both the feature representation and the DBN model structure, enabling an unsupervised approach requiring neither hand-labeled data nor hand-crafted features.
requirements: Access to a relevant theoretical construct that predicts observable patterns in the interaction data
constraints: State-of-the-art machine learning applied to conversational interactions tends to learn overly specific models that do not work well in new contexts
target_learners: collaborative learning participants in face-to-face or online group work
target_learning_goals: automatic assessment of group knowledge integration processes such as transactivity
examples: Speech Accommodation Theory motivated the DBN structure whose accommodation measure correlated with other-oriented transact prevalence
key_sources: Gweon, G., Jain, M., McDonough, J., Raj, B., & Rosé, C. P. (2013). Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2013). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9172-5

article_title: Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2011). Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 139-145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9118-8
title: Three levels of analysis in CSCL: individual, small group, and community
description: The editorial organizes CSCL theory by the unit at which learning is located: theories foreground the individual, the small group, or the community level of analysis, tracing respectively to cooperative learning research, Vygotsky's view that individual cognition is derivative of intersubjective experience, and Lave's perspective on learning as participation in a community of practice. The authors state that "a full analysis must take into account all three levels and their essential interpenetration," while noting any given analyst is usually well advised to focus on one level in accordance with a specific research interest.
requirements: Analysts choose a focal level aligned with their research interest while acknowledging the other levels
constraints: The editorial presents this as an organizing scheme for existing theories, not an empirically tested model
target_learning_goals: Selecting an appropriate unit of analysis for collaborative learning research
examples: Pifarre and Kleine Staarman's wiki study is placed in the small-group dialogicality vein; Jorczak's Collaborative Information Processing model is placed in the individual-cognition vein
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2011). Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 139-145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9118-8

article_title: Distinguishing knowledge-sharing, knowledge-construction, and knowledge-creation discourses
citation: Jan van Aalst. (2009). Distinguishing knowledge-sharing, knowledge-construction, and knowledge-creation discourses. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9069-5
title: Three modes of discourse: knowledge sharing, knowledge construction, and knowledge creation
description: The article articulates three modes of asynchronous computer-mediated discourse corresponding to three theoretical perspectives: "Knowledge sharing refers to a transmission theory of communication (see Pea 1994), knowledge construction to cognitive psychology (constructivism), and knowledge creation to interactive learning mediated by shared objects (Paavola et al. 2004)." Knowledge creation, in Bereiter and Scardamalia's model, treats a class as a community whose ideas are intellectual artifacts residing in the community's discourse, requiring design-mode work on explanations and belief-mode discourse for goals, mentoring, and evaluation. The framework is used to map four group discourses and to explain between-group differences in collective knowledge advancement.
requirements: Discourse must be examined in balance across modes, since a community may mix modes and individual epistemic beliefs differ
constraints: The article notes evidence of meta-discourse may not be strong in an inquiry of only 8 weeks
target_learning_goals: collaborative inquiry and collective knowledge advancement
examples: The four group discourses were mapped onto the modes: Group A showed threshold knowledge creation, one group knowledge sharing, and two hybrids of all three modes.
key_sources: Jan van Aalst. (2009). Distinguishing knowledge-sharing, knowledge-construction, and knowledge-creation discourses. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9069-5

article_title: Appropriation of a shared workspace: Organizing principles and their application
citation: Overdijk, M. & van Diggelen, W. (2008). Appropriation of a shared workspace: Organizing principles and their application. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-008-9038-4
title: Three basic orientations towards a shared workspace shape organizing principles
description: The paper distinguishes three orientations students may take towards a shared workspace: "(1) an orientation towards establishing and maintaining a direct and ongoing interaction between the members of the group; (2) an orientation towards the construction of a personal line of reasoning without direct interaction with the other members of the group; and (3) an orientation towards submitting contributions without expressing a relation between these contributions." These orientations lead to different principles for organization of contributions in the drawing space.
requirements: Analysis of appropriation requires distinguishing a personal dimension of actions in the tool from a collective dimension of interaction via the tool
constraints: The orientations were identified in one classroom case study of argumentative discussion
target_learners: secondary school students in small-group CSCL activities
target_learning_goals: organizing shared contributions during argumentative discussion
examples: Four focal groups were selected because each arrived at different organizing principles based on one of the three orientations
key_sources: Overdijk, M. & van Diggelen, W. (2008). Appropriation of a shared workspace: Organizing principles and their application. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-008-9038-4

article_title: Bridging research and practice: Implementing and sustaining knowledge building in Hong Kong classrooms
citation: Chan, C. K. K. (2011). Bridging research and practice: Implementing and sustaining knowledge building in Hong Kong classrooms. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9121-0
title: Three interacting themes for examining CSCL classroom innovation: context and systemic change, capacity and community building, and innovation as inquiry
description: The article proposes a conceptual framework of three interacting themes for examining how CSCL research creates innovation in classrooms: "context and systemic change, capacity and community building, and innovation as a process of inquiry." These themes organize the analysis of knowledge-building innovation in Hong Kong across macro, meso, and micro levels of the educational ecological system. The framework treats innovation as emergent changes at nested system levels rather than a single-site implementation.
requirements: Innovation must be examined at multiple interacting levels of the educational system rather than as isolated classroom change
constraints: The framework was developed from the Hong Kong knowledge-building case and its specific socio-cultural context
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge creation
Twenty-first-century skills
examples: The framework organized analysis of the Knowledge-Building Teacher Network across policy, teacher network, and classroom levels
key_sources: Chan, C. K. K. (2011). Bridging research and practice: Implementing and sustaining knowledge building in Hong Kong classrooms. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9121-0

article_title: CSCL towards the future: The second decade of ijCSCL
citation: Sten Ludvigsen. (2016). CSCL towards the future: The second decade of ijCSCL. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9230-x
title: Three interdependent layers of units of analysis in CSCL: individual, small group, and community
description: The editorial proposes a conceptual framing of CSCL research units of analysis as three interdependent layers. As printed: "Conceptually, one could frame the different units of analysis in CSCL as three interdependent layers— individual, small group and community — all of which are needed to understand and explain collaborative learning with computational tools." The framing holds that different theoretical orientations (cognitive, socio-cognitive, socio-cultural) direct analytic attention to different layers, and that a full understanding requires all three, including how individual contributions constitute group collaborative efforts.
requirements: Research designs must allow variation in units of analysis and levels of description across the three layers
constraints: The editorial presents this as a conceptual framing, not an empirically tested model
target_learners: collaborative learners in schools, higher education, and leisure time
target_learning_goals: understanding and explaining collaborative learning with computational tools
examples: The editorial notes it may be easier to design scaffolds for an individual's social and cognitive functions than for the social and content-based scaffolds of small groups and larger social units
key_sources: Sten Ludvigsen. (2016). CSCL towards the future: The second decade of ijCSCL. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9230-x

article_title: Experiences, appearances, and interprofessional training: The instructional use of video in post-simulation debriefings
citation: Elin Johansson, Oskar Lindwall, Hans Rystedt. (2017). Experiences, appearances, and interprofessional training: The instructional use of video in post-simulation debriefings. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9252-z
title: The three-phase debriefing model (description, analysis, application) structuring the post-simulation discussions
description: The investigated debriefings were organized around "a specific model for debriefing" with "three main phases: description, analysis, and application". Description begins with a 'blow out' in which each participant names one prominent feeling, followed by factual description of the scenario; the analysis phase, the most extensive part, is devoted to joint discussion and analysis of students' conduct; application involves students summarizing what they learned. Video clips of key events were introduced within the analysis phase.
requirements: A facilitator guides the phases; the analysis phase hosts the displayed key-event video clips
Participating students and observing students who watched via live video
constraints: Discussions focused primarily on what worked well and what could be improved rather than on what had not gone well
target_learners: medical and nursing students in the final phase of their educational programs
target_learning_goals: interprofessional teamwork, communication and non-technical skills such as SBAR, speak up and closed loop communication
examples: Each one-day simulation practice included five sessions of briefing (2–5 min), scenario (15–20 min), and debriefing (30–40 min) at a Swedish university hospital simulation centre
key_sources: Elin Johansson, Oskar Lindwall, Hans Rystedt. (2017). Experiences, appearances, and interprofessional training: The instructional use of video in post-simulation debriefings. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9252-z

article_title: Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings
citation: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law, Gerry Stahl, Carolyn P. Rosé. (2018). Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9274-1
title: Three interdependent planes of analysis — personal, interpersonal, and institutional — as a socio-cultural stance for CSCL
description: The editorial frames CSCL classroom analysis from a socio-cultural stance in which human development and learning rest on "the interdependencies among microgenesis, ontogenesis, and sociogenesis," which Rogoff labeled personal, interpersonal, and institutional planes of analysis. Each analytic level can be focused on individually, but actions emerge as parts of interrelated planes. Key concepts such as mediation, appropriation and emergence can be used across levels. The editorial uses this framework to discuss White's mathematics classroom-network study of connecting levels of activity.
requirements: Empirical analysis may focus on one plane, but does so with the understanding that actions emerge as parts of interrelated planes.
constraints: Digital infrastructures connecting students and teachers to multiple worlds make the connection between levels more complex than before, making the classroom more complex for both students and teachers.
target_learning_goals: understanding how individual actions, group processes and collective activities mediate each other in collaborative learning
examples: The editorial connects the three planes to White's study of Terms and Operations and Graphing in Groups digital tools in mathematics classrooms.

article_title: CSCL artifacts
citation: G. Stahl & S. Ludvigsen & N. Law & U. Cress. (2014). CSCL artifacts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 9, 237–245. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9200-0
title: Damşa's three inter-connected layers of small-group learning: productive interaction, knowledge-object development and shared epistemic agency
description: The editorial describes Damşa's analytical framework, in which she 'distinguishes three inter-connected layers of small-group learning: productive interaction, knowledge-object development and shared epistemic agency'. Productive interaction is interaction that potentially contributes to the group production of its target object; the knowledge object is the group's goal, provided from outside but interpreted and refined by the group; agency covers setting goals, pursuing them and concluding when accomplished.
requirements: The objective of producing a report must provide a grounded basis for analyzing interaction
constraints: The knowledge-object objective is largely proposed from outside the group interaction, e.g. by a university course
target_learners: university student teams working on course projects
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction through co-authored artifacts
examples: Interaction is analyzed by how it contributes to evolving the discussion and successive drafts of the team report

article_title: Evolution of the academic emotions of academically low-achieving students in knowledge building
citation: Yuqin Yang · Gaoxia Zhu · Carol K. K. Chan. (2022). Evolution of the academic emotions of academically low-achieving students in knowledge building. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09380-y
title: Three-phase principle-based pedagogical design scaffolding low-achieving students into Knowledge Building
description: A three-phased pedagogical design, refined from a previous four-phased design, that maps sixteen principle-based activities onto Knowledge Building principles (epistemic agency, community knowledge, collective responsibility, improvable ideas, embedded concurrent and transformative assessment). Phase 1 creates a collaborative and reflective culture so students "develop collaboration, inquiry, and reflection skills for productive Knowledge Building inquiry"; Phase 2 engages students in problem-centered collaborative inquiry on Knowledge Forum; Phase 3 deepens inquiry and community knowledge through student-directed portfolio assessment and field trips.
requirements: A teacher experienced with Knowledge Building pedagogy to facilitate the classes
Knowledge Forum with integrated assessment tools such as Social Network Analysis and the Note Contribution applet
constraints: Portfolio activities were not implemented in every class: group portfolio assessment only in Class C, individual portfolio assessments not in Class D, and one activity (designing questions) omitted for Class D, per Table 2
target_learners: Academically low-achieving secondary school students (Grades 9 and 11)
target_learning_goals: Inquiry, collaboration, reflection, and metacognitive skills; critical and creative thinking in Visual Arts
examples: Whole-class and small-group activities such as constructing three-dimensional objects from colorful wires, collaborative concept maps, a Knowledge Building Wall, the Crossing Your Life Point justification game, weekly collective reflection, and museum field trips
key_sources: Yuqin Yang · Gaoxia Zhu · Carol K. K. Chan. (2022). Evolution of the academic emotions of academically low-achieving students in knowledge building. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09380-y

article_title: An artificial intelligence-driven learning analytics method to examine the collaborative problem-solving process from the complex adaptive systems perspective
citation: Fan Ouyang, Weiqi Xu, Mutlu Cukurova. (2023). An artificial intelligence-driven learning analytics method to examine the collaborative problem-solving process from the complex adaptive systems perspective. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2023) 18:39–66. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09387-z
title: Three-layered AI-driven learning analytics framework for examining CPS from a complex adaptive systems perspective
description: The article proposes a three-layered analytical framework integrating AI algorithms with learning analytics to examine collaborative problem solving as complex adaptive systems: "AI algorithms were incorporated into that framework using multiple learning analytic approaches". Layer 1 codes interactive, cognitive, regulative, behavioural and socio-emotional dimensions; Layer 2 applies multichannel sequence analysis with optimal matching and Ward's clustering to detect pattern types; Layer 3 uses statistical analysis, epistemic network analysis, and hidden Markov modeling to reveal quantitative, structural, and transitional regularities per type.
requirements: Multimodal process data (verbal communication, screen recordings of clickstream behaviour, concept map products) coded into multi-dimensional sequences
constraints: Codes are "proxies for tacit learning processes" with expected overlap between dimensions, which the authors chose to retain in separate channels
Developed and demonstrated on graduate CPS activities in an online synchronous collaboration platform
target_learners: graduate students in educational technology seminar courses
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem solving skills
knowledge co-construction through concept mapping
examples: Applied to 24 datasets from four graduate-student groups completing ill-structured problems on the Huiyizhuo platform

article_title: Emergent group understanding: Investigating intersubjectivity in sociotechnical interdependencies
citation: Mørch, A. I., Andersen, R., Eie, S., & Mifsud, L. (2024). Emergent group understanding: Investigating intersubjectivity in sociotechnical interdependencies. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09432-5
title: Three-phase teaching model for social studies with Minecraft (Introduction, Reconstruction, Transformation)
description: A teaching model resulting from design-based research iterations that organizes social studies teaching with Minecraft Education in three activities: Introduction (teacher lecturing, past orientation, vague intersubjectivity, domain-specific skills), Reconstruction (collaborative design in Minecraft and role-play scriptwriting, present orientation, fragmented intersubjectivity) and Transformation (role-playing and video recording, future orientation, focused intersubjectivity). The current version "suggests how generic and domain-specific skill practices can be combined in three ways", pairing each phase with a temporal orientation, a level of intersubjectivity, and a primary/secondary skill type.
requirements: Minecraft Education environment
teacher facilitation following the model's phases
constraints: Adapted from iteration 2 and further adapted for seventh-grade school teaching, which required additional facilitators
target_learning_goals: understanding the industrial revolution in Norway
combining generic and domain-specific skills
examples: Group 7 reconstructed the nail factory's administrative buildings and a steel mill on the Aker River and staged a video-recorded role-play

article_title: Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning
citation: Lucas Paulsen, Jacob Davidsen. (2025). Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09446-7
title: Three hierarchical levels of human activity — operations, actions, activities — as the analytic spine of ABC-VR
description: Adopting activity theory, ABC-VR distinguishes "three hierarchical levels of human activity: operations, actions and activities" (Kaptelinin & Nardi, 2012), which are dynamic and context-dependent. Actions are the starting point of meaning-making; learners can shift down to ask how actions are performed and up to ask why. ABC-VR argues traditional procedural IVR training mostly moves down to isolated operations, while ABC-VR centres on identifying relevant actions and reasoning upward to the motive-level activity.
requirements: Pedagogical designs must create links between the two ends of the activity hierarchy so reflections can be tied to operations and operations to context
constraints: The boundaries between operations, actions and activities depend on the context and the learner's experience
target_learning_goals: understanding both how and why actions are performed in a practice
examples: In the medical case, students identify which knee tests to perform, how they are performed, and why and when they are performed
key_sources: Lucas Paulsen, Jacob Davidsen. (2025). Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09446-7

article_title: A collaboration literacy analytics framework (CLAF): Investigating students’ perspectives on collaboration quality indicators and feedback utilization
citation: Tochukwu Dominic Eze, Lucas Zurbuchen, Khalil Anderson, Marcelo Worsley. (2026). A collaboration literacy analytics framework (CLAF): Investigating students' perspectives on collaboration quality indicators and feedback utilization. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09475-w
title: Combine learner perspectives with theory-grounded CSCL constructs when defining collaboration quality indicators
description: The article advocates a strategy in which 'theory provides the validity anchors that delimit what counts as collaboration quality, while learners' experiential perspectives serve as empirically grounded probes to test, refine, and extend existing constructs.' This hybrid deductive-inductive, theory-anchored analytic approach treats convergence between learner perspectives and CSCL theory as validation and novel emergences as productive signals of under-specified constructs. It repositions learner voice as a mechanism for theory refinement rather than a threat to theoretical rigor.
requirements: Established CSCL frameworks must first be consolidated as theoretical coding frames before inductive analysis of learner responses
constraints: Learners' perceptions may be shaped by limited theoretical knowledge, social desirability bias, and reliance on salient but unreliable cues, so student-valued indicators must be examined as provisional constructs rather than adopted uncritically
target_learners: University students as primary end-users of collaboration analytics
CA tool designers and CSCL researchers
target_learning_goals: Designing interpretable, pedagogically grounded collaboration analytics indicators
Ensuring learner-aligned collaboration quality assessment
examples: The study benchmarked 290 students' survey perspectives against Worsley et al. (2021), Meier et al. (2007), OECD (2017), and Ofstedal and Dahlberg (2009) using a hybrid deductive-inductive thematic analysis in Taguette.

article_title: Constructivist learning (environments) and how to avoid another tower of Babel: reply to Renkl
citation: David Gijbels, Sofie M. M. Loyens. (2009). Constructivist learning (environments) and how to avoid another tower of Babel: reply to Renkl. Instructional Science, 37, 499–502. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9100-2
title: Three perspectives on constructivism: theory of learning, philosophical position, and theory of instruction
description: The article argues that debates about constructivist learning environments turn on which of three perspectives one takes. Constructivism can be seen as a learning theory that is 'student-centered, since the emphasis is on students as active learners'; as a philosophical position focused on what knowledge is; or as a theory of instruction making claims at what Renkl calls the 'prescriptive level'. The authors recommend keeping theory and pedagogy apart while acknowledging that a learning theory carries implications for practice.
requirements: The perspectives must be distinguished explicitly, as Loyens and Gijbels (2008) did, to keep theory and pedagogy apart
constraints: The learning-theory perspective is descriptive, not prescriptive; the article notes that distinguishing perspectives is needed because debates misread one for another
target_learning_goals: understanding how constructivism is defined and applied in educational settings
examples: The article contrasts defining constructivism as a reaction to the traditional classroom (learning theory) with positions such as Colliver's that treat it as an insight into the nature of human knowledge
key_sources: David Gijbels, Sofie M. M. Loyens. (2009). Constructivist learning (environments) and how to avoid another tower of Babel: reply to Renkl. Instructional Science, 37, 499–502. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9100-2

article_title: Designing to support equity-as-transformation perspectives for multilingual science learners
citation: Ashlyn Pierson, D. Teo Keifert, Bethany Daniel, Sarah Lee, Tessaly Jen, Adam Bell, Heather Johnson, Rachel Askew, Andrea Henrie. (2024). Designing to support equity-as-transformation perspectives for multilingual science learners. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09674-8
title: Three sustained PD features—immersive learning, student work analysis, and video club—support reflection and collaboration
description: The article describes its PD as built on three features for supporting reflection and collaboration: "(1) immersive learning, (2) student work analysis, and (3) video club" (PD design section). Immersive lessons in which teachers participate as learners build shared grounding in science teaching; student work analysis helps teachers understand and evaluate student thinking; video clubs anchor sensemaking in the realities of teachers' own classrooms. These features ran through both summer workshops and academic-year sessions and provided the substrate for ideological sensemaking about equity.
requirements: Sustained opportunities across summer and academic-year sessions, including collaborative reflection grounded in perspectives of young children as capable science learners
constraints: The features were studied in a multi-year elementary science PD partnership with a metropolitan district
target_learning_goals: Collaborative reflection on representations, student sensemaking, and equity
examples: The Puddles demonstration lesson served as the immersive experience, academic-year workshops analyzed student work samples such as rainbow models, and video clubs examined classroom clips

article_title: Learning Theory as Teaching Resource: Enhancing Students’ Understanding of Economic Concepts
citation: Ming-fai Pang, Ference Marton. (2005). Learning Theory as Teaching Resource: Enhancing Students' Understanding of Economic Concepts. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-2811-0
title: Three-lesson sequence on how simultaneous changes in supply and demand affect market price
description: The instructional element is a series of three lessons through which students were to come to understand "how the simultaneous change in the supply of and the demand for a certain good affects its market price." The article reports that "this study shows how the understanding of the simultaneous change in the supply of and the demand for a certain good affects its market price can be brought about in a powerful way." It was taught by theory-guided teachers and by comparison teachers, with mastery assessed after the series.
requirements: A series of three lessons planned around the object of learning, with the necessary pattern of variation and invariance brought out in the learning situation.
constraints: Demonstrated for one economic concept with secondary school students in the reported study.
target_learning_goals: understanding how simultaneous changes in supply and demand affect market price
examples: Students' mastery of the concept was compared after three lessons between theory-guided teaching and teaching without the theory.
