article_title: Do we need teachers as designers of technology enhanced learning?
citation: Kirschner, P. A. (2015). Do we need teachers as designers of technology enhanced learning? Instructional Science, 43, 309–322. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-015-9346-9
title: Prepare teachers in three fields to become competent designers of learning
description: The article concludes that teachers need to become accomplished in three fields: the domain they teach (knowing, understanding and applying subject matter at the conceptual level), the art and science of learning and teaching (the pedagogies for achieving their goals), and the science of research and design. Only then, the author argues, will teachers be competent designers of learning, including TEL. This requires drastic rethinking of initial pre-service and continuing in-service education, with teachers functioning as professional learners and co-researchers and co-designers of the technology and tools they want and need to use.
requirements: Initial and continuing teacher training must equip teachers to learn and work as co-researchers and co-designers, with expertise developed on the shop-floor
constraints: The author frames this as requiring a drastic rethinking of both pre-service and in-service education
target_learning_goals: competent design of learning, including technology enhanced learning
examples: Figure 2 visualizes the amended mapping, placing TaD of TEL motives and supports as discrete layers superimposed on the professional competencies, with customization based on student work, professional growth via collaborative design at course or lesson level, and ownership via participatory design of researchers, teachers and students
key_sources: Kirschner, P. A. (2015). Do we need teachers as designers of technology enhanced learning? Instructional Science, 43, 309–322. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-015-9346-9

article_title: The learning effects of first, second, and third order interventions in a rule-based and open simulation game
citation: Marieke de Wijse-van Heeswijk, Etienne A. J. A. Rouwette, Sander V. Meijerink. (2025). The learning effects of first, second, and third order interventions in a rule-based and open simulation game. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09715-w
title: Argyris-based framework of first-, second- and third-order interventions and learning applied to simulation-game facilitation
description: The article adapts Argyris' (1970) model, distinguishing three intervention types and three learning types. First-order interventions "aim at clarifying and applying norms", often addressing content and procedures; second-order interventions adapt a norm and change processes; third-order interventions uncover roles and behavioral patterns in an organizational context. Third-order learning is defined, based on Visser et al. (2018), as increasing insight on how to add value from a personal perspective and from one's role in the host organization. The framework grounds the study's conceptual model linking intervention type, game type, cognitive load and learning.
requirements: All three learning levels are considered necessary to achieve adaptivity because of the intricate relationships between content, processes and roles
constraints: The article notes the relations in the conceptual model are not meant to be sequential; arrows indicate the number of relations present
target_learning_goals: adaptivity to changes in the organization or its context
examples: Facilitators' interventions and participants' responses in two simulation games were coded with a codebook based on Argyris' levels of learning
key_sources: Marieke de Wijse-van Heeswijk, Etienne A. J. A. Rouwette, Sander V. Meijerink. (2025). The learning effects of first, second, and third order interventions in a rule-based and open simulation game. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09715-w

article_title: Supports for preservice teachers’ metacognitive monitoring and explanations of fraction comparisons
citation: Guba, T.-P., Barbieri, C. A., Jansen, A., & Morris, A. (2026). Supports for preservice teachers' metacognitive monitoring and explanations of fraction comparisons. Instructional Science (2026) 54:18. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09773-0
title: Three instructional supports for scaffolding preservice teachers' revision of mathematical explanations
description: The article proposes and tests three distinct supports for provoking revision of fraction comparison explanations: correct examples, defining features, and error reflection. As printed, "PSTs were randomly assigned to one of three instructional support conditions to scaffold their analysis and revision of their explanations for fraction comparisons." Correct examples provided a complete, correct explanation with a fraction-strip diagram; defining features provided "a list of steps on how to completely explain the fraction comparison" without the answer or visual; error reflection presented a fictitious student's explanation with one incorrect component and one omission. The framework links revision thinking to metacognitive monitoring and calibration.
requirements: Participants must first produce a first-draft explanation and confidence rating before encountering the condition-specific support
The supports must be presented between the first draft and the revision opportunity
constraints: The error reflection condition did not ask participants to reflect on their own errors, so the authors state they do not expect that form of reflection to impact metacognitive monitoring in particular
target_learners: elementary pre-service teachers in mathematics content courses
target_learning_goals: explaining and justifying fraction magnitude comparisons
metacognitive monitoring and calibration of one's own explanations
examples: Participants compared 7/8 and 6/7, 5/8 and 5/9, and 13/27 and 18/35, tasks chosen to evoke the distance-to-one, common numerator, and benchmark-to-one-half strategies respectively
key_sources: Guba, T.-P., Barbieri, C. A., Jansen, A., & Morris, A. (2026). Supports for preservice teachers' metacognitive monitoring and explanations of fraction comparisons. Instructional Science (2026) 54:18. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09773-0

article_title: Effects of person praise on students’ motivation and performance under ego-involving and task-involving feedback conditions
citation: Cheng-Hong Liu, Xian-Rui Yin. (2026). Effects of person praise on students' motivation and performance under ego-involving and task-involving feedback conditions. Instructional Science (2026) 54:34. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09789-0
title: Threat-conditional account of person praise: attribute affirmation mitigates threat in high-threat (ego-involving) environments but triggers self-focus distraction in low-threat (task-involving) ones
description: The article integrates self-affirmation theory and achievement goal theory into a model in which pre-task person praise functions as attribute affirmation whose effect depends on the anticipated feedback environment. Under ego-involving feedback (a high-threat, performance-goal context), the authors argue praise "may reduce the psychological threat posed by challenging learning tasks and may encourage students to approach the tasks in a positive manner"; under task-involving feedback (a low-threat, mastery context), the affirmation instead heightens self-focus and distracts from the task. Moderated serial mediation through state self-esteem supported the detrimental pathway only in the task-involving condition.
requirements: The person praise must be delivered before task engagement and paired with an anticipated feedback structure; the mechanism was tested via state self-esteem as first mediator and trials attempted as second mediator
constraints: The ego-involving condition's beneficial pathway was not mediated by state self-esteem; the article states the mechanism there remains unidentified and recommends future researchers measure other potential mediating variables. Findings apply only to pre-task affirmation with feedback expectations, not post-task praise content.
target_learners: junior high school students (aged 12–14) facing a new learning task
target_learning_goals: participation motivation in a new task
task performance
examples: In the experiment, the serial indirect effect of person praise on performance through state self-esteem and trials was negative only under task-involving feedback (−0.83, CI −2.12 to −0.06) and absent under ego-involving feedback (0.04, CI −0.19 to 0.37)
key_sources: Cheng-Hong Liu, Xian-Rui Yin. (2026). Effects of person praise on students' motivation and performance under ego-involving and task-involving feedback conditions. Instructional Science (2026) 54:34. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09789-0

article_title: Collaborative design as a form of professional development
citation: Joke Voogt, Therese Laferrière, Alain Breuleux, Rebecca C. Itow, Daniel T. Hickey, Susan McKenney (2015). Collaborative design as a form of professional development. Instr Sci (2015) 43:259-282. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-014-9340-7
title: Three key features framework for teacher learning by collaborative design: situatedness, agency, and the cyclical nature of learning and change
description: The article draws on the situative perspective of Greeno et al. (1998) and third-generation activity theory (CHAT, Engeström 1987) to propose that "three interrelated features are key to understanding learning by collaborative design in the teaching practice: the situatedness of activity, agency, and the cyclical nature of learning and educational change." Situatedness locates learning in teachers' own practice contexts; agency frames teachers as transformative agents of change, drawing on Engeström's "shared transformative agency"; the cyclical feature follows Engeström's expansive learning model of questioning, analyzing, designing, examining, implementing, and reflecting. The framework organizes the three case descriptions and the research agenda, crossed with Borko's (2004) individual, team, and system levels.
requirements: Collaborative curricular design processes must be well-scaffolded, and resulting materials must be based on up-to-date knowledge of good practice and considered usable by teachers in their contexts, per the article's introduction.
constraints: The authors state they do not establish these three characteristics as evidence-based causal factors; and the Boschman et al. (2014) study suggests that "practical concerns dominate discussion in design teams and may hinder teacher learning."
target_learning_goals: teacher professional learning through collaborative curriculum design
capacity for educational change
examples: Table 1 maps the three features against the three cases (USA, Africa, Canada) across Borko's three phases of professional development research.
key_sources: Joke Voogt, Therese Laferrière, Alain Breuleux, Rebecca C. Itow, Daniel T. Hickey, Susan McKenney (2015). Collaborative design as a form of professional development. Instr Sci (2015) 43:259-282. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-014-9340-7

article_title: The effect of contrasting cases during problem solving prior to and after instruction
citation: Loibl, K., Tillema, M., Rummel, N., & van Gog, T. (2020). The effect of contrasting cases during problem solving prior to and after instruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09504-7
title: Three-mechanism account of why problem solving before instruction can benefit conceptual understanding
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that problem solving prior to instruction (PS-I) benefits conceptual understanding through three mechanisms identified in the Loibl et al. (2017) review: "activating prior knowledge, becoming aware of knowledge gaps, and recognizing deep features of the target concept." Activating prior knowledge makes students more susceptible to subsequent instruction; incorrect attempts make knowledge gaps salient; and attention guided to deep features (functional components) prepares students to map instructed procedures onto discovered features. The study tests whether order alone (activation) versus contrasting cases (gap awareness and deep-feature discovery) trigger these mechanisms.
requirements: Each mechanism needs its own trigger; the article states the effectiveness of PS-I results from an interplay of mechanisms that each needs to be triggered.
constraints: The study found that activating prior knowledge by problem solving alone was insufficient to improve conceptual understanding, and unguided contrasting cases did not trigger the gap-awareness or deep-feature mechanisms.
target_learners: secondary education mathematics students (third year of Dutch secondary education, age 14–15)
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of the concept of variance and procedural fluency with the mean absolute deviation
examples: The experiment operationalized the mechanisms by manipulating order of phases (activation) and contrasting cases varying range, sample size, and distribution (deep-feature discovery), with no typical student solutions in instruction.
key_sources: Loibl, K., Tillema, M., Rummel, N., & van Gog, T. (2020). The effect of contrasting cases during problem solving prior to and after instruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09504-7

article_title: University students’ perceptions of using generative AI in translation practices
citation: Wenkang Zhang, Albert W. Li, Chenze Wu. (2025). University students' perceptions of using generative AI in translation practices. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09705-y
title: Three-dimensional support framework for GenAI integration: pedagogical, governance, and operational dimensions
description: The article's discussion maps its findings onto a three-dimensional framework for supporting GenAI use, which "constitutes pedagogical, governance, and operational dimensions". Pedagogically, targeted classroom strategies such as human-versus-GenAI mini-competitions and educational resources instruct students on better technology use. At the governance level, teachers and institutions offer clear guidance on GenAI implications and human translators' advantages. Operationally, the curriculum is re-evaluated and adapted for enhanced AI literacy and job-displacement concerns.
requirements: Coordination among teachers and institutions across all three dimensions to address student challenges
constraints: The framework is presented in the discussion as an alignment with Chan and Hu (2023), not as a framework tested empirically in this study
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate translation and interpreting students
target_learning_goals: effective, ethical integration of GenAI tools in translation learning and practice
examples: The study's expected teacher and institutional support strategies were interpreted as aligning with the three-dimensional framework
key_sources: Wenkang Zhang, Albert W. Li, Chenze Wu. (2025). University students' perceptions of using generative AI in translation practices. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09705-y

article_title: Relationships between students’ conceptions of constructivist learning and their regulation and processing strategies
citation: Loyens, S. M. M., Rikers, R. M. J. P., & Schmidt, H. G. (2008). Relationships between students' conceptions of constructivist learning and their regulation and processing strategies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9065-6
title: Three-tiered structure of student learning: conceptual, controlling, and operational levels
description: A framework, drawn from Vermunt's ILS tradition, in which students' learning aspects are organized into three levels: a conceptual level of ideas and beliefs (mental models of knowledge, learning orientations, and here conceptions of constructivist learning), a controlling level of regulation processes, and an operational-behavioural level of processing strategies. The article states that "the controlling level tunes the conceptual level to the operational level." The study tested this structure with SEM in a problem-based learning curriculum, finding it fully valid for MSLQ variables but only partially for ILS variables, where regulation strategies function on a controlling level but are not strict mediators.
requirements: Measurement instruments capturing conceptions, regulation strategies, and processing strategies so the three levels can be modelled separately
constraints: The article notes the three-level structure appeared valid for the MSLQ variables, but not entirely for those of the ILS
target_learners: higher-education psychology students in a problem-based learning curriculum
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning and study strategy use in higher education
examples: Structural equation models with ILS and MSLQ regulation and processing variables were tested in 98 psychology students
key_sources: Loyens, S. M. M., Rikers, R. M. J. P., & Schmidt, H. G. (2008). Relationships between students' conceptions of constructivist learning and their regulation and processing strategies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9065-6

article_title: Multimethod assessment of self-regulated learning in college students: different methods for different components?
citation: Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, Marie Weißenfels, Lea Russer, Franziska Perels. (2021). Multimethod assessment of self-regulated learning in college students: different methods for different components? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09533-2
title: Three-layer model of self-regulated learning (Boekaerts): cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational regulatory layers
description: The article adopts Boekaerts' three-layer component model as its organizing framework, in which SRL comprises interacting cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational regulatory processes on three hierarchical layers. The "inner layer comprises the regulation of information processing", the second layer covers metacognitive planning, monitoring, and reflection, and the outer layer reflects regulation of the self through motivational components, beliefs, and volitional strategies. The study operationalized all three layers across its four measures.
requirements: Layer-specific strategies are needed to optimize learning processes; the model assumes the layers interact with each other
constraints: The model is described as relatively static, treating SRL as a rather stable competence with distinct components
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategy use across cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational components
examples: The study's strategy knowledge test and microanalytic tool were constructed based on Zimmerman's (2000) and Boekaerts' (1999) models, assessing cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational components within planning, performance, and reflection phases
key_sources: Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, Marie Weißenfels, Lea Russer, Franziska Perels. (2021). Multimethod assessment of self-regulated learning in college students: different methods for different components? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09533-2

article_title: Learning the control-of-variables strategy through self-generated and vicarious errors: the mediating roles of affect, motivation, cognitive load, and error awareness
citation: Hämmerle, L., Kuhlmann, S. L., Krause-Wichmann, T., & Möller, A. (2026). Learning the control-of-variables strategy through self-generated and vicarious errors: the mediating roles of affect, motivation, cognitive load, and error awareness. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09822-2
title: Three mechanisms of learning from errors: prior-knowledge activation, motivation, and depth of cognitive processing
description: The article organizes its investigation of error-based learning around a theoretical framework, attributed to Zhang and Fiorella (2023), identifying three mechanisms that support or inhibit learning from errors. As the article states, the framework "highlights three important mechanisms: (1) activating prior knowledge, which makes existing knowledge accessible and supports its reorganization, (2) motivation, which influences the effort learners invest in engaging with errors, and (3) the depth of cognitive processing." The study operationalizes these as affect, motivation, cognitive load, and error awareness measures mediating condition effects on CVS learning, and notes the framework did not originally consider vicarious errors.
requirements: Learners must engage in deeper processing (e.g., self-explanation) rather than surface-level correction for errors to support integration into coherent knowledge structures
constraints: The article notes the framework "does not consider how these processes might be similar or different when students work with vicarious errors"
target_learning_goals: scientific inquiry skills, specifically the control-of-variables strategy for designing unconfounded experiments
examples: The study measured these mechanisms via PANAS affect, Intrinsic Motivation Inventory subscales, the Klepsch cognitive load scale, and expert-student error-assessment agreement in a four-condition PS-I intervention
key_sources: Hämmerle, L., Kuhlmann, S. L., Krause-Wichmann, T., & Möller, A. (2026). Learning the control-of-variables strategy through self-generated and vicarious errors: the mediating roles of affect, motivation, cognitive load, and error awareness. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09822-2

article_title: Minding the gender gap in advanced STEM courses: effects of student preparedness and activity level
citation: Ilana Ram, Adam Shwartz, Ido Roll. (2025). Minding the gender gap in advanced STEM courses: effects of student preparedness and activity level. Instructional Science (2025) 53:1457–1478. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09748-1
title: Multi-family explanatory framework for the STEM gender gap: learner attributes, instructional/assessment design, and motivational accounts
description: The article organizes existing explanations for the higher-STEM gender gap into three not-mutually-exclusive families. As it states, "Some focus on learner attributes such as individual level of preparation or the learner's activity level", "while others focus on instructional and assessment design", and "A third group of possible explanations look at motivational accounts" such as stereotype threat or sense of belonging. The study evaluates the first two families simultaneously using trace data, performance data on low/high-stakes assessments, and learner-attribute data, finding preparation accounts carry most explained variance.
requirements: Simultaneous modeling of multiple candidate causes (preparedness, assessment stakes, activity) to apportion explained variance
constraints: The families are not connected under a single unifying framework, possibly due to differences in epistemologies and assumptions, as the article notes
target_learning_goals: understanding and reducing the gender achievement gap in advanced STEM courses
examples: The study operationalized the framework with mixed-effects models over five assessments and hierarchical regressions with theory-driven blocks in four courses
key_sources: Ilana Ram, Adam Shwartz, Ido Roll. (2025). Minding the gender gap in advanced STEM courses: effects of student preparedness and activity level. Instructional Science (2025) 53:1457–1478. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09748-1

article_title: Sixth graders’ selection and integration when writing from multiple online texts
citation: Kullberg, N., Kiili, C., Bråten, I., González-Ibáñez, R., & Leppänen, P. H. T. (2023). Sixth graders' selection and integration when writing from multiple online texts. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09613-5
title: Thematic unit as a unit of analysis for observing integration in multiple-text writing
description: The study introduces the thematic unit, defined as "an idea or a chain of connected ideas", as a new unit of analysis for examining integration in written products. Unlike an idea unit containing a main verb, a thematic unit is broader and may span ideas within or across perspectives, from prior knowledge, or generated in response to the task. Ideas within a unit are connected by connective words, repetition of key concepts, organization, or elaborations. The authors claim it is better suited than idea units to reveal students' attempts to integrate content beyond single ideas.
requirements: Written products must be segmented into thematic units with identified sources of ideas (snippets, other text ideas, prior knowledge, task-generated ideas) before integration types can be coded.
constraints: The article reports this as a methodological contribution without evidence comparing its sensitivity to idea-unit analysis.
target_learning_goals: multiple-text comprehension
integration of ideas across texts
examples: Thematic units were identified in 162 written products, yielding 578 units coded for four integration types with 80% agreement on unit boundaries.
key_sources: Kullberg, N., Kiili, C., Bråten, I., González-Ibáñez, R., & Leppänen, P. H. T. (2023). Sixth graders' selection and integration when writing from multiple online texts. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09613-5

article_title: Exploring the association of student perceptions of science instruction and emotional engagement: The variance between grade level
citation: Xin Xia, Robert Tai. (2026). Exploring the association of student perceptions of science instruction and emotional engagement: The variance between grade level. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09800-8
title: Three-dimensional framework of student engagement (behavioral, emotional, cognitive)
description: The article adopts Fredricks et al.'s framework distinguishing three dimensions of engagement. "Behavioral engagement involves active participation in learning activities and extracurricular pursuits"; cognitive engagement reflects sustained mental effort toward deep understanding; and emotional engagement "encompasses feelings of connection to teachers, peers, and school, as well as a genuine interest in learning and enjoyment of problem-solving." The study focuses on the positive-affective dimension of emotional engagement, measured via enjoyment, interest, and desire to learn science, and distinguishes emotional engagement from interest as a relatively stable motivational state.
requirements: Measurement must distinguish emotional engagement from behavioral and cognitive dimensions and from the related but distinct construct of interest
constraints: The study operationalizes emotional engagement only through positive-affective indicators (enjoyment, interest, desire), excluding emotions such as frustration, confusion, or anxiety
target_learners: Students in grades 3–12 in science classes
target_learning_goals: Emotional engagement in science learning
examples: The study built a PCA composite of three positive-affective items (Desire, Favorite, Enjoy; Cronbach's alpha 0.881) to measure emotional engagement within this framework
key_sources: Xin Xia, Robert Tai. (2026). Exploring the association of student perceptions of science instruction and emotional engagement: The variance between grade level. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09800-8

article_title: Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared
citation: Ming Fai Pang, Lo Mun Ling. (2011). Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9191-4
title: Three types of variation structure learning study lesson planning: variation in students' ways of seeing, teachers' ways of seeing, and variation as a design principle
description: Learning study participants draw on three spelt-out types of variation when planning lessons. V1 is "Variation in students' ways of seeing the object of learning": teachers use phenomenographic insight that students understand a phenomenon in a limited number of qualitatively different ways, treating individual differences as a resource rather than an obstacle. V2 is "Variation in teachers' ways of seeing and dealing with the object of learning": sharing tacit professional knowledge across the group. V3 is "Using variation as a guiding principle of pedagogical design": consciously designing which aspects vary and which stay invariant so students discern the critical aspects.
requirements: A carefully defined object of learning with identified critical aspects
Diagnostic information on students' prior ways of understanding, e.g. via pre-tests and interviews
target_learning_goals: discernment of critical aspects of the object of learning
examples: In the mathematics case, pre-test answers were used to identify critical aspects before planning the research lesson
key_sources: Ming Fai Pang, Lo Mun Ling. (2011). Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9191-4

article_title: How multiple levels of metacognitive awareness operate in collaborative problem solving
citation: Çini, A., Järvelä, S., Dindar, M., Malmberg, J. (2023). How multiple levels of metacognitive awareness operate in collaborative problem solving. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09358-7
title: Three-level framework of metacognitive awareness (individual, social, environmental)
description: The article conceptualises metacognitive awareness as operating on three interacting levels: "oneself (the individual level), one’s interplay with others (the social level), and one’s interplay with the learning environment (the environmental level)". The individual level covers conceptual systems and regulation of cognition; the social level covers interactions with group members through written and spoken language and facial expressions; the environmental level covers interaction with the learning environment such as feedback during CPS. The study uses this framework to organise measurement (MAI, situated self-reports, feedback and facial expression data) in collaborative problem solving.
requirements: Assessment at multiple time points with situated self-reports rather than trait-based measures alone, since trait-based assessment cannot sufficiently explore metacognition in action
constraints: Developed and tested in the context of a computer-based complex CPS simulation with higher education students
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness in collaborative problem solving
examples: In the study, MAI measured the individual level, repeated metacognitive judgement and task difficulty self-reports measured the social level, and simulation feedback with facial expression data measured the environmental level.
key_sources: Çini, A., Järvelä, S., Dindar, M., Malmberg, J. (2023). How multiple levels of metacognitive awareness operate in collaborative problem solving. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09358-7

article_title: Reflection on exam grades to improve calibration of secondary school students: a longitudinal study
citation: Nederhand, M. L., Tabbers, H. K., Jongerling, J., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2020). Reflection on exam grades to improve calibration of secondary school students: a longitudinal study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09233-9
title: Three-activity framework for interventions that use grades to improve calibration accuracy
description: The article proposes that improving calibration with grades requires support on three sequential activities: making an estimate, checking the estimate against the actual grade, and reflecting on the cause of any miscalibration. As the authors put it, "First, students need to actually provide a grade estimate before receiving the actual grade. Second, students should check whether there is a mismatch between their initial estimate and their actual grade." Third, students should "reflect on the cause of their miscalibration" to improve future estimates. The study's three conditions operationalized increasing levels of support on these activities.
requirements: Interventions should provide support on all three activities: estimating, comparing estimate to grade, and reflecting on mismatch causes.
constraints: The article notes prior evidence for the third activity's benefit was mixed and dependent on performance level in university samples.
target_learning_goals: calibration accuracy; metacognitive awareness of performance estimates; self-regulated learning
examples: The study's conditions mapped onto the framework: Practice-only (activity 1), Grade comparison (activities 1–2), and Reflection (all three activities, with cue checklists and an open mismatch question for deviations of at least 0.5 points).
key_sources: Nederhand, M. L., Tabbers, H. K., Jongerling, J., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2020). Reflection on exam grades to improve calibration of secondary school students: a longitudinal study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09233-9

article_title: The underconfidence-with-practice effect in action memory: The contribution of retrieval practice to metacognitive monitoring
citation: Kubik, V., Jemstedt, A., Mahjub Eshratabadi, H., Schwartz, B. L., & Jönsson, F. U. (2022). The underconfidence-with-practice effect in action memory: The contribution of retrieval practice to metacognitive monitoring. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09288-2
title: Three theoretical accounts of the underconfidence-with-practice effect: mnemonic debiasing, memory for past test, and anchoring-and-adjustment
description: The article organizes the UWP effect around three competing explanatory accounts. The mnemonic-debiasing account holds that "the UWP effect occurs as a function of a foresight bias, which is alleviated by self-testing during practice". The Memory-for-Past-Test (MPT) account proposes that JOLs result partly from memory for the last test, producing underconfidence when previously unrecalled items are newly learned. The anchoring-and-adjustment account maintains that people set an anchor when making JOLs from which they insufficiently depart as learning progresses. The article evaluates all three against its action-memory data and concludes no single account suffices.
requirements: Repeated study–test cycles with item-based JOLs collected at study so calibration, resolution and past-test correlations can be computed
constraints: The article concludes the UWP effect cannot be explained by any single account; evidence for the anchoring-and-adjustment account in this study is correlational because the anchor point was not experimentally manipulated
target_learners: adult learners (undergraduate students) studying verbal or enacted action material
target_learning_goals: accurate metacognitive monitoring of one's own learning across repeated study–test cycles
examples: The experiment tested the accounts' predictions by comparing study–test and study–study items across three cycles with enactive and verbal encoding
key_sources: Kubik, V., Jemstedt, A., Mahjub Eshratabadi, H., Schwartz, B. L., & Jönsson, F. U. (2022). The underconfidence-with-practice effect in action memory: The contribution of retrieval practice to metacognitive monitoring. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09288-2

article_title: Sequential and temporal characteristics of self and socially regulated learning
citation: Inge Molenaar & Sanna Järvelä. (2014). Sequential and temporal characteristics of self and socially regulated learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-014-9114-2
title: Three-phase cyclical model of self-regulation: preparation, execution and reflection phases
description: The editorial describes consensus about three important phases in the process of self-regulation, drawing on Zimmerman (2002) and Winne & Hadwin (1998). In the "preparation phase students orientate on the task, activate existing knowledge and set their learning goals"; these goals guide the execution phase in which students perform the learning task; finally students reflect on their approach to optimize future process. The cyclical notion allows no strict order, as learners can jump between S-SRL actions inducing recursive sequential patterns within the cycle.
requirements: Learners' learning goals steer their learning, which entails the assumption that learners project these learning goals over time
constraints: Time window of the cycle is debated: Winne and Hadwin (2013) support a micro level COPE cycle re-occurring within one study session, whereas Zimmerman's (2002) cycle is more macro level, encapsulating one learning task possibly extending over multiple study sessions
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning of cognitive, metacognitive and motivational components
examples: Bannert et al. (2014) contributed empirical evidence of the sequential characteristics and the cyclical process in self-regulation theory via process mining of think aloud protocols
key_sources: Inge Molenaar & Sanna Järvelä. (2014). Sequential and temporal characteristics of self and socially regulated learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-014-9114-2

article_title: To what extent can think sheets with or without reflection prompts support self-regulated learning from text?
citation: Anja Prinz-Weiß & Elisa Röhm. (2025). To what extent can think sheets with or without reflection prompts support self-regulated learning from text? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09419-z
title: Use think sheets as a misconception-addressing intervention that does not require rewriting instructional texts
description: The article recommends think sheets as a practical alternative to refutation texts for addressing misconceptions during learning from text. Compared to refutation texts, "think sheets can be applied without rewriting instructional texts": the existing text stays unchanged, and a worksheet with central questions and misconceptions is added, on which learners write the correct answers using the text. The article also notes that alternating instructional methods helps keep learners motivated. In the study, this was implemented as four question-misconception blocks accompanying a statistics text.
requirements: A text providing the correct information and a worksheet listing central questions with related misconceptions.
constraints: In this study think sheets provided little benefit over having students simply read about the misconceptions and correct information, and adding reflection prompts did not improve outcomes.
target_learners: University students learning statistics content from texts
target_learning_goals: Counteracting misconceptions and supporting comprehension and transfer from text
examples: Participants in the think-sheet conditions answered four central covariance questions on a worksheet using a 539-word statistics text, with or without four reflection prompts per block.
key_sources: Anja Prinz-Weiß & Elisa Röhm. (2025). To what extent can think sheets with or without reflection prompts support self-regulated learning from text? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09419-z

article_title: Reflections on the field of metacognition: issues, challenges, and opportunities
citation: Roger Azevedo. (2020). Reflections on the field of metacognition: issues, challenges, and opportunities. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09231-x
title: Metacognitive instruction should embed instruction in content, inform learners of usefulness, and prolong training
description: The editorial states that the literature on metacognitive instruction clearly indicates three conditions for acquiring and instructing metacognition: "embedding metacognitive instruction in the content matter to ensure connectivity", informing learners about the usefulness of metacognitive activities so they exert initial extra effort, and prolonging training to guarantee smooth and maintained application of metacognitive activity. The author presents these as established global principles from the instruction literature.
requirements: Instruction must be embedded in subject-matter content to ensure connectivity between metacognitive activity and the content being learned.
constraints: Despite these global principles, the author notes the instruction of metacognition remains largely unexplored, with only a few notable examples in math, writing, and reading.
target_learners: Learners of all ages acquiring metacognitive knowledge and skills from parents, peers, and teachers
target_learning_goals: Acquisition and maintained application of metacognitive knowledge and skills
examples: The editorial cites notable examples of metacognitive instruction in math (Kramarski and Michalsky 2013), writing (Hacker 2018; Harris and Graham 2017), and reading (Griffin et al. 2019).
key_sources: Roger Azevedo. (2020). Reflections on the field of metacognition: issues, challenges, and opportunities. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09231-x

article_title: Untangling Conceptual Clutter: A Systematic Review of Adult-Reported Self-Regulation Measurement in Children Aged 0–8 Years
citation: Jiang, Y., Zhang, Y., Brown Campbell, K.-A., Zhong, T., Zehner, T., James, V., Devlin, B., Geer, E., Shire, S., & Schmitt, S. (2025). Untangling Conceptual Clutter: A Systematic Review of Adult-Reported Self-Regulation Measurement in Children Aged 0–8 Years. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10066-8
title: Three-tiered classification system of self-regulation: categories, domains, and facets
description: The review establishes a hierarchical taxonomy for organizing the variety of self-regulation terms found in early-childhood measures. As the authors state, "a three-tiered classification system was established, starting with the most detailed processes (facets), which form the domains that, in turn, contribute to the broader categories." Facets are specific processes or skills (e.g., adaptability, attention shifting), which group into domains such as cognitive flexibility, which belong to the broader categories of cognitive, emotion, or behavior regulation. The system was built by open-coding terms from measure manuals and mapping facets to established constructs.
requirements: Facets must be rated for alignment with conceptual models of self-regulation before domain and category assignment
constraints: Built from adult-reported measures only; self-reported measures were excluded from the review
target_learning_goals: self-regulation (cognitive, emotional, and behavioral regulation skills)
examples: Adaptability, attention shifting, and shifting were grouped under the domain cognitive flexibility within cognitive regulation
key_sources: Jiang, Y., Zhang, Y., Brown Campbell, K.-A., Zhong, T., Zehner, T., James, V., Devlin, B., Geer, E., Shire, S., & Schmitt, S. (2025). Untangling Conceptual Clutter: A Systematic Review of Adult-Reported Self-Regulation Measurement in Children Aged 0–8 Years. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10066-8

article_title: Bridging Reasoning in Mathematics and Science: a Document Analysis of Applying and Reasoning in the TIMSS Assessment Framework and the Case for Utilization of Resources
citation: Kyong Mi Choi, Jin Mun, Brian Hand. (2026). Bridging Reasoning in Mathematics and Science: a Document Analysis of Applying and Reasoning in the TIMSS Assessment Framework and the Case for Utilization of Resources. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10115-2
title: Three-layer hierarchical framework: Pellegrino's assessment triangle, Webb's Depth of Knowledge, and the TIMSS cognitive domains
description: The article organizes its analysis through three complementary frameworks in a hierarchical relationship: Pellegrino et al.'s assessment triangle (cognition, observation, interpretation) as meta-theory, Webb's Depth of Knowledge as taxonomic theory, and the TIMSS framework as the operational layer. The mapping holds that "DoK Level 1 corresponds to the knowing domain in TIMSS, DoK Level 2 to the applying domain, and DoK Levels 3–4 to the reasoning domain." This structure justifies analyzing TIMSS documents as evidence about cognitive structure and predicts that applying functions as a prerequisite foundation for reasoning.
requirements: Effective assessment design requires a clear theory of cognition as its foundation, with cognition, observation, and interpretation in synchrony
constraints: The knowing domains (MK, SK) were excluded from the analysis as involving reproduction and recognition of facts and terms
target_learners: Assessment developers and researchers in mathematics and science education
target_learning_goals: Understanding cognitive demand levels in mathematics and science assessment
examples: The study extracted MA, MR, SA, and SR constituent elements from TIMSS 2011, 2015, 2019, and 2023 frameworks as analytical units under this hierarchy
key_sources: Kyong Mi Choi, Jin Mun, Brian Hand. (2026). Bridging Reasoning in Mathematics and Science: a Document Analysis of Applying and Reasoning in the TIMSS Assessment Framework and the Case for Utilization of Resources. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10115-2

article_title: When is Learning “Effortful”? Scrutinizing the Concept of Mental Effort in Cognitively Oriented Research from a Motivational Perspective
citation: Axel Grund, Stefan Fries, Matthias Nückles, Alexander Renkl, Julian Roelle. (2024). When is Learning “Effortful”? Scrutinizing the Concept of Mental Effort in Cognitively Oriented Research from a Motivational Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09852-7
title: Three-fold conception of mental effort: effort-by-complexity, effort-by-need frustration, and effort-by-allocation
description: The article proposes that the term effort carries three fundamentally different meanings that should be clearly separated: effort-by-complexity (object-level processing demands), effort-by-need frustration (negatively valenced affective-emotional processing demands), and effort-by-allocation (self-initiated effort as an outcome of motivation). The authors state: "we plea for a three-fold conception of effort that clearly distinguishes the different psychological sources of experiencing and allocating effort in learning environments." Each conception has different operationalizations, theoretical roots (CLT, SDT, SEVT), and practical implications, summarized in the article's Table 1.
requirements: Researchers and instructional designers must use measurement items that distinguish the three conceptions rather than ambivalent general effort items; the article recommends a multi-facet, multimodal assessment of effort, ideally in real-time
constraints: The conceptions can be confounded in school settings where tasks are both complex and aversive; the article notes effort-by-complexity and effort-by-need frustration may often be confounded when learning at school but must not be for all learning settings
target_learners: students in formal learning settings such as school and college
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of effort and cognitive load appraisals in learning research and instructional design
examples: Table 1 pairs each conception with an ambivalent item (e.g., "How much effort do/did you have to invest in order to solve the task?") and a more specific item (e.g., "How strenuous is/was working on that task for you?")
key_sources: Axel Grund, Stefan Fries, Matthias Nückles, Alexander Renkl, Julian Roelle. (2024). When is Learning “Effortful”? Scrutinizing the Concept of Mental Effort in Cognitively Oriented Research from a Motivational Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09852-7

article_title: Conditions for Effective Learning Without Upfront Instruction: How Practice with Feedback Supports Memory, Generalization, Motivation, and Metacognition
citation: Michael W. Asher & Paulo F. Carvalho. (2026). Conditions for Effective Learning Without Upfront Instruction: How Practice with Feedback Supports Memory, Generalization, Motivation, and Metacognition. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10103-6
title: Theory of practice-centered learning: feedback can deliver lecture-equivalent instruction, while upfront practice prepares learners to encode it
description: The article proposes "a theory of practice-centered learning that integrates theoretical insights from research on problem-solving before instruction", including productive failure, pre-questioning, and replacing lecture with practice and feedback. Its premise is that effective learning requires both clear instruction and preparation to encode it; well-designed feedback can deliver the same key information as lecture, but pairing feedback with upfront practice engages attention and sharpens metacognitive monitoring. The theory predicts memory benefits from any feedback, but generalization only when feedback explains underlying principles and learners have sufficient prior knowledge.
requirements: Feedback must deliver the instructional content a lecture would provide, including facts and the rules and principles required to generalize.
For generalization, feedback must explain underlying principles and learners must have sufficient prior knowledge to engage productively with these explanations.
constraints: When the two ingredients for generalization are absent, practice may enhance retention without supporting the deeper understanding needed to apply knowledge flexibly.
Challenge from practice may feel frustrating or discouraging, particularly for learners with lower confidence or less prior knowledge.
target_learners: Adult online learners (Prolific participants) learning introductory statistics
target_learning_goals: Memory for factual statistical content
Generalization of regression concepts to novel problems
Metacognitive calibration
examples: Across two experiments, practice conditions used problem sets matched to the lecture's worked example, with feedback that either gave correct answers or explained why answers were correct.
key_sources: Michael W. Asher & Paulo F. Carvalho. (2026). Conditions for Effective Learning Without Upfront Instruction: How Practice with Feedback Supports Memory, Generalization, Motivation, and Metacognition. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10103-6

article_title: A Systematic Meta-analysis of the Reliability and Validity of Subjective Cognitive Load Questionnaires in Experimental Multimedia Learning Research
citation: Felix Krieglstein, Maik Beege, Günter Daniel Rey, Paul Ginns, Moritz Krell, Sascha Schneider. (2022). A Systematic Meta-analysis of the Reliability and Validity of Subjective Cognitive Load Questionnaires in Experimental Multimedia Learning Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09683-4
title: Three-factor model of cognitive load: intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load additively contributing to overall load
description: Cognitive load theory stipulates three additive types of cognitive load: intrinsic cognitive load (the learning task's inherent complexity, determined by element interactivity and prior knowledge), extraneous cognitive load (determined by how learning materials are presented and organized), and germane cognitive load (working memory resources devoted to schema construction, a productive load). The article states that "Perhaps the best-known version of CLT stipulates three additive types of cognitive load" and that the three-factor model "was then developed by Sweller et al. (1998) in the mid- to late 1990s." The meta-analysis used this model because the most commonly used questionnaires measure the three types separately. Recent approaches suggest intrinsic and germane loads share the same theoretical foundation and can be classified as one type.
requirements: Questionnaires must measure the three load types separately with multiple items to assess the model empirically
constraints: The additivity assumption only applies if the capacity of working memory is not exceeded; recent approaches (Kalyuga, 2011; Sweller, 2010) propose an intrinsic-extraneous two-factor alternative
target_learners: learners in multimedia learning experiments across school and adult education
target_learning_goals: managing working memory load during multimedia learning
instructional design of learning materials
examples: The meta-analysis collected Cronbach's alpha values separately for ICL, ECL, and GCL following the three-factor model
key_sources: Felix Krieglstein, Maik Beege, Günter Daniel Rey, Paul Ginns, Moritz Krell, Sascha Schneider. (2022). A Systematic Meta-analysis of the Reliability and Validity of Subjective Cognitive Load Questionnaires in Experimental Multimedia Learning Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09683-4

article_title: Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education
citation: Hoyun Cho. (2026). Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10210-y
title: Three roles of AI in generative learning: Generation Partner, Generation Substitute, Generation Catalyst
description: A typology of three roles AI can occupy relative to learners' generative processes. Partner and Substitute occupy the poles of a scaffolding–substitution continuum, while Catalyst is defined functionally: "When AI serves as a Generation Catalyst, it neither performs the learner's generative work, as in the Substitute role, nor supports the learner in performing it, as in the Partner role. It supplies an output that becomes the object of further generative work by the learner". Roles are properties of episodes, not tools, determined by tool design, task design, learner orientation, and teacher mediation.
requirements: Catalyst episodes require three jointly necessary conditions: an AI artifact the task does not treat as the answer, learner activity directed at that artifact, and activity required only because the artifact is present
constraints: Within an episode the three roles are mutually exclusive; extended interactions move among roles as trajectories
target_learners: mathematics learners using generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: sustaining learner generative cognitive engagement under AI mediation
examples: Catalyst configurations include teaching a concept to an AI and evaluating its performance, instructing the AI to find counterexamples to a learner-generated claim, and co-constructing problems by iteratively refining conditions and constraints
key_sources: Hoyun Cho. (2026). Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10210-y

article_title: Student Learning in Higher Education: a Commentary
citation: John T. E. Richardson. (2017). Student Learning in Higher Education: a Commentary. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 353–362. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9410-x
title: The presage–process–product (3P) model of student learning and its elaborations
description: Biggs' 3P model distinguishes presage variables (characteristics of students and institutional context), process variables (motives and strategies), and product variables (performance outcomes). The commentary notes Biggs (1991) added feedback loops and Biggs (1993a) adopted a systems approach allowing interactions among all components, and that Richardson (2000) argued the process component actually measures predispositions, warranting elaboration into four stages: presage, predisposition, process, and product. The commentary judges these elaborations introduce flexibility but may render the models unfalsifiable.
requirements: Requires measures of the process component, which in practice are questionnaire instruments such as the Study Process Questionnaire that capture predispositions rather than actual task processes
constraints: The commentary states that systems-style models with feedback loops and interactions seem to render these models unfalsifiable because they can accommodate virtually any pattern of empirical results
The commentary finds the assumption that personal characteristics influence learning implausible for characteristics like ethnicity, which is more likely a proxy for other characteristics
target_learning_goals: understanding and explaining individual differences in student learning approaches and outcomes
examples: Fryer critiqued the 3P model and suggested perceived control as an organizing principle for a system approach; Biggs based his account on Dunkin and Biddle's (1974) presage–process–product model of classroom teaching
key_sources: John T. E. Richardson. (2017). Student Learning in Higher Education: a Commentary. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 353–362. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9410-x

article_title: The Effects of Problem-Based, Project-Based, and Case-Based Learning on Students’ Motivation: a Meta-Analysis
citation: Wijnia, L., Noordzij, G., Arends, L. R. A., Rikers, R. M. J. P., & Loyens, S. M. M. (2024). The Effects of Problem-Based, Project-Based, and Case-Based Learning on Students' Motivation: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09864-3
title: Three-question taxonomy of motivation constructs: beliefs, task value, and reasons for engaging
description: The article organizes motivation constructs using Graham and Weiner's three basic questions — "Can I do it?", "Do I want to do it?" and "Why am I doing this task?" — mapping them onto competence and control beliefs, feelings-related and importance-related task value, and intrinsic versus extrinsic reasons for studying, plus attitudes toward school subjects including a future-interest subcategory. Figure 1 provides "a visual overview of the motivation categories used in our meta-analysis". The taxonomy structures which motivation measures were coded and how moderator analyses were run per construct.
requirements: Motivation measures must be mappable onto the constructs in Fig. 1 (competence beliefs, importance, feelings-related values such as interest/enjoyment) on Likert-type or continuous scales
constraints: Intrinsic motivation within self-determination theory is distinguished from interest value: it concerns the origin of engagement, whereas interest value concerns the source of the activity's value
target_learning_goals: Student motivation in problem-driven learning contexts
examples: The meta-analysis coded 288 effect sizes into these categories, treating reasons for studying as a dichotomous intrinsic-versus-extrinsic construct because most primary studies did so
key_sources: Wijnia, L., Noordzij, G., Arends, L. R. A., Rikers, R. M. J. P., & Loyens, S. M. M. (2024). The Effects of Problem-Based, Project-Based, and Case-Based Learning on Students' Motivation: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09864-3

article_title: The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity
citation: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. http://rer.aera.net
title: Three positions on knowledge specificity in literacy: general, task-specific, and community-specific knowledge
description: The review organizes debates in composition and literary understanding around three positions on knowledge transfer. The general knowledge position holds that writers and readers can transfer knowledge across situations; the task-specific position holds that different tasks require different knowledge; and the community-specific position holds that even similar tasks demand knowledge of particular communities, which Colomb calls specialized areas "with all the ideological, economic, political, material, linguistic, moral, and other determinants of communal life." Each position carries assumptions about learning and transfer with clear implications for curriculum and instruction.
requirements: Researchers and teachers must articulate their assumptions about knowledge and transfer to establish a coherent relationship between theory and practice
constraints: The discussion is circumscribed to extended written discourse and the reading of imaginative literature, and excludes grammatical knowledge because both readers and writers unquestionably transfer such basic knowledge
target_learners: students in school and professional writing and reading contexts
target_learning_goals: composition
literary understanding
transfer of knowledge across tasks and contexts
key_sources: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543062003279

article_title: The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity
citation: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. http://rer.aera.net
title: Three positions on knowledge specificity in literacy: general, task-specific, and community-specific knowledge
description: The review organizes literacy debates around three positions on the nature of composing and reading knowledge. The general knowledge position holds that "general knowledge is sufficient and that writers can transfer it spontaneously from situation to situation with relative ease." The task-specific position holds that different types of tasks require different types of knowledge, and the community-specific position holds that even similar tasks require knowledge of the conventions of particular discourse communities. Each position carries assumptions about learning and transfer with distinct instructional consequences.
requirements: Researchers and teachers must articulate which position they hold, since "Whenever teachers instruct, they implicitly convey their beliefs about knowledge transfer."
constraints: The discussion is circumscribed to extended written discourse and the reading of imaginative literature, and excludes grammatical knowledge because both readers and writers unquestionably transfer such basic knowledge.
target_learners: students learning composition and literary reading in secondary and higher education
target_learning_goals: writing competence across tasks and contexts
literary understanding
examples: The review illustrates the community-specific position with Pauline Kael's film criticism and Antonin Scalia's courtroom defining, both using task-specific defining skills within vastly different communities.
key_sources: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. https://doi.org/10.2307/1170740

article_title: Effective Dementia Education and Training for the Health and Social Care Workforce: A Systematic Review of the Literature
citation: Surr CA, Gates C, Irving D et al (2017) Effective Dementia Education and Training for the Health and Social Care Workforce: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Review of Educational Research. 87(5): 966-1002. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317723305
title: Underpin practice-based dementia learning with theory and support application of learning in practice
description: This principle states that dementia education for care staff should connect workplace learning to underlying theory and help learners transfer it into daily care. The synthesis found efficacious programs "underpin practice-based learning with theory" and "support application of learning in practice," linking conceptual grounding to on-the-job use for the health and social care workforce.
requirements: Education must combine practice-based learning with theoretical underpinning and include mechanisms that support applying the learning in practice.
constraints: The feature was identified in a synthesis of studies of variable quality; no effect sizes are printed in the available text.
target_learners: Health and social care workforce staff receiving dementia education and training
target_learning_goals: Applying dementia care knowledge and skills in day-to-day practice
examples: The critical interpretive synthesis listed theory-underpinned practice-based learning and support for application in practice among the common features of more efficacious programs.
key_sources: Surr CA, Gates C, Irving D et al (2017) Effective Dementia Education and Training for the Health and Social Care Workforce: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Review of Educational Research. 87(5): 966-1002. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317723305

article_title: Children’s Creativity: A Theoretical Framework and Systematic Review
citation: Kupers, E., Lehmann-Wermser, A., McPherson, G., & van Geert, P. (2019). Children's creativity: a theoretical framework and systematic review. Review of Educational Research, 89(1), 93-124. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654318815707
title: A three-dimensional taxonomy for organizing research on primary school students' creativity
description: The article introduces a three-dimensional taxonomy as the organizing scheme for its empirical integration. The taxonomy structured the systematic review of recent literature on primary school students' creativity, allowing the authors to classify the 184 reviewed studies and to identify dominant measurement practices in the field, such as treating creativity as a static, aggregated construct.
requirements: Studies must be classifiable along the taxonomy's three dimensions to be integrated in the review
constraints: The taxonomy was applied to literature from 2006–2017 on primary school students' creativity, as stated in the article
target_learning_goals: creativity assessment and research synthesis
examples: The taxonomy underpinned the systematic review of 184 studies published between 2006 and 2017
key_sources: Kupers, E., Lehmann-Wermser, A., McPherson, G., & van Geert, P. (2019). Children's creativity: a theoretical framework and systematic review. Review of Educational Research, 89(1), 93-124. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654318815707

article_title: Team-Based Professional Development Interventions in Higher Education: A Systematic Review
citation: Gast, Inken; Schildkamp, Kim; van der Veen, Jan T. (2017). Team-Based Professional Development Interventions in Higher Education: A Systematic Review. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317704306
title: Three-level framework of conditions for successful team-based professional development in higher education
description: The review organizes the conditions for successful team-based professional development into three levels: "conditions at the individual teacher level, conditions at the team level, and conditions at the organizational level." Six individual conditions were identified (attitudes, motivation, commitment, self-efficacy, professional identity, availability), five team conditions (team interaction, goals and objectives, team composition, team leadership, small group work), and four organizational conditions (organizational support, rewards, research focus, finances and resources). Only conditions mentioned in at least two articles were included.
requirements: Conditions must be mentioned in at least two of the reviewed articles to be included in the framework
constraints: The framework was derived from 18 studies in higher education, a field the review describes as fairly new, using mostly qualitative methods
target_learners: higher education faculty members who teach and/or design courses
target_learning_goals: teacher learning of new knowledge and skills for curriculum innovation and teaching practice
examples: The review's Table 3 maps each theme and condition to the supporting studies, e.g., organizational support was supported by 12 of the 18 studies
key_sources: Gast, Inken; Schildkamp, Kim; van der Veen, Jan T. (2017). Team-Based Professional Development Interventions in Higher Education: A Systematic Review. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317704306

article_title: A systematic review of the association between social and emotional competencies and student engagement in youth
citation: Anabela Caetano Santos, Celeste Simões, Márcia H.S. Melo, Margarida F. Santos, Iara Freitas, Cátia Branquinho, Carmel Cefai, Patrícia Arriaga. (2023). A systematic review of the association between social and emotional competencies and student engagement in youth. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100535
title: Three-dimensional model of student engagement (emotional, behavioural, cognitive)
description: The review adopts Fredricks et al.'s multidimensional perspective of student engagement, "which considers emotional, behavioural and cognitive engagement". Emotional engagement is students' emotional response towards school, learning and the academic community; behavioural engagement is persistence and active participation in school-based activities and adaptive school behaviour; cognitive engagement comprises self-efficacy, regulatory strategies, expectations, beliefs towards education and investment in the learning process. The review also treats disengagement, which some authors assess as the opposite end of the same continuum and others as a distinct concept (disaffection), manifesting as lack of participation and effort, disrupting class, skipping classes and poor learning strategies.
requirements: self-report measures covering at least one of the three engagement dimensions or disengagement
constraints: Most reviewed research addressed only the emotional dimension, limiting multidimensional evidence
target_learning_goals: student engagement
disengagement
