A systematic review of the association between social and emotional competencies and student engagement in youth. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100535

article_title: Using think-aloud protocol in self-regulated reading research
citation: Hu, Jingjing; Gao, Xuesong (Andy). (2017). Using think-aloud protocol in self-regulated reading research. Educational Research Review, v.22, pp. 181-193. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.09.004
title: Think-aloud protocol validity framework: reactivity and veridicality as the two central methodological concerns
description: The review organizes methodological concerns about think-aloud protocols around two constructs. Reactivity "concerns whether reporting cognitive/metacognitive processes alters the processes being reported (e.g., reading process) and/or its outcomes (e.g., comprehension or remembering of reading texts)", while veridicality "concerns whether the cognitive/metacognitive processes can be accurately and completely reported". The framework explains why design choices like training and prompting involve trade-offs: solutions to one concern may create risks for the other, a dilemma the authors highlight for self-regulated reading research.
requirements: Researchers must consider reactive effects when participants produce metacognitive verbal reports during reading tasks
Design choices must balance reactivity reduction against veridicality risks
constraints: Reactive effects are moderated by type of report, language of verbal report or learning task, and age of participants
Individual readers may no longer be conscious of habitual metacognitive processes, making them impossible to verbalize
target_learners: Researchers of self-regulated reading across educational levels
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of cognitive and metacognitive reading processes
examples: The review analyzed six experimental studies (Set 1) examining reactivity and veridicality and 23 studies using think-aloud as data collection
key_sources: Hu, Jingjing; Gao, Xuesong (Andy). (2017). Using think-aloud protocol in self-regulated reading research. Educational Research Review, v.22, pp. 181-193. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.09.004

article_title: Using think-aloud protocol in self-regulated reading research
citation: Hu, Jingjing; Gao, Xuesong (Andy). (2017). Using think-aloud protocol in self-regulated reading research. Educational Research Review, v.22, pp. 181-193. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.09.004
title: Treat think-aloud data as indicators of only part of the self-regulated reading process and triangulate with other data sources
description: Because think-aloud protocols face reactivity and veridicality risks, the review recommends that researchers "view think-aloud data as indicators of only a part of self-regulated reading process rather than a full picture of it". One or more other data sources — pre- and post-interviews, questionnaires, observations, on-line computer logs, and eye-movement registration — should be combined with think-aloud reports for a fuller picture. The review also recommends reporting details such as languages used for reading and verbalizing and participant ages.
requirements: Combine think-aloud with at least one other data collection tool
Provide detailed descriptions of participant demographics and task design in studies using think-aloud
constraints: The optimal integration of data sources is not yet identified and requires further research
target_learners: Researchers studying self-regulated reading and learning processes
target_learning_goals: Valid and complete measurement of self-regulated reading processes
examples: The review's Appendix III lists suggested solutions including combining data sources and viewing think-aloud as partial indicators
key_sources: Hu, Jingjing; Gao, Xuesong (Andy). (2017). Using think-aloud protocol in self-regulated reading research. Educational Research Review, v.22, pp. 181-193. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.09.004

article_title: Placebo or Assistant? Generative AI Between Externalization and Anthropomorphization
citation: Skulmowski, A. (2024). Placebo or Assistant? Generative AI Between Externalization and Anthropomorphization. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 58. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09894-x
title: Three-layer model of learning activities (semantic, proximal, motor)
description: The essay presents Skulmowski's (2024) model of activity-based learning, built on Pacherie's (2008) conceptualization of action planning, in which "an educational task commonly consists of a semantic part at a high level of abstraction" (e.g., the intention to write an essay), realized through proximal activities (formulating paragraphs and sentences), which are usually realized through motor activities such as typing. The semantic layer carries considerable cognitive load and requires planning, decisions, and acquired skills. The model is proposed as a guide for deciding which task layers can be externalized to AI without significant risk, with lower layers lending themselves to externalization and the semantic layer at greatest risk.
requirements: Learning tasks and objectives must be analyzed with high precision to derive guidelines on skill levels at which task parts can be offloaded.
constraints: The essay states the model is plausible as a starting point but that more empirical research is needed on effectiveness and transferability across subjects, domains, and task types.
target_learners: learners across education levels using AI tools for writing and other complex tasks
target_learning_goals: distributing learning tasks between learner effort and AI externalization without diminishing skill acquisition
examples: For essay writing: semantic activities include knowledge of style, composition, and content; proximal activities are formulating paragraphs and sentences; motor activities are typing or handwriting letters.
key_sources: Skulmowski, A. (2024). Placebo or Assistant? Generative AI Between Externalization and Anthropomorphization. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 58. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09894-x

article_title: There is an Evidence Crisis in Science Educational Policy
citation: Lin Zhang, Paul A. Kirschner, William W. Cobern, John Sweller. (2022). There is an Evidence Crisis in Science Educational Policy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09646-1
title: Three-category taxonomy of educational research evidence: program-based studies, randomized controlled studies, and correlational studies
description: The article organizes science education evidence into three research categories with different methodological strengths and different implications for policy. Program-based studies evaluate whole programs with pre-post or business-as-usual designs; controlled studies "alter only one target factor at a time to examine the effectiveness of an instructional procedure over alternatives" using random assignment; correlational studies use large datasets such as TIMSS and PISA to examine associations over large populations. The article argues the three categories yield divergent findings about inquiry-based teaching and that policy should draw on all three.
requirements: Policy recommendations should draw on all three categories rather than a single methodology
constraints: Correlational studies are limited in their capacity to claim causal relationships
Program-based studies cannot attribute program gains to any single instructional component
target_learning_goals: science conceptual and procedural understanding
examples: The article contrasts the KGS and LeTUS program evaluations (program-based) with controlled comparisons of investigation versus explicit instruction and with TIMSS/PISA correlational analyses
key_sources: Lin Zhang, Paul A. Kirschner, William W. Cobern, John Sweller. (2022). There is an Evidence Crisis in Science Educational Policy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09646-1

article_title: Teachers’ Beliefs About Inclusive Education and Insights on What Contributes to Those Beliefs: a Meta-analytical Study
citation: Dignath, C., Rimm-Kaufman, S., van Ewijk, R., & Kunter, M. (2022). Teachers' Beliefs About Inclusive Education and Insights on What Contributes to Those Beliefs: a Meta-analytical Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09695-0
title: Three-component model of teachers' belief systems about inclusive education: cognitive appraisals, emotional appraisals, and self-efficacy
description: The article organizes teachers' belief systems about inclusive education into three inter-related components: "teachers' cognitive appraisals (e.g., thoughts), emotional appraisals (e.g., feelings), and self-efficacy (e.g., agency to teach inclusive classrooms)". Drawing on Gregoire's (2003) cognitive-affective model of conceptual change, it treats these components as entangled subcomponents of a dynamic belief system that guides perceptions, interprets incoming information, and acts as a working model of the world. The framework underpins the meta-analysis's three separate syntheses and its claim that beliefs are malleable through training.
requirements: Belief components are measured separately (cognitive appraisals, emotional appraisals, self-efficacy), as the meta-analysis required three separate meta-analyses of standardized mean scores
constraints: The article notes the belief subcomponents are often entangled, and that research on teachers' beliefs about inclusive education differs from research on the effectiveness of inclusive education, which is beyond its scope
target_learning_goals: implementation of inclusive education practices
examples: The meta-analysis quantified each component separately across 102 studies and examined how career point, teacher type, and interventions contribute to each.

article_title: Validity of Early-Grade Screening Tools in the Three Tier (RTI/MTSS) Model: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Literacy, Language, and Mathematics
citation: Keles, S., ten Braak, D., Hagen, Å. M., & Melby-Lervåg, M. (2025). Validity of Early-Grade Screening Tools in the Three Tier (RTI/MTSS) Model: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Literacy, Language, and Mathematics. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10077-5
title: The Three Tier (RTI/MTSS) model as a data-informed tiered support framework in which screening is one component of broader placement decisions
description: The Three Tier model (also called MTSS with three tiers or a three-tier RTI model) is a prevention-oriented framework providing universal Tier 1 instruction, targeted Tier 2 supplemental interventions, and intensive, individualized Tier 3 support. The review emphasizes that "universal screening is not intended to serve as a definitive placement mechanism into Tiers 1, 2, or 3"; instead, screening is an initial risk-identification step within a dynamic process combining teacher judgment, contextual information, and response to intervention. The review synthesizes the validity of the screening tools that feed this process.
requirements: Screening measures should be highly predictive of future outcomes to ensure accurate identification of students at risk
Appropriate assignment of students to tiers, with ongoing adjustments informed by progress monitoring, is described as the most important prerequisite for effective implementation
constraints: The review focuses on models explicitly structured with three tiers, in ECEC through grade 2, in language, literacy, or mathematics domains
target_learners: Children in early childhood education and care (preschool/kindergarten) through grade 2 of primary school
target_learning_goals: Early identification of students at risk of learning difficulties in literacy, language, and mathematics
Accurate assignment to tiered levels of academic support
examples: The review included 127 studies in which screening tools were used as part of tier assignment, with all screeners used in Tier 1
key_sources: Keles, S., ten Braak, D., Hagen, Å. M., & Melby-Lervåg, M. (2025). Validity of Early-Grade Screening Tools in the Three Tier (RTI/MTSS) Model: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Literacy, Language, and Mathematics. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10077-5

article_title: Commentary on the Special Issue
citation: Gary D. Phye. (2012). Commentary on the Special Issue. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9211-1
title: A three-tier level of analysis implicitly exists in the study of learning, memory, and cognition
description: The author proposes that "a three-tier level of analysis implicitly exists in the study of learning, memory, and cognition (educational research, educational psychology, applied cognition)". The tiers range from global educational research on academic growth, through educational psychology, to applied cognitive psychology providing "principles of learning, memory and cognition" with classroom application. He notes someone could propose a four- or five-tier model and views the journal's special issue as a step toward enhancing communication among these research communities.
requirements: Communication across the tiers requires testable models that can serve as the basis for model-based reasoning
constraints: The author states there is a scarcity of testable models that would serve as the basis for model-based reasoning, which is critical for communication across disciplines
target_learning_goals: Classroom learning, retention, and transfer of academic content
examples: The commentary locates the special issue's applied cognitive contributors at the moderate level of precision, which it calls the functional study of memory and cognition
key_sources: Gary D. Phye. (2012). Commentary on the Special Issue. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9211-1

article_title: To Grade or Not To Grade? Demystifying a Centuries-Old Debate
citation: Nicolas Hübner, Juliane Rutsch, Ann-Kathrin Schnelle, Mia Herkommer, Evelin Ruth-Herbein, Benjamin Fauth. (2026). To Grade or Not To Grade? Demystifying a Centuries-Old Debate. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10156-1
title: Three overarching theoretical foundations structure the grades debate: motivation research, assessment and feedback research, and measurement research
description: The article's literature review of 136 studies organized the theoretical foundations of the school-grades debate into recurring fields. As the authors report, "the results of the literature review revealed three overarching recurring theoretical foundations, which stemmed from the fields of: (1) motivation research, (2) assessment and feedback research, and (3) measurement research." Within motivation research the prevalent theories were self-determination theory and its subtheories (cognitive evaluation theory, organismic integration theory); within assessment and feedback research, summative versus formative assessment and formative feedback theory; within measurement research, validity and standardization of grades and standards-based grading. Occasional topics were scored as a fourth 'other research' category.
requirements: The taxonomy emerged from a systematic literature search across four databases with AI-aided screening in ASReview, yielding 136 studies rated with a two-category scheme (interrater κ = 0.85 and κ = 0.94)
constraints: Topics that came up only occasionally were scored as a separate 'other research' category rather than integrated into the three main foundations
target_learning_goals: understanding how grading practices relate to student motivation, learning, and measurement quality
examples: The LPF school trial's features were explicitly linked back to these three theoretical foundations in Table 1
key_sources: Nicolas Hübner, Juliane Rutsch, Ann-Kathrin Schnelle, Mia Herkommer, Evelin Ruth-Herbein, Benjamin Fauth. (2026). To Grade or Not To Grade? Demystifying a Centuries-Old Debate. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10156-1

article_title: The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning
citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2024). The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09842-1
title: Three demands on limited cognitive capacity: extraneous, essential, and generative processing
description: A central tenet of CTML is that working memory capacity is limited and faces three demands during learning. The article states: "there are three demands on that limited cognitive capacity during learning: extraneous processing, essential processing, and generative processing." Extraneous processing does not support the instructional goal and depends on poor instructional design; essential processing represents the material in working memory and depends on the inherent complexity of the material; generative processing makes sense of the incoming information and depends on the learner's motivation.
requirements: Working memory capacity is limited, so capacity used for one kind of processing takes away from capacity available for the others
target_learning_goals: efficient allocation of cognitive capacity during multimedia learning
examples: Extraneous processing depends on the degree of poor instructional design, such as presenting extraneous verbal or pictorial information in a lesson.
key_sources: Richard E. Mayer. (2024). The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09842-1

article_title: The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning
citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2024). The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09842-1
title: Three instructional goals for multimedia design: minimize extraneous, manage essential, foster generative processing
description: CTML translates the three demands on cognitive capacity into a lesson-level design pattern. The article states: "The three demands on cognitive capacity give rise to three instructional goals: minimize extraneous processing, manage essential processing, and foster generative processing." Minimizing is accomplished by eliminating unneeded words and graphical elements, managing by breaking a continuous lesson into learner-paced chunks, and fostering by prompting generative learning activities such as writing a summary or self-testing.
requirements: Designers must diagnose which demand on capacity is the binding constraint for a given lesson before choosing techniques
constraints: Each design principle is subject to boundary conditions including for whom the principle applies, for which kind of lesson the principle applies, and under what circumstances the principle applies
target_learners: students in multimedia instruction across print, screen, and virtual reality
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning of academic content
examples: Managing essential processing can be accomplished by breaking a continuous lesson into manageable chunks that can be paced by the learner.
key_sources: Richard E. Mayer. (2024). The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09842-1

article_title: The Effectiveness of Concept Maps on Students’ Achievement in Science: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Dimitris Anastasiou · Clare Nangsin Wirngo · Pantelis Bagos. (2024). The Effectiveness of Concept Maps on Students' Achievement in Science: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09877-y
title: Three-theory account of concept-mapping effectiveness: Ausubel's subsumption theory, Paivio's dual coding theory, and cognitive load theory
description: The article organizes explanations of concept-mapping effects around three theories. Ausubel's subsumption theory holds that learning is facilitated when knowledge is "meaningfully acquired and hierarchically organized", matching concept maps' hierarchical structure. Dual coding theory proposes that information encoded in both verbal and visual modalities "can be more efficiently integrated and retained". Cognitive load theory holds that concept maps reduce extraneous cognitive load by visually simplifying verbal information and providing a higher degree of organization that helps students structure material into schemas.
requirements: Concept maps must connect concepts with linking words or short prepositional phrases and typically use a hierarchical structure with general concepts at the top or center
constraints: The article presents these as potential mechanisms of action explaining the observed effects, not as directly tested within the meta-analysis
target_learners: Elementary, intermediate, and secondary education students (Grades 3–12) learning science
target_learning_goals: Science achievement, including vocabulary development, understanding, and reading comprehension of scientific texts
examples: The article explains the larger physics effect by noting concept maps can help students bridge the gap between abstract theories and physical phenomena
key_sources: Dimitris Anastasiou · Clare Nangsin Wirngo · Pantelis Bagos. (2024). The Effectiveness of Concept Maps on Students' Achievement in Science: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09877-y

article_title: Without Integration, Everything Is Nothing: A Meta-Analysis of the Effectiveness of Instructional Support for Drawing-to-Learn
citation: Detlev Leutner · Johanna Biele. (2025). Without Integration, Everything Is Nothing: A Meta-Analysis of the Effectiveness of Instructional Support for Drawing-to-Learn. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10067-7
title: Three-component framework of drawing support based on generative learning and cognitive load theory
description: The article differentiates drawing support into three components: support expected to reduce extraneous cognitive load (e.g., a partially drawn background, selecting main ideas before drawing), support expected to increase germane cognitive load (e.g., explaining before or while drawing), and support expected to facilitate the integration sub-process of generative learning (e.g., comparing self-generated drawings with provided illustrations). The components are features a measure may or may not have, and are "not mutually exclusive": all integration-facilitating measures also increase germane load, but not vice versa. The framework rests on Mayer's SOI model and Cognitive Load Theory.
requirements: Studies must contrast a drawing-only condition with a drawing-support condition on a comprehension or transfer test for the components to be evaluated as moderators
constraints: The components describe potential impact on cognitive processing, not mutually exclusive categories; a single measure can address multiple sub-processes
Learners' characteristics (age, schooling level, prior knowledge) and other support kinds (extra time, drag-and-drop, tablet drawing) were not considered in greater detail
target_learners: students learning science content from text, from school to undergraduate level
target_learning_goals: comprehension and transfer of complex science content through generative drawing
examples: The meta-analysis coded each study's support measure binary on the three components and tested them as moderators of comprehension effects
key_sources: Detlev Leutner · Johanna Biele. (2025). Without Integration, Everything Is Nothing: A Meta-Analysis of the Effectiveness of Instructional Support for Drawing-to-Learn. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10067-7

article_title: Looking at Mental Effort Appraisals through a Metacognitive Lens: Are they Biased?
citation: Scheiter, K., Ackerman, R., & Hoogerheide, V. (2020). Looking at Mental Effort Appraisals through a Metacognitive Lens: Are they Biased? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09555-9
title: CLT distinguishes three load indicators—mental load, mental effort, and task performance—that map onto data-driven and goal-driven effort in metacognitive research
description: The review describes a taxonomy of three cognitive load indicators that differ in their causing factors. "Mental Load refers to the demands a task imposes on a person's cognitive resources," seen as independent of person characteristics and corresponding to data-driven effort. "Mental Effort addresses the human-centered dimension of cognitive load," affected by task, person, and their interaction, corresponding to goal-driven effort. Task performance results from the accumulation of all effort types, with effort moderating the relationship between mental load and performance.
requirements: Assumes learners are sufficiently motivated to invest all available resources in task accomplishment
constraints: CLT is commonly conceptualized as a cognitive theory that does not address student motivation
target_learning_goals: understanding how cognitive load components relate to task performance
key_sources: Scheiter, K., Ackerman, R., & Hoogerheide, V. (2020). Looking at Mental Effort Appraisals through a Metacognitive Lens: Are they Biased? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09555-9

article_title: Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science
citation: Ronnel B. King, Luke K. Fryer. (2024). Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09850-9
title: Three routes to theoretical integration: competition among theories, unified frameworks, and bridge-building integration of existing theories
description: Drawing on Gigerenzer (2010), the essay presents three routes researchers can take toward integration. Route 1 is competition among theories in the Popperian tradition, using Kuhn's criteria of accuracy, consistency, scope, simplicity, and fruitfulness. Route 2 is the formation of unified frameworks, exemplified by Dweck's program and SDT's five mini-theories. Route 3, which the authors advocate and call hybridization, is 'growth through bridge-building' — building networks between existing theories and detecting coherence among them.
requirements: Researchers must revisit their own theoretical assumptions and be willing to cross theoretical borders
constraints: The authors state Route 3 is 'perhaps the most reasonable and practical in the field of educational psychology' and nearly all special issue authors took this approach
target_learning_goals: conducting cross-theoretical research that produces cumulative knowledge
examples: Martin (2023) bridged motivation and instructional theories; Elliot bridged SDT and achievement goal theory; Hornstra et al. integrated SDT with high expectations theory; Fryer and Leenknecht integrated self-efficacy and perceived control work with higher education theorizing
key_sources: Ronnel B. King, Luke K. Fryer. (2024). Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09850-9

article_title: Promoting Argumentation Competence: Extending from First- to Second-Order Scaffolding Through Adaptive Fading
citation: Noroozi, O., Kirschner, P. A., Biemans, H. J. A., & Mulder, M. (2018). Promoting Argumentation Competence: Extending from First- to Second-Order Scaffolding Through Adaptive Fading. Educational Psychol Rev, 30, 153–176. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9400-z
title: Design second-order argument scaffolding through a three-step guideline: diagnose internal scripts, adapt support, fade adaptively
description: The article's central design principle is that argument scaffold design should extend beyond first-order scaffolding to second-order scaffolding via a guideline with three steps: "diagnosis of the internal argumentative script, adaptive external support, and adaptive fading of this external support". Diagnosis identifies learners' internal argumentative scripts; adaptive support targets missing or non-enacted script components; adaptive fading withdraws support as learners internalize the strategy, complemented by peer, automatic, and self-assessment.
requirements: Adequate and proper diagnosis of the discourse and situation is essential for realization of adaptive fading
Fading should occur only when the learner can carry out the required action, with support gradually reduced
constraints: Fading something that is not understood is not adequate for fostering acquisition of targeted argumentation activities
Evidence for fading in CABLe is mixed, so the guideline is a design proposal rather than an empirically validated recipe
target_learners: learners in natural-science education facing controversial societal issues
target_learning_goals: acquisition and transfer of argumentation competence across similar tasks
examples: The article proposes using automated analysis techniques and AI/computer-linguistic tools to detect internal scripts during discourse and deliver dynamic support and adaptive fading
key_sources: Noroozi, O., Kirschner, P. A., Biemans, H. J. A., & Mulder, M. (2018). Promoting Argumentation Competence: Extending from First- to Second-Order Scaffolding Through Adaptive Fading. Educational Psychol Rev, 30, 153–176. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9400-z

article_title: How Do Children Socially Learn from Narrative Fiction: Getting the Lesson, Simulating Social Worlds, or Dialogic Inquiry?
citation: Luciano Gasser · Yvonne Dammert · P. Karen Murphy. (2022). How Do Children Socially Learn from Narrative Fiction: Getting the Lesson, Simulating Social Worlds, or Dialogic Inquiry? Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1445–1475. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09667-4
title: Three reading stances (efferent, expressive, critical-analytic) as a taxonomy of sociomoral learning through narrative fiction
description: Drawing on Rosenblatt's transactional reading theory, the review organizes conceptions of sociomoral learning through narrative fiction into three stances. From the efferent stance, attention focuses on abstract moral propositions; from the expressive stance, readers develop mindreading and empathy by becoming immersed in the story; from a critical-analytic stance, readers critically reflect on initial responses through argument-based dialogues with peers. The review uses this taxonomy to systematize both psychological assumptions and educational programs, noting that stances are not exclusive and often overlap.
requirements: Studies and programs must be classified by their dominant stance, since readers and studies often include elements of several stances
constraints: The three stances are not exclusive; readers can take a single specific stance, but more often various stances overlap
target_learners: children and adolescents in literary education
target_learning_goals: sociomoral competence including theory of mind, empathy, and social reasoning
examples: Table 1 summarizes the three conceptions across learning mechanism, developmental outcomes, type of narrative fiction, instructional principles, and educational relationships
key_sources: Luciano Gasser · Yvonne Dammert · P. Karen Murphy. (2022). How Do Children Socially Learn from Narrative Fiction: Getting the Lesson, Simulating Social Worlds, or Dialogic Inquiry? Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1445–1475. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09667-4

article_title: The Powerful Teacher: A Power Hypothesis for the Benefits of Learning-by-Teaching
citation: Sarah Shi Hui Wong, Stephen Lim. (2026). The Powerful Teacher: A Power Hypothesis for the Benefits of Learning-by-Teaching. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10097-1
title: Three extant theoretical accounts of learning-by-teaching benefits
description: The article organizes prior mechanism accounts into a three-part framework: "Three main non-mutually exclusive accounts have been proposed to explain the benefits of learning-by-teaching: (a) the retrieval hypothesis, (b) the generative hypothesis, and (c) the social presence hypothesis." The retrieval hypothesis attributes benefits to retrieval practice; the generative hypothesis to selecting, organizing, integrating, and metacognitive monitoring during teaching; the social presence hypothesis to feelings that an audience is real and present. The review argues each account has contested evidence.
requirements: Each account is evaluated against empirical tests; the article treats them as non-mutually exclusive and requires process measures (retrieval, elaborations, monitoring statements, self-other referential terms) to test them.
constraints: The article reports mixed or contested evidence for each account: the social presence hypothesis is summarized as showing that increasing social presence does not necessarily enhance learning outcomes.
target_learners: learners in peer tutoring and teachable-agent settings
target_learning_goals: retention and comprehension of studied material
higher-order outcomes such as question generation and argumentative reasoning
examples: The article reviews Koh et al.'s teaching-with-retrieval versus teaching-no-retrieval comparison and Sibley et al.'s open- versus closed-book teaching as tests of the retrieval hypothesis.
key_sources: Sarah Shi Hui Wong, Stephen Lim. (2026). The Powerful Teacher: A Power Hypothesis for the Benefits of Learning-by-Teaching. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10097-1

article_title: Reporting of Methodological Rigor in Empirical Mixed Methods Research in Educational Psychology
citation: Matthew T. McCrudden · Macy Bowman · Gala Sofia Campos Oaxaca. (2025). Reporting of Methodological Rigor in Empirical Mixed Methods Research in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10090-8
title: Creswell and Plano Clark's three core mixed methods designs (convergent, explanatory sequential, exploratory sequential)
description: A taxonomy of three basic mixed methods research designs in which researchers combine quantitative and qualitative approaches in a single study. The review adopts this typology "because it is widely used in educational psychology and many other disciplines" and uses it both to explain design logic (rationales of comparison, explanation, and exploration) and to classify the designs of the 57 reviewed articles. Each design specifies the timing and sequence of the two strands and the typical rationale for mixing.
requirements: Researchers choose a design and report the quantitative and qualitative strands and their interface (e.g., timing, integration)
constraints: Other design types and typologies/labels exist beyond the three core designs
target_learning_goals: designing and reporting mixed methods empirical studies
examples: The review classified 30 reviewed articles as explanatory sequential, 23 as convergent, and 4 as exploratory sequential using this typology
key_sources: Matthew T. McCrudden · Macy Bowman · Gala Sofia Campos Oaxaca. (2025). Reporting of Methodological Rigor in Empirical Mixed Methods Research in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10090-8

article_title: Examining Black and Latine Students’ Sense of Belonging within the Mathematics Classroom: A Narrative Review
citation: Harris-Thomas, B., Nicolai, K. D., Chen, X.-Y., & Areizaga Barbieri, C. (2026). Examining Black and Latine Students' Sense of Belonging within the Mathematics Classroom: A Narrative Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10181-0
title: Three considerations for researching and supporting Black and Latine students' mathematics belonging
description: The review's organizing framework proposes that belonging researchers consider three areas "that would allow them to study belonging in productive and not harmful ways": "(1) Contextual Factors that Shape a Sense of Belonging to Mathematics, (2) Positionality and Framing of Investigations of Belonging, and (3) Recognizing the Whole Student." Each consideration is broken down into practical ways researchers might consider context, framing, and the whole student, along with future research considerations. The framework rests on the review's premise that belonging is dynamic, situated, and shaped by race, ethnicity, and culture.
requirements: Researchers must examine the educational contexts in which Black and Latine students engage with mathematics alongside the prevailing frameworks and assumptions of their studies
constraints: The review presents the list of contextual factors as non-exhaustive and based on the 20 reviewed studies
target_learners: Black and Latine adolescent mathematics students in U.S. schools
target_learning_goals: Supporting students' sense of belonging in mathematics learning environments
examples: The review organizes its Findings and Interpretation section around the three considerations, drawing on studies such as Gray et al. (2024) and Maloney and Matthews (2020)
key_sources: Harris-Thomas, B., Nicolai, K. D., Chen, X.-Y., & Areizaga Barbieri, C. (2026). Examining Black and Latine Students' Sense of Belonging within the Mathematics Classroom: A Narrative Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10181-0

article_title: Navigating Spatial Ability for Mathematics Education: a Review and Roadmap
citation: Kelsey E. Schenck, Mitchell J. Nathan. (2024). Navigating Spatial Ability for Mathematics Education: a Review and Roadmap. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09935-5
title: Make three explicit design decisions — taxonomy, analytical framework, and task selection — when studying spatial ability in mathematics education
description: The review proposes a guiding framework identifying three major design decisions for scholars using spatial skills in mathematics education research: selecting a spatial ability taxonomy, selecting corresponding analytical frameworks, and selecting spatial tasks for assessing spatial performance. The review states this framework "is intended to provide educational researchers and practitioners with a common language and decision-making process for conducting research and instruction that engages learners' spatial abilities," aiming to improve understanding of associative and causal links between spatial and mathematical abilities.
requirements: Researchers must align taxonomy, analytical framework, and task choices with one another and with their research goals, since the review shows divergent choices yield conflicting interpretations.
constraints: The review explicitly declines to offer overly optimistic proposals for resolving long-standing complexities, instead helping researchers operate within them from an informed perspective.
target_learners: mathematics and STEM education researchers and practitioners
target_learning_goals: designing spatial skills interventions and selecting appropriate spatial measures for mathematics education studies
examples: The review compiled Table 1 of instruments organized by Ramful et al.'s (2017) three-factor framework and grouped tasks into spatial orientation, non-rotational spatial visualization, and mental rotation categories chosen for their empirical links to mathematical thinking.
key_sources: Kelsey E. Schenck, Mitchell J. Nathan. (2024). Navigating Spatial Ability for Mathematics Education: a Review and Roadmap. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09935-5

article_title: The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies
citation: Charlotte Dignath & Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2021). The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09534-0
title: Three levels of strategy instruction: blind, informed, and self-control training (WWW&H rule)
description: Drawing on Brown et al., the article differentiates three levels of strategy instruction. In blind training, students are induced to use a strategy without information about its significance; informed training adds information about the strategy's benefits; and "the self-control training, the highest level of instruction, combines the informed training with an explicit instruction of how to manage, monitor, check, and evaluate strategy application." Self-control training best facilitates transfer. Explicit instruction follows the WWW&H rule—What to do, When, Why, and How—so students develop metacognitive knowledge about strategies.
requirements: Students first need explicit training in self-regulation strategies before they can benefit from implicit instruction and modeling
constraints: Blind training might fail to maintain strategy production in the future and its generalization to similar useful contexts
target_learning_goals: metacognitive strategy use
transfer of strategy application
examples: The article's Table 1 lists examples of explicit strategy instruction: explicit demonstration, explicit explanation, explicit call, and explicitly asking about strategy use
key_sources: Charlotte Dignath & Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2021). The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09534-0

article_title: The Case for Multifaceted, Integrative Motivation Interventions Embedded in Classrooms
citation: Linnenbrink-Garcia, L., Wigfield, A., Cabrera, L., Mouzaoir, S., McKinney, D., Liu, P. P., Marchand, G., Schmidt, J. A., Harris, C. J., & Guthrie, J. (2026). The Case for Multifaceted, Integrative Motivation Interventions Embedded in Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10177-w
title: Theoretical integration rationale: no single motivation theory captures all relevant constructs, so interventions should integrate carefully across theories
description: The paper argues that "no theory captures all relevant motivation constructs that impact student learning outcomes. Perhaps no one theory ever can", echoing Graham and Kelly that theories have foci and a range of convenience. Because constructs overlap across theories yet each theory holds unique constructs, integrative approaches should let interventions reach more students. The authors caution, following Pekrun and Ryan, that integration must be done carefully and conceptually: integrate theories studying the same phenomena or making converging predictions, and specify how integration yields new insights rather than merely adding constructs.
requirements: Integration should follow Pekrun's rules: same phenomena or converging predictions, plus a specified account of new insights gained
constraints: The authors state the motivation field's knowledge about integrating across motivation, metacognition, self-regulation, and personality is not complete enough to recommend interventions spanning those constructs
target_learning_goals: designing motivation interventions that support multiple forms of student motivation
examples: CORI integrated goal, interest, self-determination, expectancy-value, and social cognitive theories; M-PLANS built on five motivational design principles integrated across theories
key_sources: Linnenbrink-Garcia, L., Wigfield, A., Cabrera, L., Mouzaoir, S., McKinney, D., Liu, P. P., Marchand, G., Schmidt, J. A., Harris, C. J., & Guthrie, J. (2026). The Case for Multifaceted, Integrative Motivation Interventions Embedded in Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10177-w

article_title: Development and Validation of a Theory-Based Questionnaire to Measure Different Types of Cognitive Load
citation: Krieglstein, F., Beege, M., Rey, G. D., Sanchez-Stockhammer, C., & Schneider, S. (2023). Development and Validation of a Theory-Based Questionnaire to Measure Different Types of Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09738-0
title: Three types of cognitive load within Cognitive Load Theory: intrinsic, extraneous, and germane
description: The article organizes cognitive load into three types within Cognitive Load Theory. Intrinsic load "refers to the load imposed by the learning task's complexity", reflected in element interactivity and reduced by prior knowledge. Extraneous load "results from processes that are not relevant to learning" and is determined by the presentation format of the material. Germane load is the learning-relevant, productive load: learners "must actively invest cognitive resources" to construct and automate schemata, so GCL should be as high as possible. ICL and ECL are assumed to be additive, and design aims to reduce ECL to free resources for dealing with ICL.
requirements: Measurement instruments must be able to differentiate between the three load types to assess the effectiveness of specific instructional designs and principles.
constraints: The article states the role of GCL within CLT is still controversial concerning its measurement and theoretical embedding.
target_learners: learners acquiring secondary knowledge in educational and training contexts
target_learning_goals: efficient use of limited working memory for construction and automation of schemata in long-term memory
examples: The questionnaire items were formulated to reflect these definitions: ICL items address perceived task complexity and prior knowledge, ECL items address the design of the learning material, and GCL items address mental effort and schema construction.
key_sources: Krieglstein, F., Beege, M., Rey, G. D., Sanchez-Stockhammer, C., & Schneider, S. (2023). Development and Validation of a Theory-Based Questionnaire to Measure Different Types of Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09738-0

article_title: Culture and school belonging: Towards a global research agenda
citation: Ronnel B. King, Faming Wang. (2026). Culture and school belonging: Towards a global research agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10213-9
title: Three forms of cultural variation in school belonging: level-oriented, structure-oriented, and meaning-oriented differences
description: The commentary organizes how culture can shape school belonging into three forms, drawing on van de Vijver and Leung's distinction between level-oriented and structure-oriented differences and adding meaning-oriented differences. Culture "could impact the mean levels of school belonging in a given population (i.e., level-oriented differences)", could "modify the relationship between school belonging and other constructs in the nomological network", and could shape the very meaning of belonging across contexts. The commentary uses this framework to structure its PISA 2018 reanalyses and its argument for emic approaches.
requirements: Cross-cultural studies must specify which form of cultural variation they are testing (means, associations, or meanings)
constraints: Level comparisons of means can be open to numerous interpretations, per the authors
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students across cultural contexts
target_learning_goals: Understanding how cultural context shapes students' sense of school belonging and its links to motivation and achievement
examples: The commentary's PISA 2018 reanalyses illustrate level-oriented differences (Table 3 rankings) and structure-oriented differences (Figure 2 ecological correlations)
key_sources: Ronnel B. King, Faming Wang. (2026). Culture and school belonging: Towards a global research agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10213-9

article_title: Visuospatial Processing Decline Due to Cannabis Consumption in Nondependent High School Students
citation: Goycolea, Rodrigo; Castro Alonso, Juan; Dörr Álamos, Anneliese. (2020). Visuospatial Processing Decline Due to Cannabis Consumption in Nondependent High School Students. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09564-8
title: Three-type taxonomy of correlational studies of cannabis-related visuospatial decline
description: The review organizes its correlational evidence into three types: comparisons of declines between visuospatial processing and other cognitive tasks, studies comparing declines between high school students and adult participants, and stringent correlational studies such as large samples, longitudinal data, and twin studies. This taxonomy structures how the review weighs evidence of visuospatial processing decline associated with cannabis use in nondependent high school students, alongside experimental evidence and evidence from abstinent conditions.
requirements: Correlational evidence must be classified by design features such as sample size, longitudinal data, or twin design to count as stringent
constraints: The taxonomy applies to correlational studies of cannabis-related cognitive decline in nondependent or nonclinical high school students
target_learning_goals: visuospatial processing
learning performance
key_sources: Goycolea, Rodrigo; Castro Alonso, Juan; Dörr Álamos, Anneliese. (2020). Visuospatial Processing Decline Due to Cannabis Consumption in Nondependent High School Students. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09564-8

article_title: The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education
citation: Rexigel, E., Kuhn, J., Becker, S., & Malone, S. (2024). The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09958-y
title: Three categories of representational competencies for learning with multiple external representations
description: Drawing on Rau (2017), the article distinguishes three categories of representational competencies needed to profit from MERs. Conceptual representational competencies are the abilities and knowledge learners apply when associating an external representation with a specific concept and drawing conclusions from it, including discerning superficial versus conceptually significant similarities between representations. Perceptual representational competencies include visual fluency (effortlessly reading a representation) and connectional fluency (quickly matching and connecting multiple representations). Meta-representational competencies are essential for selecting an appropriate representation according to the task and one's own abilities. These skills can be developed through targeted interactions with representations.
requirements: To benefit from MERs, learners need representational competence; when it is lacking, students face a representational dilemma of learning unfamiliar content from as-yet-unfamiliar representations.
constraints: Representational competencies are rarely studied as outcomes of learning with multimedia educational resources.
target_learners: Students of any age learning with multiple external representations
target_learning_goals: Developing representational competencies for learning and problem-solving with MERs
examples: The article cites eye-tracking studies showing different combinations of representations triggered distinct processing of mathematical problems.
key_sources: Rexigel, E., Kuhn, J., Becker, S., & Malone, S. (2024). The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09958-y

article_title: Moving Beyond Reflection: Reflexivity and Epistemic Cognition in Teaching and Teacher Education
citation: Feucht, F. C., Lunn Brownlee, J., & Schraw, G. (2017). Moving beyond reflection: Reflexivity and epistemic cognition in teaching and teacher education. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 234-241. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1350180
title: Three waves of personal epistemology research: development, beliefs, and justification/epistemic cognition
description: Drawing on Hofer (2016), the article organizes five decades of personal epistemology research into three waves: epistemological development, epistemological beliefs, and more recent work on justification and epistemic cognition. Developmental frameworks (Perry; Kuhn & Weinstock) describe progression from absolutist through subjectivist to evaluativist positions. Schommer-Aikins proposed independent multidimensional beliefs, while Hofer's epistemological theories and Elby and Hammer's epistemological resources offer fine-grained, context-specific accounts. The article notes that 'no specific framework (or even framework type) has achieved prevalence to enable systematic and focused research'.
requirements: Understanding of the framework distinctions requires familiarity with the cited primary works, which this article only summarizes
constraints: The article presents these as descriptive overviews of others' frameworks rather than tested models
target_learning_goals: understanding the nature of knowledge and processes of knowing
framing research on teachers' personal epistemologies
examples: The article applies the developmental levels to teachers: absolutist teachers view knowledge as transmissible, subjectivist teachers as personal opinion, evaluativist teachers as requiring adjudication among perspectives
key_sources: Feucht, F. C., Lunn Brownlee, J., & Schraw, G. (2017). Moving beyond reflection: Reflexivity and epistemic cognition in teaching and teacher education. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 234-241. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1350180

article_title: A critical analysis of the current motivation theories in educational psychology: Why the same theories continue to dominate
citation: Murayama, K., & von Keyserlingk, L. (2025). A critical analysis of the current motivation theories in educational psychology: Why the same theories continue to dominate.
title: Distinction between descriptive and explanatory aspects of theory, and between theory, phenomenon, and data
description: Drawing on Greene (2022) and Borsboom et al. (2021), the article distinguishes the descriptive aspect of a theory (a broad, concise picture of a phenomenon) from its explanatory aspect (an account of the causal mechanisms, the "how"). It further distinguishes data (direct observations such as survey responses or classroom behavior) from phenomena (robust empirical generalizations across data, such as the positive manifold or named effects), with "A theory provides a causal explanation for the phenomena". The authors argue existing motivation theories largely describe phenomena in the Figure 1 scheme but lack detailed causal explanation, making them hard to falsify.
requirements: A theory should make predictions about new phenomena that can be tested with empirical data
constraints: The distinction between data and phenomenon is relative, not absolute, per the article
target_learning_goals: understanding how theories are formulated and evaluated in motivation science
examples: The article uses the positive manifold as an example: general intelligence theory and mutualism-style accounts (van der Maas et al., 2006) are alternative theories explaining the same phenomenon
key_sources: Murayama, K., & von Keyserlingk, L. (2025). A critical analysis of the current motivation theories in educational psychology: Why the same theories continue to dominate. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2025.2473894

article_title: Exploring the links between students' engagement in cooperative learning, their goal preferences and appraisals of instructional conditions in the classroom
citation: Hijzen, D., Boekaerts, M., & Vedder, P. H. (2007). Exploring the links between students' engagement in cooperative learning, their goal preferences and appraisals of instructional conditions in the classroom. Learning And Instruction, 17(6), 673-687. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2007.09.020
title: Three types of engagement during cooperative learning: task-relevant, task-irrelevant, and socially oriented task engagement
description: Following Chapman (2003), the article distinguishes "three types of engagement that may occur during CL". Task-relevant engagement characterizes students who are active, focus on the task and persist; task-irrelevant engagement characterizes disaffected students who "do not try hard, give up easily" and chat or disturb others; socially oriented task engagement involves students "primarily involved in social activities such as providing help and emotional support". The study operationalizes these as subscales of an observation rating list and uses them to define effective versus ineffective CL teams.
requirements: Engagement must be observed during actual CL sessions and rated with items covering the three engagement types
constraints: The article treats engagement as students' actual involvement, distinct from motivation, which concerns underlying cognitions
target_learning_goals: engagement in cooperative learning tasks
examples: The 18-item rating list contained three subscales with sample items such as "this student chats" (α = 0.89), "this student concentrates on the task" (α = 0.95), and "this student offers team members help" (α = 0.90).
key_sources: Hijzen, D., Boekaerts, M., & Vedder, P. H. (2007). Exploring the links between students' engagement in cooperative learning, their goal preferences and appraisals of instructional conditions in the classroom. Learning And Instruction, 17(6), 673-687. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2007.09.020

article_title: The relation between text comprehension and computation in mathematical word-problem solving
citation: Strohmaier, A. R., Schons, C., Knabbe, A., Vogel, M., Saado, K., & Obersteiner, A. (2025). The relation between text comprehension and computation in mathematical word-problem solving. Learning and Instruction, 101, 102235. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102235
title: Three categories of attentional effects (canonical, phase-crossover, attention-crossover) for discriminating process models
description: The article proposes a categorization of effects on cognitive processing during word-problem solving: "Canonical effects" are predicted by all process models; "Phase-crossover effects" occur when a difficulty or ability affects the phase opposite to its canonical one (predicted by flexible models); "Attention-crossover effects" occur when a factor affects attention on the problem part opposite to its canonical one (predicted by integrated models). This framework converts model differences into empirically testable predictions about fixation durations on numbers and situational text in two solution phases.
requirements: Independent variation of linguistic and mathematical problem difficulty, standardized ability measures, and phase-distinguishing process data
constraints: Flexible and integrated models predict opposite attention-crossover effects for question position, "which might also cancel each other out"
target_learning_goals: diagnosing the sequence and integration of comprehension and computation processes
key_sources: Strohmaier, A. R., Schons, C., Knabbe, A., Vogel, M., Saado, K., & Obersteiner, A. (2025). The relation between text comprehension and computation in mathematical word-problem solving. Learning and Instruction, 101, 102235. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102235

article_title: Increasing the use of conceptually-derived strategies in arithmetic: using inversion problems to promote the use of associativity shortcuts
citation: Joanne Eaves, Nina Attridge, Camilla Gilmore. (2018). Increasing the use of conceptually-derived strategies in arithmetic: using inversion problems to promote the use of associativity shortcuts. Learning and Instruction. https://figshare.com/s/230ee9491e0b67d9d3f3
title: Three proposed mechanisms linking inversion problem exposure to associativity shortcut use
description: The article proposes three non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms through which solving inversion problems may encourage associativity shortcut use: conceptual knowledge association, spatial attention, and strategy validation. The authors state they "suggest three possible (not mutually exclusive) mechanisms through which this could operate, a) conceptual knowledge, b) spatial attention, and c) validation of a strategy." Conceptual association activates linked principles in memory; spatial attention directs focus to the right-hand side where the shortcut is located; validation communicates that a right-to-left strategy is legitimate. The mechanisms are likely to interact.
requirements: For the conceptual mechanism, individuals must have at least some understanding of both principles stored in memory
For the validation mechanism, top-down manipulation of arithmetic knowledge is required rather than a simple general stimulus
constraints: The mechanisms are proposed as explanations, not independently tested in the available text; the authors note they are likely to interact and are discussed separately only for clarity
target_learning_goals: use of associativity shortcuts in arithmetic
conceptual knowledge of arithmetic principles
examples: Study 3 was designed to discriminate between mechanisms by comparing 'a + b – b' inversion, 'a + b – a' inversion, and two-term control conditions
key_sources: Joanne Eaves, Nina Attridge, Camilla Gilmore. (2018). Increasing the use of conceptually-derived strategies in arithmetic: using inversion problems to promote the use of associativity shortcuts. Learning and Instruction. https://figshare.com/s/230ee9491e0b67d9d3f3

article_title: Contrasting school dropout: The protective role of perceived teacher justice
citation: Grazia, V., Molinari, L., Mameli, C. (2024). Contrasting school dropout: The protective role of perceived teacher justice. LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION, 89, 1-9. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101826
title: Three-wave teacher justice and dropout-intention questionnaire
description: A repeated questionnaire measuring students' perceptions of teacher justice and their intentions to drop out, administered at the beginning (T1), middle (T2) and end (T3) of the school year. Participants "answered a questionnaire on teacher justice and intentions to drop out" at each wave. The three-wave design enabled latent growth modeling of change in intentions and of the justice association over time.
requirements: Administration at three time points across the school year to capture growth
constraints: Self-report measure with 9th-grade students; perception-based rather than observational
target_learning_goals: Measuring perceived teacher justice and dropout intentions over time
examples: Administered to 547 students (56% male, 94% born in Italy, Mage = 13.92)
key_sources: Grazia, V., Molinari, L., Mameli, C. (2024). Contrasting school dropout: The protective role of perceived teacher justice. LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION, 89, 1-9. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101826

article_title: Examining myside bias on a controversial historical event after engagement in dialogic argumentation: Insights from a think aloud study
citation: Iordanou, K., Fotiou, C., Manoli, A., & Zembylas, M. (2025). Examining myside bias on a controversial historical event after engagement in dialogic argumentation: Insights from a think aloud study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102209
title: Think-aloud methodology as a tool for identifying myside bias and the conditions that facilitate or impede its change
description: The article proposes the think-aloud methodology, in which participants read sentence-by-sentence flashcards and verbalize thoughts and feelings, as a way to assess myside bias during reading rather than only in argument generation or evaluation tasks. It argues the method captures not just final judgments but the reasoning behind them, and that "it uncovers when and under which conditions myside bias occurs, changes, or fails to change." The study applied it pre- and post-intervention with authentic biased historical texts.
requirements: Participants must be able to meet the demands of thinking aloud while reading; in this study teachers selected students on that criterion.
constraints: Assessed myside bias for one ethnic community's students on one controversial historical event; the method was previously validated for this purpose in an adult sample.
target_learning_goals: reasoning and myside bias during reading of conflicting historical accounts
examples: Pre- and post-intervention think-aloud sessions of 20-25 minutes with flashcards of sentences from Greek-Cypriot and Turkish-Cypriot historian texts, coded with an adapted reading-comprehension scheme (inter-rater κ = 0.849).
key_sources: Iordanou, K., Fotiou, C., Manoli, A., & Zembylas, M. (2025). Examining myside bias on a controversial historical event after engagement in dialogic argumentation: Insights from a think aloud study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102209

article_title: Differential effects of the classroom on African American and non-African American’s mathematics achievement.
citation: Schenke, K., Nguyen, T., Watts, T. W., Sarama, J. H., & Clements, D. H. (2017). Differential effects of the classroom on African American and non-African American’s mathematics achievement. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(6), 794–811. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000165
title: Three observed dimensions of the early-childhood classroom learning environment
description: The article organizes the observed classroom-learning environment into three dimensions measured with the COEMET observation protocol: (1) teachers' expectations and the developmental appropriateness of their instruction, (2) teachers' confidence and enthusiasm in their teaching, and (3) teachers' support for mathematical discourse. The authors state, "we described the classroom environment as: (1) teachers’ expectations and the developmental appropriateness of their instruction... (2) teachers’ confidence and enthusiasm in their teaching, and (3) teachers’ support for mathematical discourse." Factor composites were weighted by standardized factor loadings, and the three factors were moderately to strongly intercorrelated (r = .48 to .66).
requirements: Trained observers blind to experimental condition conducting COEMET observations twice during the school year, with ratings averaged across time points and mathematics activities
constraints: Developmental appropriateness is operationalized specifically as the expectations teachers have of what preschool students are capable of learning, including engagement in higher-level thinking rather than only play-based activities
target_learning_goals: early mathematics achievement (number and geometry skills)
examples: The dimensions were used as mediators in multigroup multilevel mediation models linking the TRIAD treatment to student posttest mathematics achievement
key_sources: Schenke, K., Nguyen, T., Watts, T. W., Sarama, J. H., & Clements, D. H. (2017). Differential effects of the classroom on African American and non-African American’s mathematics achievement. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(6), 794–811. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000165

article_title: Expanding the developmental models of writing: A direct and indirect effects model of developmental writing (DIEW).
citation: Kim Young-Suk Grace, Schatschneider Christopher. (2017). Expanding the developmental models of writing: A direct and indirect effects model of developmental writing (DIEW). Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000129
title: Three levels of mental representation in discourse comprehension and production
description: The article describes theoretical models of discourse comprehension and production positing three levels of mental representations: the situation model, textbase, and surface code. The situation model, the highest level, requires linking propositions across the text and to background knowledge to integrate and infer meanings. The article maps language and cognitive skills onto these levels, with higher-order cognitive skills (inference, theory of mind) supporting global coherence (situation model) and foundational skills supporting textbase construction. As printed: 'The situation model is the interlocutor's representation of the events, actions, and characters (what the text is about; van Dijk & Kintsch, 1983), and is the highest level of mental representation.'
requirements: Linking propositions across the text and to general background knowledge to establish a coherent whole
target_learning_goals: Discourse-level oral language comprehension and production
examples: The direct and mediated model of discourse-level language maps inference and theory of mind onto the situation model and vocabulary, grammatical knowledge, and working memory onto the textbase
key_sources: Kim Young-Suk Grace, Schatschneider Christopher. (2017). Expanding the developmental models of writing: A direct and indirect effects model of developmental writing (DIEW). Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000129

article_title: Research versus Propaganda in Visual Education.
citation: Frank N. Freeman. (1922). Research Versus Propaganda in Visual Education. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. XI, No. 5. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/13/5/
title: Three-stage model of how educational movements are adopted: propaganda, reaction, and equilibrium
description: Freeman proposes that an educational movement typically passes through three stages: undiscriminating propaganda that awakens enthusiasm, a second stage of reaction and decline in which claims are found overstated, and a third stage of equilibrium in which the movement's true value is estimated. He argues the wasteful cycle could be shortened if the critique of later stages were applied at the beginning and classroom trial supplemented by systematic experimentation.
requirements: Scientific technique of investigation, including laboratory experimentation and statistical methods, must be available to test new movements before adoption
constraints: The analysis is framed for new materials or methods adopted through large-scale schoolroom practice rather than tested in advance
target_learning_goals: judicious adoption of new instructional materials and methods
examples: Freeman applies the model to visual education, which he sees as showing signs of the first, propaganda stage
key_sources: Frank N. Freeman. (1922). Research Versus Propaganda in Visual Education. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. XI, No. 5. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/13/5/

article_title: Form and position in handwriting interpretation. Part I.
citation: Downey, J. E., and Anderson, J. E. (1914). Form and Position in Handwriting Interpretation. Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Form+and+position+in+handwriting+interpretation%22+Downey+Anderson
title: Three-way taxonomy of readers of illegible writing: combined form-and-meaning readers, meaning-dominant readers, and form-dominant readers
description: The article classifies subjects' procedures in reading illegible writing into three classes. Some place 'dependence being placed exclusively on neither meaning or form, but on a combination of both as occurs in ordinary reading'; a second class depends largely on meaning, making substitutions on a meaning basis without noticing the difference; a third depends greatly on form while paying little attention to meaning, producing context-free substitutions. The authors stress these divisions shade into each other, and the same three classes recur with mutilated specimens where meaning plays a smaller part.
requirements: Samples of genuinely illegible adult handwriting, read aloud once under time, so that substitution and omission behavior can be observed
constraints: The divisions are not hard and fast but shade into each other; the article says it is often difficult to tell whether a person is using a meaning or form basis
target_learning_goals: perception of handwriting form and meaning in reading
examples: In Test C 1 a subject read 'latest list of all' as 'taxes this year' (meaning-based); in Test A 1 a subject read 'Review Monograph Series' as 'Reverend Negotiable Fines' (form-based)
key_sources: Downey, J. E., and Anderson, J. E. (1914). Form and Position in Handwriting Interpretation. Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Form+and+position+in+handwriting+interpretation%22+Downey+Anderson

article_title: Problems in the experimental pedagogy of geometry.
citation: William H. Metzler. (1912). Problems in the Experimental Pedagogy of Geometry. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Three lines of experimental investigation for the pedagogy of geometry
description: The article organizes experimental work on geometry teaching around three questions: whether the desired results are obtained under a given method, what the best method of obtaining them is, and whether obtaining them transfers to other subjects. It states that "If the three lines of investigation indicated were carefully carried out and the questions involved settled, there would be no doubt as to the correct aims and proper methods in teaching the subject." The framework links aim-verification, method comparison, and transfer testing into one research program.
requirements: Experiments must be performed "with the utmost care and under the most certain conditions," since overlooked factors can spoil an experiment's value
constraints: Testing for transfer is described as not easy and in some phases almost, if not entirely, impossible
target_learning_goals: logical thinking
concentration
transfer of general powers
examples: The article derives suggested tests for knowledge of fundamentals, reasoning, and concentration from the first line of investigation
key_sources: William H. Metzler. (1912). Problems in the Experimental Pedagogy of Geometry. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070947

article_title: Problems in the experimental pedagogy of geometry.
citation: William H. Metzler. (1912). Problems in the Experimental Pedagogy of Geometry. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Three recognized general methods of teaching geometry: textbook, suggestive, and syllabus methods
description: The article identifies "the textbook method, the suggestive method, and the syllabus method" as the three fairly well recognized general methods of teaching geometry, alongside many special devices. It proposes that their relative merits be determined by well-selected experiments testing the results, and that because different schools use different methods, the same test could be given across schools to compare outcomes.
requirements: Method comparison requires well-selected experiments testing the results, or same tests administered across schools using different methods
target_learning_goals: acquisition of the ten desired outcomes of geometry study
examples: The article suggests giving the same test to different schools that use different methods as one route to comparison
key_sources: William H. Metzler. (1912). Problems in the Experimental Pedagogy of Geometry. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070947

article_title: Recent studies in handwriting.
citation: Thompson, M. E. (1911). Recent Studies in Handwriting. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 41-45.
title: Thorndike's objective scale for measuring handwriting quality
description: Thorndike devised a standard scale for objectively measuring the quality of handwriting, resting on the consensus of many competent judges rather than on individual biased impressions. Samples from pupils in grades V to VIII were sorted into twenty quality groups by thirty or forty judges, and scale points were constructed equidistant from each other, with a copy-book model at the top and artificially produced very bad writing at the bottom.
requirements: Several competent judges independently compare a sample with the scale and indicate the quality it most resembles
constraints: The author admits the scale is not yet perfect; few of the steps contain a sufficient number of different styles of writing
Individuals will vary somewhat in their ratings, so the scale will not work automatically
target_learners: pupils in grades V to VIII
target_learning_goals: handwriting quality measurement
examples: A scale of six points was also constructed for the quality of adult women's handwriting
key_sources: Thompson, M. E. (1911). Recent Studies in Handwriting. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 41-45. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0068789

article_title: Recent studies in handwriting.
citation: Thompson, M. E. (1911). Recent Studies in Handwriting. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 41-45.
title: Thompson's resume organizes psychological research on writing for teachers, from alphabet history to neural bases to pedagogy
description: Thompson's book brings together widely scattered experimental data on handwriting, published in technical journals inaccessible to the average teacher, and presents them in orderly fashion with emphasis on their pedagogical applications. It traces the historical development of the alphabet, summarizes views on the neural activities underlying writing including the agraphia question, and reviews experimental studies of movement, practice, and intelligence before re-examining the results from the teacher's practical standpoint.
requirements: Intended for teachers and laymen rather than the psychological expert
constraints: For the specialist in psychology she has nothing new to offer; she made no original researches nor novel theories
The historical sketch ends with the printing form of the Latin alphabet and does not trace cursive development
target_learning_goals: evidence-based understanding of handwriting pedagogy
examples: The final chapter on the pedagogy of writing incorporates a portion of Thorndike's scale and includes a bibliography of 44 numbers and an index
key_sources: Thompson, M. E. (1911). Recent Studies in Handwriting. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 41-45. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0068789

article_title: Measuring arithmetic: A psychometric approach to understanding formatting effects and domain specificity.
citation: Rhodes Katherine T., Branum-Martin Lee, Washington Julie A., Fuchs Lynn S. (2017). Measuring arithmetic: A psychometric approach to understanding formatting effects and domain specificity. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000189
