title: Four competing theories of arithmetic cognition as measurement hypotheses (Abstract Code, Encoding Complex, Triple Code, Exact versus Approximate)
description: The article frames four leading theories of arithmetic cognition as competing, testable measurement hypotheses. Abstract Code Theory holds that a single abstract code represents all numeric information regardless of format, so "formatting exerts no effect on numeric processing." Encoding Complex Theory posits format-specific codes in an associative network relying on domain-general capacities. Triple Code Theory posits visual Arabic, verbal word frame, and analog magnitude representations determined by stimulus format, with Exact versus Approximate Calculations as its extension for calculation tasks. The study operationalizes each theory as a confirmatory factor model.
requirements: Measurement requires multitrait multimethod data: arithmetic measured across formats alongside language and executive attention measures, analyzed with confirmatory factor analysis.
constraints: The factor analytic framework cannot distinguish the abstract-code and encoding-complex single-factor models, which the authors note as a limitation.
target_learning_goals: arithmetic cognition and measurement of mathematical ability
examples: The study tested 11 models, presenting full results for the four theory-guided full measurement models plus a post-hoc hybrid model.
key_sources: Rhodes Katherine T., Branum-Martin Lee, Washington Julie A., Fuchs Lynn S. (2017). Measuring arithmetic: A psychometric approach to understanding formatting effects and domain specificity. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000189

article_title: Expanding autonomy psychological need states from two (satisfaction, frustration) to three (dissatisfaction): A classroom-based intervention study.
citation: Sung Hyeon Cheon, Johnmarshall Reeve, Youngsun Lee, Nikos Ntoumanis, Nicolas Gillet, Bo Ram Kim, Yong-Gwan Song. (2019). Expanding Autonomy Psychological Need States from Two (Satisfaction, Frustration) to Three (Dissatisfaction): A Classroom-Based Intervention Study. Journal of Educational Psychology, 111(4), 685-702. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000306
title: Three-state model of the psychological need for autonomy: satisfaction, frustration, and dissatisfaction
description: The article expands the SDT dual-process model by adding autonomy dissatisfaction as a third need state. It argues that "need satisfaction represented the 'bright side' of student motivation" while need frustration represented the "dark side," and that dissatisfaction arises when the learning environment is indifferent to students' needs. Teacher indifference—neglecting students' needs, goals, or concerns—produces an "energy-depleting experience" of dissatisfaction marked by boredom, amotivation, and apathy, distinct from the energy-disorganizing frustration produced by teacher control.
requirements: A learning environment that offers need indifference—activities unrelated or disconnected from students' psychological needs—for dissatisfaction to occur
constraints: The study focused only on the psychological need for autonomy, not competence or relatedness
target_learners: secondary school students in physical education
target_learning_goals: classroom engagement and prevention of disengagement
examples: Figure 1 illustrates how a teacher's motivating style (need supportive, need indifferent, or need thwartive) yields one of three student need states during instruction
key_sources: Sung Hyeon Cheon, Johnmarshall Reeve, Youngsun Lee, Nikos Ntoumanis, Nicolas Gillet, Bo Ram Kim, Yong-Gwan Song. (2019). Expanding Autonomy Psychological Need States from Two (Satisfaction, Frustration) to Three (Dissatisfaction): A Classroom-Based Intervention Study. Journal of Educational Psychology, 111(4), 685-702. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000306

article_title: An approach to the synthetic study of interest in education: Part I.
citation: Waples, D. (1920). An Approach to the Synthetic Study of Interest in Education: Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, XI(6).
title: Three types of interest: intrinsic, practical, and cognitive
description: Waples proposes a theoretical classification of expressed interest into three attitudes distinguished by types of experience: "the types are three: an intrinsic, which seeks indulgence of feeling toward the situation; practical, which seeks usefulness, or directs action towards the situation; and cognitive, which seeks meaning." Each type is conceived to be differentiated by socialized expression, with some elements becoming prominent only after infancy. He argues discovery of the appropriate type and knowledge of its limitations is the theoretical prerequisite of effective motivation, and notes substantial agreement among authorities on this logical classification.
requirements: Diagnosis of the individual's appropriate type of interest and knowledge of its limitations before applying motivational principles
constraints: The pure type probably exists only in abstraction, so the classification's application depends largely on the specific case
target_learners: school pupils at successive stages of development
target_learning_goals: effective motivation through accurate diagnosis of pupil interest
examples: Waples traces the classification to Herbart's three-fold division under knowledge and participation and lists Kilpatrick, Dewey, McDougall, and others as employing substantially the same terms
key_sources: Waples, D. (1920). An Approach to the Synthetic Study of Interest in Education: Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, XI(6). https://doi.org/10.1037/h0076045

article_title: An approach to the synthetic study of interest in education: Part I.
citation: Waples, D. (1920). An Approach to the Synthetic Study of Interest in Education: Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, XI(6).
title: Three-class taxonomy of sources on interest: introspective, descriptive-psychological, and statistical
description: The article organizes previous investigations of interest into three general classes: works where analysis is largely introspective (with or without direct pedagogical reference), descriptive psychology ranging from laboratory analysis to childhood and adolescence biographies, and statistical child-study investigations recording group preferences and reactions. Each class is further distributed between strictly pedagogical and strictly psychological approaches and between direct and incidental study of interest. Waples judges the incidental classes generally the more reliable despite greater difficulty of adaptation.
requirements: Selection of representative works from each class so the student can cover the field with the greatest economy of time
constraints: Very few of the statistical studies had made any real contribution to the theory of interest, rendering those few easy to distinguish
target_learners: education researchers and students of educational psychology
target_learning_goals: understanding the nature, development, and educational bearing of interest
examples: Illustrative works named include Herbart's Outlines and Science of Education, Mitchell's The Structure and Growth of the Mind, and Croswell's, Chapman and Feeler's, and Thorndike's studies
key_sources: Waples, D. (1920). An Approach to the Synthetic Study of Interest in Education: Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, XI(6). https://doi.org/10.1037/h0076045

article_title: The decision of African American students to complete high school: An application of the theory of planned behavior.
citation: Davis, L., Ajzen, I., Saunders, J., & Williams, T. (2002). The decision of African American students to complete high school: An application of the theory of planned behavior. Journal of Educational Psychology, 94(4), 810–819. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.94.4.810
title: Theory of planned behavior as a framework for explaining students' completion decisions
description: The theory of planned behavior (Ajzen, 1991) explains behavior via intentions shaped by three constructs: attitudes toward the behavior, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control. In this article it structures a questionnaire about completing high school, and its constructs "accurately predicted from attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control" students' intentions to complete the year, demonstrating the framework's applicability to academic persistence decisions among African American adolescents.
requirements: A questionnaire measuring attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control toward the target behavior
constraints: Applied here to one population: African American high-school students aged 14 to 17, and to the specific behavior of completing the school year
target_learners: African American high-school students aged 14 to 17
target_learning_goals: Intention to complete the high-school year and persist to graduation
examples: Students completed a questionnaire based on the theory of planned behavior early in their second year of high school
key_sources: Davis, L., Ajzen, I., Saunders, J., & Williams, T. (2002). The decision of African American students to complete high school: An application of the theory of planned behavior. Journal of Educational Psychology, 94(4), 810–819. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.94.4.810

article_title: The Devious Path of Slow Work.
citation: Bird, Grace E. (1921). The Devious Path of Slow Work. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ123456
title: Pupils should think in terms of results more than in terms of the process.
description: Bird concludes that pupils "should think in terms of results more than in terms of the process," because this economical method encourages speed and is more conducive to concentration, being in less danger of distraction elements which tend to alter the character of the work. The recommendation follows from her observation that rapid calculation crowds out irrelevant intermediate performances.
requirements: Practice must be properly focalized and motivated so that learners exercise optimum effort.
target_learning_goals: rapid and accurate computation
concentration on task goals
examples: In her experiment, students during rapid adding stated as their central thought a desire to get the answer, while slow adding produced varied distractions.

article_title: The power of the eye to sustain clear seeing under different conditions of lighting.
citation: C. E. Ferree and Gertrude Rand. (1917). The Power of the Eye to Sustain Clear Seeing Under Different Conditions of Lighting. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Three-minute acuity-sustain test of the eye's power to sustain clear seeing under lighting conditions
description: A laboratory test combining two principles: visual acuity may be measured by the smallest angle the eye can discriminate, and loss of efficiency shows more plainly in prolonged than momentary performance. As printed, "The power of the eye to sustain a certain standard of acuity for three minutes is measured before and after a period of reading from uniform type and paper under the lighting conditions to be tested." A kymograph and chronograph record time at standard versus below it, and the ratio measures the ability to sustain clear seeing. Observers were trained to precision and results were accepted only when condition effects exceeded the mean variation.
requirements: Observers trained to satisfactory precision in the three-minute record and the three-hour test before taking part
Results accepted only when the variation from changing conditions largely exceeded the mean variation for the condition
target_learners: adult observers under 30 years of age with no uncorrected defects of consequence
target_learning_goals: measuring sustained visual efficiency under different lighting conditions
examples: Used to compare direct, semi-indirect, and indirect installations at four positions in a test room and across lamp wattages and reflector densities
key_sources: C. E. Ferree and Gertrude Rand. (1917). The Power of the Eye to Sustain Clear Seeing Under Different Conditions of Lighting. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0072369

article_title: Testing a three-phase model of the relationship between motivational appraisals, observable engagement, and subjective engagement: Insights from combining mobile learning data and daily diaries.
citation: Breitwieser, J., Brod, G., & Malmberg, L.-E. (2026). Testing a three-phase model of the relationship between motivational appraisals, observable engagement, and subjective engagement: Insights from combining mobile learning data and daily diaries. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001009
title: A three-phase model positioning observable engagement as the mediator between motivational appraisals and retrospective subjective engagement
description: The model integrates SEVT, engagement, and self-regulated learning process models by dividing learning into before, during, and after phases. It hypothesizes that appraisals of expectancy, value, and cost before learning drive observable behaviour during learning, and that post-learning perceptions of satisfaction, effort, and task delay are shaped by, but not identical to, that behaviour. A key contribution is "the explicit positioning of observable engagement as a mediator, highlighting the role of actual behaviour in linking motivational appraisals to retrospective perceptions of engagement." Direct effects of appraisals on subjective engagement are assumed to be tentative and subject to exploratory investigation.
requirements: Data capturing appraisals before learning, objective behaviour during learning, and subjective perceptions after learning in temporal order
constraints: Only the quantity, not the quality, of observable engagement is modelled as a mediator
Direct effects of appraisals on subjective engagement are tentative and not strong predictions
target_learners: school-aged learners in informal mobile learning settings
target_learning_goals: understanding how motivational appraisals relate to actual and perceived engagement in self-directed learning
examples: In the study, appraisals were measured in a morning diary, observable engagement as app log counts of vocabulary items studied, and satisfaction, effort, and task delay in an after-learning diary
key_sources: Breitwieser, J., Brod, G., & Malmberg, L.-E. (2026). Testing a three-phase model of the relationship between motivational appraisals, observable engagement, and subjective engagement: Insights from combining mobile learning data and daily diaries. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001009

article_title: Social learning through prediction error in the brain
citation: Jessica Joiner, Matthew Piva, Courtney Turrin and Steve W. C. Chang. (2017). Social learning through prediction error in the brain. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0009-2
title: Two developmental accounts of representing others: theory-theory and simulation theory
description: The review presents two historically competing developmental accounts of how we represent others. In theory-theory, "like small scientists testing causal relations, children are constantly gathering data from the world and testing the predictions they make using the collected data"; in simulation theory, we understand others egocentrically by using the machinery of our own mental processes and projecting it onto others' behaviors. The review notes these accounts predict different neural implementations (allocentric vs egocentric mechanisms).
requirements: A proposal for how other-referenced information is represented in the brain to distinguish the two accounts empirically
constraints: The review states its current understanding of how the brain implements these processes is not complete
target_learners: children and nonhuman animals developing representations of others
target_learning_goals: understanding and modeling other individuals' internal states
key_sources: Jessica Joiner, Matthew Piva, Courtney Turrin and Steve W. C. Chang. (2017). Social learning through prediction error in the brain. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0009-2

article_title: Triggers of curiosity in social constructivist classroom discourse
citation: Ali, F., Wang, Y., Wang, S. J.-W. & Zhu, G. (2025). Triggers of curiosity in social constructivist classroom discourse. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00330-5
title: Three discourse patterns sustain curiosity chains: sustained teacher-student episodes, one student's question sparking another's, and consecutive student question turns
description: This lesson-level pattern describes three qualitatively identified configurations in which curiosity chains (S:CUR4→S:CUR2→S:CUR) occur in classroom discourse. The first is a sustained dialogue between teacher and one student using probing questions, encouragement, and confirmation-seeking; the second occurs when "the teacher engages in a discussion with one student, subsequ ently stimulating the curiosity of another student regarding the same topic"; the third involves "various students posing different questions," including consecutive student question turns when the teacher refrains from interrupting.
requirements: Knowledge Building classroom discourse in which students are free to pose questions and the discourse alternates between teacher and students
constraints: Patterns were qualitatively interpreted from two KB classrooms (one per grade) in one Canadian private school
target_learning_goals: sustaining chains of student curiosity and question asking during collaborative knowledge building
examples: Qualitative examples include a second-grade student's seed-germination question sparking another student's question about planting seeds on rock, and consecutive student questions about worms and compost.
key_sources: Ali, F., Wang, Y., Wang, S. J.-W. & Zhu, G. (2025). Triggers of curiosity in social constructivist classroom discourse. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00330-5

article_title: Exploring the potential of LLM to enhance teaching plans through teaching simulation
citation: Bihao Hu, Jiayi Zhu, Yiying Pei & Xiaoqing Gu. (2025). Exploring the potential of LLM to enhance teaching plans through teaching simulation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00300-x
title: Refining problem chains into context-based, trap-based, and summary-based types improves LLM teaching plan design
description: The article replaces a generic numbered problem-chain output format with three distinct chain types that structure classroom questioning across a lesson. Context-based chains introduce new knowledge through scenarios, trap-based chains pose medium- to high-difficulty questions that provoke critical thinking and productive failure, and summary-based chains support review and further interest. The authors report that "this subdivision approach enhances the LLM’s understanding of the teaching process, progressing from basic to advanced levels, and leads to better outcomes when designing andimproving teaching plans."
requirements: Prompts must include the lesson's knowledge points, instructional objectives, and teaching priority and challenge, with examples supplied for each chain type
constraints: Trap-based problem chains score slightly lower in usability than the other two types, indicating LLM limits in designing deep and challenging questions
target_learning_goals: gradual understanding and mastery of mathematical concepts through sequenced problem chains
examples: In the Stratified Random Sampling lesson example (Fig. 2), GPT-4 simulated teacher-student dialogs, generated reflections, and produced the enhanced plan with the three chain types in the Statistics module
key_sources: Bihao Hu, Jiayi Zhu, Yiying Pei & Xiaoqing Gu. (2025). Exploring the potential of LLM to enhance teaching plans through teaching simulation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00300-x

article_title: Executive functions as mediators of early educational disparities by SES, gender and birth month
citation: Rémeau, M., Schmitt, P., & Borst, G. (2026). Executive functions as mediators of early educational disparities by SES, gender and birth month. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00422-w
title: Three-core executive function framework as foundational for early academic learning
description: The article defines executive functions as distinct but interrelated higher-order neurocognitive processes, largely dependent on the prefrontal cortex, that regulate thought, behavior and emotion toward goal-directed outcomes. It states "Three core EFs have been identified: working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility", and treats a general EF factor combining these three as the mediating mechanism linking sociodemographic factors to pre-academic abilities in preschoolers.
requirements: The framework presumes EFs are measurable as a one-factor latent construct; the article's one-factor CFA including inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility and working memory showed excellent fit
constraints: The study aggregated EF dimensions into a broad latent construct, so it does not identify the most influential EF subcomponent for each pre-academic sub-domain
Only cool EFs were assessed; hot EFs such as self-control and delay of gratification were not included
target_learning_goals: pre-academic abilities including early oral language and early numeracy
examples: A one-factor CFA of inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility and working memory fit the data with CFI = 1.000 and standardized loadings from .40 to .78
key_sources: Rémeau, M., Schmitt, P., & Borst, G. (2026). Executive functions as mediators of early educational disparities by SES, gender and birth month. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00422-w

article_title: Effects of different AI-driven Chatbot feedback on learning outcomes and brain activity
citation: Yin, J., Xu, H., Pan, Y., & Hu, Y. (2025). Effects of different AI-driven Chatbot feedback on learning outcomes and brain activity. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00311-8
title: Three educational chatbots providing metacognitive, affective, or neutral feedback during human-cardiovascular-system learning
description: The article designed and developed three educational chatbots differing only in feedback type: metacognitive feedback posing questions to "evaluate, re ﬂect, monitor, or regulate the learning process", affective feedback with "encouragement and praise" statements, and neutral feedback ("Let’st a k ea break ﬁrst") serving as a non-judgmental control that "does not interfere with the learning process". Each chatbot delivered 15 personalized, conversational learning modules on the human heart and blood (approximately 1846 Chinese characters) with learning, self-assessment, and feedback phases.
requirements: Feedback delivered after the self-assessment phase in every trial; students rate confidence or emotional state on five-point Likert-type scales.
constraints: The neutral feedback is not typical feedback and serves only as a break prompt / control condition.
target_learning_goals: biology conceptual knowledge
retention
transfer
metacognitive monitoring
examples: Personalization included replacing "the" with "your" in statements, interactive lead-in sentences, and using the student's name, e.g., "Yin, do you understand heart tissue now?"
key_sources: Yin, J., Xu, H., Pan, Y., & Hu, Y. (2025). Effects of different AI-driven Chatbot feedback on learning outcomes and brain activity. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00311-8

article_title: Disentangling the contribution of individual and social learning processes in human advice-taking behavior
citation: Maayan Pereg, Uri Hertz, Ido Ben-Artzi and Nitzan Shahar. (2024). Disentangling the contribution of individual and social learning processes in human advice-taking behavior. npj Science of Learning 9:4. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00214-0
title: Three-process account of advice-taking: individual learning, informed advice-taking, and non-informed advice-taking
description: The article proposes and substantiates an explanatory framework in which choice behavior in repeated advice environments integrates three latent processes: "individual learning (i.e., learning the value of actions, independent of advice)", "informed advice-taking (i.e., learning the value of following advice)", and "non-informed advice-taking (i.e., a constant bias to follow advice regardless of outcome history)". Prediction-error-based Q-learning models estimate each component, with the winning mixture model assigning value to the instructed card (φ) and updating the value of following advice from outcomes (ω-weighted). The authors link the non-informed bias to social norms such as reciprocity or epistemic trust in advisors.
requirements: A repeating advice environment with interleaved revealed and concealed advice trials to disentangle the three processes
constraints: The authors note the results "do not necessarily expand to other forms of social learning that were not explicitly examined here", such as observational learning
Only prediction-error-based RL models were examined; alternative frameworks like active inference were not explored
target_learners: adult online participants (Prolific) performing value-based decision-making
target_learning_goals: disentangling how learners integrate personal experience with repeated external advice
key_sources: Maayan Pereg, Uri Hertz, Ido Ben-Artzi and Nitzan Shahar. (2024). Disentangling the contribution of individual and social learning processes in human advice-taking behavior. npj Science of Learning 9:4. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00214-0

article_title: Combining perspectives in multidisciplinary research on inequality in education
citation: Louise Elffers, Eddie Denessen and Monique Volman. (2024). Combining perspectives in multidisciplinary research on inequality in education. npj Science of Learning 9:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00215-z
title: Three dimensions along which disciplinary perspectives on educational inequality vary
description: The article identifies a taxonomy of three dimensions on which perspectives on inequality in education differ between academic disciplines. As the authors state, "These dimensions pertain to (1) how the problem of inequality in education is framed, (2) how inequality in education is empirically evaluated, and (3) how the role of education in fostering (in)equality is conceptualized." The taxonomy organizes the article's argument that combining disciplinary insights requires awareness of these varying lenses.
requirements: Researchers combining insights across disciplines must be aware of and able to locate their work on each of the three dimensions
constraints: The authors note the brief comment "cannot do justice to all theoretical perspectives on inequality in education, nor to the rich empirical literature on the topic from all disciplines"
target_learners: Researchers studying inequality in education across academic disciplines
target_learning_goals: Understanding and addressing educational inequality through multidisciplinary research
key_sources: Louise Elffers, Eddie Denessen and Monique Volman. (2024). Combining perspectives in multidisciplinary research on inequality in education. npj Science of Learning 9:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00215-z

article_title: Toward a unified vocabulary for embodiment research challenges and solutions
citation: Peng Wang, Jingming Li, Qian Yu, Liye Zou, Xia Xu, Myrto Mavilidi, Ryan S. Falck, Fabian Herold, Robert J. Schinke, Markus Raab & Fred Paas. (2026). Toward a unified vocabulary for embodiment research: challenges and solutions. npj Science of Learning 11:36. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00413-x
title: Apply the 3 Cs—clear, concise, consistent terminology—in embodiment research communication
description: The authors propose that embodiment research language should be "clear, concise, and consistent". Clear means pairing precise scholarly terms with plain-language glosses; concise means shorter self-descriptive labels (e.g., embodiment-informed instruction) with practice-facing descriptors; consistent means defining terms at first use, aligning with established frameworks, and avoiding scope drift. They argue adopting the 3 Cs makes studies easier to line up side by side and supports cumulative knowledge generation.
requirements: Define terms at first use and align with established frameworks; when theories truly differ, give them distinct labels rather than overloading the term embodied cognition
constraints: Conciseness should not come at the expense of precision, especially when a term signals theoretical assumptions; the goal is a shared vocabulary that makes differences explicit, not a single theory of embodiment
target_learning_goals: clear cross-disciplinary scientific communication about embodiment and embodied learning
examples: The article suggests pairing a technical term such as embodied pedagogical dynamics with an explanatory gloss about how bodily action and perception are intentionally leveraged during instruction
key_sources: Peng Wang, Jingming Li, Qian Yu, Liye Zou, Xia Xu, Myrto Mavilidi, Ryan S. Falck, Fabian Herold, Robert J. Schinke, Markus Raab & Fred Paas. (2026). Toward a unified vocabulary for embodiment research: challenges and solutions. npj Science of Learning 11:36. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00413-x

article_title: Dissociable sensory, motor, and visuomotor predictive functions
citation: Inmaculada Márquez & Mario Treviño. (2025). Dissociable sensory, motor, and visuomotor predictive functions. npj Science of Learning 10:85. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00377-4
title: Three-task sensorimotor prediction battery (interception, detection, motor variability)
description: A battery of three joystick- and keyboard-based tasks administered to the same participants to quantify distinct components of predictive processing. As the authors write, "we developed a battery of three tasks targeting distinct com- ponents of predictive processing, all of which were performed by the same group of participants": (1) a visuomotor adaptation task with angular and speed perturbations during target interception; (2) a sensory detection task requiring judgments about brief changes in target direction or speed; and (3) a motor variability task assessing directional consistency during blindfolded joystick movements. Performance was quantified using eye movements, interception accuracy, detection accuracy, response times, and movement variability.
requirements: A calibrated computer and joystick, an eye tracker for gaze recording, and counterbalanced task order with a minimum 1-day interval between sessions.
constraints: Task sessions occurred on different days, leaving performance susceptible to shifts in internal states such as arousal or fatigue.
target_learners: adults aged 19–30 with normal or corrected-to-normal vision
target_learning_goals: measuring sensory detection, motor execution, and visuomotor adaptation
examples: Angular discrepancies were imposed by rotating joystick output by ±30° to ±180°; speed discrepancies scaled velocity to 50%–150% of joystick input.
key_sources: Inmaculada Márquez & Mario Treviño. (2025). Dissociable sensory, motor, and visuomotor predictive functions. npj Science of Learning 10:85. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00377-4

article_title: The influence of task and interpersonal interdependence on cooperative behavior and its neural mechanisms
citation: Zijun Yin, Bin Xuan, Chengchi Liu, Jingchao Yi, Xiaoyan Zheng & Mingming Zhang. (2025). The influence of task and interpersonal interdependence on cooperative behavior and its neural mechanisms. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00303-8
title: Three-dimensional structural model of social interaction behaviors (goal, interactive, and task structure)
description: The article adopts a three-dimensional structural model for dissecting social interaction behaviors, "delineating it into goal structure (cooperation versus competition), interactive structure (synchronous versus turn-based), and task structure (interdependent versus independent)". The study fixes goal structure at cooperation and interactive structure at synchronous, and varies the task-structure subdimension by contrasting high and low task interdependence within cooperation key-pressing tasks. The model thus provides the design axis along which the experimental tasks were refined.
requirements: Prior three-dimensional SIB conceptualization (Liu & Pelowski) is used to classify tasks along the three structures
constraints: The study examines only the cooperative, synchronous, interdependent subdimensions
target_learning_goals: cooperative behavior and inter-brain coordination
examples: Cooperation key-pressing tasks refined into HICT (synchronous key presses scored for response-time similarity) and LICT (individual speed against standard times)
key_sources: Zijun Yin, Bin Xuan, Chengchi Liu, Jingchao Yi, Xiaoyan Zheng & Mingming Zhang. (2025). The influence of task and interpersonal interdependence on cooperative behavior and its neural mechanisms. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00303-8

article_title: Trajectories of performance change indicate multiple dissociable links between working memory and fluid intelligence
citation: Aaron Cochrane and C. Shawn Green. (2021). Trajectories of performance change indicate multiple dissociable links between working memory and fluid intelligence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00111-w
title: Three-account framework for why aggregated WM performance correlates with fluid intelligence
description: The article frames three candidate explanations for observed links between WM and Gf: (1) Gf shares "processing constraints with WM", predicting stationary correlations; (2) Gf reflects "the ability to learn", predicting correlations with the rate of change; (3) Gf relates to performing novel tasks well "from the very ﬁrst attempt", predicting correlations with initial performance. All three, the authors note, are confounded by aggregation of performance over time.
requirements: Requires time-sensitive modeling of task performance to dissociate the three accounts, since aggregation over trials confounds them
constraints: The possibilities are described as neither exhaustive nor necessarily independent
target_learning_goals: understanding individual differences in cognitive task performance and fluid intelligence
examples: The 87-participant study tested all three accounts by modeling WM trajectories into initial accuracy, rate of change, and final accuracy components
key_sources: Aaron Cochrane and C. Shawn Green. (2021). Trajectories of performance change indicate multiple dissociable links between working memory and fluid intelligence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00111-w

article_title: The effect of low-intensity exercise on emotional and cognitive engagement in the classroom
citation: Ayame Tamura, Kou Murayama, Ryo Ishii, Michiko Sakaki and Ayumi Tanaka. (2022). The effect of low-intensity exercise on emotional and cognitive engagement in the classroom. npj Science of Learning 7:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00125-y
title: Three-minute slow aerobics programme (expert-created DVD)
description: The specific exercise artifact used in the intervention: a short slow-aerobics routine developed by experts, delivered via DVD with music. The article describes slow aerobics as combining upper limb, lower limb and trunk movements at an intensity that does not cause average heart rate to exceed 110 bpm, and notes the three-minute version was developed to encourage reasonable and habitual exercise and is practicable for people with low physical strength.
requirements: DVD and music; brief practice of body movements in initial lessons
constraints: Low-intensity by design (heart rate not exceeding 110 bpm); selected for classroom practicality rather than maximal physiological stimulus
target_learners: university students (designed also for people with relatively low physical strength)
target_learning_goals: classroom motivation and emotional engagement
examples: Participants followed the DVD through three movements (arm extensions, hip and hand shaking with overhead extension, and body-wrapping twists) in time with music
key_sources: Ayame Tamura, Kou Murayama, Ryo Ishii, Michiko Sakaki and Ayumi Tanaka. (2022). The effect of low-intensity exercise on emotional and cognitive engagement in the classroom. npj Science of Learning 7:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00125-y

article_title: Frontal midline theta transcranial alternating current stimulation enhances early consolidation of episodic memory
citation: Limor Shtoots, Asher Nadler, Roni Partouche, Dorin Sharir, Aryeh Rothstein, Liran Shati & Daniel A. Levy. (2024). Frontal midline theta transcranial alternating current stimulation enhances early consolidation of episodic memory. npj Science of Learning 9:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00222-0
title: Theta oscillatory upregulation inherently benefits early episodic memory consolidation, independent of mental-state strategies
description: The article proposes that theta-band oscillatory activity is intrinsically beneficial to early consolidation of newly formed episodic memories, likely via cortico-hippocampal communication during waking replay. Because tACS entrains neural firing "not linked with particular cognitive/affective strategies," finding a theta advantage under tACS indicates the benefit is not attributable to relaxation or attentional strategies used in prior neurofeedback work. The authors speculate that "theta entrainment might lead to greater waking replay of an encoding-related pattern of neural activity," strengthening memory representations.
requirements: Theta-frequency stimulation applied during the post-learning consolidation window, following encoding of the material to be consolidated
constraints: The study could not measure hippocampal activity, so whether effects arose from hippocampal or cortico-hippocampal modulation or other processes remains unknown
The authors acknowledge the alternative that frontal theta stimulation relaxed participants, and a quiet mind rather than direct circuit modulation benefited memory
target_learning_goals: episodic memory for studied object pictures
examples: Four groups received frontal theta, parietal theta, frontal beta, or sham stimulation for 20 min after three study-test cycles, then completed recall tests after 2 h, 24 h, and 1 week
key_sources: Limor Shtoots, Asher Nadler, Roni Partouche, Dorin Sharir, Aryeh Rothstein, Liran Shati & Daniel A. Levy. (2024). Frontal midline theta transcranial alternating current stimulation enhances early consolidation of episodic memory. npj Science of Learning 9:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00222-0

article_title: A practical implementation science framework for education
citation: Allen, S. E., Bardach, L., Jirout, J., Mackey, A., McCoy, D., Pesando, L. M., & Kizilcec, R. F. (2026). A practical implementation science framework for education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00430-w
title: Thorough Inquiry: implementation projects should continually deepen understanding of learners' needs and monitor for unforeseen issues
description: One of three complementary principles for success the article offers as a positive reframing of the failure modes. Thorough Inquiry holds that "Successful projects continually strive to gain a deep understanding of students' needs, explore multiple possible ways to meet those needs, consider the unique constraints in the local context, and closely monitor for unforeseen issues." It requires committing time and resources to understanding the problem before committing to a solution.
requirements: An intentional allocation of time and resources to understand the problem before committing to a solution
constraints: The authors state the three failure modes are more likely where time and resources are not specifically allocated in those areas
target_learners: Students and teachers in schools undergoing implementation of new practices or technologies
target_learning_goals: Selecting and sustaining interventions that genuinely meet local student learning needs
examples: The Milpitas superintendent opened the initiative by asking teachers and principals what the school of the future would look like, rather than negotiating with vendors first as the LAUSD did
key_sources: Allen, S. E., Bardach, L., Jirout, J., Mackey, A., McCoy, D., Pesando, L. M., & Kizilcec, R. F. (2026). A practical implementation science framework for education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00430-w

article_title: Design of generative AI-powered pedagogy for virtual reality environments in higher education
citation: Ulla Hemminki-Reijonen, Noha M. A. M. Hassan, Minna Huotilainen, Jaana-Maija Koivisto & Benjamin Ultan Cowley. (2025). Design of generative AI-powered pedagogy for virtual reality environments in higher education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00326-1
title: Three-step design model for GAI-powered characters in IVR
description: The article's Pedagogical Design answer to RQ2 is a three-step design model integrating pedagogy with GAI and VR: "selecting the applicable reference framework, identifying the learning objectives and the instructional methods that could be feasible in IVR, and designing the GAI characters." It was applied in a sustainability education context, grounding character design in the refined sustainability competence framework and producing the Tero and Madida use cases. The authors present it as how AI technologies, learning content, and pedagogical approaches "can be integrated having the form of a pedagogical GAI character in IVR."
requirements: A reference framework covering the needed competencies with learning objectives and instructional methods
Iterative prompt engineering with domain-expert testing of the designed characters
constraints: The model covers only the Needs Analysis and Pedagogical Design phases; Development, Evaluation, and Reflection phases were beyond the report's scope
target_learning_goals: sustainability systems-thinking and values-thinking competencies
examples: Applied to design Tero, a forest-owner character for interviewing (Fact Finding in participatory modelling), and Madida, a companion for the backcasting exercise

article_title: Helping children with reading difficulties: some things we have learned so far
citation: Genevieve McArthur and Anne Castles. (2017). Helping children with reading difficulties: some things we have learned so far. npj Science of Learning (2017) 2:7. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0008-3
title: Assess reading behaviours, proximal causes, and comorbidities before designing an individualised intervention
description: The article recommends a three-step assessment sequence that exploits heterogeneity rather than despairing of it. Practitioners first assess different aspects of reading (word reading accuracy, fluency, comprehension) with standardized tests, then test potential proximal causes using cognitive models as a roadmap, and finally assess comorbid spoken language, attention, anxiety, depression, and self-concept problems. The resulting profile makes it possible to design an intervention matched to the child's needs, targeting proximal impairments while accommodating comorbidities.
requirements: Teachers need appropriate training in administering the standardized reading and cognitive tests, and specialists (speech and language therapists, neuropsychologists, clinical psychologists) are needed for comorbidity assessment.
constraints: The article bases this approach on evidence "thus far", describing it as tentative and requiring coordinated efforts of teachers, specialists and parents.
target_learning_goals: word reading accuracy
reading fluency
reading comprehension
examples: The article names commercially available and free tests for each step, including the York Assessment for Reading Comprehension, the Castles and Coltheart Word Reading Test (CC2), the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test, and the Letter-Sound Test available at www.motif.org.au.
key_sources: Genevieve McArthur and Anne Castles. (2017). Helping children with reading difficulties: some things we have learned so far. npj Science of Learning (2017) 2:7. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0008-3

article_title: Toward an understanding of when prior knowledge helps or hinders learning
citation: Garvin Brod. (2021). Toward an understanding of when prior knowledge helps or hinders learning. npj Science of Learning 6:24. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00103-w
title: A hierarchical three-determinant framework of when prior knowledge helps or hinders learning
description: The article proposes that whether and how prior knowledge affects learning depends on three determinants: whether it is activated, whether it is relevant, and whether it is congruent with the to-be-learned content. These are arranged hierarchically in Figure 1, so relevance only matters once knowledge is activated, and congruency only once knowledge is activated and relevant. The determinants are dichotomies meant as "the extreme ends of one scale/dimension", all acting at an intra-individual level.
requirements: Prior knowledge must be activated (retrieved from memory) before it can affect learning at all
constraints: The determinants are intra-individual; inter-individual and environmental determinants such as age or intervention duration are not considered
The dichotomies are the extreme ends of one scale/dimension, not true categories
target_learners: school and adult learners generally, as discussed across cited memory and conceptual-change research
target_learning_goals: acquisition of new domain knowledge in instruction
examples: Figure 1 maps combinations: not activated → negligible effects; activated but irrelevant → negligible or hindering via intrusions; activated, relevant, incongruent → mostly hindering; only activated, relevant, congruent knowledge reliably helps
key_sources: Garvin Brod. (2021). Toward an understanding of when prior knowledge helps or hinders learning. npj Science of Learning 6:24. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00103-w

article_title: Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives
citation: Mizoguchi, R., & Bourdeau, J. (2015). Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0077-5
title: Three-level ontology engineering methodology anchored in a top-level ontology (YAMATO)
description: The article's methodology evolved from a three-layer model (common vocabulary, formal definition of concepts, operational building blocks such as task ontology) into an approach anchored on YAMATO, a top-level ontology released in 2010. Anchoring ensures specification of the most abstract basic concepts such as event, process and system, and the authors claim it "provides a common vocabulary, and on the scientific level, it allows for refutation or discussion at the most abstract and even philosophical level". OMNIBUS was reoriented under this constraint.
requirements: Ontologies must be related to a top-level ontology
target_learning_goals: Building interoperable, refutable conceptual foundations for AIED systems
examples: Mizoguchi's YAMATO top-level ontology and the later MAUOC ontology of culture were both built with reference to this anchoring principle
key_sources: Mizoguchi, R., & Bourdeau, J. (2015). Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0077-5

article_title: Intelligent Tutoring Systems by and for the Developing World: A Review of Trends and Approaches for Educational Technology in a Global Context
citation: Benjamin D. Nye. (2015). Intelligent Tutoring Systems by and for the Developing World: A Review of Trends and Approaches for Educational Technology in a Global Context. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0028-6
title: Three stakeholder patterns for developing-world ITS: transferred, home-grown, and new systems designed for a target region
description: The article observes three patterns among reviewed papers, depending on stakeholders. In the first, an established ITS from a higher-income country is transferred and localized for less developed countries; these tend to be mature with numerous evaluations. The second is a home-grown system developed by researchers in a developing region targeting local or national needs. The third is a new system designed predominantly in a most-developed country but intended for a less developed area, grouped with transfers due to low numbers.
requirements: Transferred and collaborative systems depend on stakeholders from both a high-income country and a lower-income country
constraints: The review found collaborations and transfers addressed mobile platforms and data costs in none of the reviewed papers, while home-grown ITS more often addressed mobile platforms, data costs, and student basic ICT skills
target_learners: learners in developing regions served by transferred or locally developed tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: delivery of adaptive tutoring suited to local infrastructure, language, and culture
examples: Examples of transferred/collaborative ITS were Cognitive Tutor in Latin America, the LISTEN Reading Tutor in Africa, the Single Display Groupware system, and the Braille Tutor; home-grown ITS were most strongly represented by China, India, and Mexico
key_sources: Benjamin D. Nye. (2015). Intelligent Tutoring Systems by and for the Developing World: A Review of Trends and Approaches for Educational Technology in a Global Context. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0028-6

article_title: Against Personalised Learning
citation: Caroline Pelletier. (2023). Against Personalised Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2024) 34:111–115. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00348-z
title: Three political-philosophical questions AI education research should answer about personalisation
description: The commentary proposes that AI research in education should provide 'nuanced, thoughtful and empirically-grounded responses' to three historically central educational questions: what the purpose of education is; what vision of a better world education sustains; and how education practises equality as a political claim, understood as self-determination rather than indoctrination. It argues AI has been treated as a mere technique, which 'has the effect of de-politicising education'.
requirements: Researchers and teachers treating questions of purpose as within their remit, since teaching or research invokes a sense of purpose.
constraints: The author does not claim everyone should have clear and categorical answers; the questions are offered to trouble assumptions and open possibilities.
target_learners: teacher educators and MA students in education and technology
target_learning_goals: critical examination of the purposes and political commitments of educational technology research
examples: The commentary returns to the three standard claims about personalised learning to illustrate how each question troubles their assumptions.
key_sources: Caroline Pelletier. (2023). Against Personalised Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2024) 34:111–115. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00348-z

article_title: Mapping Artificial Intelligence in Education Research: a Network-based Keyword Analysis
citation: Shihui Feng & Nancy Law. (2021). Mapping Artificial Intelligence in Education Research: A Network-based Keyword Analysis. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 277–303. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00244-4
title: Three-step multi-scale (macro, meso, micro) framework for analyzing keyword co-occurrence networks of a research field
description: The article proposes a network-based review method that analyzes keyword co-occurrence networks at three levels: macro-level distribution of keyword structural importance, meso-level community detection of knowledge clusters, and micro-level identification of trending and bridging keywords. As the authors state, "A novel three-step approach in the analysis of the keyword co-occurrence networks (KCN) is proposed to identify the knowledge structure, knowledge clusters and trending keywords within AIED over time." Temporal KCNs on two-year windows support evolution analysis. The authors argue the framework generalizes beyond AIED.
requirements: A corpus of keyworded articles from a field, standardized keywords, and construction of undirected weighted KCNs with fast-greedy modularity clustering
constraints: Applied and demonstrated on the AIED literature from 2010 to 2019
target_learners: researchers mapping the development of a scientific field
target_learning_goals: understanding knowledge structure, clusters, and trends of a research field
examples: Applied to 1830 AIED articles from five publication sources, with five temporal KCNs each covering a two-year window
key_sources: Shihui Feng & Nancy Law. (2021). Mapping Artificial Intelligence in Education Research: A Network-based Keyword Analysis. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 277–303. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00244-4

article_title: Different Topics, Similar Patterns: The Consistency of Learners and Learning Across Interactive STEM Simulations
citation: Jade Mai Cock · Ido Roll · Käser Tanja. (2025). Different Topics, Similar Patterns: The Consistency of Learners and Learning Across Interactive STEM Simulations. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00512-7
title: Three-paradigm feature-abstraction framework with spectral clustering for cross-topic inquiry-pattern analysis
description: The article presents a clustering framework to analyze log data from interactive simulations under three levels of topic abstraction: variable (simulation-specific qualification by independent variable), relationship (qualification by the nature of the variable–outcome relationship, generalizable across isomorphic simulations), and focus (simulation-agnostic qualification by number of involved variables). Sequences are transformed into Markov transition matrices and clustered with spectral clustering, which handles non-convex data. The framework aims to "identify productive inquiry patterns without relying on predefined behavior assumptions" and to offer insight into the trade-offs between topic-agnostic and context-rich representations.
requirements: Log data retaining timestamps and the simulation elements learners interact with, so interactions can be extracted into chronological action sequences.
Sufficient interaction log coverage per learner to build a transition matrix for each simulation activity.
constraints: The relationship paradigm is only generalizable across isomorphic simulations with similar types of relationships between independent and dependent variables.
The focus paradigm is very coarse and mainly captures context switching between variables.
Break thresholds were data driven (3s merge, 20s break) for these two labs and may not transfer to other environments.
target_learning_goals: Scientific inquiry skills such as forming hypotheses, collecting and interpreting data, and uncovering relationships between variables in interactive simulations
examples: Applied to Beer's Law Lab and Capacitor Lab logs: sequences were encoded per paradigm, transformed into transition matrices, and clustered with spectral clustering using k-means, yielding two clusters per lab with optimal nc = 2 and gamma = 10^-4.
key_sources: Jade Mai Cock · Ido Roll · Käser Tanja. (2025). Different Topics, Similar Patterns: The Consistency of Learners and Learning Across Interactive STEM Simulations. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00512-7

article_title: Short-Answer Grading for German: Addressing the Challenges
citation: Ulrike Padó, Yunus Eryilmaz, Larissa Kirschner. (2024). Short-Answer Grading for German: Addressing the Challenges. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00383-w
title: Three-challenge framework for broad-scale adoption of automated short-answer grading: technical, usability, and trust
description: The article organizes the barriers to classroom adoption of automated short-answer grading into three challenges: "A technical challenge regarding the need for high-quality models, which is exacerbated for languages with fewer resources than English; a usability challenge in adapting high-quality research prototypes to the needs of non-expert users, and a trust challenge in communicating the abilities and limitations of the tools." The framework draws on the Technology Acceptance Model and usability research, and structures the paper's contributions: a German Transformer model, the ASYST interface, and a hybrid human-machine grading workflow.
requirements: Meeting the trust challenge requires users' understanding of tool capabilities and preserved teacher agency, per Nazaretsky et al. as the article reports
constraints: Technical quality is harder for languages with fewer training resources than English
target_learners: teachers using automated grading tools in classrooms
target_learning_goals: adoption of reliable, usable, and trusted automated grading support
examples: The paper addresses each challenge in turn with German data as the instantiation: model training and evaluation, the ASYST GUI, and the automated grading workflow
key_sources: Ulrike Padó, Yunus Eryilmaz, Larissa Kirschner. (2024). Short-Answer Grading for German: Addressing the Challenges. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00383-w

article_title: SMILI☺: a Framework for Interfaces to Learning Data in Open Learner Models, Learning Analytics and Related Fields
citation: Susan Bull & Judy Kay. (2016). SMILI☺: a Framework for Interfaces to Learning Data in Open Learner Models, Learning Analytics and Related Fields. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0090-8
title: Three classes of learner model: cognitive, pragmatic and data-intensive
description: The article identifies three important classes of learner model. The earliest days saw a dichotomy between cognitive and pragmatic learner models; more recently a third class of data-intensive, automatically generated models has emerged that harnesses large bodies of learning data. Despite this diversity, there is "a consistent view of the learner model as a dynamic representation of the learner's knowledge (lack of it, misconceptions and similar) as it evolves through the learning interactions". The representation requires two key elements: an ontology for the aspects to be modelled, and a means to use learning data to infer what the learner knows.
requirements: A learner model representation requires an ontology for the aspects to be modelled and a means to use learning data, as it becomes available, to infer what the learner knows.
target_learners: learners in intelligent tutoring systems and adaptive learning environments
target_learning_goals: personalised learning through accurate learner modelling
key_sources: Susan Bull & Judy Kay. (2016). SMILI☺: a Framework for Interfaces to Learning Data in Open Learner Models, Learning Analytics and Related Fields. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0090-8

article_title: Scaling Academic Writing Instruction: Evaluation of a Scaffolding Tool (Thesis Writer)
citation: Rapp, C., & Kauf, P. E. (2018). Scaling academic writing instruction: evaluation of a scaffolding tool (Thesis Writer). International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0162-z
title: Thesis Writer (TW): domain-specific online scaffolding environment with an academic-text editor
description: Thesis Writer is described as "a domain-specific, online learning environment for the scaffolding of student academic writing, combined with an online editor optimized for producing academic text." It targets theses and research article writing using the IMRD scheme rather than the essay genre, and unlike automated essay scoring tools it focuses on "instruction, planning, and genre mastery" rather than feedback. It was evaluated with first-year business administration students writing research proposals.
requirements: Used for domain-specific academic writing tasks such as research proposals and theses
constraints: Tailored to thesis and research article writing (IMRD scheme), not the essay genre
target_learning_goals: academic writing
research proposal writing
genre mastery
examples: Test run with a first-year course of 102 business administration students writing research proposals
key_sources: Rapp, C., & Kauf, P. E. (2018). Scaling academic writing instruction: evaluation of a scaffolding tool (Thesis Writer). International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0162-z

article_title: Commentary on: “Toward Computer-Based Support of MetaCognitive Skills: a Computational Framework to Coach Self Explanation”
citation: Conati, C. (2016). Commentary on: “Toward Computer-Based Support of MetaCognitive Skills: a Computational Framework to Coach Self Explanation”. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0074-8
title: Three-level incremental scaffolding for self-explanation: masking interface, uncovered-step prompts, and menu-based explanation tools
description: The SE-Coach delivers "incremental guidance" via "three levels of scaffolding": (i) a masking interface requiring students to mouse over each solution step to see it, helping focus attention; (ii) explicit self-explain prompts next to each uncovered step; and (iii) menu-based tools offering "constructive but controllable ways to generate the different types of explanations relevant for a solution step". The philosophy is to provide guidance to self-explanation incrementally, interfering as little as possible with spontaneous behaviors.
requirements: Menu-based tool explanations are evaluated for correctness against the information contained in the solution graph
constraints: Students with low tendency for self-explanation may not be receptive to interface scaffolding alone and may need more direct tutorial interventions
target_learning_goals: self-explanation of worked-out example solutions
key_sources: Conati, C. (2016). Commentary on: “Toward Computer-Based Support of MetaCognitive Skills: a Computational Framework to Coach Self Explanation”. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0074-8

article_title: Preface to Special Issue on User Modelling to Support Personalization in Enhanced Educational Settings
citation: Olga C. Santos, Milos Kravcik, Jesus G. Boticario. (2016). Preface to Special Issue on User Modelling to Support Personalization in Enhanced Educational Settings. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:809–820. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0114-z
title: Three-aspect taxonomy of user modelling research for personalization in learning environments
description: The article organizes personalization research in learning environments into three main areas, derived from analysing 39 PALE workshop contributions: "1) modelling learners and their performance to provide engaging learning experiences, 2) designing adaptive support, and 3) building standards-based models to cope with interoperability and portability". The first area covers modelling affective states, confusion, self-regulation, reputation and open learner models; the second covers adaptive study plans, hints, recommendations and educator involvement; the third covers standards such as IMS LIP, IMS RDCEO and IMS AFA. The four special-issue papers are each situated within one of these aspects.
requirements: Suitable user models that deal with the evolving nature of learner's current needs
target_learners: learners in technology-enhanced educational settings across formal and informal contexts
target_learning_goals: effective, active, efficient and satisfactory learning through personalization
examples: The special issue maps Ghergulescu and Muntean and Janning et al. to aspect 1, Dennis et al. to aspect 2, and Valdés Aguirre et al. to aspect 3.
key_sources: Olga C. Santos, Milos Kravcik, Jesus G. Boticario. (2016). Preface to Special Issue on User Modelling to Support Personalization in Enhanced Educational Settings. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:809–820. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0114-z

article_title: Negotiating Meaning with Machines: AI’s Role in Doctoral Writing Pedagogy
citation: Jessica L. Parker, Veronica M. Richard, Alexandra Acabá, Sierra Escoffier, Stephen Flaherty, Shannon Jablonka, Kimberly P. Becker. (2025). Negotiating Meaning with Machines: AI's Role in Doctoral Writing Pedagogy. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00425-x
title: Three-step AI discussion prompt (original response, AI interaction, comparison and revision decision)
description: A discussion-board structure created by the professor in which step one is the original pre-AI discussion task, step two asks students to "Interact with an LLM like ChatGPT to check your responses", and step three asks students to compare their observations with the AI's insights and decide whether to change their original responses, explaining why. Steps two and three were not graded to encourage honesty. The prompt frames AI as "a tool to facilitate self-reflection and critical thinking" rather than an authority.
requirements: Each discussion prompt modified to include the three steps; students must explain any decision to change their original response
constraints: Steps two and three were ungraded in this course to encourage honesty and transparency
target_learners: first-year doctoral students in a Doctor of Healthcare Administration program
target_learning_goals: academic argument structure, critical reading, revision and editing, self-reflection on writing
examples: Sample prompt in Table 2 asks students to identify reporting verbs and transition words, check their answers with ChatGPT, then compare and justify revisions

article_title: The Use of Large Language Models in Education
citation: Wanli Xing, Nia Nixon, Scott Crossley, Paul Denny, Andrew Lan, John Stamper, Zhou Yu. (2025). The Use of Large Language Models in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00457-x
title: Three-strand framework for research on LLMs in education
description: The editorial organizes special-issue research on LLMs in education into three strands. The first applies open-source and proprietary LLMs to streamline educational tasks "such as feedback analysis and automated grading, mainly through diverse prompting strategies"; the second focuses on fine-tuning and pretraining LLMs for specific educational environments; the third focuses on enhancing adaptive digital learning environments with LLMs. The framework maps how LLM integration moves from off-the-shelf prompting toward domain adaptation and adaptive learning support.
requirements: Research investigating the use of LLMs in educational contexts, addressing deployment challenges and opportunities, to fill the strands
constraints: The editorial notes little is known empirically about learning experience design of LLM-enabled applications, and that LLMs trained on broad, non-specialized datasets may generate irrelevant or inaccurate outputs for specific educational tasks
target_learning_goals: feedback and assessment processes
adaptive support for self-regulated learning
domain-specific learning in mathematics and reading
examples: The editorial assigns Parker et al. and Lin et al. to the prompting strand, Morris et al., Zhang et al., and Acosta et al. to the fine-tuning strand, and Norberg et al. and Goslen et al. to the adaptive environments strand
key_sources: Wanli Xing, Nia Nixon, Scott Crossley, Paul Denny, Andrew Lan, John Stamper, Zhou Yu. (2025). The Use of Large Language Models in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00457-x

article_title: Detecting and Addressing Frustration in a Serious Game for Military Training
citation: DeFalco, J. A., Rowe, J. P., Paquette, L., Georgoulas-Sherry, V., Brawner, K., Mott, B. W., Baker, R. S., & Lester, J. C. (2018). Detecting and Addressing Frustration in a Serious Game for Military Training. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0152-1
title: Theory-based motivational feedback design for addressing learner frustration in military training
description: The article designs frustration interventions using motivationally designed feedback messages grounded in three theoretical constructs chosen for the military population: control-value theory (indicating the value of the activity), social identity theory (targeting military identity), and self-efficacy theory (supporting learners' ability to achieve goals through effort). Grounded in Amsel's frustration theory, the approach favors helping learners "recover, manage, and persist" through frustration rather than removing its source or giving explicit corrective feedback. Messages were also designed to be fail-soft, minimizing negative impact if triggered by a detector false positive.
requirements: Messages should be meaningful, relevant, and support goal-oriented efforts
Interventions selected with the goal of being fail-soft against detector false positives
constraints: Theoretical constructs were selected to reflect the unique profile of the target population, USMA cadets
target_learners: US Army combat medics and combat lifesavers in tactical combat casualty care training
target_learning_goals: Tactical combat casualty care skills including hemorrhage control and care under fire
Persisting through frustration during game-based training
examples: Experiment 2 tested control-value, social identity, self-efficacy, non-motivational, and no-message conditions with 124 cadets in TC3Sim via GIFT
key_sources: DeFalco, J. A., Rowe, J. P., Paquette, L., Georgoulas-Sherry, V., Brawner, K., Mott, B. W., Baker, R. S., & Lester, J. C. (2018). Detecting and Addressing Frustration in a Serious Game for Military Training. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0152-1

article_title: Research–practice interactions as reported in recent design studies: still promising, still hazy
citation: Ormel, B. J. B., Pareja Roblin, N. N., McKenney, S. E., Voogt, J. M., & Pieters, J. M. (2012). Research–practice interactions as reported in recent design studies: still promising, still hazy. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-012-9261-6
title: Three sources of knowledge inform the design of instructional solutions: literature, project data, and practical knowledge
description: The article distinguishes "three sources of knowledge that we see are commonly used to inform the design of solutions, often in combination with one another: literature, project data, practical knowledge". Literature-based design builds upon theory and/or evidence found in literature; data-driven design is steered by empirical findings from field investigation during project development; and practical knowledge-informed design incorporates the wide range of insights and knowledge about research, design, teaching, learning and schooling. This framework is used to map all 18 reviewed projects in a Venn diagram according to the sources said to have informed the (re)designed product.
requirements: Sources must be said to have informed the (re)designed product, not merely gathered as research data
constraints: The sources in Fig. 1 do not represent all the data gathered in the studies but only those sources which were said to have informed the (re)designed product
target_learning_goals: designing instructional solutions informed by research
examples: Only two projects clearly indicated that they used all three sources of knowledge to inform their work: Flannery and Pragman (2008) and Gu et al. (2009).
key_sources: Ormel, B. J. B., Pareja Roblin, N. N., McKenney, S. E., Voogt, J. M., & Pieters, J. M. (2012). Research–practice interactions as reported in recent design studies: still promising, still hazy. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-012-9261-6

article_title: Enhancing self-regulated learning in online environments: challenges and opportunities for recommender system algorithms
citation: Long Zhang, Khe Foon Hew & Gulipari Maimaiti. (2026). Enhancing self-regulated learning in online environments: challenges and opportunities for recommender system algorithms. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10618-x
title: Three-level analytical framework for analyzing SRL-promoting recommender systems
description: The article develops a three-tiered analytical framework that considers challenges in three areas: data and experiments, user experience/interface design, and technical factors. It uses this framework to systematically examine foundational recommendation methods, their integration into comprehensive systems, and the experimental validation of their effectiveness for supporting SRL in online environments.
requirements: Applied to recommender systems that provide clear guidance or advice to the user for at least one specific SRL (sub)strategy
constraints: Challenges related to experimental design such as participant recruitment and content alignment are outside the scope of system design and implementation
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
