article_title: Weaving in: shifts in youth mathematical engagement through weaving
citation: Thompson, N. (2024). Weaving in: shifts in youth mathematical engagement through weaving. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10316-y
title: Three instantiations of mathematics in weaving: arithmetic and calculations, image and shape transformations, and multiple embedded patternings
description: A taxonomy from the author's prior work with experienced weavers, describing three simultaneous, overlapping mathematical instantiations that emerge through weaving practice. The article states: "These instantiations are (1) arithmetic and calculations, (2) image and shape transformations, and (3) multiple embedded patternings." Image and shape transformations deal with designing with regard to space, shape, proportion, symmetry, while multiple embedded patternings encompasses invention and experimentation with patterns, sequences, and structure. The current study operationalizes two of these instantiations to analyze youth artifacts.
requirements: Prior work with experienced weavers (Thompson, 2022) that identified the three instantiations
constraints: The current study operationalizes only two of the three instantiations: image and shape transformations and multiple embedded patternings
target_learning_goals: mathematical engagement through making
pattern and shape reasoning
key_sources: Thompson, N. (2024). Weaving in: shifts in youth mathematical engagement through weaving. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10316-y

article_title: Supporting struggling readers with digital game-based learning
citation: Ronimus, M., Eklund, K., Pesu, L., & Lyytinen, H. (2019). Supporting struggling readers with digital game-based learning. Education Tech Research Dev, 67, 639–663. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09658-3
title: Three-component engagement framework (behavioral, cognitive, emotional) applied to game-based learning
description: The article applies Fredricks et al.'s (2004) three-component engagement framework to game-based reading training. Behavioral engagement is defined as observable behaviors such as attentiveness and persistence; cognitive engagement covers "internal investment in learning, that is, the learner's efforts and persistence in attempting to understand and master the given tasks"; emotional engagement refers to positive and negative emotions experienced during the activity. In this study, behavioral engagement was operationalized as exposure time from game logs, cognitive and emotional engagement were measured via child self-reports and parent/teacher evaluations, and in-game success rate was used as a potential mediator between engagement and learning.
requirements: Because self-report measures are problematic with young children, the study used both self-report measures and teachers' and parents' evaluations
constraints: Engagement was assessed only at posttest in a small intervention sample
target_learning_goals: word reading
reading fluency
examples: The study measured engagement with five-item self-report scales (alphas .79 and .69) and parent/teacher online surveys (alphas .77 and .82), plus log-based exposure time
key_sources: Ronimus, M., Eklund, K., Pesu, L., & Lyytinen, H. (2019). Supporting struggling readers with digital game-based learning. Education Tech Research Dev, 67, 639–663. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09658-3

article_title: Tracking public opinion about online education over COVID-19 in China
citation: Mingming Zhou, Hao Mou. (2022). Tracking public opinion about online education over COVID-19 in China. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10080-5
title: Threefold typology of Chinese public opinion profiles toward online education across pandemic phases: affirmative, achievement-based, and critical users
description: The article proposes a typology of public opinion profiles derived from LDA topic modeling of Weibo microblogs across the three pandemic phases. Before the pandemic, users were profiled as "affirmative" because the positive tone in both topics confirmed online education's power to help level up life standards. During the pandemic, when online education became a dominant mode, users were profiled as "achievement-based", concerned with curriculum design and learning effectiveness. After the pandemic, users were profiled as "critical", attending to socio-political consequences, life impacts, and technological aspects.
requirements: LDA topic modeling with perplexity-based selection of the optimal number of topics per phase (2, 4, and 7 topics respectively)
constraints: The authors caution that topics obtained through LDA might not be optimal and that different hyperparameters could have generated more coherent topics
target_learners: Chinese general public discussing online education on Weibo
K-12 and higher education students and their families
target_learning_goals: Understanding public perceptions and acceptance of online learning modes during emergency remote teaching
examples: LDA analysis identified 2 topics pre-pandemic, 4 amid-pandemic, and 7 post-pandemic, with the top 15 tokens per topic translated and thematically integrated into the three profiles
key_sources: Mingming Zhou, Hao Mou. (2022). Tracking public opinion about online education over COVID-19 in China. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10080-5

article_title: DUDA: a digital didactic learning unit based on educational escape rooms and multisensory learning activities for primary school children during COVID-19 lockdown
citation: Walter Setti, Rebecca Tarello, Erica Volta, Lucia Ferlino, Monica Gori, Gualtiero Volpe. (2025). DUDA: a digital didactic learning unit based on educational escape rooms and multisensory learning activities for primary school children during COVID-19 lockdown. Education Tech Research Dev 73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10407-4
title: Three-dimensional construct of student engagement (behavioral, emotional, cognitive)
description: The article adopts the framework that engagement is a multidimensional construct underpinning academic success. As printed: "Scholarly discourse further delineates engagement as a complex construct, comprising three essential dimensions: behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement (Fredricks et al., 2004)." Behavioral engagement covers participation in academic, social, or extracurricular pursuits; emotional engagement covers attitudes toward teachers, peers, academics, and school; cognitive engagement entails thoughtful effort with intricate concepts. D-UDA's multisensory group activities were designed to enhance behavioral engagement and teamwork.
requirements: Motivation is treated as a prerequisite of students' engagement in learning
target_learning_goals: Behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement in learning activities
examples: D-UDA's cooperative multisensory games were chosen to highlight effects on teamwork and potential to enhance students' behavioral engagement
key_sources: Walter Setti, Rebecca Tarello, Erica Volta, Lucia Ferlino, Monica Gori, Gualtiero Volpe. (2025). DUDA: a digital didactic learning unit based on educational escape rooms and multisensory learning activities for primary school children during COVID-19 lockdown. Education Tech Research Dev 73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10407-4

article_title: Designing and using digital platforms for 21st century learning
citation: Meier, E. B. (2021). Designing and using digital platforms for 21st century learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09880-4
title: Theory of change perspective for evaluating online learning design heuristics
description: The article applies a "theory of change" lens to review the Nacu et al. heuristic for educator learning-support roles in networked technologies. It frames the heuristic as one component within a larger system: platforms must address twenty-first century learning goals and support equitable access, and a theory of change could identify the critical variables needed for teachers and designers to transition to student-centered online learning. The framework positions online learning as a knowledge-building environment rather than a delivery channel.
requirements: A holistic approach that repositions online learning as a knowledge-building environment
constraints: Heuristics alone do not prepare designers or teachers to enact this work
target_learning_goals: pursue their interests and take ownership of their learning

article_title: Developing digital formative assessment for deep conceptual learning goals: Which topic-specific research gaps need to be closed?
citation: Hankeln, C., Kroehne, U., Voss, L., Gross, S., & Prediger, S. (2025). Developing digital formative assessment for deep conceptual learning goals: Which topic-specific research gaps need to be closed? Education Tech Research Dev, 73, 1953–1973. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10486-x
title: Three quality criteria for digital formative assessment of deep conceptual understanding: relevance, validity, and in-depth informativity
description: The article proposes that a DFA for deep conceptual understanding must fulfill three criteria: relevance (focusing on the most relevant components of a topic), validity (appropriateness of inferences, including actionable diagnostic information for teachers), and in-depth informativity (combining in-depth insights into student thinking with automatable analysis). These criteria structure the four-step design process and are summarized in Fig. 5.
requirements: Prior to item construction, epistemological and empirical research in the subject-matter area is required to unpack topics into the most relevant concept elements
constraints: The digital assessment of deep conceptual understanding is more challenging to realize than the digital assessment of procedural skills
target_learners: Grade 5–7 students who struggle in mathematics
target_learning_goals: Deep conceptual understanding of basic arithmetic concepts

Developing digital formative assessment for deep conceptual learning goals: Which topic-specific research gaps need to be closed? article_title: Measuring learning in serious games: a case study with structural assessment
citation: Wouters, P., van der Spek, E. D., & van Oostendorp, H. (2011). Measuring learning in serious games: A case study with structural assessment. Educational Technology Research and Development, 59(6), 741–763. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9183-0
title: Three-step structural assessment process: elicitation, representation, evaluation
description: The article distinguishes three consecutive steps to implement a structural approach to measure and interpret knowledge structures. Knowledge elicitation captures the underlying organization of knowledge through methods such as card sorting or rating relatedness between concept pairs. Knowledge representation transforms ratings into a graphical network. Knowledge evaluation compares the learner's structure with a referent knowledge structure using similarity or coherence measures.
requirements: Selection of important domain concepts through cognitive task analysis, instructional material analysis, or expert interviews
A referent knowledge structure derived from an instructor, an expert, or an analysis of instructional material
target_learning_goals: Assessment of knowledge organization in complex-skill domains

article_title: Connecting sustainability and computer science curricula through website learning projects embedding different types of student-generated content
citation: Blanco, J. M., Domínguez, C., Jaime, A., & Usandizaga, I. (2024). Connecting sustainability and computer science curricula through website learning projects embedding different types of student-generated content. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10376-8
title: A three-project progression (video → channel → website) where students create, review, and reuse peer-generated content about SDG topics.
description: The article describes a "series of three learning projects whose outcome is content addressing the computer engineering profession and its relationship to SDGs". Students first create a video on a specific SDG, then create derivative videos in a shared channel, and finally build a multilingual website integrating content from previous projects and peers. The design embeds "the exchange of information and the sharing of opinions" through teamwork and progressive content building.
requirements: Instructor-provided presentation documents and materials
Video channel and website hosting infrastructure
Team-based work with 3–8 members per project
constraints: SDG-related content is "not assessed in exams or other tests, and is used purely for formative assessment"
Time-constrained: video and channel projects last 3 weeks each, website project lasts 8 weeks
target_learning_goals: Project management skills
Understanding of the impact of ICT on Sustainable Development Goals
examples: Teams of three or four students produced a video on one SDG in three weeks; later teams of six to eight built a multilingual website with videos, web articles, and self-assessment questionnaires organised by SDG.
key_sources: Blanco, J. M., Domínguez, C., Jaime, A., & Usandizaga, I. (2024). Connecting sustainability and computer science curricula through website learning projects embedding different types of student-generated content. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10376-8

article_title: Validation of a peer observation and evaluation tool for online teaching in the U.S.
citation: Jia, Y., Spagnolo, A. B., Barrett, N., Murphy, A. A., Basto, P. M., Rothpletz-Puglia, P., & Luther, S. (2025). Validation of a peer observation and evaluation tool for online teaching in the U.S. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10428-z
title: Three models of teaching observation: evaluation, developmental, and collaborative
description: The article describes "three models of teaching observation—evaluation, developmental, and collaborative—are commonly recognized in the literature (Yiend et al., 2014)." The evaluation model is managerial and judgmental, overseeing teaching quality for compliance. The developmental model is less judgmental and more formative, involving an educational expert as observer. The collaborative model, also formative, entails mutual observation between academic colleagues. The POET-O assumes the collaborative model with the purpose of improving teaching through constructive dialogue.
constraints: The article notes the collaborative model "in nature has a greater chance of ongoing success" per Fletcher (2018)
target_learning_goals: understanding frameworks for peer review of teaching
key_sources: Jia, Y., Spagnolo, A. B., Barrett, N., Murphy, A. A., Basto, P. M., Rothpletz-Puglia, P., & Luther, S. (2025). Validation of a peer observation and evaluation tool for online teaching in the U.S. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10428-z

article_title: Toward a Learning Technologies knowledge network
citation: Roy D. Pea, Robert Tinker, Marcia Linn, Barbara Means, John Bransford, Jeremy Roschelle, Sherry Hsi, Sean Brophy, Nancy B. Songer. (1999). Toward a Learning Technologies Knowledge Network. title: Theme-team workshops as a mechanism for spawning cross-institution research partnerships
description: A reusable organizational pattern in which national workshops convene experts around designated theme areas, and the collaborations formed there are converted into funded partnership projects across institutions. The article reports "first-year progress in d+ning a set of CILT partnership projects with many other institutions that came out $our national theme-team workshops." The pattern links agenda-setting (choosing themes where research is likely to yield major gains) to concrete multi-institution projects.

Designated theme areas to focus the workshops
constraints: Applied at the level of a national research center coordinating many institutions

examples: CILT's first-year partnership projects with many other institutions, which came out of its national theme-team workshops

article_title: AI-enhanced legal pedagogy: a case study of generative AI integration in property law courses
citation: Haifang Liu. (2026). AI-enhanced legal pedagogy: a case study of generative AI integration in property law courses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10698-9
title: Three-phase instructional workflow with iFlytek Spark in property law sessions
description: Each class session during the 16-week intervention followed a three-phase workflow (Fig. 2): pre-AI preparation, in which the instructor presents a case scenario and students draft an initial analysis independently; AI interaction, in which students submit to iFlytek Spark, compare with their own draft, engage in iterative dialogue and follow-up probing, and integrate AI feedback; and post-AI reflection, with whole-class discussion evaluating AI versus student analysis and a reflection journal entry documenting the reasoning process. The design operationalizes the constructivist scaffolding rationale of the intervention.
requirements: Students submit only hypothetical case scenarios and avoid personally identifiable information, per the study's data governance measures
constraints: The workflow was implemented with iFlytek Spark, a Chinese-language commercial platform selected for language appropriateness, ease of use, and compatibility with national data governance norms
target_learners: third-year law students in property law courses
target_learning_goals: legal reasoning
iterative analysis refinement
metacognitive awareness of reasoning processes
examples: Figure 6 shows a representative student revision trajectory across three successive AI exchanges, moving from initial draft to multi-perspective analysis acknowledging legal weakness
key_sources: Haifang Liu. (2026). AI-enhanced legal pedagogy: a case study of generative AI integration in property law courses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10698-9

article_title: Computational thinking beyond coding: exploring student computational practices while playing and modifying a socio-scientific simulation game with integrated computational tools
citation: Marianthi Grizioti. (2025). Computational thinking beyond coding: exploring student computational practices while playing and modifying a socio-scientific simulation game with integrated computational tools. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10477-y
title: Three-axis framework for CT in socio-scientific contexts: computational tools, engagement process and content
description: The article proposes a framework organizing the development of computational literacy around three axes. The first concerns the representational tools provided to learners, where the study introduced "multiple interconnected representations" combining data handling, map-based interface and coding. The second concerns the engagement process and learner roles, scaffolded by the three-stage PFO model. The third concerns content, integrating societal and scientific aspects of the simulated issue to support critical computational thinking. The themes and codes are offered as guidelines for designing CT activities and evaluation instruments.
requirements: Tools must interconnect multiple computational affordances beyond coding, such as databases, map editors and block-based programming
constraints: The article states the results cannot be applied to the general population without validation with a larger number of students with different backgrounds
target_learning_goals: computational thinking practices (abstraction, pattern recognition, automation)
critical engagement with socio-scientific issues
systems thinking
examples: The CT-Chef game in ChoiCo was used across Play, Focused Modifications and Open design stages in a 7-week school project
key_sources: Marianthi Grizioti. (2025). Computational thinking beyond coding: exploring student computational practices while playing and modifying a socio-scientific simulation game with integrated computational tools. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10477-y

article_title: Approaches to illuminate content-specific gameplay decisions using open-ended game data
citation: Rosenheck, Louisa; Cheng, Meng-Tzu; Lin, Chen-Yen; Klopfer, Eric. (2021). Approaches to illuminate content-specific gameplay decisions using open-ended game data. Springer US. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09989-0
title: Three-approach analysis pattern for distinguishing player methods in open-ended game data
description: The article's reusable analytic pattern consists of three complementary lenses: "looking at actions and tool use, play patterns and player types, and tool input patterns". Applied together to one open-ended quest, these lenses identify content-specific gameplay decisions and distinguish players utilizing different methods. The pattern is intended to generalize as guiding questions for learning games designers and data scientists.
requirements: Rich, granular log data covering actions, tool use and tool inputs
An open-ended task context within the target domain
constraints: Illustrated in the context of a single selected game quest in genetics
target_learning_goals: Revealing domain-specific problem-solving methods in gameplay
examples: The study distinguished players utilizing different methods of completing genetics game tasks using the three lenses

article_title: Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development
citation: Sara van der Linden, Susan McKenney. (2020). Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09772-7
title: Three-step reflection procedure: preparation, image forming, conclusion drawing
description: As the procedural (recurrent) aspect of united reflection, the article adopts a generic three-step procedure from Reymen et al. in the context of engineering design: preparation, image forming, and conclusion drawing. Preparation requires practitioners "to detail the reflective question and to collect facts related to it"; image forming investigates the identified phenomena using the framing to interpret or anticipate the teaching situation; conclusion drawing contrasts findings and considers implications for practice, determining the ZPP or ZPI.
requirements: A detailed reflective question and collected facts in the preparation step
Framing that guides interpretation, whether framework-driven or context-driven
constraints: The procedure was originally described in the context of engineering design and is here adapted to teaching
target_learning_goals: Structured reflection on teaching practice
examples: Table 1 cross-tabulates the three steps with deliberate and aware perspective variants, plus comparing perspectives
key_sources: Sara van der Linden, Susan McKenney. (2020). Uniting epistemological perspectives to support contextualized knowledge development. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09772-7

article_title: Development research on an AI English learning support system to facilitate learner-generated-context-based learning
citation: Donghwa Lee, Hong-hyeon Kim, Seok-Hyun Sung. (2023). Development research on an AI English learning support system to facilitate learner-generated-context-based learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10172-2
title: Three design principles for an AI system facilitating LGC-based learning
description: From a literature review on LGC, self-determined learning, and second-language strategies, the authors derived three design principles: learners are "creators capable of generating their own contexts and studying autonomously based on such contexts, through personalized learning assistance and continuous interactions with resources"; the system provides personalized support for determining learning content, plans, and strategies; and an open platform of learning resources with a content curation tool encourages interaction with resources and context expansion.
requirements: Functionalities include mobile and web-based anytime/anywhere learning, learner-generated content, OERs and online media resources, multisensory strategy choice, multimedia and natural language processing technologies, and an intelligent agent providing guidance without human instructors
constraints: Principles were derived for English language education in South Korea with secondary students as the priority population
target_learning_goals: autonomous English learning
learner-generated content creation
learning strategy selection
examples: The principles guided development of the four-module AI web-based system evaluated in the field test

article_title: The ever evolving MOOC
citation: Patricia A. Young. (2021). The ever evolving MOOC. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09959-6
title: Three generations of MOOCs: cMOOCs, xMOOCs, and hybrid MOOCs
description: The editorial organizes MOOC development into a three-generation taxonomy, citing Bozkurt et al. (2018): "the basic MOOC has transformed into cMOOCs (first generation); xMOOCs (second generation) and third generation Hybrid MOOCs". This framework frames the special section's discussion of how the platform's educational function is merging with social and political functions.

constraints: The taxonomy is attributed to Bozkurt et al. (2018) and presented as a historical framing rather than a tested model

article_title: Taking adaptive learning in educational settings to the next level: leveraging natural language processing for improved personalization
citation: Mathias Mejeh, Martin Rehm. (2024). Taking adaptive learning in educational settings to the next level: leveraging natural language processing for improved personalization. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10345-1
title: Threshold-triggered automated prompting combined with personalized strategy delivery in a daily feedback loop
description: This pattern divides learning into episodes that proceed cyclically, with a feedback loop in which preceding phases influence subsequent phases. Learners answer brief daily surveys (morning and afternoon); "If a student does not exceed a specific threshold, the app automatically prompts them with an appropriate regulation strategy." Personalized strategy recommendations are then grounded in personal motivation, emotion, cognition, metacognition, and resource management data, delivered as short videos using pictographs and text, and adjusted after each data collection before and after tasks.
requirements: A questionnaire-based mechanism that systematically gathers SRL-related data from learners over time
Strategy content; the majority of strategies are based on the German version of the Learning and Study Strategies Inventory (LASSI)
constraints: When learners receive adaptive feedback depends on which learning episodes are defined and how long they are
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategy use and reflection on the learning process
examples: Example strategies include creating a sense of achievement for motivation, expressive writing for emotion, the slow down strategy for cognition, task management for metacognition, and the flow place strategy for resource management
key_sources: Mathias Mejeh, Martin Rehm. (2024). Taking adaptive learning in educational settings to the next level: leveraging natural language processing for improved personalization. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10345-1

article_title: Taking adaptive learning in educational settings to the next level: leveraging natural language processing for improved personalization
citation: Mathias Mejeh, Martin Rehm. (2024). Taking adaptive learning in educational settings to the next level: leveraging natural language processing for improved personalization. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10345-1
title: Three-tier NLP analysis pipeline: opinion mining, part-of-speech tagging, and sentiment analysis
description: To analyze how integrating NLP into an ALT could provide just-in-time SRL support, the authors "employed a three-tier approach, namely using opinion mining, POS, and sentiment analysis." Opinion mining compares learner lexicons against reference lexicons built from SRL components of the MSLQ and LASSI using cosine similarity (0 to 1); POS tagging assigns syntactic tags to contextualize word pairs; sentiment analysis uses the DE-LIWC2015 dictionaries covering positive and negative emotions. The approach is explicitly informed by qualitative interview data from the co-design process.
requirements: Reference lexicons grounded in identified (meta-)cognitive, motivational, and emotional SRL components
Qualitative research and sound theoretical considerations informing the quantitative NLP configurations
constraints: In its current form the word network remains somewhat unclear from a purely descriptive standpoint, per the authors
target_learners: high school students whose interview and verbal input is analyzed
target_learning_goals: identifying learners' SRL-related terminology, context, and emotional disposition to tailor adaptive support
examples: Analysis was performed in R using the textstem, udpipe, and quanteda libraries, with LIWC software for sentiment analysis
key_sources: Mathias Mejeh, Martin Rehm. (2024). Taking adaptive learning in educational settings to the next level: leveraging natural language processing for improved personalization. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10345-1

article_title: Authenticity in a high school data science curriculum
citation: Rotem Israel-Fishelson, David Weintrop. (2026). Authenticity in a high school data science curriculum. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10622-1
title: Thick Authenticity framework (Shaffer & Resnick, 1999) as the organizing lens for analyzing curriculum authenticity
description: The study operationalizes Shaffer and Resnick's (1999) 'thick authenticity' framework, which the article describes as "a comprehensive view of authentic learning, defined as 'thick authenticity.'" It comprises four interconnected dimensions: personal authenticity (alignment with interests, values, goals), real-world authenticity (tasks mirroring professional contexts), disciplinary authenticity (thinking in the modes of a discipline), and authentic assessment (assessment reflecting real-world knowledge application). The researchers coded 108 relevant interview segments against these four dimensions to assess student perceptions.
requirements: Coding requires segments assignable to one or more dimensions, as instances of authenticity are not always mutually exclusive
constraints: The framework is applied to a single interest-driven high school data science curriculum context
target_learning_goals: data science practices
perceiving authenticity and relevance of learning activities
examples: Two researchers independently coded 350 interview segments, identified 108 authenticity-related segments, and achieved Cohen's Kappa of 0.79 (relevancy) and 0.89 (dimension coding)
key_sources: Rotem Israel-Fishelson, David Weintrop. (2026). Authenticity in a high school data science curriculum. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10622-1

article_title: Revisiting Kuo and Belland’s exploratory study of undergraduate students’ perceptions of online learning: minority students in continuing education
citation: Beth Beschorner. (2021). Revisiting Kuo and Belland’s exploratory study of undergraduate students’ perceptions of online learning: minority students in continuing education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09900-3
title: Three types of online interaction: content, instructor, and other learners
description: The article organizes online course design around three interaction types, following the interaction framework it attributes to Moore (1989) and Kuo and Belland (2016): learners' interaction "with the content, with the instructor, and with other learners." Instructors are advised to determine, for each type, how students will interact when designing online coursework. constraints: Applied here to undergraduate online courses in the context of the COVID-19 shift to online delivery
target_learning_goals: designing equitable online learning experiences across content, instructor, and peer interaction
examples: The commentary uses the three interaction types to structure its advice on creating more equitable online courses

article_title: Examining the use of digital technology in schools with a school-wide approach to personalized learning
citation: Schmid, R., Pauli, C., & Petko, D. (2023). Examining the use of digital technology in schools with a school-wide approach to personalized learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10167-z
title: Three types of digital technology integration in schools with school-wide personalized learning
description: The article systematizes its three case analyses into a taxonomy of how schools integrate digital tools into daily practices under a school-wide personalized learning policy. As the authors state, "A systematization of our analyses resulted in three different types in terms of how schools integrate digital tools into their daily practices": selective use according to individual teacher preference, selective use according to individual student preference, and structural use in accordance with a school-wide strategy. The taxonomy is derived from qualitative content analysis of interviews, observations, and documents in three contrasting Swiss lower-secondary schools.
requirements: Derived from multiple-case analysis of schools that have implemented personalized learning school-wide, with data triangulated across student questionnaire, interviews, observations, and curriculum documents
constraints: Based on three cases selected as the schools with the most frequent digital technology use among 31 Swiss lower-secondary schools; the authors present the types as indications for future research and practice rather than a validated typology
target_learners: lower-secondary students (8th grade) in schools with personalized learning concepts
target_learning_goals: implementation of personalized learning through digital technology use
examples: The three case-study schools each exemplified one type: School A (teacher preference), School B (student preference), and School C (school-wide strategy)
key_sources: Schmid, R., Pauli, C., & Petko, D. (2023). Examining the use of digital technology in schools with a school-wide approach to personalized learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10167-z

article_title: Actualization of teaching conceptions in lesson design: how teaching conceptions shape TPACK regarding spherical video-based virtual reality-supported writing instruction
citation: Mengyuan Chen, Ching-sing Chai, Morris Siu-Yung Jong. (2023). Actualization of teaching conceptions in lesson design: how teaching conceptions shape TPACK regarding spherical video-based virtual reality-supported writing instruction. title: Three orientations of teaching conceptions for SVVR-supported writing: skill, community, and identity

article_title: Shooting live television shows on film
citation: Sherburne, E. G., Jr. (1953). Research Abstracts 77. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Three-camera film technique for shooting live television shows on film
description: Freund's abstracted article describes producing the weekly half-hour program "I Love Lucy" on film with three motion picture cameras shooting simultaneously: the middle camera on a long shot and the two side cameras on closeups. This "provides more flexibility in editing, and better photographic quality than in kinescope recording", placing the technique at an intermediate point on the film-to-kinescope continuum described on the page.
requirements: Three motion picture cameras with a crew of four men per camera, plus roughly four days of rehearsal and shooting per weekly show.

article_title: Activity-Centred Analysis and Design (ACAD): Core purposes, distinctive qualities and current developments
citation: Peter Goodyear. (2015). Teaching as design. HERDSA Review of Higher Education. https://www.herdsa.org.au/herdsa-review-higher-education-vol-2/27-50
title: Three design components: learning tasks, supportive environments, and social organisation
description: An activity-centered approach focuses on "three main classes of things which can be designed: (i) good learning tasks, (ii) properly supportive physical and digital environments, and (iii) forms of social organisation and divisions of labour". The components entangle in students' actual learning activity but are best kept conceptually distinct during design, which allows shifting elements between components, e.g. offloading an over-complicated task specification to scaffolding in digital tools.
requirements: Each component must be designed and managed at multiple scale levels by people in different roles
constraints: Learning, activity and experience cannot be designed, only designed for (Wenger, 1998)
target_learning_goals: productive learning activity at learntime
examples: If a groupwork design may go awry, the teacher-designer can supplement the social design with additional instructions about how to co-ordinate work

article_title: Relational topologies in the learning activity spaces: operationalising a sociomaterial approach
citation: Linda Castañeda, Victoria I. Marín, Daniel Villar-Onrubia. (2024). Relational topologies in the learning activity spaces: operationalising a sociomaterial approach. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10296-z
title: Three relational topologies for sociomaterial analysis of learning spaces
description: The article proposes a methodological framework built on three sequential topologies for the sociomaterial analysis of teaching and learning spaces. As the authors state, the approach is based on "three different topologies: (1) Topologies of influence and activity in the learning space, focused on the use of tools; (2) Topologies for the multi-spatial learning context... and (3) Entanglements in multi-spatial contexts". The first topology is described as "the seed of the second one, and so on", so they were developed iteratively. Each topology starts from a guiding question (who introduces tools; where learning happens; how devices, interfaces and spaces entangle) and is operationalised through concrete data-collection and visualisation procedures.
requirements: Combination of "topologies of digital data practices" with the three ACAD design dimensions (set, epistemic, social)
Mixed qualitative and quantitative data collection with participants' self-reports
constraints: Applying topologies can be challenging due to their complex, non-linear, and heterogeneous nature
Specialised software is required to visualise and analyse the multiple data layers
target_learning_goals: Understanding technology-mediated learning activity across spaces, tools and devices
examples: The three topologies were developed and illustrated sequentially using data from the RICT course case study

article_title: Learners and learning contexts: international perspectives on new alignments for the digital age
citation: Joke Voogt, Gerald Knezek. (2021). Learners and learning contexts: international perspectives on new alignments for the digital age. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09985-4
title: Three clusters of needed alignments: learning and learning contexts, technology integration and teachers, and partnerships
description: The editorial organizes the special issue's twelve papers into three thematic clusters where new alignments are needed for technology to foster learning. As the authors state, "The papers in this special issue identified three clusters where new alignments are needed in order to make technology work in the practice of education." The clusters span what is worth learning, teacher technology integration, and stakeholder partnerships, with recommendations at macro, meso and micro levels.
requirements: Papers addressing the theme from research, policy and practice perspectives
target_learning_goals: effective technology-supported learning across formal and non-formal contexts
examples: Ten Thematic Working Groups from EDUsummIT 2019 published in the special issue, plus two additional accepted papers

article_title: Generic service integration in adaptive learning experiences using IMS learning design
citation: Luis de-la-Fuente-Valentín, Abelardo Pardo, Carlos Delgado Kloos. (2011). Generic service integration in adaptive learning experiences using IMS learning design. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.12.007
title: Three-type taxonomy of adaptive learning schemes: content, flow and interface adaptation
description: The article adopts, citing He, Kinshuk and Patel (2002), a taxonomy of adaptive learning schemes by the element modified: "content adaptation, where the same learning activity is presented to all the students but with different material; flow adaptation, where a different set of activities is chosen for each student; and interface adaptation, where the same information is presented to all the students but with different layouts". It uses this taxonomy to argue, following Burgos, Tattersall and Koper (2007), which types IMS LD supports: flow and content via properties, conditions and visibility attributes, but not interface modification inside a Unit of Learning.
requirements: Any adaptation type must be generalizable to one of the three described types
constraints: Interface modifications are not supported by adaptation inside a UoL, since IMS LD says nothing about how compliant players present information
target_learning_goals: classifying and implementing adaptation in learning experiences
examples: The workshop UoL used flow adaptation: the second act depended on questionnaire results gathered in the first act

article_title: Instagram as a platform for teacher collaboration and digital social support
citation: Eric Richter, Jeffrey P. Carpenter, André Meyer, Dirk Richter. (2022). Instagram as a platform for teacher collaboration and digital social support. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2022.104624
title: Three-form conceptualization of teacher collaboration on social media (information seeking, information sharing, co-creating)
description: The article develops a multi-faceted, theory-driven conceptualization of teacher collaboration on social media, distinguishing "information seeking, information sharing, co-creating". It builds on Gräsel et al.'s (2006) forms of teacher collaboration and the low-cost/high-cost distinction, positioning seeking and sharing as lower-cost activities and co-creating as a higher-cost form requiring greater investment. The study operationalizes the framework in a 10-item survey instrument and validates it via CFA on Instagram users.
requirements: The framework assumes collaboration activities can be self-reported via Likert-scale items and differentiated as latent factors, as operationalized in the study's instrument.
constraints: The instrument was developed and validated for Instagram use among German teachers; the article calls for replication on other platforms and more balanced samples.
target_learners: in-service teachers using social media for professional collaboration
target_learning_goals: teacher professional development through peer collaboration and digital social support
examples: The study measured the three forms with items such as "I use Instagram to look for teaching related information" and "I prepare lessons together with my colleagues on Instagram."
key_sources: Eric Richter, Jeffrey P. Carpenter, André Meyer, Dirk Richter. (2022). Instagram as a platform for teacher collaboration and digital social support. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2022.104624

article_title: The influences of lecturer charismatic leadership and technology use on student online engagement, learning performance, and satisfaction
citation: Hazzam, J., & Wilkins, S. (2023). The influences of lecturer charismatic leadership and technology use on student online engagement, learning performance, and satisfaction. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104809
title: Three-dimensional model of student online engagement (cognitive, emotional, behavioral)
description: The article adopts Sun and Rueda's (2012) conceptualization that "student online engagement has three dimensions": cognitive engagement (effort and investment in learning, such as reading extra materials), emotional engagement (feelings about the online learning experience, such as excitement), and behavioral engagement (observable behavior, such as completing online tasks or following classroom rules). This taxonomy structures the study's measurement and hypotheses, with each dimension measured by validated scales and hypothesized to relate to lecturer characteristics and outcomes.
requirements: Measured with validated multi-item scales (Sun and Rueda's cognitive, emotional, and behavioral engagement scales)
constraints: The article focuses on the learning aspect of self-efficacy rather than other efficacies such as computer self-efficacy
target_learners: higher education students in online courses
target_learning_goals: student engagement in online learning
key_sources: Hazzam, J., & Wilkins, S. (2023). The influences of lecturer charismatic leadership and technology use on student online engagement, learning performance, and satisfaction. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104809

article_title: Framework for the evolution of acquiring knowledge modules to integrate the acquisition of high-level cognitive skills and professional competencies: Principles and case studies
citation: Warin, B., Kolski, C., & Sagar, M. (2011). Framework for the evolution of acquiring knowledge modules to integrate the acquisition of high-level cognitive skills and professional competencies. Computers and Education, 57(2), 1595-1614. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.02.013
title: Three case studies of disciplinary module evolution
description: The article presents and analyzes three case studies showing the evolution of three disciplinary course modules. Each case study documents how a module was transformed using the framework and what learning outcomes resulted. The case studies serve as concrete demonstrations of the framework applied in different disciplinary contexts, providing the empirical grounding for the article's claims about motivation, efficiency, and employer alignment.
requirements: Each case study requires a disciplinary module that has undergone evolution using the framework
constraints: The case studies are limited to three specific disciplinary modules in higher education
target_learning_goals: disciplinary knowledge
professional competencies

article_title: How stress influences creativity in game-based situations: Analysis of stress hormones, negative emotions, and working memory
citation: Yeh, Y.-C.; Lai, G.-J.; Lin, C. F.; Lin, C.-W.; Sun, H.-C. (2015). How stress influences creativity in game-based situations: Analysis of stress hormones, negative emotions, and working memory. Computers and Education, v.81, pp. 143-153. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2014.09.011
title: Three-dimensional theory of emotion and creativity (valence, activation, regulatory focus)
description: The article describes a three-dimensional theory developed by Baas et al. (2008) to explain the relationship between emotion and creativity. The three dimensions proposed are "valence (positive vs. negative), level of activation (activating vs. deactivating), and regulatory focus (promotion vs. prevention)." This framework underpins the study's Inventory of Three-dimensional Emotions (I3E) and its hypotheses about how specific emotion types influence WM and creativity during gaming.
requirements: The article uses this theory to structure the measurement of emotions along three dimensions.
target_learning_goals: creativity in game-based learning situations

article_title: Can teaching simulations in a virtual classroom help trainee teachers to develop oral communication skills and self-efficacy? A randomized controlled trial.
citation: Angélique Remacle, Stéphane Bouchard, Dominique Morsomme. (2023). Can teaching simulations in a virtual classroom help trainee teachers to develop oral communication skills and self-efficacy? A randomized controlled trial. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104808
title: Theoretical Framework for Teachers' Vocal Behavior
description: The article develops a Theoretical Framework for Teachers' Vocal Behavior that "draws on principles of vocology (i.e., vocal behavior, vocal health), acoustics (i.e., background noise), pedagogy (i.e., teachers and students' behavior), and psychology (i.e., self-efficacy)". It relies on ecological models of health behaviors, focusing on the nature of individuals' interactions with their physical and sociocultural environments. The framework depicts a feedback loop between the teacher's vocal behavior, background noise level, students' behavior, vocal health, and communication self-efficacy, with ten numbered interactions including the Lombard effect. It can guide the development of oral communication-related interventions.
requirements: Designed as a reference point to guide oral communication- and particularly voice-related interventions
target_learning_goals: oral communication skills
healthy and effective voice use

article_title: Instruments for Assessing Basic Life Support Knowledge in Secondary School Students: A Scoping Review and Expert Panel.
citation: Mecías‐Calvo M., Sobrido‐Prieto M., Navarro‐Patón R. (2026). Instruments for Assessing Basic Life Support Knowledge in Secondary School Students: A Scoping Review and Expert Panel. The Journal of School Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.70223
title: Three-level relevance classification of questionnaire content: mandatory, recommended, and optional
description: The expert panel proposed a reusable structure for designing comparable BLS knowledge questionnaires adaptable to different educational contexts. It classifies questionnaire content into three relevance levels: "mandatory (present in any questionnaire); recommended (depending on the scope of the training program or the time available); and optional (more specific or advanced aspects)." This classification supports instrument adaptation across varied program scopes and time constraints while preserving a common core of assessed content.
requirements: Questionnaire designers assign each content element to one of the three relevance levels to enable comparability across contexts.
target_learning_goals: basic life support knowledge assessment
examples: The panel proposed the classification to facilitate the design of comparable instruments adaptable to different educational contexts.

article_title: Clinical teaching models for the instruction of healthcare trainees in the 21(st) century: a scoping review.
citation: Munguiko Clement, Masereka Enos Mirembe, Atukwatse Joseph, Smitha Joseph, Kateregga James, Nankinga Clare, Collete Alice Alum, Namujju Josephine, Akello Safina, Nalubega Sylivia. (2026). Clinical teaching models for the instruction of healthcare trainees in the 21st century: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09710-w
title: Three pedagogical orientations organize contemporary clinical teaching models: learner-centred reasoning, procedural skills-based, and workplace-based reflective teaching
description: The review groups the eight mapped models into three dominant pedagogical orientations, stating they "can broadly be grouped according to their dominant pedagogical orientation, namely learner-centred reasoning models, procedural and skills-based models, and workplace-based reflective teaching models." Learner-centred reasoning models (OMP, SNAPPS, RIME, Aunt Minnie) emphasize clinical reasoning, diagnostic thinking, and metacognition; procedural models (STEPS, BOPPPS) emphasize deliberate practice and structured instructional sequencing; workplace-based models (MiPLAN, ED STAT) emphasize contextual learning, role modelling, and adaptive supervision in authentic settings.
requirements: The grouping assumes models can be assigned a dominant pedagogical orientation, which the review presents as a broad interpretive categorization rather than a mutually exclusive classification
constraints: The review presents this as a broad grouping of mapped models, not a validated typology
target_learners: healthcare trainees including medical, nursing, midwifery, and allied health students
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning
procedural skills acquisition
professionalism and workplace-based competence
examples: The review assigns OMP, SNAPPS, RIME, and Aunt Minnie to the reasoning orientation, STEPS and BOPPPS to procedural skills, and MiPLAN and ED STAT to workplace-based teaching

article_title: Pedagogical Innovation in Digital Environments: A Systematic Review Focused on Higher Education.
citation: Casimiro Urcos CN, Casimiro Urcos WH, Alberca Pintado NE, Ostos Miraval RM, Carrasco Muñoz MA, Piñas Rivera LC. (2026). Pedagogical Innovation in Digital Environments: A Systematic Review Focused on Higher Education. F1000Research 15:522. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.176682.1
title: Three-category organizing framework: pedagogical innovations, digital environments, and higher-education experiences/results
description: The review organizes the literature into three analytic categories: pedagogical innovations (active methodologies such as PBL, flipped learning, collaborative learning), digital environments (evolving from LMS to instructional ecosystems with simulation, analytics, and collaboration layers), and higher-education experiences and results. Studies were coded to one of these categories, with the review aiming to "characterize how these categories have been investigated" through contributions, limitations, and results.
requirements: Studies must address at least one of the three analysis categories in a university context with explicit methodological design, defined sample, peer review, and accessible data
constraints: Excluded reviews, grey literature, articles without a specific sample or with unmitigated methodological bias
target_learning_goals: pedagogical innovation in digital environments
contributions and limitations of technology-mediated higher education
examples: The 39 included studies in Table 2 were classified as 1 = Pedagogical innovations; 2 = Digital environments; 3 = Higher education – experiences/outcomes

article_title: Artificial intelligence generated virtual patients in health professions education: a scoping review.
citation: Fang Eric Kin Meng, Boon Yuru, Ho Jin Yang, Tey Natasha, Low Matthew Jian Wen. (2026). Artificial intelligence generated virtual patients in health professions education: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10028-w
title: Three-domain development framework for AI-generated virtual patients: clinical accuracy, degree of anthropomorphism, and adaptability
description: The review organizes development strategies around a conceptual model, credited to Wang et al., with "three major domains: clinical accuracy, degree of anthropomorphism, and adaptability". These domains are said to contribute toward constructive alignment between learning tasks and workplace tasks, and to align with the limitations the review identified. The review also presents its own synthesized framework (Fig. 4) consolidating these strategies, explicitly framed as a conceptual synthesis of exploratory scoping findings rather than definitive directives, applying mostly to LLM-based virtual patients.
requirements: Development strategies require reviewing case content and platform outputs by clinical experts and learners, and iterative prompt engineering.
The framework presupposes defined use cases whose required clinical content, realism and adaptability can be specified.
constraints: The review emphasizes the framework is a conceptual synthesis of exploratory findings, not definitive directives.
Strategies mostly apply to LLM-based virtual patients, with limited generalizability to rule-based dialog systems.
Recommendations were not weighted by methodologic strength because study quality was not appraised.
target_learners: Health professions students and postgraduate trainees across nursing, pharmacy, medicine, dentistry and allied health
target_learning_goals: Clinical communication skills
Diagnostic and management reasoning
examples: The review charts strategies per domain: expert-validated case content for accuracy; behavioral rules and few-shot prompting for anthropomorphism; fallback responses and temperature customization for adaptability.
key_sources: Fang Eric Kin Meng, Boon Yuru, Ho Jin Yang, Tey Natasha, Low Matthew Jian Wen. (2026). Artificial intelligence generated virtual patients in health professions education: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10028-w

article_title: Microvascular errors of technique: a systematic review.
citation: Esanu V, Marziali E, Gaspar O, Agoston S, Carciumaru T, Stoia A, Paun C, Colosi HA, Dindelegan G, Dirven C, Meling TR, Vasilic D, Volovici V. (2026). Microvascular errors of technique: a systematic review. Acta Neurochirurgica. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00701-026-06810-w
title: A three-phase taxonomy of microvascular anastomosis errors (pre-operative, intra-operative, post-operative)
description: The review organizes microsurgical errors by operative phase, subdividing the intra-operative phase into dissection, needle passage, and suture handling domains. It states: "Errors were categorized according to the operative phase: preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative." Tables 1–3 enumerate specific errors per phase, e.g. empty grasp, backwall suture, tight suture tear, and crushing patency tests.
requirements: Errors must be defined as observable end-product deviations, with causes treated separately as contributory factors
constraints: Derived from 34 heterogeneous studies; the authors note heterogeneity made developing standardized rubrics challenging
target_learning_goals: recognizing and classifying technical errors in microvascular anastomosis
examples: Tables 1–3 list pre-operative errors (tool selection, microscope calibration), intra-operative errors (dissection, needle passage, suture handling), and post-operative errors (patency testing, leaks, obstruction)

title: Three-level classification of mechanistic evidence: direct biological, indirect physiological, and inferred mechanistic
description: The review proposes a qualitative classification of mechanistic evidence into three levels to improve transparency and limit overinterpretation. It states that "direct biological evidence was defined as evidence derived from objective biological, biochemical, neuroimaging, or neurophysiological measurements", indirect physiological evidence rests on validated proxies such as heart rate variability, and inferred mechanistic evidence proposes a pathway without direct measurement. requirements: Mechanistic relevance must be assigned only when a study directly measures biological markers, assesses validated physiological proxies, or explicitly tests a predefined mechanistic hypothesis
constraints: Applied to scoping-review synthesis in student populations; intended to limit overinterpretation of mechanistic claims rather than to grade study quality

academic achievement
examples: The review used the classification to restrict its focused mechanistic table to studies providing the most explicit and directly assessed biological information

description: The review develops an inductive thematic structure organising reported influences on ALS competence maintenance into three overarching domains: individual (e.g., experience, self-confidence, stress and cognitive load, non-technical skills), institutional (e.g., assessment systems, institutional support, standardisation, training access), and educational (e.g., simulation-based training, feedback and debriefing, spaced repetition and LDHF models, gamification, blended learning). citation: Varpula Jaakko, Askola Riitta, Kahsay Desale Tewelde, Axelin Anna, Virtanen Laura, Maijala Riikka, Peltonen Laura‐Maria. (2026). Enhancing Nurse Leaders Evidence‐Based Practice Implementation Leadership Competence. A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis of Educational Interventions. description: The review describes how the six included interventions, while sharing the goal of enhancing leadership competencies and fostering a supportive EBP environment, drew on different theoretical mechanisms: supportive leadership and team dynamics, organizational behavior, experiential learning and social networks, adult learning and leadership behavior, proactive behavior and organizational readiness, and self-efficacy and implementation science. As the review states, "the mechanism behind the intervention effects differed" across studies. constraints: Mechanisms differed across interventions, limiting generalization about how the effects arise

description: The review organizes the six included studies into three themes: "(1) preparation to care for people living with dementia, (2) impact of dementia care training and (3) experience of caring of people living with dementia." Preparation covers undergraduate curriculum needs; training impact covers knowledge, confidence and empathy outcomes; experience covers transition challenges, barriers and facilitators in acute care. article_title: Learning curve for lateral lymph node dissection in rectal cancer - a systematic review of literature.
citation: Kehagias D., Baldari L., Cassinotti E., Boni L., Lampropoulos C., Kehagias I. (2025). Learning curve for lateral lymph node dissection in rectal cancer – a systematic review of literature. Techniques in Coloproctology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10151-025-03214-3
title: Three-phase learning curve model: learning, competence, and proficiency
description: The review applies a standardized three-phase learning curve model consisting of learning, competence, and proficiency phases, supported by several studies in minimally invasive surgery. The learning curve follows a characteristic pattern: an initial phase of rapid learning and improvement, followed by a plateau phase indicating competence, and ultimately a phase of mastery or proficiency. Studies reporting only two phases were classified as learning and competence; studies with four phases were classified as two learning phases followed by competence and proficiency.
requirements: CUSUM or similar quantitative method for learning curve analysis
constraints: Several confounding factors can affect the shape and interpretation of a learning curve, including prior experience, individual background, and the availability of appropriate equipment
target_learning_goals: Achieving surgical competence in new procedures
key_sources: Kehagias D., Baldari L., Cassinotti E., Boni L., Lampropoulos C., Kehagias I. (2025). Learning curve for lateral lymph node dissection in rectal cancer – a systematic review of literature. Techniques in Coloproctology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10151-025-03214-3

article_title: The Effectiveness of Community Nurse Training Programs to Improve Nurses' Competency in Community Settings: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
citation: Pumsopa, N., Jirapongsuwan, A., Kalampakorn, S., Siri, S., and Klainin‐Yobas, P. (2025). The Effectiveness of Community Nurse Training Programs to Improve Nurses' Competency in Community Settings: a Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis. International Journal of Nursing Practice. https://doi.org/10.1111/ijn.70090
title: Three‐method taxonomy of community nurse training delivery: online, hybrid and onsite training
description: The review organises community nurse training programs (CNTPs) by delivery method using Allen and Seaman's classification, distinguishing "online, hybrid and onsite training". Onsite training "delivers 0%–29% of the materials online" with all class meetings face to face; hybrid training delivers "a substantial portion of the training content (30%–79%) online"; online training delivers "more than 80% of its content online" with no required face‐to‐face meetings. Seven included studies used onsite, one online and six hybrid training. This taxonomy structures the review's subgroup analyses of knowledge and skills outcomes.
requirements: Training programs must be classifiable by the proportion of content delivered online per the Allen and Seaman thresholds
constraints: The review notes a small number of eligible studies on the online training platform and nurses' traits, limiting meta‐analysis for those categories
target_learning_goals: nursing knowledge
nursing skills
nursing traits
examples: Seven studies conducted onsite training with workshops, lectures, feedback, seminars, experience sharing, discussions, demonstrations and brainstorming; six studies used hybrid combinations such as e‐learning with onsite sessions or WeChat group online interaction
key_sources: Pumsopa, N., Jirapongsuwan, A., Kalampakorn, S., Siri, S., and Klainin‐Yobas, P. (2025). The Effectiveness of Community Nurse Training Programs to Improve Nurses' Competency in Community Settings: a Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis. article_title: Beyond traditional teaching: a systematic review of innovative pedagogical practices in higher education.
citation: Suyo-Vega JA, Fernández-Bedoya VH, Meneses-La-Riva ME. (2024). Beyond traditional teaching: a systematic review of innovative pedagogical practices in higher education. F1000Research. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.143392.1
title: Three-category taxonomy of innovative pedagogical practices in higher education
description: The review organizes its findings into three distinct teaching strategies: "the first emphasizing student-centered approaches, the second showcasing the integration of educational technology, and the third highlighting evaluation and feedback methodologies." This taxonomy emerged from categorizing the 25 included articles and structures the review's analysis of strategies, pedagogical approaches, and their impact. It provides a framework for examining how innovative practices in university settings promote teaching and learning effectiveness.
requirements: Articles must address innovative pedagogical practices in university settings
constraints: Taxonomy derived from 25 articles published 2015-2023 in ERIC, Scopus, and ProQuest
target_learning_goals: improved teaching and learning effectiveness
key_sources: Suyo-Vega JA, Fernández-Bedoya VH, Meneses-La-Riva ME. (2024). Beyond traditional teaching: a systematic review of innovative pedagogical practices in higher education. F1000Research. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.143392.1

article_title: Facilitating clinical reasoning for medical students in clinical settings: a scoping review.
citation: Cahyaningrum Yeny Dyah, Suhoyo Yoyo, Rahayu Gandes Retno. (2025). Facilitating clinical reasoning for medical students in clinical settings: a scoping review. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2025.333
title: Three-theme framework for clinical reasoning facilitation in clinical settings
description: This scoping review proposes an organizing framework comprising three themes for understanding how clinical reasoning is facilitated in clinical settings. The review states these themes "encompass the responsibilities of clinical teachers, strategies employed in the process of clinical reasoning, and factors that impact clinical reasoning learning in clinical settings." The framework maps facilitator roles (environment creation, process demonstration, assessment, technique implementation), specific facilitation techniques organized by thinking process, and internal/external influencing factors. It provides a structure for medical educators to optimize clinical reasoning instruction.
requirements: Clinical teachers in clinical settings who facilitate medical students' clinical reasoning learning
constraints: The review notes specific strategies that enhance clinical reasoning abilities need further investigation
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning
Diagnostic reasoning
Clinical decision-making
