article_title: The efficacy of simulation-based learning versus non-simulation-based learning in endocrinology education: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Wu Zeyu, Huang Yiling, Lyu Ling, Huang Yu, Ping Fan. (2024). The efficacy of simulation-based learning versus non-simulation-based learning in endocrinology education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06010-z
title: Three-type taxonomy of simulation techniques in endocrinology education: computer-based simulation, scenario-based simulation, and standardized patients
description: The article organizes the simulation interventions in the reviewed trials into three primary types. "Computer-based simulations employ software applications" offering adaptability and scalability for repetitive practice; "Scenario-based simulations utilize prearranged scenarios and settings," often with role-playing and tangible equipment; and "Standardized patients involve trained actors or volunteers who simulate real patient scenarios," supporting communication and clinical reasoning. The taxonomy structures both the included studies and the subgroup analysis by simulation technique.
requirements: Each technique requires interactive design, timely feedback, and a safe learning environment for developing medical skills, as the article states these are common features
constraints: The article notes notable disparities exist among the three methods, so their attributes are not interchangeable across learning goals
target_learning_goals: endocrine theoretical knowledge
clinical and communication skills
clinical decision-making
examples: In the included trials, 10 studies used standardized patients, 6 employed computer-based simulations, and 6 used scenario-based simulation methods
key_sources: Wu Zeyu, Huang Yiling, Lyu Ling, Huang Yu, Ping Fan. (2024). The efficacy of simulation-based learning versus non-simulation-based learning in endocrinology education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06010-z

article_title: Automated analysis of operative video in surgical training: scoping review.
citation: Dick L, Boyle CP, Skipworth RJE, Smink DS, Tallentire VR, Yule S. (2024). Automated analysis of operative video in surgical training: scoping review. BJS Open. https://doi.org/10.1093/bjsopen/zrae124
title: Evidence corpus of 13 real-world operative video analytics studies
description: The review's evidence base comprises 13 studies applying automated video analysis to trainee-performed real-world operations, identified from 6736 screened articles. The median number of videos included for analysis was 69 (range 6–1107), with a total of 107 trainees and 152 attendings or experts reported across studies. Cataract surgery and cholecystectomy were the two most common operations assessed, and the mean adjusted MERSQI quality score was 12.73 out of 18. All studies were published within the last 10 years, with 8 within the last 5 years.
requirements: Studies must use real-world operations, trainee-performed video, automated analysis, and metrics with potential to facilitate feedback and training
constraints: Simulated or virtual reality settings were excluded, which the review notes may have under-represented minimally invasive surgery
target_learning_goals: automated assessment of operative technical performance
examples: Included study designs were predominantly prospective cohort studies (8), with 4 retrospective cohort studies and 1 qualitative study
key_sources: Dick L, Boyle CP, Skipworth RJE, Smink DS, Tallentire VR, Yule S. (2024). Automated analysis of operative video in surgical training: scoping review. BJS Open. https://doi.org/10.1093/bjsopen/zrae124

article_title: A scoping review to inform the development of dementia care competencies.
citation: Kay Kelly, Metersky Kateryna, Smye Victoria, McGrath Colleen, Johnson Karen, Astell Arlene, Sun Winnie, Bartfay Emma. (2023). A scoping review to inform the development of dementia care competencies. Dementia. https://doi.org/10.1177/14713012231165568
title: Thirteen organizing principles for dementia care competencies adapted from Bardsley (2011)
description: The article adapts Bardsley's (2011) UK framework into 13 principles organizing dementia care competencies for the Ontario context, spanning promoting health and social well-being, identifying dementia, assessment and diagnosis, sensitive communication, supporting living well, responding to unmet needs and distress, valuing care partners, multi-agency teamwork, understanding context of care, end of life care, worker self-care, leader accountability, and embedded quality improvement. The authors state "Bardsley (2011) identified 13 principles to organize dementia care competencies within the UK context" and used them as the review's organizing framework.
requirements: Competency statements for dementia care across the lay-to-professional continuum must be organized under the 13 principles
constraints: Adapted from a UK framework with minor wording changes for the Ontario, Canada context
target_learning_goals: dementia care knowledge, skills and actions
examples: Table 4 maps each of the 22 included studies to the principles they support, with totals per principle ranging from 2 to 11 references
key_sources: Kay Kelly, Metersky Kateryna, Smye Victoria, McGrath Colleen, Johnson Karen, Astell Arlene, Sun Winnie, Bartfay Emma. (2023). A scoping review to inform the development of dementia care competencies. Dementia. https://doi.org/10.1177/14713012231165568

article_title: The role of WhatsApp® in medical education; a scoping review and instructional design model.
citation: Coleman E., O'Connor E. (2019). The role of WhatsApp® in medical education; a scoping review and instructional design model. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1706-8
title: Three strategies for WhatsApp use in medical education: pre-defined curriculum, education without curriculum, and primarily non-educational use
description: The review organises the 23 included studies into three usage strategies distinguished by educational intent, curriculum presence, moderation, setting and scale. As printed, "Three strategies for WhatsApp use were apparent; primarily educational use with a pre-defined curriculum (n = 5), primarily educational use without a curriculum (n = 11), and primarily non-educational use (n = 7)." Curriculum groups were local, moderated and short-duration; non-educational groups were national or international and seldom moderated. The taxonomy anchors the authors' proposed design model.
requirements: Classification requires judging each study's primary purpose, curriculum presence, moderator presence and setting scale from the published report.
constraints: Derived from 23 studies published 2015–2018 in medical education; the review notes possible omission of relevant publications.
target_learning_goals: discipline-specific medical knowledge
clinical case discussion and information sharing
examples: The review tabulated all 23 studies against the strategies, finding moderated local groups for educational use and unmoderated national or international groups for primarily non-educational use.
key_sources: Coleman E., O'Connor E. (2019). The role of WhatsApp® in medical education; a scoping review and instructional design model. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1706-8

article_title: Professional Reasoning in Occupational Therapy: A Scoping Review.
citation: Márquez-Álvarez L.-J., Calvo-Arenillas J.-I., Talavera-Valverde M.-Á., Moruno-Millares P. (2019). Professional Reasoning in Occupational Therapy: A Scoping Review. Occupational Therapy International. https://doi.org/10.1155/2019/6238245
title: Three-phase historical development of professional reasoning research in occupational therapy: exploratory, transition, and consolidation
description: The review proposes that research on professional reasoning in occupational therapy evolved through three historical periods with distinct characteristics: "(a) exploratory phase (1982-1993), (b) transition phase (1994-2003), and (c) consolidation phase (2005-present)". The exploratory phase is characterised by nonempirical qualitative studies using ethnographic and phenomenological approaches; the transition phase shows considerable increase and diversification of studies with empirical work outweighing nonempirical; the consolidation phase shows a reversed trend with quantitative approaches predominating and more literature reviews. The phases are grounded in the statistically significant period-methodology associations the review reports.
requirements: The phase division rests on statistical comparison of articles grouped into 10-year periods, with articles published between 2015 and 2017 excluded from the statistical analyses
constraints: The phase characterisation derives from indexed-journal articles (original studies and reviews) published between 1982 and 2017 (n = 208)
A detailed analysis of the findings of the included papers was beyond the scope of the study, and scientific quality of the literature was not assessed
target_learning_goals: understanding the historical development of research on professional reasoning in occupational therapy
examples: The review classifies 1982–1993 as exploratory with similar numbers of nonempirical (n = 10) and empirical (n = 11) articles, mainly exploratory and descriptive; 1994–2003 as transition with qualitative phenomenological studies predominating among empirical work; and 2005 onward as consolidation with quantitative studies (n = 29) outweighing qualitative ones (n = 23) in 2004–2014.
key_sources: Márquez-Álvarez L.-J., Calvo-Arenillas J.-I., Talavera-Valverde M.-Á., Moruno-Millares P. (2019). Professional Reasoning in Occupational Therapy: A Scoping Review. Occupational Therapy International. https://doi.org/10.1155/2019/6238245

article_title: A scoping review of medical education research in family medicine.
citation: Webster F, Krueger P, MacDonald H, Archibald D, Telner D, Bytautas J, Whitehead C. (2015). A scoping review of medical education research in family medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4407512/
title: Explicitly ground education research in theoretical frameworks
description: The review recommends that family medicine education research be explicitly theoretically informed, arguing that articulation of underlying assumptions is needed for researchers to critically engage with study findings. The authors state: "research should be explicitly theoretically informed; this can be achieved by engaging scholars with diverse areas of theoretical expertise." The principle addresses the observed lack of stated research paradigms and epistemological assumptions in the field.
requirements: Research must articulate its underlying theoretical framework and epistemological assumptions
constraints: Recommended for a field where most studies did not identify methodology; authors note broader medical education research shares this limitation
target_learning_goals: strengthening theoretical grounding and critical engagement in education research
examples: The authors cite Bunniss and Kelly's argument that articulation of underlying assumptions is needed to critically engage with findings
key_sources: Webster F, Krueger P, MacDonald H, Archibald D, Telner D, Bytautas J, Whitehead C. (2015). A scoping review of medical education research in family medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4407512/

article_title: What Are We Looking for in Computer-Based Learning Interventions in Medical Education? A Systematic Review.
citation: Taveira-Gomes T, Ferreira P, Taveira-Gomes I, Severo M, Ferreira MA. (2016). What Are We Looking for in Computer-Based Learning Interventions in Medical Education? A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.5461
title: Three latent classes characterize intervention end points in medical CBL research: knowledge and attitudes, knowledge-attitudes-skills, and online activity
description: A second latent class model grouped the 212 intervention studies by measured end points. The review reports: "We found 3 classes for intervention outcomes: knowledge and attitudes (175/212, 82.6%), knowledge, attitudes, and skills (11.8%), and online activity (12/212, 5.7%)." The dominant class assesses knowledge and attitudes only; a small class adds skills assessment; the smallest measures online activity such as number of posts and reads, with knowledge and skill assessment nearly absent.
requirements: Class models were fitted on end point variables reported in at least 2% of studies, with class number chosen by lowest BIC and interpretability
constraints: Derived from the 212 of 251 articles reporting interventions on the end points of interest
target_learning_goals: characterizing outcome measurement in CBL intervention research
key_sources: Taveira-Gomes T, Ferreira P, Taveira-Gomes I, Severo M, Ferreira MA. (2016). What Are We Looking for in Computer-Based Learning Interventions in Medical Education? A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.5461

article_title: The Impact of Reading Success Academy on High School Reading Achievement
citation: Burlison, K., & Chave, J. (2014). The Impact of Reading Success Academy on High School Reading Achievement. Journal for Leadership and Instruction. https://www.scopeonline.us
title: Three-stage reading lesson structure with focus lesson, mini-lesson, and instructional passage
description: Each Reading Success Academy small-group session was organized around a focus lesson, mini-lesson, and instructional passage, and followed "the three reading stages of pre, during, and post -reading strategies." All students completed the required pre-reading, during reading, and post-reading activities for each lesson. Pre-reading strategies included predicting content, anticipation guides, previewing text features, and setting a purpose for reading; post-reading strategies had students revisit predictions, analyze or evaluate the passage, and build upon key ideas.
requirements: Students complete all required pre-reading, during reading, and post-reading activities for each lesson
constraints: Evaluated in this study only with nonproficient ninth-grade readers in small-group pull-out sessions over eight weeks
target_learners: struggling adolescent readers in small groups
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
activating prior knowledge
decoding and processing text
examples: Teachers used pre-reading strategies such as predicting the content, completing anticipation guides, previewing and clarifying text features, and setting a purpose for reading
key_sources: Burlison, K., & Chave, J. (2014). The Impact of Reading Success Academy on High School Reading Achievement. Journal for Leadership and Instruction. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1081400

article_title: Empirical Benchmarks for Planning and Interpreting Causal Effects of Community College Interventions
citation: Michael J. Weiss, Marie-Andrée Somers, & Colin Hill. (2023). Empirical Benchmarks for Planning and Interpreting Causal Effects of Community College Interventions. Journal of Postsecondary Student Success 3 (1). https://doi.org/10.33009/fsop_jpss132759
title: THE-RCT restricted-access database and the public empirical-benchmarks effect-size dataset
description: THE-RCT RAF is MDRC's restricted-access student-level database of postsecondary RCTs conducted 2003–2019, housed at ICPSR, containing design indicators, student characteristics, and semester-level outcomes (enrollment, credits, degree completion) from college records, the National Student Clearinghouse, and baseline surveys. From it the authors built a public-use dataset of study-level effect estimates: "A public database with effect sizes is available to researchers." The full sample includes "39 postsecondary interventions and a total of 65,604 students."
requirements: Access to THE-RCT RAF is limited to qualified researchers with few restrictions
constraints: Version 1.0 of THE-RCT RAF excludes individual-level data from five CUNY RCTs, which the present analysis supplemented
target_learners: postsecondary students mostly from low-income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: enrollment persistence
credit accumulation
degree or certificate completion
examples: The article's analyses draw on 30 MDRC RCTs, 27 of which met WWC evidence standards without reservations, across 44 institutions in 12 states

article_title: Improving Reading Comprehension Skills with Children's Books through Metacognitive Strategy: The Turkish Context
citation: Erkan Çer, Ertuğrul Şahin. (2016). Improving Reading Comprehension Skills with Children's Books through Metacognitive Strategy: The Turkish Context. Journal of Education and Training Studies. http://dx.doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i9.1566
title: Three-phase metacognitive reading instruction: planning before, self-monitoring during, and self-evaluation after reading
description: The experimental instruction organized metacognitive strategy into three parts explaining "what to do before, during, and after the reading activity". Before reading, a Pre-Reading Plan technique used teacher questions to activate foreknowledge and planning; during reading, four self-monitoring questions (e.g., "Do I clearly grasp what I am reading?") regulated comprehension; after reading, nine reflection questions targeted autonomy and self-regulation. This pattern was delivered over an 8-week period alongside books of literary quality.
requirements: Instruction must cover all three phases (pre-, during-, post-reading) so planning, self-monitoring, self-evaluation and self-regulation processes are exercised
constraints: Evaluated in this study only with 5th-grade students in one private secondary school over 8 weeks
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
metacognitive awareness
self-regulation
higher-order thinking
examples: The experimental group received this instruction with five award-winning children's books of literary quality, while the control group read 100 Basic Works texts with no strategies applied
key_sources: Erkan Çer, Ertuğrul Şahin. (2016). Improving Reading Comprehension Skills with Children's Books through Metacognitive Strategy: The Turkish Context. Journal of Education and Training Studies. http://dx.doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i9.1566

article_title: Model Debate for the Yellow Book Learning in Islamic Boarding School
citation: Apdoludin, Abdul Rahim Saidek, Raisul Islami. (2016). Model Debate for the Yellow Book Learning in Islamic Boarding School. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.23. https://www.iiste.org
title: Three-framework grounding of the debate model: behaviorism, cognitivism, and constructivism
description: The article organizes its theoretical rationale around three learning theory categories: "behaviorism learning theory, learning theory cognitivism, and constructivism learning theory". Behaviorism treats debate as stimulus-response practice strengthening habits; cognitivism, via Piaget's assimilation and accommodation, frames debate as situations applying mastered concepts; constructivism holds that students actively build new concepts from their own activity. The authors argue cognitivism "can support the learning model of debate in the yellow book that equally emphasize on intellectual progress, intelligence and critical thinking".
requirements: Learning designed so students organize their own experiences into meaningful knowledge (constructivist condition stated by the authors)
target_learners: Boarding school students in religion-focused secondary education
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking
Conceptual understanding of yellow book material
examples: The article contrasts behaviorism, where behavior is changed by manipulating conditions and reinforcement, with cognitivism, where knowledge itself is studied
key_sources: Apdoludin, Abdul Rahim Saidek, Raisul Islami. (2016). Model Debate for the Yellow Book Learning in Islamic Boarding School. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.23. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1112798

article_title: Design and Validation of a Questionnaire to Measure Research Skills: Experience with Engineering Students
citation: Cobos Alvarado, F., Peñaherrera León, M., & Ortiz Colon, A. M. (2016). DESIGN AND VALIDATION OF A QUESTIONNAIRE TO MEASURE RESEARCH SKILLS: EXPERIENCE WITH ENGINEERING STUDENTS. Journal of Technology and Science Education. http://dx.doi.org/10.3926/jotse.227
title: Three-factor structure of self-rated research skills: process, managing and developing scientific information
description: The validated AHABI organizes research skills into three correlated factors. Factor 1, "Process scientific information", covers organizing, analysing, reflecting on, summarizing and critically discussing scientific information; factor 2, "Managing scientific information", covers searching and managing scientific sources; factor 3, "Develop scientific information", covers producing new outputs such as abstracts, essays, keywords and oral communication of results. The article states the factors "indicate relationship and dependence between them", supporting the questionnaire's validity.
requirements: Items must saturate on their assigned factor as shown in the rotated component matrix
constraints: Derived from a sample of 150 basic-cycle engineering students; the authors propose further studies in other knowledge areas
target_learning_goals: research skills across information processing, management and production
examples: Factor 1 groups items 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 17; factor 2 groups items 1-6 and 18; factor 3 groups items 14, 15, 16, 19 and 20
key_sources: Cobos Alvarado, F., Peñaherrera León, M., & Ortiz Colon, A. M. (2016). DESIGN AND VALIDATION OF A QUESTIONNAIRE TO MEASURE RESEARCH SKILLS: EXPERIENCE WITH ENGINEERING STUDENTS. Journal of Technology and Science Education. http://dx.doi.org/10.3926/jotse.227

article_title: The Effect of (Think-Pair-Share) Strategy on the Achievement of Third Grade Student in Sciences in the Educational District of Irbid
citation: Dr. Ribhi Khaleel Ahmad Hamdan. (2017). The Effect of (Think – Pair – Share) Strategy on the Achievement of Third Grade Student in Sciences in the Educational District of Irbid. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.9. https://www.iiste.org
title: Think–Pair–Share three-step discussion pattern: individual thinking, pair discussion, whole-class sharing
description: Think–Pair–Share is a cooperative learning technique in which students "think through questions using three distinct steps, encouraging individual participation". The teacher poses a question, gives students timed individual thinking with no talking, then students pair with a neighbour to exchange views and reach a common answer, and finally pairs share solutions with the class, sometimes joined into squares of two pairs to save the teacher time. The article applied it to third-grade science units on plant parts and functions over 25 classroom periods in five weeks.
requirements: A question exciting to think or a problem related to the lesson topic
A specific time allocated for individual reflection based on students' knowledge and question complexity
Teachers trained and ready to implement the strategy
constraints: The study applied it only to third-grade science material in two schools in the educational district of Irbid
target_learning_goals: science achievement of scientific concepts
communication skills and thinking refinement
examples: In the study, teachers taught material units on plant parts and functions using the strategy in a particular pattern and specific mechanism, two servings per week for a total of 16 classes of 45 minutes
key_sources: Dr. Ribhi Khaleel Ahmad Hamdan. (2017). The Effect of (Think – Pair – Share) Strategy on the Achievement of Third Grade Student in Sciences in the Educational District of Irbid. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.9. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1139082

article_title: The Effect of (Think-Pair-Share) Strategy on the Achievement of Third Grade Student in Sciences in the Educational District of Irbid
citation: Dr. Ribhi Khaleel Ahmad Hamdan. (2017). The Effect of (Think – Pair – Share) Strategy on the Achievement of Third Grade Student in Sciences in the Educational District of Irbid. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.9. https://www.iiste.org
title: 20-item multiple-choice science achievement test for third grade
description: The study's measuring instrument was an achievement test of scientific concepts developed for the study: initially 22 multiple-choice questions with 4 options, reduced after arbitrator review to 20 questions scored one mark per correct answer. Difficulty indices ranged between (0.41 - 0.66) and discriminate indices between (0.41 - 0.67), with a whole-test difficulty index of 0.52 and discriminate index of 0.58. Reliability via Cooder Richardson equation (20) was 0.841, and test-retest Pearson correlation over two weeks on 25 students outside the sample was 0.89.
requirements: Validation by 8 arbitrators from experts in learning and modern teaching methods
constraints: Developed specifically for the plant parts and functions material of the third-grade science curriculum in 2016/2017
target_learning_goals: measuring achievement of scientific concepts
examples: The test was applied twice in two weeks on a prospective sample of 25 students from outside the study sample to obtain the test-retest correlation

article_title: Formative Research in Ubiquitous and Virtual Environments in Higher Education
citation: Cristian Velandia-Mesa, Francisca-José Serrano-Pastor, María-José Martínez-Segura. (2017). Formative Research in Ubiquitous and Virtual Environments in Higher Education. Comunicar, 51, XXV. https://doi.org/10.3916/C51-2017-01
title: Three-stage model of articulating educational research with professional practice
description: The article frames formative research as systematization of the pedagogical experience, "an ongoing exercise in the production of critical knowledge from practice." The articulation of educational research with professional practice "has 3 stages that are sequenced and called referencing, systematization, and analysis": referencing builds antecedents and theoretical referents, systematization embraces data collection and processing of context, and analysis corresponds to triangulation, interpretation, and discussion of findings.
requirements: Technological assistance that allows access and ongoing information tracking, plus formative evaluation providing students with feedback
constraints: The process cannot be limited to a physical and temporal space, since knowledge is built at any time and place
target_learners: Higher education students in professional teaching practice
target_learning_goals: Educational research competence and critical knowledge production from practice
examples: The quasi-experiment evaluated outcomes at each of the three stages using a 41-item rubric distributed across them.
key_sources: Cristian Velandia-Mesa, Francisca-José Serrano-Pastor, María-José Martínez-Segura. (2017). Formative Research in Ubiquitous and Virtual Environments in Higher Education. Comunicar, 51, XXV. https://doi.org/10.3916/C51-2017-01

article_title: Causal Mediation in Educational Intervention Studies
citation: Greg Roberts, Nancy Scammacca, and Garrett J. Roberts. (2018). Causal Mediation in Educational Intervention Studies. Behavioral Disorders, 43(4), 457–465. https://doi.org/10.1177/0198742917749560
title: Base mediation modeling on theory and use sensitivity analysis for omitted variables
description: The article argues that omitted variables causing both mediator and outcome bias Paths b and c′ and can mask full mediation, so "statistical modeling should be based on theory and informed by prior research." It frames causal mediation as "a tool for evaluating the extent to which a conceptual model grounded in theory is supported by sample data," and recommends sensitivity analysis to evaluate the potential that a model has omitted variables. Randomization protects Paths a and c from this bias but not b and c′.
requirements: A conceptual model grounded in theory and prior research to guide which potential mediators are included
constraints: Omitted-variable bias affects Paths b and c′ even in randomized designs; randomization only protects Paths a and c
target_learners: educational researchers analyzing randomized school-based intervention studies
target_learning_goals: valid identification of the mechanisms through which interventions affect student outcomes
examples: In the running example, only the PSRA effortful control subtest was modeled; the article notes attention/impulsivity and executive functioning subtests were omitted and could be included if researchers had theoretical support
key_sources: Greg Roberts, Nancy Scammacca, and Garrett J. Roberts. (2018). Causal Mediation in Educational Intervention Studies. Behavioral Disorders, 43(4), 457–465. https://doi.org/10.1177/0198742917749560

article_title: Empirical Benchmarks for Planning and Interpreting Causal Effects of Community College Interventions
citation: Michael J. Weiss, Marie-Andrée Somers, & Colin Hill. (2023). Empirical Benchmarks for Planning and Interpreting Causal Effects of Community College Interventions. Journal of Postsecondary Student Success 3(1). https://doi.org/10.33009/fsop_jpss132759
title: THE-RCT: The Higher Education Randomized Controlled Trials Restricted Access File and associated public benchmark database
description: THE-RCT RAF is a restricted-access student-level database created by MDRC and housed at ICPSR, including all RCTs MDRC conducted in postsecondary education from 2003–2019, with design indicators, student characteristics, and semester-level outcomes (enrollment, credits, degree completion). The present analysis uses 39 interventions and "a total of 65,604 students" across 44 institutions. A companion public-use dataset with study-level effect estimates and an online adjustment tool are available at the MDRC benchmarks site.
requirements: Access to THE-RCT RAF is restricted to qualified researchers with few restrictions
constraints: The RCT samples focus on students already enrolled who agreed to participate, so effects may not generalize to all community college students or to prospective students and applicants
target_learning_goals: enrollment persistence
credit accumulation
degree or certificate completion
examples: The article's benchmarks were computed from THE-RCT data on 39 interventions, with analytic samples ranging from 21,163 to 65,604 students depending on outcome and semester
key_sources: Michael J. Weiss, Marie-Andrée Somers, & Colin Hill. (2023). Empirical Benchmarks for Planning and Interpreting Causal Effects of Community College Interventions. Journal of Postsecondary Student Success 3(1). https://doi.org/10.33009/fsop_jpss132759

article_title: A Field Study about the Impact of a VR Learning Unit
citation: Thomas Keller, Fabian Hagen and Elke Brucker-Kley. (2019). A FIELD STUDY ABOUT THE IMPACT OF A VR LEARNING UNIT. 16th International Conference on Cognition and Exploratory Learning in Digital Age (CELDA 2019). https://doi.org/10.33965/celda2019_201911L038
title: Immersive learning framed by the three I's: imagination, immersion and interaction
description: The article adopts the account that learning in virtual worlds, called "immersive learning", rests on three factors: "Imagination, immersion and interaction seem to be important factors for immersive learning." Immersion is described as the degree to which individuals perceive interacting more with the virtual than the real environment, determined by representation of the learners, presence and possibilities of interaction. The framework is used to situate the VR mathematics unit as an immersive learning environment with high interaction.
requirements: The learning environment must provide real-time visualizations and reactions giving users immediate feedback on their inputs, with multimodal information recording
constraints: The support of immersion on learning processes via flow and presence is presented as a thesis, and the same effects are also discussed in the context of computer game addiction
target_learning_goals: mathematics learning (measures and masses) through immersive VR
examples: The study's VR unit "So small! - So big!" was developed to exhibit a degree of interaction close to doing, in the sense of involvement in learning
key_sources: Thomas Keller, Fabian Hagen and Elke Brucker-Kley. (2019). A FIELD STUDY ABOUT THE IMPACT OF A VR LEARNING UNIT. 16th International Conference on Cognition and Exploratory Learning in Digital Age (CELDA 2019). https://doi.org/10.33965/celda2019_201911L038

article_title: Effects of a Text-Processing Comprehension Intervention on Struggling Middle School Readers
citation: Amy E. Barth, Sharon Vaughn, Philip Capin, Eunsoo Cho, Stephanie Stillman-Spisak, Leticia Martinez, and Heather Kincaid. (2016). Effects of a Text-processing Comprehension Intervention on Struggling Middle School Readers. Top Lang Disord. 2016; 36(4): 368–389. https://doi.org/10.1097/TLD.0000000000000101
title: Three-component text-processing lesson model for building comprehension of informational science texts
description: The article's intervention operationalizes a lesson model in which "Each instructional lesson consisted of three components: 1) identifying key words and main ideas through text-based discourse, 2) synthesizing information within a single text for summarization and making inferences, and 3) integrating information across multiple texts". Interventionists model components through think-alouds, provide guided practice and corrective feedback, and gradually release responsibility as students show proficiency. The model targets both lower-level and higher-level language processes hypothesized to restrict struggling readers' synthesis of central ideas.
requirements: Interventionists use explicit instructional routines, quality feedback, and gradual release of responsibility, supported by semi-scripted lessons and weekly research-team support
constraints: The article reports the feedback loop for main idea statements was challenging for undergraduate interventionists and required ongoing weekly professional development and script modifications
target_learners: middle grade students (grades 6-8) reading below Basic or Basic on a state reading assessment
target_learning_goals: identifying key words and main ideas in informational science texts
summarizing and making inferences
integrating information across multiple texts
vocabulary knowledge
examples: Students received 40 minutes of small group instruction (4-6 students per group) four times per week for approximately eight weeks, organized around four two-week thematic science units with texts at grade 6-8 Lexile levels
key_sources: Amy E. Barth, Sharon Vaughn, Philip Capin, Eunsoo Cho, Stephanie Stillman-Spisak, Leticia Martinez, and Heather Kincaid. (2016). Effects of a Text-processing Comprehension Intervention on Struggling Middle School Readers. Top Lang Disord. 2016; 36(4): 368–389. https://doi.org/10.1097/TLD.0000000000000101

article_title: Effects of Instruction on Chinese College Students' Use of Thematic Progression in English Essays
citation: Jing Wei. (2017). Effects of Instruction on Chinese College Students' Use of Thematic Progression in English Essays. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.8. https://www.iiste.org
title: Thematic progression patterns as an analytic framework for English essay writing
description: Thematic progression (TP), first proposed by Daneš (1974), concerns "the way that the texts develop the ideas they present" in Theme-Rheme structure. The study identifies five TP patterns (linear, constant, summative, split Theme, split Rheme) and three types of unmotivated Themes (back, contextual, new), counting connections between contiguous T-units. The framework is used to code 150 essays and quantify how instruction changes learners' information structuring.
requirements: Theme/Rheme division following Halliday's first experiential constituent, with the T-unit as the unit of analysis
constraints: Only connections between contiguous T-units were counted as linear or constant progressions, with the exception of Themes in split and summative progressions
target_learners: Chinese college English majors writing in English
target_learning_goals: Discourse-level coherence and information structuring in English essay writing
examples: Five TP patterns and three unmotivated Theme types were identified and counted in 150 essays totaling 33,134 words, analyzed in SPSS with independent and paired-samples t-tests
key_sources: Jing Wei. (2017). Effects of Instruction on Chinese College Students' Use of Thematic Progression in English Essays. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.8. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1139060

article_title: Experimental Design: Utilizing Microsoft Mathematics in Teaching and Learning Calculus
citation: Rina Oktaviyanthi, Yani Supriani. (2015). Experimental Design: Utilizing Microsoft Mathematics in Teaching and Learning Calculus. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.25. https://www.iiste.org
title: Three-purpose framework for using Microsoft Mathematics in Calculus lectures
description: The article organizes its lecture activities around three main purposes of using a tool in teaching and learning, adapted from Wilson (2008): promoting drill and practice (problem solving and calculation), variation of parameters (visualization and graphing), and conceptual understanding (exploratory and confirmatory use). Within these, students tried graphical, numerical, or algebraic approaches, changed parameters of Calculus functions and observed graphical changes, and validated their answers in problem solving tasks. The article states a pedagogical benefit that "Direct feedback is helpful to make the relation between the parameters in Calculus functions".
requirements: Activities must be organized around stated purposes of tool use, as the study planned activities based on three main purposes of using a tool in teaching and learning process
constraints: The framework was applied in a single first-year Calculus lecture setting at one university
target_learners: first-year university students in a Faculty of Information Technology
target_learning_goals: understanding Calculus concepts including limits, derivatives, and integration
problem solving and connecting multiple mathematical representations
examples: Students used Microsoft Mathematics to try different approaches to solve a given Calculus problem, to graph functions and solve problems related to area under a curve, and to explore integration in algebraic and graphical representation
key_sources: Rina Oktaviyanthi, Yani Supriani. (2015). Experimental Design: Utilizing Microsoft Mathematics in Teaching and Learning Calculus. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.25. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1078520

article_title: Enhancement of Performance and Motivation through Application of Digital Games in an English Language Class
citation: Saovapa Wichadee and Fasawang Pattanapichet. (2017). Enhancement of Performance and Motivation through Application of Digital Games in an English Language Class. Teaching English with Technology, 18(1), 77-92. http://www.tewtjournal.org
title: Theory of gamified learning: games affect learning through a direct mediating process and a less direct moderating process
description: The article adopts Landers' theory of gamified learning as its explanatory framework for how digital games influence outcomes. It states that "two major psychological proce sses in which games can affect learning include a more direct mediating process and a less direct moderating process". Because learning occurs through an intermediary attitude or behavior, games should vary in context: specific rules or goals can raise motivation to learn, while adapting a game to learner ability can enhance cognitive strategies. The study's Kahoot intervention is interpreted against this framework.
requirements: Games should be designed to vary in context because learning occurs through an intermediary attitude or behavior
target_learning_goals: grammar and vocabulary knowledge
learning motivation
examples: The study embedded Kahoot quizzes in a fundamental English course to reinforce attention and engagement, interpreting the performance and motivation gains through this framework
key_sources: Saovapa Wichadee and Fasawang Pattanapichet. (2017). Enhancement of Performance and Motivation through Application of Digital Games in an English Language Class. Teaching English with Technology, 18(1), 77-92. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1170635

article_title: Impact of Smartphone Based Activities on EFL Students' Engagement
citation: Pir Suhail Ahmed Sarhandi, Ayman Bajnaid & Tariq Elyas. (2017). Impact of Smartphone Based Activities on EFL Students' Engagement. English Language Teaching, 10(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n6p103
title: Three-strand task engagement framework: behavioural, cognitive, and emotional realisations
description: The article adopts a three-strand interpretation of task engagement drawn from Skinner & Belmont (1993): behavioural engagement evidenced through task initiation and sustained involvement, cognitive engagement including concentration, and generally positive emotions. The authors state that "task engagement can be deconstructed into three realisations" and note task engagement exists on a continuum from flow to superficial engagement and disaffection. They operationalise the behavioural and emotional strands for their smartphone study and treat behavioural engagement as an indicator of some cognitive engagement.
requirements: Measurement requires observation of initiation, sustained involvement, and emotional display; the article notes no instrument "can comprehensively assess student engagement on all of the construct dimensions listed"
constraints: Cognitive engagement was not measured in this study because teachers could not reliably comment on it
target_learning_goals: Student task engagement during classroom EFL activities
examples: Teachers recorded initiation times in seconds and Likert-scale distraction and negative-emotion ratings after each of 19 treatment sessions
key_sources: Pir Suhail Ahmed Sarhandi, Ayman Bajnaid & Tariq Elyas. (2017). Impact of Smartphone Based Activities on EFL Students' Engagement. English Language Teaching, 10(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n6p103

article_title: The Effects of Training and Other Factors on Problem Solving in Students
citation: Robabeh Puran, Mohamad Hasan Behzadi, Ahmad Shahvarani, Farhad Hosseinzadeh Lotfi. (2017). The Effects of Training and Other Factors on Problem Solving in Students. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 6(3): 448-460. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2017.3.448
title: Three teaching methods mapping onto three historical stages of education: teaching-centred, information processing, and student-centred
description: The article organises mathematics problem-solving instruction into three methods — traditional, heuristic, and active — and states "These three methods correspond with the three historical stag es of education (teaching-centred, information processing and student-centred)." The traditional method has the teacher presenting predefined materials orally while students memorise; the heuristic method teaches named strategies such as drawing a picture, systematic tables, and eliminating inappropriate possibilities; the active method centres on students solving problems themselves with teacher guidance. The framework frames the study's comparison of the three conditions.
requirements: Teachers must know the methods and their underlying strategies; the article says instruction in the use and selection of explorative problem-solving strategies is very important
constraints: Heuristics, per Schoenfeld as cited, cannot be generalised due to the complexity of utilising them in practice
target_learning_goals: problem-solving skill
creative thinking
examples: The heuristic condition introduced two heuristics per session, including drawing a picture for the chickens-and-cows problem and systematic tables for the orange-salesman problem
key_sources: Robabeh Puran, Mohamad Hasan Behzadi, Ahmad Shahvarani, Farhad Hosseinzadeh Lotfi. (2017). The Effects of Training and Other Factors on Problem Solving in Students. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 6(3): 448-460. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2017.3.448

article_title: Influence of Conflict Resolution Training on Conflict Handling Styles of College Students
citation: Abel Gitimu Waithaka, Shante' Moore-Austin, Priscilla N. Gitimu. (2015). Influence of conflict resolution training on conflict handling styles of college students. Research in Higher Education Journal, 28. http://www.aabri.com/copyright.html
title: Thomas-Kilmann Conflict MODE instrument for measuring conflict handling styles
description: The MODE instrument measures individual conflict handling styles by allocating respondents to the assertiveness and cooperativeness dimensions. "The MODE instrument consists of 30 paired items, which makes a total of 60 statements." Participants choose from each pair the statement that best describes how they usually behave in conflict situations, yielding scores on five modes. The study used it for both pre- and post-testing of experimental and control groups.
requirements: Participants choose the response from each pair that best describes their usual behavior in conflict situations
target_learning_goals: measuring conflict handling styles
examples: Used as the pre-test and post-test measure of conflict handling styles in this study's control-group design
key_sources: Abel Gitimu Waithaka, Shante' Moore-Austin, Priscilla N. Gitimu. (2015). Influence of conflict resolution training on conflict handling styles of college students. Research in Higher Education Journal, 28. http://www.aabri.com/copyright.html

article_title: A Comparative Study of the Effects of the Neurocognitive-Based Model and the Conventional Model on Learner Attention, Working Memory and Mood
citation: Sanit Srikoon, Tassanee Bunterm, Teerachai Nethanomsak & Tang Keow Ngang. (2017). A comparative study of the effects of the neurocognitive-based model and the conventional model on learner attention, working memory and mood. Malaysian Journal of Learning and Instruction, 14(1), 83-110. https://mjli.uum.edu.my
title: Thai computerized attention and working memory battery tests and the Bond-Ladder mood scale
description: The study used three instruments to measure learning outcomes: an attention computerized battery test, a working memory computerized battery test, and a 16-item Bond-Ladder visual analogue scale for mood. The article states "The attention battery test consisted of 14 sub-tests or 14 tasks" and the working memory battery test comprised 13 tasks, all in Thai, measuring accuracy and reaction time. Test-retest reliability ranged from 0.939 to 0.998 for attention sub-tests and 0.822 to 0.979 for working memory tasks; the mood scale's KR20 was 0.888.
requirements: Administration in the Thai language; construct validity previously evaluated by Bunterm et al. (2015) and Srikoon (2015)
constraints: Mood measured by self-report visual analogue scale covering alertness, calmness, and contentedness only
target_learning_goals: measuring attention accuracy and reaction time
measuring working memory accuracy and reaction time
measuring mood
examples: Students were given 50 trials in each attention task; the working memory battery included stroop, flanker-arrow, n-back, and Thai word span tasks
key_sources: Sanit Srikoon, Tassanee Bunterm, Teerachai Nethanomsak & Tang Keow Ngang. (2017). A comparative study of the effects of the neurocognitive-based model and the conventional model on learner attention, working memory and mood. Malaysian Journal of Learning and Instruction, 14(1), 83-110. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1150726

article_title: The Impact of Providing Performance Feedback to Teachers and Principals. NCEE 2018-4001
citation: Garet, M.S., Wayne, A.J., Brown, S., Rickles, J., Song, M., and Manzeske, D. (2017). The Impact of Providing Performance Feedback to Teachers and Principals (NCEE 2018-4001). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: Three-measure low-stakes educator performance feedback system (CLASS/FFT observations, value-added growth reports, VAL-ED leadership feedback)
description: The study provided eight districts resources and support to implement three performance measures: a classroom practice measure "with subsequent feedback sessions conducted four times per year based on a classroom observation rubric" (CLASS or FFT), a student growth measure (value-added scores provided once per year), and a principal leadership measure (VAL-ED) with feedback sessions twice per year. No formal stakes were attached; measures were used to give educators and supervisors information about performance. Schools were randomly assigned to implement the measures or not.
requirements: Districts needed data systems sufficient to support value-added analysis
Feedback sessions with trained observers and printed or online report dissemination
constraints: The measures were not used for staffing decisions such as tenure or continued employment, with exceptions in three districts where principal observations counted in official ratings
Rubric assignment was by district preference, not random, so CLASS/FFT differences cannot be attributed to the observation systems
target_learners: Grades 4–8 teachers of reading/ELA and mathematics
target_learning_goals: Improving classroom instructional practice
Improving principal instructional leadership
Raising student mathematics and reading achievement
examples: Treatment teachers received an average of 3.7 and 3.9 observations with feedback sessions in Years 1 and 2 respectively
key_sources: Garet, M.S., Wayne, A.J., Brown, S., Rickles, J., Song, M., and Manzeske, D. (2017). The Impact of Providing Performance Feedback to Teachers and Principals (NCEE 2018-4001). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee

article_title: The Effectiveness of Using WhatsApp Messenger as One of Mobile Learning Techniques to Develop Students' Writing Skills
citation: Said Fathy El Said Abdul Fattah. (2015). The Effectiveness of Using WhatsApp Messenger as One of Mobile Learning Techniques to Develop Students' Writing Skills. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.32. https://www.iiste.org
title: Three-question writing pre/post test (punctuation, sentence structure, essay)
description: The study's instrument was a pre/post test built from curriculum standards and previous studies, consisting of "three questions": punctuating a 15-sentence paragraph with ten punctuation mistakes, correcting grammatical mistakes in sentence structure, and writing a five-paragraph essay on one of three topics. Content validity was judged by two EFL assistant professors and one lecturer, and test-retest reliability with 13 students yielded a Pearson coefficient of 0.72.
requirements: Administered before and after the program to establish group equivalence and measure gains.
constraints: The article limits the research to punctuation marks, sentence structures and generating ideas.
target_learning_goals: writing skills: punctuation, sentence structure, essay writing
examples: The jury suggested offering more than one essay topic and adding capitalization to the paragraph mistakes.
key_sources: Said Fathy El Said Abdul Fattah. (2015). The Effectiveness of Using WhatsApp Messenger as One of Mobile Learning Techniques to Develop Students' Writing Skills. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.32. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1083503

article_title: Humour in the Teaching of English and German Equivocal Words
citation: Sanchez, A. C. & Magro, L. J. C. (2018). Humour in the teaching of English and German equivocal words. Cypriot Journal of Educational Sciences, 13(4), 645-653. https://www.cjes.eu
title: Three-test retention design for vocabulary teaching (pre-test, immediate post-test, two-week delayed post-test)
description: The study's measurement instrument is a translation test of ten sentences, each containing one target equivocal word, administered three times. Test I before instruction showed participants did not know the words; Test II immediately after instruction checked understanding; Test III two weeks later measured retention and correct use. German learners took an inverse translation from German into Spanish.
requirements: The same ten-sentence translation test administered at all three time points to both control and experimental groups
constraints: Retention was assessed only at a two-week delay in this pilot study
target_learners: Adult Spanish foreign-language learners of English and German (B1)
target_learning_goals: Retention and correct use of equivocal vocabulary
examples: Test III was "done two weeks later because it will shed light upon the question whether or not EG and CG retain and remember the lexicon taught"
key_sources: Sanchez, A. C. & Magro, L. J. C. (2018). Humour in the teaching of English and German equivocal words. Cypriot Journal of Educational Sciences, 13(4), 645-653. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1202228

article_title: Effects of Worksheets Base the Levels of Inquiry in Improving Critical and Creative Thinking
citation: Muskita, M., Subali, B., & Djukri. (2020). Effects of Worksheets Base the Levels of Inquiry in Improving Critical and Creative Thinking. International Journal of Instruction, 13(2), 519-532. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13236a
title: Three-level inquiry-based biology worksheets (structured, guided, open) for plant morphology, ecology, and physiology
description: Printed student worksheets designed around three levels of inquiry — structured, guided, and open — each organized by the syntax of formulating problems, submitting hypotheses, collecting data, analyzing, and drawing conclusions. Each worksheet material is arranged in a sequent order including "material descriptions, material summaries, practice questions, and assignments". The worksheets were developed for plant morphology, plant ecology, and plant physiology courses and validated by a curriculum expert and science material experts.
requirements: Designed to suit the characteristics of the learning materials and courses; validated by curriculum and science material experts
constraints: Developed and tested with biology education students in plant morphology, ecology, and physiology at Pattimura University
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills
creative thinking skills
examples: Worksheets were used weekly over three months (February to April 2018) across twelve science topics, with 120-minute class meetings
key_sources: Muskita, M., Subali, B., & Djukri. (2020). Effects of Worksheets Base the Levels of Inquiry in Improving Critical and Creative Thinking. International Journal of Instruction, 13(2), 519-532. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13236a

article_title: Application of Meta-Cognitive Strategy Instruction in Listening Comprehension to the Level III Student-Teachers
citation: Evangelin Whitehead. (2019). Application of Meta-Cognitive Strategy Instruction in Listening Comprehension to the Level III Student-Teachers. The Excellence in Education Journal, 8(2). https://excellenceineducationjournal.org
title: Three-stage metacognitive listening instruction model (planning, listening, post-listening)
description: The article operationalizes metacognitive strategy instruction in listening comprehension as three stages. The planning stage uses "planning and directed attention" with pre-questioning advance organizers; the listening stage has students hear the task three times in pairs, applying selective attention, monitoring, problem solving and self-management; the post-listening stage is a self-assessment stage using class discussion, a check back system, learning logs and reflection and evaluation strategies.
requirements: Instruction delivered across a semester within the regular listening comprehension course, with the teacher demonstrating and assisting the strategies
constraints: Stated limitation: the experiment ran for only one term with a very small group in a single class of students
target_learners: Level III EFL student-teachers of average to below average listening proficiency
target_learning_goals: EFL listening comprehension
metacognitive awareness of listening strategies
examples: Students wrote their ideas about the topic before listening, compared predictions across three listenings, kept learning logs noting peers' strategies, and answered comprehension questions
key_sources: Evangelin Whitehead. (2019). Application of Meta-Cognitive Strategy Instruction in Listening Comprehension to the Level III Student-Teachers. The Excellence in Education Journal, 8(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1228050

article_title: The Impact of Educational Infographic on Students' Interaction and Perception in Jordanian Higher Education: Experimental Study
citation: Alqudah, D., Bidin, A., & Md Hussin, M. A. H. (2019). The Impact of Educational Infographic on Students’ Interaction and Perception in Jordanian Higher Education: Experimental Study. International Journal of Instruction, 12(4), 669-688. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2019.12443a
title: Three-stage infographic lesson design: divide lecture into introduction, content and conclusion, vary graphic elements, then select semiotic forms
description: The article's procedure for developing infographics for selected chapters proceeds in three stages. "The first stage was dividing each lecture material into three parts: Introduction and main concepts for the taught course, lesson's content  explanation which have abundance in text" and a conclusion with less text. The second stage divides the design into multiple graphic presentations, changing graphical elements such as colors, sizes and spatial distribution each lesson according to student inferences. The third stage selects semiotic forms — icon, index and symbol — singly or in mutual links representing the overall idea of a topic.
requirements: researcher collaboration with subject tutors to ensure harmony between infographic design and tutors' subject knowledge
constraints: the researcher was not a specialist in the courses and needed tutor supervision to design the medium
target_learners: first-year higher education students in scientific and humanistic colleges
target_learning_goals: receiving, comparing and considering lesson information through visual communication
examples: Infographic videos presented concepts in the introduction and reviewed concluded points at the end, with several infographic designs and semiotic selections presented during content explanation at a longer duration
key_sources: Alqudah, D., Bidin, A., & Md Hussin, M. A. H. (2019). The Impact of Educational Infographic on Students’ Interaction and Perception in Jordanian Higher Education: Experimental Study. International Journal of Instruction, 12(4), 669-688. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2019.12443a

article_title: Effects of Etymological Elaboration on the EFL Learners' Comprehension and Retention of Idioms
citation: Bagheri, M. S., & Fazel, I. (2010). Effects of Etymological Elaboration on the EFL Learners’ Comprehension and Retention of Idioms. Journal of Pan-Pacific Association of Applied Linguistics, 14(1), 45-55. https://www.paaljapan.org
title: Three-part 15-idiom pen-and-paper test replicated from Boers et al. (2007)
description: The study's instrument is "a pen and paper test comprising 15 idioms" replicated from Boers et al. (2007), with three parts: a matching exercise pairing idioms with origins, a multiple-choice exercise on idiom definitions, and a gap-filling exercise with meaningful sentences. Validity was checked by three experienced university lecturers and reliability by Cronbach's alpha, reported as r=0.88.
requirements: The same 15 idioms are used across all three parts; the gap-filling task is administered a week after the first two exercises.
constraints: The instrument was validated locally by three lecturers at Islamic Azad University and Shiraz State University.
target_learning_goals: Assessing idiom comprehension and retention
examples: The appendix prints the matching exercise with 15 idioms such as 'a rule of thumb' and 'to tie the knot' paired with origin descriptions A–O.
key_sources: Bagheri, M. S., & Fazel, I. (2010). Effects of Etymological Elaboration on the EFL Learners’ Comprehension and Retention of Idioms. Journal of Pan-Pacific Association of Applied Linguistics, 14(1), 45-55. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ920503

article_title: ThinkForward: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Sean Demack, Colin McCaig, Claire Wolstenholme, Anna Stevens and Laura Fumagalli. (2016). ThinkForward: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/evaluation/projects/think-forward
title: ThinkForward four-step coaching process with GROW model and SMART targets
description: The ThinkForward intervention places a trained, full-time coach in a school to work with pupils aged 14 onwards identified as most at risk of becoming NEET, through one-to-one and group sessions. "Coaches follow a four step process in order to carry out their work with pupils": identify participants via a bespoke NEET-risk scoring mechanism, understand needs using the Personal Development tracker and Apollo psychometric platform, design action plans using the GROW coaching model with SMART targets, and do and review through regular sessions. In late Year 10/early Year 11 pupils also undertake 6-8 business mentoring sessions with corporate partners covering CV writing and interview practice.
requirements: Coaches are employed full time and should develop a relationship with pupils, with good knowledge of opportunities open to young people to signpost pupils outside of school
All sessions are recorded on a management information system, and coaches have termly review meetings with the school lead
constraints: This evaluation was undertaken when ThinkForward was in a relatively early stage of its development, and the findings should be considered in this context
target_learners: Secondary school pupils aged 14-16 identified as most at risk of becoming NEET
target_learning_goals: Successful transition into adulthood through further education, employment or vocational training
Building life skills and confidence, and access to employers and the world of work
examples: Coaches typically see pupils approximately twice per half term for a planned, structured session lasting around 45 minutes as well as informal check ups in the interim
key_sources: Sean Demack, Colin McCaig, Claire Wolstenholme, Anna Stevens and Laura Fumagalli. (2016). ThinkForward: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/evaluation/projects/think-forward

article_title: The Effect of Explicit Metapragmatic Instruction on Request Speech Act Awareness of Intermediate EFL Students at Institute Level
citation: Fatemeh Abdollahizadeh Masouleh, Masoumeh Arjmandi, Fereydoon Vahdany. (2014). The Effect of Explicit Metapragmatic Instruction on Request Speech Act Awareness of Intermediate EFL Students at Institute Level. Universal Journal of Educational Research 2(7): 504-511. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2014.020702
title: Three factors causing pragmatic failure in L2 communication
description: The article identifies three causes of pragmatic failure: "cultural differences, pragmatic transfer, and the lack of pragmatic knowledge". Cultural differences between L1 and target culture may cause negative transfer; pragmatic transfer involves L1 speech patterns used in L2 utterances, such as using a direct speech act where a native speaker would use an indirect one; and lack of pragmatic knowledge mainly affects inefficient communication. The article frames explicit teaching of rules of appropriate language use as the teacher's response, since pragmatic failures often pass unchecked or are attributed to rudeness.
requirements: Both linguistic and pragmatic competence are required to achieve communicative goals efficiently
constraints: Presented in the article's introduction as background framing, not tested in this study
target_learning_goals: pragmatic competence and appropriate language use across cultures
key_sources: Fatemeh Abdollahizadeh Masouleh, Masoumeh Arjmandi, Fereydoon Vahdany. (2014). article_title: The Effects of Learning-Style Based Activities on Students' Reading Comprehension Skills and Self-Efficacy Perceptions in English Foreign Language Classes
citation: Özgül Balcı. (2017). The Effects of Learning-Style Based Activities on Students' Reading Comprehension Skills and Self-Efficacy Perceptions in English Foreign Language Classes. Higher Education Studies, 7(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v7n4p35
title: Three-phase EFL reading lesson cycle with warm-up and evaluation, delivered through learning-style varied activities
description: The article's instructional pattern organizes each weekly reading lesson into a short warm-up followed by pre-reading, while-reading, and post-reading phases, ending with an evaluation on a similar text. Pre-reading activities activate background knowledge; while-reading activities guide strategic reading; post-reading activities extend content through other skills. The article states "reading lessons were conducted through activities divided into three phases after a short warm-up period". Both experimental and control groups followed this structure; only the activity design differed.
requirements: Texts selected at appropriate difficulty, with suitable syntactic structures, appropriate length, age and interest appropriateness, and a reasonable amount of new information
Teaching delivered across repeated weekly sessions (three one-hour sessions weekly in the study)
constraints: The study ran over a limited 8-week, 24-class-hour period, which the author lists as a limitation on generalization
target_learners: freshmen university students at low English proficiency (A1/A2 self-reported)
target_learning_goals: English reading comprehension
English self-efficacy across the four language skills
examples: Eight texts, one per week, were arranged from easy to difficult based on Gunning Fog readability analyses; each class ended with an evaluation using a different text on a similar topic with the same target vocabulary

article_title: A Comparison of Heritage Learners and L2 Learners of Spanish: A Study on Compliment Sequences in the Classroom
citation: Bachelor, J. W., & Barros García, M. J. (2019). A comparison of heritage learners and L2 learners of Spanish: A study on compliment sequences in the classroom. Journal of Foreign Language Education and Technology, 4(1). http://jflet.com/jflet/
title: Three-lesson explicit pragmatic intervention sequence on compliment sequences
description: The intervention consisted of three classroom lessons of approximately 15 minutes each, totaling 45 minutes across a semester. The first lesson gave an explicit explanation of compliment sequences followed by practice exercises; the second used video clips from the Spanish-speaking world for learners to identify compliments, responses, speaker relationships, and purposes; the third was a condensed, video-supported modification of CARLA's lesson on compliment sequences.
requirements: Video clips providing authentic context for compliment sequences
Explicit explanation of compliment norms in Spanish followed by examples
constraints: The intervention lasted half of a semester, which the authors list as a limitation
target_learning_goals: recognizing and responding appropriately to Spanish compliment sequences
examples: One lesson occurred approximately every three weeks after the pretest, which was given two months into the semester
