article_title: Virtual Laboratory as an Element of Visualization When Teaching Chemical Contents in Science Class
citation: Nataša Rizman Herga, Milena Ivanuš Grmek, Dejan Dinevski. (2014). Virtual Laboratory as an Element of Visualization when Teaching Chemical Contents in Science Class. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 13(4). https://www.tojet.net
title: Three levels of scientific concept presentation (macroscopic, submicroscopic, symbolic)
description: The article describes chemical concepts as describable on three levels: "The first concrete and actual level is the macroscopic level; the second  is the actual phenomenon explaining the submicroscopic level; and the third level is symbolic". Pupils struggle to bridge the gaps between these levels, which the authors say visualization elements such as virtual laboratories can overcome, so that all three levels meaningfully overlap during learning and appropriate mental models develop.
requirements: All three levels should meaningfully overlap during the learning process for adequate mental models to develop
target_learning_goals: understanding of chemical concepts at macroscopic, submicroscopic and symbolic levels
examples: Figure 1 depicts the three levels of scientific concepts' presentation and the role of the virtual laboratory in bridging them
key_sources: Nataša Rizman Herga, Milena Ivanuš Grmek, Dejan Dinevski. (2014). Virtual Laboratory as an Element of Visualization when Teaching Chemical Contents in Science Class. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 13(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1043246

article_title: Short-Term and Long-Term Retention of Vocabulary through Authentic Subtitled Videos
citation: Nader Asadi Aidinlou & Alireza Moradinejad. (2016). Short-term and Long-term Retention of Vocabulary through Authentic Subtitled Videos. Advances in Language and Literary Studies. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.5p.14
title: Three types of audio-subtitle combinations in foreign-language video
description: Drawing on Zanon, the article distinguishes three combinations of audio and subtitles: "standard subtitles (the combination of foreign language audio and mother tongue captions)", bimodal subtitles (foreign-language audio with foreign-language subtitles), and reversed subtitles (mother-tongue audio with foreign-language captions). It reports that the bimodal, intra-lingual type is the most common in classroom activities. The framework explains how subtitles support monitoring of speech and vocabulary recognition.
requirements: Subtitles are presented as needing appropriate guidance and training to give learners subjective support and objective aid in recognition, maintenance, and production of linguistic items
constraints: The article notes subtitles have sometimes been regarded as distracting and as tending to slow the development of listening skills
target_learners: foreign language learners watching authentic video
target_learning_goals: vocabulary recognition and retention from audiovisual input
examples: The experimental treatment used subtitled sitcom viewing: first with subtitles, then a second viewing without subtitles
key_sources: Nader Asadi Aidinlou & Alireza Moradinejad. (2016). Short-term and Long-term Retention of Vocabulary through Authentic Subtitled Videos. Advances in Language and Literary Studies. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.5p.14

article_title: How Much Videos Win over Audios in Listening Instruction for EFL Learners
citation: Yasin, B., Mustafa, F., & Permatasari, R. (2018). How Much Videos Win Over Audios in Listening Instruction for EFL Learners. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(1). https://tojet.net/
title: Three models of listening processes: bottom-up, top-down, and interactive processing
description: The article presents, citing Flowerdew and Miller (2010), a three-part account of how listeners construct meaning. In bottom-up processing, listeners "mentally construct the meaning of information heard in chunks, starting with individual sounds to words, phrases, clauses and sentences"; in top-down processing listeners rely on prior knowledge and experience; interactive processing mixes the two simultaneously. The article uses this framework in its literature review to ground how listening should be taught.
requirements: Teachers must understand the processes of listening and strategies for teaching listening before teaching it, as the article states
target_learning_goals: listening comprehension
key_sources: Yasin, B., Mustafa, F., & Permatasari, R. (2018). How Much Videos Win Over Audios in Listening Instruction for EFL Learners. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1165770

article_title: How Much Videos Win over Audios in Listening Instruction for EFL Learners
citation: Yasin, B., Mustafa, F., & Permatasari, R. (2018). How Much Videos Win Over Audios in Listening Instruction for EFL Learners. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(1). https://tojet.net/
title: Three-stage listening lesson: pre-listening, while-listening, post-listening
description: The article describes a lesson-level structure for listening instruction in which "A good listening activity consists of three stages: pre-listening, while-listening and post-listening". Pre-listening prepares students for what they will hear (about 10 to 15 minutes at most, per Houston); while-listening has students listen and complete tasks, with the recording played a few times with a different task each time; post-listening gives feedback and lets the teacher analyse difficulties. Table 1 contrasts early practices (pre-teaching vocabulary for maximum understanding) with current practices (establishing context, creating motivation, pre-teaching only critical vocabulary, and final play with transcripts).
requirements: Each stage needs its own activity: preparation before listening, a task during listening, and feedback after listening
constraints: The pre-listening stage should not be too long, about 10 to 15 minutes at the most, per the article citing Houston (2016)
target_learning_goals: listening comprehension
examples: The article's treatment lessons followed the 2013 Curriculum's scientific approach across four 90-minute meetings focused on identifying main ideas and supporting details in exposition texts
key_sources: Yasin, B., Mustafa, F., & Permatasari, R. (2018). How Much Videos Win Over Audios in Listening Instruction for EFL Learners. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1165770

article_title: The Impact of Explicit Instruction and Intentional Learning in the Reception of Vocabulary--An Experimental Study
citation: R. Infanta Vincy. (2018). The Impact of Explicit Instruction and Intentional Learning in the Reception of Vocabulary - An Experimental Study. i-manager's Journal on English Language Teaching, Vol. 8 No. 2. https://journals.imanager.com/jelt
title: Design vocabulary textbook materials and teaching methodologies on the basis of theoretical understanding of vocabulary knowledge and acquisition
description: The article's key implication is that "the theoretical understanding of the available concepts of vocabulary knowledge and the process of vocabulary acquisition is mandatory in designing the textbook materials and in framing methodologies for the teaching of vocabulary". It further argues that beyond methodologies and tasks, there is a need for consciousness of vocabulary in both teacher and learners.
requirements: Teachers and learners should both be conscious that vocabulary learning is occurring
constraints: The qualitative findings are strictly limited to the Tamil Nadu Uniform Syllabus textbooks
target_learners: learners of English as a second language in early language learning phases
target_learning_goals: receptive and eventual productive vocabulary knowledge
examples: The study analysed the textbook's vocabulary aspects and observed teaching before testing the explicit-plus-intentional alternative.
key_sources: R. Infanta Vincy. (2018). The Impact of Explicit Instruction and Intentional Learning in the Reception of Vocabulary - An Experimental Study. i-manager's Journal on English Language Teaching, Vol. 8 No. 2. https://journals.imanager.com/jelt

article_title: Are They Climbing the Pyramid? Rating Student-Generated Questions in a Game Design Project
citation: Jason Paul Siko. (2011). Homemade PowerPoint Games. http://it.coe.uga.edu/wwild/pptgames
title: Three philosophical justifications for homemade PowerPoint games: constructionism, microtheme writing, and question writing
description: The article organizes the rationale for homemade PowerPoint games around three justifications: "constructionism, microtheme writing, and question writing." Constructionism holds that students learn through building artifacts; microtheme writing draws on writing-across-the-curriculum research showing enhanced effects with shorter assignments; question writing draws on self-questioning research showing learning gains, greatest with emphasis on higher-order questions, longer processing time, and direct instruction. The article tests whether the question-writing justification is actually realized in practice.
requirements: Students must construct coherent multiple-choice questions with plausible incorrect alternatives for the game to be challenging
constraints: Prior studies have not shown performance gains over traditional instruction despite these justifications
target_learning_goals: content learning through game design
question-writing skills
examples: Games built from a template with introductory, narrative, directions, and question slides, played by answering multiple-choice questions
key_sources: Jason Paul Siko. (2011). Homemade PowerPoint Games. http://it.coe.uga.edu/wwild/pptgames

article_title: A Story-Telling Approach to Teaching English to Young EFL Iranian Learners
citation: Farzaneh Kalantari & Mahmood Hashemian. (2016). A Story-Telling Approach to Teaching English to Young EFL Iranian Learners. English Language Teaching, 9(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n1p221
title: Three-stage storytelling lesson plan: preteaching, while-teaching, and postteaching stages
description: The article's storytelling treatment was organized as a lesson plan "had three sections: preteaching, while-teaching, and postteaching stages". In the pre-storytelling stage learners received comprehensible input through talk, games, reading and listening and learned key vocabulary via pictures and gestures. In the while-storytelling stage the teacher told the story with PowerPoint visual support and interaction, and in the post-storytelling stage learners played vocabulary games and role-played the story by memorizing dialogues.
requirements: Teacher-prepared stories based on the course's units, a PowerPoint visual presentation, and data-show hardware in the classroom
constraints: Developed and evaluated with young upper-beginner EFL learners in a private language institute in Isfahan, Iran
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary knowledge
listening comprehension and engagement with stories
examples: The experimental group's lessons followed the preteaching, while-teaching, and postteaching sequence, ending with vocabulary games and role-play of the story dialogues
key_sources: Farzaneh Kalantari & Mahmood Hashemian. (2016). A Story-Telling Approach to Teaching English to Young EFL Iranian Learners. English Language Teaching, 9(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n1p221

article_title: Management of Teacher Scientific-Methodical Work in Vocational Educational Institutions on the Basis of Project-Target Approach
citation: Elena A. Shakuto, Evgenij M. Dorozhkin and Anastasia A. Kozlova. (2016). Management of Teacher Scientific-Methodical Work in Vocational Educational Institutions on the Basis of Project-Target Approach. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(16), 8834-8845. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
title: Manage teacher scientific-methodical work through three organizational-pedagogical conditions: a management system, purposeful motivation, and a training system
description: The article proposes that efficient teacher scientific-methodical work on a project-target basis requires a complex of organizational-pedagogical conditions. As printed, "The complex of organizational -pedagogical conditions includes the management system of teacher scientific -methodical work in vocational educational institutions; purposeful motivation of teachers for scientific -methodical work" plus stimulating self-development and a complex of events raising teachers' qualification. The conditions were defined taking into account each organization's facilities and federal state educational standard requirements.
requirements: A management system of teacher scientific-methodical work built on the structural-functional model
Building profound teacher motivation, including discovering and eliminating factors of teachers' dissatisfaction
A system of teacher training in scientific-methodical work on the basis of project-target approach
constraints: Conditions were defined for specific secondary vocational educational institutions and the requirements of the federal state educational standard for secondary vocational education
target_learners: teachers in secondary vocational educational institutions
heads and deputy heads of vocational educational organizations
target_learning_goals: scientific-methodical competence
professional reflexion and educational mobility of teachers
examples: The second condition involved discovering and eliminating teachers' inner psychological reasons for dissatisfaction, such as uncertainty in developing content and forms of control in academic disciplines programs

citation: Elena A. Shakuto, Evgenij M. Dorozhkin and Anastasia A. Kozlova. (2016). Management of Teacher Scientific-Methodical Work in Vocational Educational Institutions on the Basis of Project-Target Approach. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(16), 8834-8845. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
title: Three-stage implementation of the model: propaedeutic, activity-based, and outcome-correction
description: The method of implementing the structural-functional model for teachers' professional development proceeds through three stages. At the propaedeutic stage the authors "defined the targets, objectives, methods of data collection, the evaluation criteria of teachers scientific and methodical work" and provided primary evaluation. At the activity-based stage the model content was introduced and teachers took part in the training program with monitoring. The outcome-correction stage analyzed monitoring data and corrected indicators, program content, organizational forms and monitoring tools.
requirements: Pedagogical monitoring tools and evaluation criteria defined before the activity-based stage
Correction of model components based on monitoring data at the outcome-correction stage
constraints: Applied within a professional training program for teachers working in secondary vocational institutions in the city of Ekaterinburg
target_learning_goals: raising the level of knowledge, skills and professionally important qualities in scientific-methodical work
examples: At the outcome-correction stage the teachers' knowledge and skills acquired during the course were consolidated and indicators of knowledge and skills were corrected

article_title: The Effect of Differentiated Mathematics Programs on the Mathematics Attitude of Gifted Children
citation: Deringöl, Y., & Davaslıgil, Ü. (2020). The effect of differentiated mathematics programs on the mathematics attitude of gifted children. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Sciences, 8(1). http://mojes.um.edu.my/
title: Theme-based interdisciplinary differentiation pattern combining content, process and product differentiation with interest-driven activities
description: The program's design pattern: a single theme ('Balance') organises differentiated content, process and product; the topic is transposed across disciplines; learning environments include "projects, discussions, and games based on the interests of the students"; and students pursue research themes individually or in small or large groups with presentations. Activities were designed to engage students emotionally as well as cognitively and to focus on understanding instead of memorization. This pattern operationalises Tomlinson's advice to differentiate content, processes, or products based on student readiness, interests, and student profile.
requirements: a selected theme for content, process and product differentiation
flexible learning environments designed to maximize creativity
constraints: developed and applied for mathematically gifted and talented fifth-grade students
target_learning_goals: positive mathematics attitudes
high-level thinking skills
research and presentation skills
examples: Two guest academicians (an architect and a music educator) worked with students in and out of the classroom in a master-apprentice fashion under the Connections Curriculum

article_title: Replication of Effects of the "Positive Action" Program in Randomized Trials in Hawai'i and Chicago Schools
citation: Brian R. Flay, D.Phil. (2014). Replication of effects of the Positive Action program in randomized trials in Hawai'i and Chicago schools. SREE Spring 2014 Conference Abstract. https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT01025674
title: Thoughts-Actions-Feelings about Self Circle: the Positive Action program's core philosophy unit
description: The Positive Action curriculum is founded on a philosophy taught in its first unit: the Thoughts-Actions-Feelings about Self Circle. The article states that the first unit "teaches the philosophy of the program and the Thoughts-Actions-Feelings about Self Circle, and provides an introduction to the nature and relevancy of positive and negative actions/behaviors," while Units 2-6 teach positive actions across physical, intellectual, social and emotional areas. The authors interpret the trial results as "consistent with the presumed theory of action of the Positive Action program," since both trials found strong effects on school quality/climate indicators.
requirements: Delivered as the first of six curriculum units forming the foundation of the whole program
target_learners: Elementary and middle school students (grades K-8)
target_learning_goals: Understanding that thoughts, actions and feelings about self are interconnected
choosing positive behaviors

article_title: An Integrated Approach to Teaching Literature in an EFL Classroom
citation: Supaporn Yimwilai. (2015). An Integrated Approach to Teaching Literature in an EFL Classroom. English Language Teaching, 8(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n2p14
title: Carter and Long's three models of teaching literature: language model, cultural model, and personal growth model
description: The article presents three main approaches to teaching literature. In the language model, "texts are used as a focus for grammatical and structural analysis"; in the cultural model, texts are treated as cultural artifacts requiring exploration of social, political, literary, and historical context; and in the personal growth model, texts are "considered a stimulus for personal growth activities", bridging the other two by connecting language use, cultural context, and students' personal experiences. The article argues each has strengths and weaknesses and that an integrated approach combining key elements of all three makes literature most beneficial for EFL students.
requirements: An integrated approach model comprising key elements of all three models is needed so that literature becomes accessible to EFL students
constraints: The cultural model tends to be teacher-centered, with little opportunity for extended language work, per Savvidou (2004) as cited in the article
target_learning_goals: language knowledge
cultural understanding
personal growth and interpretative abilities
examples: The study's lesson plan operationalized the three models as Language Consideration, Cultural Consideration, and Enrichment Consideration phases
key_sources: Supaporn Yimwilai. (2015). An Integrated Approach to Teaching Literature in an EFL Classroom. English Language Teaching, 8(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n2p14

article_title: An Integrated Approach to Teaching Literature in an EFL Classroom
citation: Supaporn Yimwilai. (2015). An Integrated Approach to Teaching Literature in an EFL Classroom. English Language Teaching, 8(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n2p14
title: Three-phase integrated literature lesson: Language, Cultural, and Enrichment Consideration
description: The article's lesson plan teaches literature in three phases. In Language Consideration, students read a literary text at home with a vocabulary list including culturally meaningful items; in Cultural Consideration, the instructor provides background and cultural information in a pre-reading stage; in Enrichment Consideration, the class holds an instructor-facilitated discussion followed by post-reading writing and language activities. The author states these stages "assisted students in acquiring language knowledge effectively and facilitated their cultural competence and interpretative abilities".
requirements: A literary text, vocabulary list with cultural items, instructor-provided background information, and facilitated discussion with post-reading activities
constraints: Evaluated over eight weekly sessions of two and a half hours with Thai English-major undergraduates
target_learners: Thai EFL university students majoring in English
target_learning_goals: literature knowledge
critical thinking skills
positive attitudes toward reading literature
examples: Experimental groups were taught with lesson plans based on this three-phase design for eight two-and-a-half-hour sessions while controls received conventional instructor-led instruction
key_sources: Supaporn Yimwilai. (2015). An Integrated Approach to Teaching Literature in an EFL Classroom. English Language Teaching, 8(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n2p14

article_title: The Application of Technology in Teaching Grammar to EFL Learners: The Role of Animated Sitcoms
citation: Zari Saeedi and Aso Biri. (2014). THE APPLICATION OF TECHNOLOGY IN TEACHING GRAMMAR TO EFL LEARNERS: THE ROLE OF ANIMATED SITCOMS. Teaching English with Technology, 16(2), 18-39. https://www.tewtjournal.org
title: Larsen-Freeman's three-dimensional grammar framework (form, meaning, use) as an account of why contextualized video supports grammar learning
description: The article uses Larsen-Freeman's framework, in which "form, meaning, and use are interrelated", to interpret its results: the form dimension concerns lexicogrammatical and morphosyntactic construction, meaning the sense of a construction, and use how a construction is used in context. It argues the subtitled sitcom addressed all three dimensions, while explicit instruction taught form only. Grammar is treated as "a dynamic system" that must be taught in meaningful, psychologically authentic ways.
requirements: Instruction must give learners opportunities to encounter, process and use forms in their various form-meaning relationships, as the article quotes Larsen-Freeman (2003) stating
constraints: The article notes the explicit approach was useful for the form dimension but not equally useful for the meaning and use dimensions
target_learning_goals: understanding and use of conditional sentences across form, meaning, and use
examples: The article argues the English subtitles familiarized students with the form dimension while hearing and seeing conditionals in contexts supported meaning and use
key_sources: Zari Saeedi and Aso Biri. (2014). THE APPLICATION OF TECHNOLOGY IN TEACHING GRAMMAR TO EFL LEARNERS: THE ROLE OF ANIMATED SITCOMS. Teaching English with Technology, 16(2), 18-39. https://www.tewtjournal.org

article_title: The Influence of Explicit Cross-Linguistic Consciousness-Raising on the EL Writing of the Iranian English Language Learners
citation: Seyyed Yavar Hosseininik & Hamid Rahmani Sangani. (2014). The Influence of Explicit Cross-Linguistic Consciousness-Raising on the EL Writing of the Iranian English Language Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 5(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.3p.147
title: Three-test battery measuring recognition, translation, and writing production of target grammar items
description: The study used three parallel pre/post instruments: a twenty-item recognition test in which participants underlined errors in sentences and wrote their correct forms; a translation test of ten Persian-to-English sentences; and a written performance test with two picture-cued tasks eliciting paragraphs and answers about each picture. Post-tests were "designed in harmony with pre-tests, so the number of tasks, items and sentences were exactly the same as those in the pre-tests."
requirements: Tests must be parallel across pre- and post-test administrations to support paired comparisons
constraints: The battery targets only the chosen language items (subject-verb agreement and adverb position) at intermediate proficiency
target_learning_goals: recognition of errors, proper use, and correct production of targeted grammatical structures
examples: The recognition test mixed correct and incorrect sentences so there was "not an identifiable pattern of correct or incorrect sentences"

article_title: Organization and Carrying out the Educational Experiment and Statistical Analysis of Its Results in IHL
citation: Oleg V. Sidorov, Lyubov’ V. Kozub, Alexander V. Goferberg, Natalya V. Osintseva. (2018). Organization and Carrying out the Educational Experiment and Statistical Analysis of its Results in IHL. European Journal of Contemporary Education. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.1.177
title: Three-stage comparative educational experiment: stating, forming, and control stages
description: The article presents a reusable experimental design for psychoeducational research in which, as it prints, the comparative experiment "as a rule it includes three stages": a stating stage choosing experimental and control groups and determining the initial level of formation of students' technological training via testing; a forming stage introducing the didactic set into the educational process in the experimental group while the control group uses the traditional technique; and a control stage performing a final check (cutoff test) of the forming stage's results and final confirmation of the research hypothesis. The design rests on comparing control and experimental groups and registering corresponding changes.
requirements: Groups chosen to be completely identical (same year of beginning study, year of study, age, level of knowledge, number of students)
Planning that defines the character of separate stages and the order of their realization
Diagnostic tools for determining the efficiency of students' educational cognitive activity
constraints: The article presents this as the comparative experiment used in psychoeducational researches more often, illustrated on one course example
target_learners: second-year university students in teacher-training programs
target_learning_goals: validating the effectiveness of a teaching technique through controlled comparison
examples: The authors equipped the laboratory, created the installations, introduced the course, and ran preexperimental testing, forming-stage teaching, and a final cutoff test

article_title: Developing Cognitive Independence of Future Informatics Teachers by Multimedia Tools
citation: Yakymchuk, N. V., Kazachenok, V. V. (2018). Developing Cognitive Independence of Future Informatics Teachers by Multimedia Tools. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(3), 581-597. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.3.581
title: Three-stage methodology for developing cognitive independence of future Informatics teachers through multimedia tools
description: The article proposes a staged methodology in which the role of multimedia expands across a theoretical stage (semesters 3-4), an integrating stage (semesters 5-6), and a practical stage (semesters 7-8). At the initial stage multimedia is "a means of visual presentation of educational material", at the integrating stage students learn to create multimedia tools, and at the practical stage they "carry out creative multimedia projects, both group and individual ones". The methodology aims to deepen multimedia knowledge, shape positive attitudes, and develop skills to create and apply multimedia products in teaching.
requirements: Purposeful, consistent work across all three stages of university study, with updated course topics that merge into existing curricula without changing total hours
constraints: Developed and tested specifically for future Informatics teachers within a credit-based education system at one university
target_learning_goals: Cognitive independence across informative, operational, motivational, emotional-volitional, and reflexive components
examples: The experimental group used electronic textbooks, interactive whiteboard lessons, screencasts, a multimedia game, and the MEMC 'Multimedia in education', while the control group received only traditional media
key_sources: Yakymchuk, N. V., Kazachenok, V. V. (2018). Developing Cognitive Independence of Future Informatics Teachers by Multimedia Tools. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(3), 581-597. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.3.581

article_title: Students' Experimental Research Competences in the Study of Physics
citation: Bakytzhan A. Kurbanbekova, Torebai A. Turmambekova, Usen A. Baizaka, Pulat A. Saidakhmetova, Rakhymzhan T. Abdraimova, Aigerim E. Bekayevaa, and Kuldarkhan O. Orazbayevab. (2016). Students’ Experimental Research Competences in the Study of Physics. INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL & SCIENCE EDUCATION, 2016, VOL. 11, NO. 18, 13069-13078. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
title: Three-level diagnostic framework for experimental research competencies based on degree of autonomy
description: The article defines a three-level diagnostic framework in which formedness of experimental research competencies is judged by the degree of autonomy a student shows on diagnostic tasks. High level means a student independently performs the first-level creative task without assistance cards; mid level means fulfilling a second-level task using one or two assistance cards; low level presupposes performing the third-level task with more than two cards. Diagnostic tasks were drawn from methodological literature and the authors' own teaching and research, with requirements of availability, equivalence of options, available instruments and literature, ease of experiments, and completion within one 80-minute session.
requirements: Diagnostic tasks must satisfy the article's stated requirements: availability for the students' stage of training, equivalence of options, availability of instruments and materials, availability of required literature, ease of experiments, and the ability to perform the work in one 80-minute session
constraints: The framework was developed and applied with undergraduate physics students at pedagogical universities in Kazakhstan
target_learners: undergraduate physics students at pedagogical universities
target_learning_goals: experimental research competencies in physics
examples: Students' work was examined both by teachers of core courses and by those holding laboratory classes, a double assessment intended to reduce subjectivity in level evaluation

article_title: Students' Experimental Research Competences in the Study of Physics
citation: Bakytzhan A. Kurbanbekova, Torebai A. Turmambekova, Usen A. Baizaka, Pulat A. Saidakhmetova, Rakhymzhan T. Abdraimova, Aigerim E. Bekayevaa, and Kuldarkhan O. Orazbayevab. (2016). INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL & SCIENCE EDUCATION, 2016, VOL. 11, NO. 18, 13069-13078. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
title: Three-level creative tasks with assistance cards for mini investigations in physics laboratory work
description: Within each laboratory work, creative tasks for mini investigations were developed at three levels of difficulty and presented in methodological guidelines for students' independent work under control. First-level tasks are most difficult and only specify the problem; second-level tasks keep the problem but add clues such as a limited range of devices and materials and outlined ways of performance; the third level is maximally simplified with more tips while retaining creativity elements. Individual tasks are provided with assistance cards containing a pre-arranged question, scheme, pattern or formula. The stated main purpose is development of experimental research competencies of all undergraduate students regardless of their abilities.
requirements: Assistance cards must narrow potentialities to find a solution without giving a direct answer
constraints: The pattern was implemented within the laboratory workshop of the general physics course at pedagogical universities
target_learning_goals: experimental research competencies
creativity
independent experimental work
examples: Training manuals 'Workshop on general physics' and 'Guidelines for the implementation of tasks for students’ independent work under control in the course of general physics' were developed as components of the General Course of Physics Training Package

article_title: Management of Development of Creative Civil Activity of Student's Youth
citation: Belentsov S.I., Gribanova V.A., Brasnik O.U., Pozdniakov A.V. (2018). Management of Development of Creative Civil Activity of Student's Youth. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(2): 257-264. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.2.257
title: Three-stage model of formation of creative civil activity of student youth
description: The article presents formation of civil activity as a model realized during three interconnected stages: a theoretical-procedural (search) stage, an interiorization (transformative-reflexive) stage, and an eksteriorization (practice-oriented) stage. Each stage includes purposes, psychology and pedagogical conditions, contents and a system of pedagogical means, and the stages are "directed on formation of theoretical, practical and personal readiness of students". The model structures civil activity as a three-part unity of informative, motivationally-demanding and personal-reflexive components, grounded in personally focused, activity and axiological approaches.
requirements: Educational work must be structured to match the three stages and their purposes, conditions, contents and pedagogical means
constraints: The model was approved in skilled and experimental work at one institute (Taganrog institute of A. P. Chekhov) during the 2017-2018 academic years
target_learning_goals: creative civil activity
theoretical, practical and personal readiness for civil activity
examples: The interiorization stage was implemented via a youth forum, school of the young citizen, personal growth trainings and project work; the eksteriorization stage via patriotic propaganda teams and volunteering
key_sources: Belentsov S.I., Gribanova V.A., Brasnik O.U., Pozdniakov A.V. (2018). Management of Development of Creative Civil Activity of Student's Youth. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(2): 257-264. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.2.257

article_title: Management of Development of Creative Civil Activity of Student's Youth
citation: Belentsov S.I., Gribanova V.A., Brasnik O.U., Pozdniakov A.V. (2018). Management of Development of Creative Civil Activity of Student's Youth. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(2): 257-264. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.2.257
title: Three-tier system of priority forms of educational work for civil activity formation
description: The article enumerates a system of priority and effective forms of work of a modern higher education institution for forming students' civil activity, organized in three tiers: "search (interview, situations of civil dialogue, business and role-playing games, debate)"; converting and reflexive forms (academy of the young citizen, school of social development, personal growth trainings, school of leadership, youth forums, project work); and practice-oriented forms (patriotic propaganda teams, volunteering). Practical coordination of all these forms was carried out by the department of educational work and employment of the Taganrog institute of A. P. Chekhov.
requirements: Coordination of all forms across the institution, here by a dedicated department of educational work and employment
constraints: Evaluated within one institute's educational work during 2017-2018
target_learning_goals: civil activity
positive and creative civil personal qualities
examples: The plan of work built from student survey answers included a School of the young citizen, personal growth trainings, a school of leadership, a youth forum, project work, elections of student's deans, discussion platforms and flashmobs
key_sources: Belentsov S.I., Gribanova V.A., Brasnik O.U., Pozdniakov A.V. (2018). Management of Development of Creative Civil Activity of Student's Youth. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(2): 257-264. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.2.257

article_title: Using Tablet and iTunesU as Individualized Instruction Tools
citation: Libor Klubal, Katerina Kostolanyova and Vojtěch Gybas. (2017). Using Tablet and iTunesU as Individualized Instruction Tools. 13th International Conference Mobile Learning 2017. ISBN: 978-989-8533-61-6
title: Three-activity self-paced lesson sequence: interactive app practice, written proof exercise, then skill-based competitive game
description: The individualized lesson was structured as three sequenced activities through which students progressed at their own pace: solving 10 equations in the Algebra Touch application with interactive tools, a written exercise with the problem distributed as a PDF in iTunesU requiring a full solution with proof in notebooks, and the Orbit Integers game in which up to four students compete on one racetrack. Finishing one activity visibly signalled the transition to the next, making progress easy to monitor.
requirements: Each student needs a tablet with access to the iTunesU course, and notebooks for the written activity; the teacher sets rules for notebook work at the start.
constraints: The game component requires an internet connection to place up to four students on one racetrack.
target_learners: 12-13-year-old students in a regular mathematics classroom
target_learning_goals: practicing simple equations
developing general math skills needed for solving equations
examples: Students who finished the Algebra Touch task moved to the written exercise, and the order of finishing the second part naturally formed the competing groups.
key_sources: Libor Klubal, Katerina Kostolanyova and Vojtěch Gybas. (2017). Using Tablet and iTunesU as Individualized Instruction Tools. 13th International Conference Mobile Learning 2017. ISBN: 978-989-8533-61-6. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED579278

article_title: Digital Literacy and New Technological Perspectives
citation: Elvia Ilaria Feola. (2016). Digital Literacy and New Technological Perspectives. Universal Journal of Educational Research 4(9): 2174-2180. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2016.040929
title: Three-dimensional vision of digital literacy: technological, cognitive/metacognitive and ethical/social dimensions
description: The article frames digital literacy as "a complex combination of skills, abilities and knowledge" organised in a "three -dimensional vision technology; cognitive/metacognitive; ethical/social". It stresses that what matters is "not only the technical and computer skills of the learner, but especially critical thinking, problem solving, collaboration, research". The framework drives both the training methodology design and the choice of the Instant DCA instrument, whose three dimensions mirror it, and draws on Gilster's emphasis on critical thinking and evaluation of information over technical skills.
requirements: Assessment must cover all three dimensions (technological, cognitive, ethical) rather than technical skills alone, as operationalised in the Instant DCA.
constraints: The article notes integration of new media and technology in education is still poor despite the concept being in vogue for over thirty years.
target_learning_goals: digital competence
critical thinking and evaluation of information
ethical responsibility in media use
examples: The Instant DCA questionnaire operationalises the framework with items on the technological, cognitive and ethical dimensions, and the 15 course activities were designed five for each dimension.
key_sources: Elvia Ilaria Feola. (2016). Digital Literacy and New Technological Perspectives. Universal Journal of Educational Research 4(9): 2174-2180. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2016.040929

article_title: Forming Well Organized Writing Activities
citation: Irfan Tosuncuoğlu. (2018). Forming a Well Organized Writing Activities. Journal of Education and Training Studies, Vol. 6, No. 6. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v6i6.3111
title: Three main qualities of a well-organized text: outlining, coherence, and unity
description: The article proposes that well-organized writing rests on three text qualities: outlining, the organized listing of ideas that shows relationships among groups; coherence, the logical and orderly arrangement of ideas so the reader is carried forward; and unity, discussing only one main idea per paragraph under a controlling idea. The author derives this framework from linguo-methodological literature and uses it to structure the supplementary exercises, which "are divided into three main groups; outline, coherence, unity."
requirements: Instruction must address all three qualities, since each element pays attention to the well organization of the text
target_learners: EFL school students learning English writing
target_learning_goals: organizing ideas in written compositions
examples: The experimental group's supplementary exercises were organized into outline, coherence, and unity exercise groups
key_sources: Irfan Tosuncuoğlu. (2018). Forming a Well Organized Writing Activities. Journal of Education and Training Studies, Vol. 6, No. 6. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v6i6.3111

article_title: Inquiry-Based Integrated Thematic Instruction on Character Education of Primary School Students
citation: Chumdari, Sri Anitah, Budiyono, & Nunuk Suryani. (2018). Inquiry-based Integrated Thematic Instruction On Character Education Of Primary School Students. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.6n.2p.69
title: Three-stage implementation of thematic and inquiry-based integrated thematic learning: preparation, implementation, evaluation
description: Both the thematic instruction model and the inquiry-based integrated thematic instructional model are implemented through three linked stages. The article states "three stages are required in the implementation of thematic learning, namely the preparation, implementation, and evaluation", and repeats that the inquiry-based integrated model "also consists of three stages, namely preparation, implementation and evaluation". Figures 1 and 2 illustrate the correlation of components in these stages in relation to character education in primary school.
requirements: Preparation includes lesson plan (RPP) development; implementation and evaluation stages are linked to character education outcomes as illustrated in the article's Figures 1 and 2
constraints: The article reports teacher obstacles at each stage: difficulty elaborating competencies into indicators and developing themes at preparation, limited knowledge, materials and facilities at implementation, and difficulty assessing grade-1 students and documenting results at assessment
target_learning_goals: Character values
Integrated subject-matter learning
examples: The experimental treatment ran six meetings, two per sub-theme, with lesson plans scored at each meeting.
key_sources: Chumdari, Sri Anitah, Budiyono, & Nunuk Suryani. (2018). Inquiry-based Integrated Thematic Instruction On Character Education Of Primary School Students. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.6n.2p.69

article_title: Fostering Creativity in Engineering Universities: Research Activity and Curriculum Policy
citation: Kozlo, A. V., & Shemshurina, S. A. (2018). Fostering Creativity in Engineering Universities: Research Activity and Curriculum Policy. International Journal of Instruction, 11(4), 93-106. https://www.e-iji.net
title: Three-component diagnostic taxonomy of engineering students' research competence
description: The article defines research competence as a training outcome and indicator of a student's readiness to conduct research, assessed through three components: motivational (studied by questioning), cognitive (assessed via end-of-course paper test or oral questioning), and operational (assessed by comparative analysis of grades and observation results). Each component is graded high, average, or low with printed level characteristics (Tables 1-3); for example, a high operational-level student can "state the research purpose fully and clearly" and independently develop a testing technique. The taxonomy grounds the experiment's pre/post diagnostics.
requirements: Determination of indicators without which assessment criteria and diagnostic methods cannot be found
Personal self-improvement as a dominant motive for activity to count as competent
target_learning_goals: diagnosing research competency level
examples: Tables 1, 2, and 3 print the level characteristics for the motivational, cognitive, and operational components used in pedagogical monitoring at the early stage of the experiment.
key_sources: Kozlo, A. V., & Shemshurina, S. A. (2018). Fostering Creativity in Engineering Universities: Research Activity and Curriculum Policy. International Journal of Instruction, 11(4), 93-106. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1191553

article_title: Pragmatic Instruction May Not Be Necessary among Heritage Speakers of Spanish: A Study on Requests
citation: Barros García, M. J., & Bachelor, J. W. (2018). Pragmatic Instruction May Not Be Necessary Among Heritage Learners of Spanish: A Study on Requests. Journal of Foreign Language Education and Technology, 3(1). https://jflet.com/jflet/
title: Three-part pragmatic lesson sequence on Spanish request strategies
description: An instructional element consisting of three 20-minute classroom sessions (approximately 60 minutes total) on request strategies in Spanish, delivered to the SHL and L2 experimental groups during a spring 2017 semester. The first session was an explicit lesson displaying typical request strategies by level of imposition and explaining the hearer-oriented nature of Spanish requests; the remaining sessions followed a more implicit approach, including categorizing request clips from popular Spanish films. The lessons were adapted from Langer (2013), CARLA (2006), and Martín Ruiz (2011) to student proficiency level.
requirements: Delivery within existing courses without modifying departmental or course outcomes, so no additional variables arise between control and experimental groups; materials adapted to students' proficiency level.
constraints: The lessons addressed only request strategies (formal vs. informal situations, imposition levels, indirect and hearer-oriented requests), not pragmatics broadly.
target_learners: college students of Spanish, both heritage and L2, at intermediate to intermediate-high proficiency
target_learning_goals: selecting pragmatically appropriate request strategies in Spanish according to social distance, power, and imposition
examples: In the final lesson, students viewed clips from popular Spanish films containing a variety of requests and categorized them per the instructions in Martín Ruiz (2011).
key_sources: Barros García, M. J., & Bachelor, J. W. (2018). Pragmatic Instruction May Not Be Necessary Among Heritage Learners of Spanish: A Study on Requests. Journal of Foreign Language Education and Technology, 3(1). https://jflet.com/jflet/

article_title: Implementing Environmental Culture in the Language Learning Laboratory
citation: Aida G. Sadykova, Marianna E. Yashina & Luiza R. Zakirova. (2014). Implementing Environmental Culture in the Language Learning Laboratory. English Language Teaching, 7(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n12p85
title: Three-criteria framework for diagnosing environmental education: cognitive, relational, and activity criteria
description: The article defines three criteria for measuring formation of environmental education in senior pupils. The "Cognitive criterion" reflects "the depth and stability of interest, the level and breadth of environmental awareness"; the relational (moral and ethical) criterion covers tolerance, value orientations and respect for nature; the activity (communicative-pragmatic) criterion identifies practical and communicative skills, including the correct use of environmental knowledge in practice. Together these criteria let the authors measure and assign pupils to three levels of formation.
requirements: Integrated and systematic presentation of all three criteria is needed to measure levels of formation
constraints: Developed and applied to senior pupils in foreign-language instruction
target_learning_goals: environmental awareness
value orientations toward nature
communicative-pragmatic skills
examples: Diagnostics used conversation, observation, testing, interviewing and checking of empirical skills across preparatory, forming and control phases
key_sources: Aida G. Sadykova, Marianna E. Yashina & Luiza R. Zakirova. (2014). Implementing Environmental Culture in the Language Learning Laboratory. English Language Teaching, 7(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n12p85

article_title: Implementing Environmental Culture in the Language Learning Laboratory
citation: Aida G. Sadykova, Marianna E. Yashina & Luiza R. Zakirova. (2014). Implementing Environmental Culture in the Language Learning Laboratory. English Language Teaching, 7(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n12p85
title: Three text types for environmental education, with problem-definition-without-solution texts most valued
description: For didactically correct selection of foreign-language material, the article distinguishes three types of texts: those containing the description of a problem's definition and its decision, those with only the solution, and those with only the problem definition. The authors write that "The last type of texts refers to the number of problematic and has the particular value". Text work was supported by tasks such as paragraphing, formulating the main idea, and annotating articles around environmental problems.
requirements: Text selection must account for language feasibility and the reasonability of the environmental information covered
constraints: Applied to senior pupils reading foreign-language texts on ecology
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
ecological and linguistic competence
critical reflection on environmental problems
examples: Experimental groups read authentic texts from foreign teaching aids with card-supported tasks, then discussed them in training conferences
key_sources: Aida G. Sadykova, Marianna E. Yashina & Luiza R. Zakirova. (2014). Implementing Environmental Culture in the Language Learning Laboratory. English Language Teaching, 7(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n12p85

article_title: An Empirical Study on the Application of Theme Theory in the Field of Writing Pedagogy
citation: Liu Jingxia & Liu Li. (2013). An Empirical Study on the Application of Theme Theory in the Field of Writing Pedagogy. English Language Teaching, 6(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n5p117
title: Theme Theory and Danes' thematic progression patterns as a framework for textual coherence
description: Theme Theory, from Systemic-functional Linguistics, divides each clause into a theme (the point of departure) and a rheme (what is said about it), with simple, multiple and clausal theme types. Thematic progression (TP), defined by Danes as "the choice and ordering of utterance themes, their mutual concatenation hierarchy", describes how themes and rhemes chain across clauses to display connexity. The article uses six TP patterns (linear, constant, focused, derived-theme, split-rheme, summarized) both to analyze texts and to structure writing instruction aimed at discourse-level coherence.
requirements: Instruction must cover theme/rheme identification across moods, the theme-information structure relation, and the TP patterns before students apply them
constraints: The authors note the theory is complex for undergraduates, who found applying TP patterns "a bit stiff and unnatural"
target_learners: Chinese university English majors (second-year EFL learners)
target_learning_goals: Discourse-level writing coherence
Text organization in EFL composition
examples: The experimental class analyzed model CET-4 passages for their TP patterns and evaluated model writing from the perspective of thematic structure
key_sources: Liu Jingxia & Liu Li. (2013). An Empirical Study on the Application of Theme Theory in the Field of Writing Pedagogy. English Language Teaching, 6(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n5p117

article_title: The Effectiveness of Using Blogs as an Independent Learning Tool to Develop Reading Skills for University Students
citation: Said Fathy El Said Abdul Fattah. (2016). The Effectiveness of Using Blogs as an Independent Learning Tool to Develop Reading Skills for University Students. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.32. http://www.iiste.org
title: Campbell's three-type taxonomy of blogs in language teaching
description: The article adopts Campbell's (2003) classification of educational blogs into three types: the tutor blog created by the teacher, the class blog produced by the whole class, and the learner's blog created by an individual student. It describes the tutor blog as "the gateway for learners to develop their language skills" and a source of daily reading practice and syllabus information; the class blog as a shared space for comments on assignments and quizzes; and the learner's blog as a venue for personal expression read by classmates. The study's treatment used the teacher's blog.
requirements: A teacher or learner must create and maintain the blog; the article notes no HTML or programming knowledge is required
constraints: The article notes many students are not familiar with the blog tool
target_learning_goals: reading skills
writing skills
learner autonomy
examples: The study's experimental treatment used a teacher's blog hosting an independent reading program
key_sources: Said Fathy El Said Abdul Fattah. (2016). The Effectiveness of Using Blogs as an Independent Learning Tool to Develop Reading Skills for University Students. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.32. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1122464

article_title: Formation of Future Teachers' Professional Competence on the Basis of Polylingual Approach: The State Analysis
citation: Zhorabekova, A. N. (2015). Formation of Future Teachers' Professional Competence on the Basis of Polylingual Approach: The State Analysis. International Education Studies, 8(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v8n12p130
title: Three-component diagnostic model of future teachers' professional competence on a polylingual basis
description: According to the developed model, professional competence consists of three components: motivational, cognitive and operational. The motivational component "performs a regulatory function in the structure of formation, expresses a conscious attitude of the student to polylingual approach"; the cognitive component covers pedagogical, special, methodological and polylingual knowledge; the operational component ensures abilities and skills for practical experience. Each component carries a criterion with three indicators (Table 1).
requirements: Diagnostic methodology with defined evaluation criteria, indicators and levels of professional competence formation
target_learning_goals: formation of professional competence for teaching subjects in Kazakh, Russian and foreign languages
examples: Criteria include student's presence of needs to master the professional competence, knowledge of polylingual approach, and mastery of competencies implementing it
key_sources: Zhorabekova, A. N. (2015). Formation of Future Teachers' Professional Competence on the Basis of Polylingual Approach: The State Analysis. International Education Studies, 8(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v8n12p130

article_title: The Impact of Early Algebra: Results from a Longitudinal Intervention
citation: Brizuela, B.M., Martinez, M.V., and Cayton-Hodges, G.A. (2013). The Impact of Early Algebra: Results from a Longitudinal Intervention. Journal of Research in Mathematics Education, 2(2), 209-241. https://doi.org/10.4471/redimat.2013.28
title: Thread algebra throughout the elementary mathematics curriculum rather than treating it as an add-on unit
description: The article argues that early access to algebra should be sustained and frequent rather than confined to a late unit: "alge bra cannot be conside re d as an add-on unit for the e nd ofthe curriculum ,but ne e ds to be thre ade d throughout the m athe m atics curriculum". The authors hypothesize access to algebra needs to happen early, be sustained over time, and occur frequently, and present their longitudinal intervention results as initial support for this position.
requirements: Algebra instruction must begin in the earliest grades and be sustained and frequent over time rather than delivered as a single end-of-curriculum unit
constraints: The authors state further evidence in support of this hypothesis is still needed
target_learning_goals: algebraic reasoning
functional relations
variables and algebraic expressions
examples: The research team implemented 104 EA lessons across grades 3-5 (50 in 3rd, 36 in 4th, 18 in 5th) in addition to the regular Investigations curriculum, with weekly lessons and homework review sessions
key_sources: Brizuela, B.M., Martinez, M.V., and Cayton-Hodges, G.A. (2013). The Impact of Early Algebra: Results from a Longitudinal Intervention. Journal of Research in Mathematics Education, 2(2), 209-241. https://doi.org/10.4471/redimat.2013.28

article_title: An EFL Flipped Learning Course Design: Utilizing Students' Mobile Online Devices
citation: Ishikawa, Y., Akahane-Yamada, R., Smith, C., Kondo, M., Tsubota, Y., & Dantsuji, M. (2015). An EFL flipped learning course design: utilizing students’ mobile online devices. Critical CALL – Proceedings of the 2015 EUROCALL Conference, Padova, Italy. http://dx.doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2015.000343
title: Three-phase flipped learning unit: pre-class online tasks, in-class problem-solving, post-class self-assessment
description: Each learning unit of the two-semester EFL flipped course had three phases: "1) pre-class online completion of TOEIC course materials; 2) individualized problem-solving instruction in class; and 3) post-class online completion of self-assessment and reflection learning tasks". This structure integrates online and in-class tasks in a single learning environment, reserving classroom time for teacher-student analysis of performance on the pre-class learning tasks.
requirements: Students complete the online pre-class materials before class so classroom time can support them through interaction and problem-solving
target_learning_goals: TOEIC score improvement
self-regulated learning attitudes, skills and behavior
examples: Implemented from April 2014 to January 2015 at a university in Japan with 551 first-year students
key_sources: Ishikawa, Y., Akahane-Yamada, R., Smith, C., Kondo, M., Tsubota, Y., & Dantsuji, M. (2015). An EFL flipped learning course design: utilizing students’ mobile online devices. article_title: A Comparative Analysis of Point-of-View Modeling for Industrial and Technology Education Courses
citation: Petros J. Katsioloudis, Todd D. Fantz, Millie Jones. (2012). A Comparative Analysis of Point-of-View Modeling for Industrial and Technology Education Courses.
title: Three point-of-view categories for instructional video: subjective, reportorial, and objective
description: The article organizes instructional video by the camera point of view used while filming, drawing on Burrows and Wood (1986): "The three main points of view used for instructional videos are: (a) subjective, (b) reportorial, and (c) objective". The subjective view shows everything from the instructor's eyes; the reportorial view shows the scene as if standing beside the instructor; the objective view provides face-to-face instruction with the instructor facing the camera. The study operationalizes each with a differently placed camera filming the same lathe demonstrations.
requirements: Each point of view requires a specific camera placement: head-mounted overhead for subjective, to the side of the instructor for reportorial, facing the instructor for objective.
constraints: The taxonomy is applied to hands-on demonstration videos in industrial and technology education contexts in this study.
target_learners: college students in industrial and technology education
target_learning_goals: hands-on psychomotor skills such as lathe turning, facing, and drilling
examples: Three films demonstrating facing, turning, and drilling on a lathe were created with identical narrative and length, differing only in point of view.
key_sources: Petros J. Katsioloudis, Todd D. Fantz, Millie Jones. (2012). A Comparative Analysis of Point-of-View Modeling for Industrial and Technology Education Courses. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1020186

article_title: Understanding Atmospheric Carbon Budgets: Teaching Students Conservation of Mass
citation: Collin Reichert, Cinzia Cervato, Dale Niederhauser, and Michael D. Larsen. (2015). Understanding Atmospheric Carbon Budgets: Teaching Students Conservation of Mass. Journal of Geoscience Education 63, 222–232. https://doi.org/10.5408/14-055.1
title: Thinkspace online problem-solving intervention with four scenario-based budget tasks
description: Thinkspace is an online problem-solving e-learning system used to deliver a stand-alone remediation during one 2-hour lab period, chosen to test efficacy in a large lecture course "where signiﬁcant instructor–student interaction is limited." Students role-play a snow-cone business owner and complete four tasks applying budget concepts in different contexts: a water-tank simulation with real-time feedback, a radiation-budget task using National Climate Data Center data, a bank-account task explicitly confronting the pattern-matching misconception, and an ill-structured atmospheric carbon task based on IPCC (2007) scenarios. Feedback comes from the program itself, via the Task 1 simulation and a Task 3 short-answer explanation of a contradictory example.
requirements: Students work through a series of challenges applying budget concepts to new scenarios, with feedback provided by the Thinkspace program rather than the instructor
constraints: Instructor interaction was limited to assisting with technical issues and encouraging students
A new version of the e-learning platform was still being developed and tested in summer 2015
target_learning_goals: understanding stock-flow (budget) systems and conservation of mass
reducing pattern-matching misconceptions about atmospheric carbon dioxide levels
examples: Students adjusted faucet inflow rates (0.0–10.0 L/h) against a constant 1.0 L/h drain to reach a 70 L maximum, interpreting 24-h graphs of inflow, outflow, and water level

article_title: Organizing Educational Activity of a Pupil on the Basis of Learning Technologies
citation: Tatiana V. Sibgatullina and Olga G. Selivanova. (2016). Organizing Educational Activity of a Pupil on the Basis of Learning Technologies. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(13), 6056-6067. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
title: Three learning technologies matched to a pupil's degree of subjectness: 'I want to learn', 'I can learn', 'I know how to learn'
description: The article defines a learning technology as "a system of actions of a pupil aiming at achieveing personally and socially important aims" and works out three technologies matched to pupils' degree of subjectness. 'I want to learn' targets low-motivated pupils with teacher-initiator/pupil-performer interaction and a staged sequence from self-estimation to subjective aim-setting. 'I can learn' targets pupils with intermittent positive attitudes, making the pupil a co-manager of education quality via personal aiming and choice situations. 'I know how to learn' targets pupils with formed learning skills, where the teacher acts as consultant to an individual educational program.
requirements: Each technology must correspond to the pupil's educational needs and learning abilities, as the article states the technologies contribute to subjectness only "if they correspond to his/her educational needs and learning abilities".
constraints: The technologies were developed and tested in the Kirov region and Surgut district school systems under Russian state educational standards.
target_learners: school pupils from elementary to high school with varying degrees of subjectness
target_learning_goals: self-analysis, self-goal-setting, self-planning, self-organization, self-control, self-assessing, self-correction
examples: Teachers worked individually with pupils who chose (sometimes with parents) whether to use a given technology during the forming stage of the experiment.
key_sources: Tatiana V. Sibgatullina and Olga G. Selivanova. (2016). Organizing Educational Activity of a Pupil on the Basis of Learning Technologies. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(13), 6056-6067. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

article_title: Valuing a More Rigorous Review of Formative Assessment's Effectiveness
citation: Apthorp, H., Klute, M., Petrites, T., Harlacher, J., & Reale, M. (2016). Valuing a more rigorous review of formative assessment's effectiveness. SREE Spring 2016 Conference Proposal. https://www.relcentral.org/news-and-events/the-essence-of-formative-assessment-creating-a-common-understanding-of-the-formative-assessment-process/
title: Three-level classification of outcome assessments by alignment with the intervention
description: To describe variation in effectiveness, the review classified outcome assessments "into one of three levels of alignment with the intervention": (1) broadly focused standardized tests such as a reading achievement test; (2) narrowly focused standardized tests targeting a subdomain such as passage comprehension; and (3) specialized topic tests developed specifically for an intervention. This classification draws on prior research relating intervention effects to type of outcome assessment, and is used in cross-tabulations with intervention type, student sample, and study context.
requirements: Each outcome assessment must be assignable to one of the three alignment levels based on its focus relative to the intervention
target_learning_goals: interpreting formative assessment effects in relation to outcome measure alignment
examples: A specialized topic test example quoted from Hill, Bloom, Black, & Lipsey (2008): a reading comprehension measure developed by the researcher for text similar to that used in the intervention
key_sources: Apthorp, H., Klute, M., Petrites, T., Harlacher, J., & Reale, M. (2016). Valuing a more rigorous review of formative assessment's effectiveness. article_title: Efficiency of Using a Web-Based Approach to Teach Reading Strategies to Iranian EFL Learners
citation: Elham Dehghanpour & Mahmood Hashemian. (2015). Efficiency of Using a Web-Based Approach to Teach Reading Strategies to Iranian EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 8(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n10p30
title: Three-stage cognitive-theory sequence for Web-based reading strategy training
description: The article organizes its 20-hour Web-based reading strategy program around Anderson's (1993) cognitive theory, in which "L2 learning proceeds through three stages: Cognitive, associative, and autonomous". In the cognitive stage the teacher explicitly explains each strategy and learners verbalize and apply it; in the associative stage learners complete tasks independently with teacher support for fluency; in the autonomous stage learners apply all strategies independently while reading hypertexts. The four strategies taught were note taking, skimming, inferring, and using context clues.
requirements: A teacher who explicitly explains strategies and supports learners during the associative stage
Web-based hypertext reading tasks for practice across the three stages
constraints: The article reports the sequence only for upper-intermediate learners, arguing lower levels may lack the grammar and vocabulary to employ the strategies effectively
target_learners: upper-intermediate adolescent EFL learners (15-18 years old)
target_learning_goals: L2 hypertext and general reading comprehension
use of general reading strategies (skimming, inferring, context clues, note taking)
examples: The 30 participants attended twice-weekly 2-hr sessions for 20 hours, practicing the four strategies on Internet texts through the cognitive, associative, and autonomous stages
key_sources: Elham Dehghanpour & Mahmood Hashemian. (2015). Efficiency of Using a Web-Based Approach to Teach Reading Strategies to Iranian EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 8(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n10p30

article_title: A Qualitative Perspective: Pre-Service Teachers Discuss Educational Technology Online
citation: Spatariu, A., & Winsor, D. L. (2010). A Qualitative Perspective: Pre-Service Teachers Discuss Educational Technology Online. i-manager's Journal of School Educational Technology, 6(1). https://eric.ed.gov
title: Three-level content analysis coding scheme for online argumentation discourse
description: The article developed and released a qualitative coding scheme for analyzing online discussion transcripts, applied to 272 postings in Atlas-Ti with open, selective, and axial coding and inter-rater reliability of .90. Level 1 conventional analysis produced 84 codes; Level 2 directed analysis organized them into five boldface categories: "(i) position on dilemma; (ii) support of position on dilemma; (iii) perspective of dilemma evaluation; (iv) nature of dilemma evaluation; and (v) nature of response to others." Appendix C is presented to allow other researchers to use a similar coding scheme.
requirements: Two researchers coding independently for inter-rater reliability, plus graduate assistant reliability checks by reviewers not involved in data collection
constraints: Space did not permit extrapolation of the full coding scheme in the article text
target_learners: pre-service teachers in undergraduate online courses
target_learning_goals: analyzing argumentation quality and discourse processes in online discussion
examples: Sample codes include TEBSP (Treatment Group Evaluation Based on Student Perspective), TEPE (Evaluation Based on Personal Experience), and TB (Treatment Both, it depends)
key_sources: Spatariu, A., & Winsor, D. L. (2010). A Qualitative Perspective: Pre-Service Teachers Discuss Educational Technology Online. i-manager's Journal of School Educational Technology, 6(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1102777

article_title: The Impact of Task-Based Instruction Program on Fostering ESL Learners' Speaking Ability: A Cognitive Approach
citation: Mohammad Mohammadipour & Sabariah MD Rashid. (2015). The Impact of Task-Based Instruction Program on Fostering ESL Learners' Speaking Ability: A Cognitive Approach. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.2p.113
title: Three-phase task-based teaching strategy integrating communicative tasks with the cognitive approach
description: The article proposes a teaching strategy in which "each speaking lesson was divided into three main phases: pre-task phase, during-task phase and post- task phase". The pre-task phase uses planning, consciousness raising and teaching to prepare learners and draw attention to form; the during-task phase focuses on communicating meaning while the teacher facilitates, records performance and assigns peer observers; the post-task phase uses self/peer evaluation of recordings and supportive feedback to remedy errors and raise awareness of accuracy and restructuring. The strategy operationalises the cognitive-approach goal of managing learners' focus of attention across fluency, accuracy and complexity.
requirements: Tasks should not be so easy that learners do not engage seriously nor so difficult that excessive mental processing is required
A set of target structures, skills or elements made prominent in attentional terms
constraints: The programme was implemented with freshmen university students in a Malaysian ESL context over eleven weeks
target_learning_goals: overall speaking proficiency
fluency, accuracy and complexity in spoken language
examples: Each lesson used pre-task activities such as planning and consciousness raising, during-task performance with peer observers and recording, and post-task self/peer evaluation of recorded extracts
key_sources: Mohammad Mohammadipour & Sabariah MD Rashid. (2015). The Impact of Task-Based Instruction Program on Fostering ESL Learners' Speaking Ability: A Cognitive Approach. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.2p.113

article_title: The Effects of Classic and Web-Designed Conceptual Change Texts on the Subject of Water Chemistry
citation: Taş, E., Gülen, S., Öner, Z., & Özyürek, C. (2015). The effects of classic and web-designed conceptual change texts on the subject of water chemistry. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 7(2), 263-280. http://www.iejee.com
title: Three-stage diagnostic test for identifying conceptual errors
description: A 30-item instrument measuring attainment, reasons for answers, and confidence in one test. The article states it can "find out the conceptual errors of a great number of people simultaneously and in a short time." Items were refined via pilot item analysis (two items removed for distinctiveness below 0.2; difficulty index p = 0.51; distinctiveness r = 0.43; Cronbach's alpha = 0.69).
requirements: Requires pilot item analysis to remove low-distinctiveness items
Requires confidence ('sure, not sure, I guessed') items to distinguish errors from guesses
constraints: Developed specifically for water chemistry content with 8th-9th grade students
target_learning_goals: Water chemistry concepts: hardness, softening, chlorination, ion exchange
examples: Used as pre-test, post-test, and three-month permanency test in this study
