article_title: Assessing the Promise of a Supplemental Reading Intervention for At-Risk First Grade Students in a Public School Setting
citation: Mokhtari, K., Neel, J. L., Kaiser, F., & Le, H.-H. (2015). Assessing the Promise of a Supplemental Reading Intervention for At-Risk First Grade Students in a Public School Setting. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 7(3), 281-300. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1072447
title: Three-component tutoring framework: familiar reading, shared reading, and interactive writing segments
description: The article describes a research-based instructional framework for organizing one-on-one tutoring sessions, comprising "(a) a 20-minute reading or re-reading of an easy or familiar text, (b) a 20-minute shared or interactive reading of a self-selected text, and (c) a 20-minute interactive writing segment targeting specific writing skills and strategies". Together the three components take approximately 50-55 minutes. The framework was designed to be flexible enough for tutors to adapt lessons while enabling close supervision and monitoring of implementation fidelity.
requirements: Tutors must be trained to implement the framework; fidelity of lesson implementation was monitored via protocols and lesson observations, with tutors implementing lessons as intended or with slight adaptations about 85% of the time
constraints: The framework was designed for one-on-one tutoring of at-risk first grade readers in a supplemental Tier 3 before-school program
target_learners: At-risk first grade readers in the lowest performing quartile
target_learning_goals: Early literacy skills including reading fluency, comprehension, and writing strategies
examples: Tutors delivered the three-component lessons three times a week for 10 weeks during fall and spring semesters
key_sources: Mokhtari, K., Neel, J. L., Kaiser, F., & Le, H.-H. (2015). Assessing the Promise of a Supplemental Reading Intervention for At-Risk First Grade Students in a Public School Setting. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 7(3), 281-300. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1068056

article_title: The Three Block Model of Universal Design for Learning (UDL): Engaging Students in Inclusive Education
citation: Jennifer Katz. (2013). The Three Block Model of Universal Design for Learning (UDL): Engaging students in inclusive education. Canadian Journal of Education, 36(1). https://journals.sfu.ca/cje/index.php/cje
title: The Three Block Model of Universal Design for Learning
description: The Three Block Model of UDL (Katz, 2012a) "provides teachers with a method for creating inclusive environments and improving student engagement," organized into three blocks. Block 1 addresses social and emotional learning through compassionate learning communities, the Respecting Diversity program, and democratic classroom management. Block 2, Inclusive Instructional Practice, is a planning and instructional framework combining Understanding by Design, Differentiated Instruction, curriculum integration, inquiry, and assessment for learning, with heterogeneous groupings in which "ALL students work together ... to master curriculum through differentiated inquiry activities." Block 3 completes the model as described in Appendix A.
requirements: Teachers co-plan integrated units, determine essential understandings, create differentiated inquiry projects, and develop rubrics allowing differentiated assessment
Professional development and follow-up consultation support implementation
constraints: In this study only Block 2 instructional practices were implemented; teachers were not asked to implement the RD program or classroom meetings
target_learners: All K-12 students in inclusive classrooms, including students with disabilities, ESL learners, and gifted students
target_learning_goals: Academic and social inclusion
Student engagement
Mastery of complex concepts through higher-order inquiry
examples: Treatment teachers co-planned integrated units, created inquiry-based projects and multiple intelligences activities differentiating complexity and modality, and developed rubrics for differentiated assessment
key_sources: Jennifer Katz. (2013). The Three Block Model of Universal Design for Learning (UDL): Engaging students in inclusive education. Canadian Journal of Education, 36(1). https://journals.sfu.ca/cje/index.php/cje

article_title: Metacognitive Awareness and the Fluency of Task-Based Oral Output across Planning Conditions: The Case of Iranian TEFL Students
citation: Seifoori, Z. (2016). Metacognitive awareness and the fluency of task-based oral output across planning conditions: The case of Iranian TEFL students. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research, 4(1), 11-26. https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr
title: Three models of second-language fluency development: accelerating, restructuring, and instance models
description: The article presents three competing accounts of how fluency develops. Accelerating models rest on "the proceduralization of declarative knowledge", whereby rules are applied more quickly with less demand on mental resources. Restructuring models link fluent performance to better-organized rules, and instance-based models attribute fluency to "contextually-coded exemplars" stored and retrieved as wholes, requiring less processing capacity. The author uses this framework, following Schmidt (1992) and Skehan (1996), to interpret why combined planners gained the most fluency.
requirements: Fluent performance is explained relative to the processing demands of rule application, rule organization, or exemplar retrieval
constraints: The article treats these as competing explanatory accounts rather than tested models in this study
target_learning_goals: oral fluency in a second language
examples: The author interprets the POLP planners' advantage as their use of extra pre-task and on-line planning time to choose attentional direction and employ mental resources more rapidly

article_title: The 4C/ID-Model in Physics Education: Instructional Design of a Digital Learning Environment to Teach Electrical Circuits
citation: Melo, M. (2018). The 4C/ID-Model in Physics Education: Instructional Design of a Digital Learning Environment to Teach Electrical Circuits. International Journal of Instruction, 11(1), 103-122. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1118a
title: Three-level categorization of multimedia cognitive learning theories underlying 4C/ID
description: Following van Merriënboer and Kester, the article categorizes general multimedia cognitive learning theories in three levels: psychological theories of memory systems and cognitive processes (information processing theory), theories for designing educational messages including Sweller's Cognitive Load Theory and Mayer's Multimedia Learning Theory, and theories and models prescribing how to develop educational programs with the 4C/ID-model. The article writes that "the general (multimedia) cognitive learning theories can be categorized in three levels" and uses this framing to justify its design choices.
requirements: Instruction must obey experimentally tested procedures that reduce working memory load to facilitate schema construction
constraints: Working memory is limited in capacity and duration until transformed by knowledge held in long-term memory
target_learners: Learners of digital educational resources, here 9th-grade physics students
target_learning_goals: Construction and automation of mental schemas for complex skills
examples: The article cites the coherence, contiguity and modality principles from Mayer's theory as guides for designing its supportive information videos

article_title: Effect of Instructional vs. Authentic Video Materials on Introvert and Extrovert Iranian EFL Learners' Vocabulary Learning
citation: Isazadeh, P., Makui, S. M. Z., & Ansarian, L. (2016). Effect of Instructional vs. Authentic Video Materials on Introvert and Extrovert Iranian EFL Learners' Vocabulary Learning. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 4(4). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.4n.4p.1
title: Three-phase video session: pre-movie, movie, and post-movie activities
description: Each treatment session followed a three-part structure for exploiting video clips: "1) pre-movie activities, in which the teacher will activate the participants' schemata by asking relevant questions about the movie topic. 2) Movie activities", in which the movie was watched and learners could take notes, and "3) post-movie activities", in which new vocabulary was introduced and practiced followed by free discussion. The article also recommends clips be short, around 2 or 3 minutes, and clear, self-contained and engaging.
requirements: Teacher guidance and well-chosen materials; clips prepared ahead with appropriate pre-viewing, viewing and post-viewing activities
constraints: Clips should be short (around 2 or 3 minutes) to allow exploitation of their contents in class
target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning from video materials
examples: Experimental groups watched POD English Series videos in 10 sessions of 45 minutes, each divided into pre-movie, movie, and post-movie sections
key_sources: Isazadeh, P., Makui, S. M. Z., & Ansarian, L. (2016). Effect of Instructional vs. Authentic Video Materials on Introvert and Extrovert Iranian EFL Learners' Vocabulary Learning. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 4(4). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.4n.4p.1

article_title: Cognitive Factors That Influence Children's Learning from a Multimedia Science Lesson
citation: Anggoro, F. K., Stein, N. L., & Jee, B. D. (2012). Cognitive factors that influence children's learning from a multimedia science lesson. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 5(1), 93-108. https://www.iejee.com
title: Theory of complex learning: three types of learning required for science knowledge acquisition
description: The article describes a theory of complex learning in which "knowledge acquisition in the sciences requires three types of learning: concept learning, causal explanation-based learning, and argument learning." Concept learning requires explicitness and compare/contrast procedures for novices. Causal explanation-based learning provides transferable knowledge of mechanisms, and failing to provide causal explanations results in superficial understanding. Argument learning emphasizes correcting learners' misconceptions by providing evidence in favor of correct concepts. The article used this theory to design a causally coherent multimedia lesson about the states of water.
requirements: Learning materials must describe all dimensions of the concept as well as dimensions that are not part of the concept
Explicit visual models are needed to teach complex spatial and causal properties difficult to convey in words
constraints: These elements of complex learning cannot be supported through text-based instruction alone
target_learning_goals: understanding observable and molecular properties of the three states of water
causal explanation of physical science phenomena
examples: The article adopted two learning modules from Stein et al. designed using this theory, teaching about matter, states of water, and molecular properties
key_sources: Anggoro, F. K., Stein, N. L., & Jee, B. D. (2012). Cognitive factors that influence children's learning from a multimedia science lesson. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 5(1), 93-108. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1068621

article_title: Difficulties That English Teachers Encounter While Teaching Listening Comprehension and Their Attitudes towards Them
citation: Alrawashdeh, A. I. & Al-zayed, N. N. (2017). Difficulties That English Teachers Encounter while Teaching Listening Comprehension and Their Attitudes towards Them. English Language Teaching, 10(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n5p167
title: Three-domain framework of difficulties in teaching listening comprehension
description: The article organizes difficulties English teachers encounter while teaching listening comprehension into three questionnaire domains: problems related to the proficiency of teachers, problems regarding the teaching-learning environment, and problems related to availability of resources and teaching aids. Each domain was measured with Likert-scale items and rated low, medium or high by mean score.
requirements: A questionnaire covering the three domains with Likert-scale scoring
constraints: Developed in the context of Jordanian Karak schools
target_learning_goals: Teaching listening comprehension
examples: The questionnaire contained 8 items on teacher proficiency, 9 on teaching environment and 6 on resources and teaching aids

citation: Hmidani, T. (2017). Didactic model: Teaching the English temporal system to Arabic freshman learners of English. Profile: Issues in Teachers' Professional Development, 19(Suppl. 1), 81-97. https://doi.org/10.15446/profile.v19n_sup1.68617
title: Three-section self-assessment journal for monitoring language-learning progress
description: Students keep a journal or diary completed on three occasions during the course, divided into three sections: "questions for direct assessment", a list of new lexis and grammatical points with sentences illustrating proper use, and a section where students write their own mistakes and provide corrections. The journal is submitted to the teacher to be reviewed, discussed, and graded. It helps students monitor their progress and serves as a reference containing a stock of new vocabulary items.
requirements: Completed on three occasions during the course and submitted to the teacher for review, discussion, and grading
target_learners: Freshman university students in an intensive English course
target_learning_goals: self-assessment and monitoring of language-learning progress
vocabulary building
error correction
examples: The journal was used as the fourth, ongoing Self-Assessment Phase of the didactic model throughout the semester

article_title: A Blended Education Program Based on Critical Thinking and Its Effect on Personality Type and Attribution Style of the Students
citation: Mosalanejad, L., Alipor, A., & Zandi, B. (2010). A Blended Education Program Based on Critical Thinking and Its Effect on Personality Type and Attribution Style of the Students. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education, 11(2). http://tojde.anadolu.edu.tr/tojde39/articles/article_12.htm
title: Three categories of blended learning assumptions: needed skills, needed perceptions, needed capability
description: The article organizes assumptions about blended learning into three categories drawn from Harvey (2003): a personal method supported by an educational mediator for developing special skills and knowledge; integration of different learning methods into communicational means for developing special behaviors and perceptions; and integrated learning with knowledge management and leadership for developing capabilities of the work environment. The authors use this taxonomy to justify combining teaching kinds in medical sciences education.
requirements: A change of individuals' attitudes and conceptions has priority in the medical sciences, completed by development of capabilities and skills needed for learning

skill development
professional capability

article_title: Integrated Reading and Writing: A Case of Korean English Language Learners
citation: Cho, H., & Brutt-Griffler, J. (2015). Integrated reading and writing: A case of Korean English language learners. Reading in a Foreign Language, 27(2), 242-261. http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl
title: Thinksheet and questionsheet worksheets for integrated reading and writing instruction
description: The thinksheet is a three-step worksheet modified from the WIRC project's thinksheet (Englert & Raphael, 1989) to suit ELL students. Step 1 asks students to read a chunk of the story, identify one or two important ideas, and paraphrase the main ideas. Step 2 asks students to select the most important ideas and reflect on them. Step 3 asks students to write a summary and reflection. An additional worksheet called a questionsheet was created for this study, providing students with space to work cooperatively on their questions about vocabulary, grammar, and the story. The worksheets serve as a cognitive model while students read and write, helping each other achieve both "process goals" and "content goals."
requirements: Teachers are provided with orientation materials about paraphrasing, questioning, and summarizing, answer keys to the student worksheets, and synonym lists.
constraints: The thinksheet and questionsheet were designed so as to allow teachers to "step-in" when explaining, correcting, and scaffolding and to "step-back" when giving students time to work individually or as part of a group.
target_learners: Korean middle school EFL students at beginning, intermediate, and advanced proficiency levels
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Summary writing
Paraphrasing
Reflection writing
examples: Students read a page or two, wrote questions about words, grammar, and the story, discussed them with peers and the teacher, then identified and paraphrased main ideas on the thinksheet, repeating until the story was finished.
key_sources: Cho, H., & Brutt-Griffler, J. (2015). Integrated reading and writing: A case of Korean English language learners. Reading in a Foreign Language, 27(2), 242-261. http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl

article_title: Exploring the Classroom: Teaching Science in Early Childhood
citation: Dejonckheere, P.J.N., De Wit, N.L., Van de Keere, K., & Vervaet, S. (2016). Exploring the classroom: Teaching science in early childhood. European Journal of Educational Research, 5(3), 149-164. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.5.3.149
title: Three-phase structure for inquiry-based preschool science activities
description: The article's intervention activities followed a consistent three-part structure: an introduction phase where the teacher presented materials and linked them to prior knowledge without instructions, an exploration phase of free play in small groups, and a trigger phase where the teacher posed probe questions. This structure aims to "focus the exploration activities to the causal and non -causal variables" while preserving child-initiated exploration.
requirements: Activities must be connected to classroom themes and children's interests; materials must allow manipulation of multiple variables.
constraints: The article states it could not determine the exact contribution of each phase (e.g., whether free exploration alone would suffice).
target_learning_goals: scientific reasoning skills
control of variables strategy
domain-general process skills such as observing, predicting, and experimenting
examples: In the sinking and floating activity, the introduction phase involved brainstorming and demonstration, the exploration phase involved free play with water materials, and the trigger phase used probe questions like 'Do large objects always float? How would you investigate this?'

article_title: A Thematic-Based Meta Analytic Study Regarding the Effect of Creativity on Academic Success and Learning Retention
citation: Faysal Özdas & Veli Batdi. (2017). A Thematic-based Meta Analytic Study Regarding the Effect of Creativity on Academic Success and Learning Retention. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v5i3.2043
title: Thematic-based meta-analytic framework categorizing creativity interventions into four themes
description: The article organizes creativity research into four themes: "creative thinking, creative thinking activities, creative thinking techniques and creative writing applications" (CT, CTA, CTT, CWA). Studies are coded in three phases—study identity, study characteristics (course type, grade levels, duration), and study data (sample sizes, means, standard deviations)—then pooled using Hedges' d under fixed-effect and random-effects models with Q-test homogeneity checks and fail-safe number analysis.
requirements: Included studies must use experimental and control groups (pretest-posttest control group model)
Studies must report sample sizes, means and standard deviations, or t-test, F-test, or p-values so effect sizes can be calculated
constraints: Only studies from 2001–2011 available in English or Turkish were included
target_learners: students across grade levels in experimental creativity studies
target_learning_goals: academic success
learning retention
examples: Eighteen of 230 studies met the inclusion criteria and were analyzed using CMA and MetaWin programs

article_title: Engaging Engineering Students in Geoscience through Case Studies and Active Learning
citation: Elizabeth A. Holley. (2017). Engaging Engineering Students in Geoscience Through Case Studies and Active Learning. Journal of Geoscience Education. https://doi.org/10.5408/16-145.1
title: Three-component curricular revision combining faculty case studies, student presentations, and active learning exercises
description: The 2015 redesign of the Earth Materials and Resources course had three components: "geological concepts were taught in the context of case studies presented by the faculty, teams of students gave case study presentations, and active learning exercises were incorporated into class meetings." The components were aligned with course learning outcomes and survey questions (Table I), and active learning techniques were selected using Bonwell and Sutherland's active learning continuum framework.
requirements: Team-teaching by faculty to support breakout sessions and monitor activity effectiveness
Advance selection of active learning techniques to scaffold and formatively assess learning outcomes
constraints: Implemented in a single 4-credit junior-level mining engineering geoscience course with 30 students
target_learning_goals: connecting geoscience concepts to mining engineering applications
improving attitudes toward geoscience
examples: Class meetings began with student case study presentations and peer evaluations, followed by faculty-led case studies with interspersed active learning exercises such as minute papers, think–pair–share, and small-group discussion
key_sources: Elizabeth A. Holley. (2017). Engaging Engineering Students in Geoscience Through Case Studies and Active Learning. Journal of Geoscience Education. https://doi.org/10.5408/16-145.1

article_title: The Courseware of Discontinuous Nature of Matter in Teaching the States of Matter and Their Changes
citation: Sopandi, W., Kadarohman, A., Rosbiono, M., Latip, A., & Sukardi, R. R. (2018). The Courseware of Discontinuous Nature of Matter in Teaching the States of Matter and Their Changes. International Journal of Instruction, 11(1), 61-76. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1115a
title: Three levels of chemical representation (macroscopic, sub-microscopic, symbolic)
description: The article adopts the framework that studying chemistry includes aspects of the macroscopic, sub-microscopic, and symbolic levels. Students observe phenomena at the macroscopic level, explain them via particles at the sub-microscopic level, and communicate them with chemical terminology at the symbolic level. The article treats the sub-microscopic level as "a bridge between macroscopic and symbolic levels" and as the level students find most difficult.
requirements: Instruction should develop all three levels, as the study's lesson plans were prepared to do
constraints: The sub-microscopic level is the most difficult to learn, partly due to lack of introduction and students' concrete thinking
target_learners: Junior and senior high school chemistry students
target_learning_goals: Explaining chemical phenomena at macroscopic, sub-microscopic, and symbolic levels
examples: The study measured conceptual mastery of changing states of matter separately at each of the three levels
key_sources: Sopandi, W., Kadarohman, A., Rosbiono, M., Latip, A., & Sukardi, R. R. (2018). The Courseware of Discontinuous Nature of Matter in Teaching the States of Matter and Their Changes. International Journal of Instruction, 11(1), 61-76. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1115a

article_title: Developing Formative Assessment Practices in Instruction: Recommendations from a Meta-Aggregation
citation: Lolkus, M., Kenney, R., & Maeda, Y. (2022). Developing formative assessment practices in instruction: Recommendations from a meta-aggregation. Practical Assessment, Research, & Evaluation, 27(26). https://scholarworks.umass.edu/pare/vol27/iss1/26
title: Three-phase framework of formative assessment practice: planning, gathering/responding, and reflecting
description: The article organizes teachers' formative assessment practices into three sub-domains of an expanded assessment cycle: planning for FA before gathering evidence, teaching and adjusting instruction with FA while gathering and responding to student thinking, and reflecting on FA practices afterward. Double-sided arrows in the framework figure signal that FA "does not necessarily follow an orderly cyclical pattern" but can move among phases in any direction. The framework framed the analysis and synthesis of the 11 primary studies.
requirements: Teachers connect the framework's phases to daily instructional practice rather than a simplified assessment cycle
constraints: Developed from US secondary mathematics qualitative studies published 2008–2019
target_learning_goals: formative assessment practice
responsive mathematics instruction
key_sources: Lolkus, M., Kenney, R., & Maeda, Y. (2022). Developing formative assessment practices in instruction: Recommendations from a meta-aggregation. Practical Assessment, Research, & Evaluation, 27(26). https://scholarworks.umass.edu/pare/vol27/iss1/26

article_title: An Investigation of Teaching Strategy in the Distance Learning Mathematics Classroom
citation: DePriter, T. (2012). An Investigation of Teaching Strategy in the Distance Learning Mathematics Classroom. Journal of Educators Online, 9(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ975633
title: Constructivist group projects structured across three weeks with mixed-ability groups
description: In the constructivist-based section, each of three group projects spanned three weeks: week one for contacting group members and submitting a plan, week two for solving and submitting the problem, and week three for presenting findings electronically and discussing other groups' work. Groups of "three to four participants with a mix of high and low achieving students as determined by the pretest" were used, which the article says is supported by constructivist theory because students construct knowledge in relation to life experiences.
requirements: A study-group area in the online classroom where groups can discuss assigned problems
Problems complex enough that groups can transcend what individuals could accomplish
constraints: Student withdrawal in the first weeks of class made establishing and maintaining groups difficult
target_learners: adult distance learners in developmental mathematics
target_learning_goals: mathematics content knowledge and collaborative problem solving
examples: Group problems were posted without a set of instructions so members discussed solution strategies, and the researcher posed follow-up questions to take concepts to a higher level
key_sources: DePriter, T. (2012). An Investigation of Teaching Strategy in the Distance Learning Mathematics Classroom. Journal of Educators Online, 9(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1020037

article_title: The Impact of Training Metacognitive Strategies on Reading Comprehension among ESL Learner's
citation: Habibian, M. (2015). The Impact of Training Metacognitive Strategies on Reading Comprehension among ESL Learner’s. Journal of Education and Practice, 6(28). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1082693
title: Three-phase metacognitive knowledge framework for strategy instruction design
description: The article describes a twelve-week instructional design in which students are taught three knowledge-based components: "declarative knowledge (learning what are the strategies), situational knowledge (learning in which context strategy can be applied), and procedural knowledge (learning how to employ the strategy)." This structure organizes explicit strategy instruction across knowing what, when, and how.
requirements: Sessions must address all three knowledge types across the instructional period
constraints: Studied among first-level reading Malaysian ESL undergraduates; generalization to other ESL contexts is limited per the author
target_learning_goals: metacognitive strategy use in reading
examples: The strategy-based design was based on Wade et al. (1990) and comprised highlighting main points, paraphrasing, identifying keywords, using diagrams, mental integration, using background knowledge, problem solving, monitoring, re-reading, self-testing, and adjusting reading rate
key_sources: Habibian, M. (2015). The Impact of Training Metacognitive Strategies on Reading Comprehension among ESL Learner’s. Journal of Education and Practice, 6(28). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1081318

article_title: Effects of Theory Training, Hands-on Supervision and a Self-Instructional Treatment Manual on Staff Competency
citation: Hatlenes, L. T., & Eikeseth, S. (2016). Effects of Theory Training, Hands-on Supervision and a Self-instructional Treatment Manual on Staff Competency. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 9(2), 373-384. https://www.iejee.com
title: Pair theory training with hands-on supervision to reach mastery-level teaching skills
description: The article's findings indicate that theoretical training alone increased correct teaching procedures but not to mastery levels, while adding hands-on supervision produced the greatest gains. The authors state "mastery criterion on clinical skills was reached only when theory training was followed by hands-on supervision." This supports sequencing theory before supervised practice.
requirements: Theory training should cover the specific teaching procedures staff will perform
constraints: The study did not assess generalization across clients and target skills
The study had a low number of participants
target_learners: staff working with individuals with developmental disorders
target_learning_goals: correct teaching skills
theoretical competence in behavior analysis
examples: After the manual group received hands-on supervision, their mean correct teaching skills reached 90%

article_title: The Attitude of the Students towards the Value of "Paying Attention to Being Healthy" in 4th Grade Elementary Social Sciences Course
citation: Turhan ÇETİN & Mustafa TAHİROĞLU. (2012). The Attitude of the Students towards the Value of “Paying Attention to Being Healthy” in 4th Grade Elementary Social Sciences Course. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 12(2). www.edam.com.tr/estp
title: Three approaches to values teaching: Value Explanation, Value Analysis, and Moral Judgement
description: The article describes three approaches used in values teaching and development. Value Explanation is "based on how individuals define what is important for them in their life" with processes of Choice, Appreciation, and Acting. Value Analysis helps people learn a step-by-step logical process for moral decisions. Moral Judgement presents real-life dilemmas where "two different value principles clash."
requirements: Teachers and students should refrain from attitudes that make it hard to think on subjects of value
constraints: Dilemmas must be simple, open-ended, related to class subjects, and appropriate to student level
target_learning_goals: adopting and experiencing values
key_sources: Turhan ÇETİN & Mustafa TAHİROĞLU. (2012). The Attitude of the Students towards the Value of “Paying Attention to Being Healthy” in 4th Grade Elementary Social Sciences Course. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 12(2). www.edam.com.tr/estp. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ987865

article_title: SMS as a Learning Tool: An Experimental Study
citation: Gutiérrez-Colon Plana, M., Gallardo Torrano, P. and Grova, M. E. (2012). SMS as a learning tool: an experimental study. The EUROCALL Review, 20(2).
title: M-learning evaluation at micro and macro levels (Vavoula and Sharples three-level framework)
description: The article adopts Vavoula and Sharples's (2009) three-level evaluation framework for mobile learning scenarios: "(1) the usability of the technology (micro level); (2) education/learning (meso level); and (3) organisation/practicability (macro level)". The study positions itself at both micro and macro levels, investigating exercise types following Gu et al.'s design principles for content, activity and usability, and organisational issues such as timing and message quantity.
requirements: Evaluation of mobile learning scenarios should address usability, learning, and organisation/practicability levels
constraints: The present study addresses only the micro and macro levels, not the meso level in depth
target_learners: researchers and designers evaluating mobile learning interventions
target_learning_goals: evaluating mobile learning methodology viability
examples: The study examined exercise design (micro) and timing, student preferences and organisation of messages (macro)

article_title: Using Anticipatory Reading Guides to Improve Elementary Students' Comprehension
citation: Ortlieb, E. (2013). Using Anticipatory Reading Guides to Improve Elementary Students' Comprehension. International Journal of Instruction, 6(2), 145-162. https://www.e-iji.net
title: Three-column anticipatory reading guide worksheet.
description: The anticipatory reading guide material was "a three column spreadsheet where the first column told the student which paragraph to read. The second column stated what to look for and the third column gave space to record responses." Students completed the guide before answering multiple-choice questions, focusing their reading on targeted content. This tool served as the primary intervention material across reading and social studies lessons during the six-week study.
requirements: Passages with identifiable paragraph structure and questions that can be previewed before reading
constraints: Originally designed for secondary grades; adapted here for elementary use
target_learning_goals: Directed reading comprehension and standardized test performance

article_title: Development of Subject Position as a Condition for Forming Communicative Competence of a Future Teacher
citation: Yarullina, A. Sh., & Araslanova, A. T. (2016). Development of Subject Position as a Condition for Forming Communicative Competence of a Future Teacher. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(9), 2311-2322.
title: Three-level progression of communicatively-oriented tasks of increasing complexity
description: Students solve a set of communicatively-oriented tasks which gradually became more complex. The first level develops informational skills (diagnostic questions, verbal and non-verbal expressive means, coding and decoding non-verbal signals); the second develops empathic perceptive skills (emotional reaction, empathic listening); the third develops interactive-relation skills such as "establishing psychological contact" and correct behavior in conflict situations.
requirements: Tasks must be sequenced from informational to empathic to interactive complexity
target_learning_goals: communicative skills with pupils
empathic perceptive skills
interactive relations with pupils
examples: Tasks included "Forming informational data about pupils", "Talks with the pupils' parents", and "Designing maps of psychological state of pupils"

article_title: Modern English Drama and the Students' Fluency and Accuracy of Speaking
citation: Kian Pishkar, Ahmad Moinzadeh & Azizallah Dabaghi. (2017). Modern English Drama and the Students’ Fluency and Accuracy of Speaking. English Language Teaching, 10(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n8p69
title: Segalowitz's three notions of fluency as the study's organizing framework
description: The article organizes its measurement of speaking around Segalowitz's distinction among cognitive fluency, utterance fluency and perceived fluency. Cognitive fluency concerns "the speaker’s abilities to efficiently plan and execute his speech", while utterance fluency is measured in a speech sample. Following Skehan and Tavakoli, the study further splits utterance fluency into breakdown, speed and repair fluency and selects measures so these aspects are not confounded.
requirements: Measures of pausing and speed of delivery must be kept unconfounded, as the article states its measures "were chosen such that breakdown fluency, speed fluency, and repair fluency were not confounded"
target_learning_goals: L2 speaking fluency
key_sources: Kian Pishkar, Ahmad Moinzadeh & Azizallah Dabaghi. (2017). Modern English Drama and the Students’ Fluency and Accuracy of Speaking. English Language Teaching, 10(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n8p69

article_title: Using Convergent and Divergent Tasks to Improve Writing and Language Learning Motivation
citation: Marashi, H., & Tahan-Shizari, P. (2015). Using convergent and divergent tasks to improve writing and language learning motivation. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research, 3(1), 99-117. https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr
title: Three-phase pre-writing, while-writing, and post-writing task structure for collaborative writing instruction
description: The article describes a lesson-level instructional pattern in which writing sessions are organized into pre-task, while-task, and post-task phases. The authors state that "applying the three phases of pre-writing, while-writing, and post-writing plays particularly important roles in helping learners comprehend the text better with less effort." In both experimental conditions, pre-task activities activated background knowledge and vocabulary, while-task phases involved collaborative writing in groups of five, and post-task phases included error correction, discussion, and individual rewriting.
requirements: Learners work in small groups (five learners per group in the study) with teacher-guided error correction during and after the writing phases.
target_learners: intermediate EFL learners in language school classes
target_learning_goals: improve L2 writing through structured collaborative task phases
examples: Pre-task activities included listing topic-related words, matching words to definitions, and discussing questions to activate background knowledge before group writing.

article_title: Effectiveness of an AI-augmented teacher feedback model in improving medical students' clinical documentation skills: a retrospective cohort study.
citation: Hu Shuai, Du Fei, Fang Can, Zheng Xiyan, Shi Xianjie, Zhou Zheng. (2026). Effectiveness of an AI-augmented teacher feedback model in improving medical students' clinical documentation skills: a retrospective cohort study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09953-7
title: Three-phase validation paradigm: tool validity, predictive validity, and effectiveness evaluation
description: The study introduces a reusable three-phase evidence chain for evaluating AI teaching tools: Phase 1 assessed AI scoring reliability using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) based on 20 records blindly evaluated by two experts; Phase 2 analyzed the correlation between post-rotation AI scores and Mini-CEX scores; Phase 3 used ANCOVA for comparing post-rotation AI scores between groups. The authors state this is "the first study to chain instrument validation, predictive validity, and effectiveness evaluation in a single three-phase paradigm, offering a reusable framework for evaluating AI-assisted teaching tools in clinical documentation training."
requirements: Requires establishing AI scoring tool reliability against expert ratings before testing effectiveness
constraints: Developed and applied in the context of clinical documentation training for medical interns
target_learning_goals: evaluating AI-assisted teaching tools
clinical documentation skills assessment

Effectiveness of an AI-augmented teacher feedback model in improving medical students' clinical documentation skills: a retrospective cohort study. article_title: Simulation-based education in undergraduate psychiatry: a focused review and interpretive analysis of clinical competence representation.
citation: Pulido Francisco Rodríguez, García Ángeles Rodríguez, Estebaranz Nayra Caballero. (2026). Simulation-based education in undergraduate psychiatry: a focused review and interpretive analysis of clinical competence representation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09885-2
title: Three-domain framework of psychiatric competence: behavioural, relational and integrative
description: The review conceptualises psychiatric competence as comprising three interrelated domains. Behavioural competence refers to observable clinical actions such as information gathering and interview organisation; relational competence encompasses empathy, rapport and therapeutic engagement; and integrative competence involves "the formulation of clinically meaningful understandings through the synthesis of biological, psychological and social information". The review uses this framework deductively to analyse which domains are explicitly represented in published assessment approaches.
requirements: Assessment frameworks must specify which competence domains are explicitly operationalised for the framework to be applied in analysing representation
constraints: The domains are closely interconnected in practice but may differ in how explicitly they are represented within assessment systems
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in psychiatry clerkships
target_learning_goals: psychiatric interviewing
clinical communication
biopsychosocial formulation
examples: The review analysed four included studies against the three domains, classifying each domain in each study as explicitly represented, implicitly addressed, or not reported
key_sources: Pulido Francisco Rodríguez, García Ángeles Rodríguez, Estebaranz Nayra Caballero. (2026). Simulation-based education in undergraduate psychiatry: a focused review and interpretive analysis of clinical competence representation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09885-2

article_title: Educational impact of a simulation-based renal biopsy workshop for medical students during nephrology clerkship.
citation: Onishi Yasuhiro, Tsuji Kenji, Nakanoh Hiroyuki, Uchida Naruhiko, Fukushima Kazuhiko, Mise Koki, Takeuchi Hidemi, Tanaka Keiko, Tanabe Katsuyuki, Morinaga Hiroshi, Uchida Haruhito A., Kitamura Shinji, Wada Jun. (2026). Educational impact of a simulation-based renal biopsy workshop for medical students during nephrology clerkship. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09805-4
title: Three-phase renal biopsy simulation workshop: lecture, peer ultrasound practice, hands-on simulated biopsy
description: The workshop comprised "three sequential phases: a brief introductory lecture, ultrasound practice, and hands-on biopsy simulation", delivered in small groups of four to five students over approximately 50 minutes per group. A ~5-minute lecture covered indications, complications, ultrasound principles, sterile technique, and needle handling; students then scanned each other (~5 minutes per student) and practiced simulated biopsy (~5 minutes each), supervised by a single board-certified nephrologist.
requirements: Small groups of four to five students to allow close supervision and active participation
Supervision by an experienced nephrologist instructor
constraints: Total training time was limited; the authors state it did not provide sufficient repetition or mastery-based progression
target_learners: fifth-year medical students on nephrology clerkship
target_learning_goals: renal biopsy procedure knowledge
ultrasound probe handling
biopsy needle handling confidence
examples: Delivered to an entire cohort of 113 students as part of the regular clerkship curriculum

article_title: Development and validation of the teachers generative AI professional competence scale.
citation: Aldighrir Wafa Mohammed. (2026). Development and validation of the teachers generative AI professional competence scale. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-65021-6
title: Three-domain framework for teachers' generative AI professional competence
description: The article proposes that teachers' generative AI professional competence comprises three related yet empirically distinguishable domains: pedagogical judgment (evaluating AI-supported suggestions in relation to learning aims), ethical leadership (modeling and sustaining morally responsible AI use), and professional agency (acting intentionally and autonomously within changing technological conditions). The framework is unified by a human-centered AI perspective arguing that AI should enhance rather than diminish human capabilities, responsibility, and dignity in educational settings.
requirements: The three domains are expected to correlate because they arise from the same professional ecology, yet should remain empirically distinguishable
constraints: The framework is deliberately measurement-focused and assumes generative AI competence is not captured by these three domains alone
target_learning_goals: Understanding what it means for teachers to remain professionally responsible, morally credible, and agentically engaged in classrooms shaped by generative AI
key_sources: Aldighrir Wafa Mohammed. (2026). Development and validation of the teachers generative AI professional competence scale. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-65021-6

article_title: Full-Scale high-fidelity simulation compared to procedural simulation workshop for veno-arterial ECMO cannulation during refractory cardiac arrest: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Bouras Marwan, Senage Thomas, Meule Emma, David Charles-Henri, Guimbretière Guillaume, Cadiet Julien, Bazin Olivier, Rozec Bertrand, Lejus-Bourdeau Corinne, Vourc’h Mickael. (2026). Full-Scale high-fidelity simulation compared to procedural simulation workshop for veno-arterial ECMO cannulation during refractory cardiac arrest: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09618-5
title: Three-hour procedural simulation workshop for VA-ECMO cannulation technical skills
description: A focused 3-hour workshop led by a cardiac surgeon in a cardiothoracic intensive care unit room, where residents in small groups engage in hands-on, apprenticeship-style learning. The session covers equipment introduction, step-by-step ultrasound-guided puncture, wire handling, key maneuvers, and common pitfalls, with practice on a CREAPLAST Evolution III mannequin with simulated arterial and venous flows. The training focuses exclusively on technical skills, without covering ECMO patient management or refractory cardiac arrest algorithms.
requirements: A CREAPLAST Evolution III mannequin with simulated flows, ultrasound equipment, and an instructor (cardiac surgeon); prior e-learning module completion
constraints: Does not cover ECMO patient management or refractory cardiac arrest algorithms; conducted in a controlled, cost-effective setting
target_learning_goals: Technical skills for ultrasound-guided femoro-femoral VA-ECMO cannulation
examples: In the trial, 15 residents completed this workshop and were later evaluated on the same mannequin type used during training

article_title: Bridging the gap in pre-hospital maternity care: emergency personnel's knowledge and clinical skills in managing obstetric emergencies.
citation: Shahbazi Sighaldeh S, Norollahpour Z, Nekoolaltak M, Khosravi S, Saberian P, Rahimi Foroushani A, Shateranni F. (2026). Bridging the gap in pre-hospital maternity care: emergency personnel’s knowledge and clinical skills in managing obstetric emergencies. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09636-3
title: Three Delays Model of maternal mortality
description: The article invokes the "Three Delays Model" proposed by Thaddeus and Maine as an explanatory framework for maternal mortality. The model identifies "delays in seeking care, reaching a health facility, and receiving adequate treatment as major contributors to maternal mortality." Within this framework, pre-hospital emergency services play an important role in reducing delays in reaching appropriate care, positioning P-HEP proficiency as essential for positive maternal and neonatal outcomes.
requirements: An emergency care system capable of reducing delays in reaching appropriate care
target_learning_goals: Understanding the system-level factors contributing to maternal mortality
Reducing delays in reaching appropriate maternity care
examples: The article applies the model to frame the role of Tehran Emergency Center personnel in reducing the second delay (reaching a health facility)

article_title: Practice and application of blended teaching based on RG-UClass in a preventive medicine course.
citation: Liu Sha, Zhang Jiale, Shang Yuqi, Jiang Yufei, Zhang Xueyan, Hu Zhiyong, Chen Caiyun, Mi Wei. (2026). Practice and application of blended teaching based on RG-UClass in a preventive medicine course. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1885005
title: Three-stage blended teaching workflow: online independent learning plus offline flipped classroom
description: The RG-UClass model organizes teaching into three stages: pre-class online preview and testing, in-class combination of online lecturing and offline interactive discussion, and post-class online assignments, feedback, and discussion. The article describes this as an "online independent learning" plus "offline flipped classroom" model that eliminates time and space restrictions of traditional education to achieve complementary advantages, shifting students from passive to active learning and from shallow to deep knowledge acquisition.
requirements: A smart platform supporting pre-class material delivery, in-class interaction, and post-class assignment and feedback workflows
constraints: The integrated model makes it impossible to separate the independent effect of any single teaching format, resulting in confounding effects
target_learning_goals: active learning
deep learning strategies
knowledge application
examples: Theoretical knowledge-based chapters were taught online via the platform's live-streaming mode, while practical knowledge-based content (cohort studies, case-control studies, screening experiments) was taught offline face-to-face

article_title: The effect of video assisted instruction on central venous catheter application skills, anxiety and satisfaction in nursing students: a randomised controlled study.

BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09532-w
title: Three training videos for central venous catheter care (10 min total)
description: Three training videos were prepared for the experimental group, covering skills for taking blood from the central venous catheter, administering drugs, and providing care. The videos were organised to cover different stages of central venous catheter care and lasted 10 min in total. Each video contains detailed steps in the Central Venous Catheter Care Skills Assessment Form and shows how to perform each step correctly, allowing students to learn each step accurately and improve their practice.
requirements: Videos must be reviewed by experts to evaluate whether the steps in the assessment form were handled correctly.
Students should be encouraged to watch each video repeatedly to reinforce learning.
constraints: The frequency, duration, and completeness of students' engagement with the videos could not be objectively monitored, so the actual level of exposure to the intervention may have varied among participants.
target_learning_goals: psychomotor skills (blood collection, drug administration, dressing care)
examples: The videos were used as reference material during the students' applications in the experimental group in the laboratory environment and became an important support tool in the realization of these applications.

article_title: Building consensus on the core clinical competencies and outcomes related to effective child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS) crisis team provision: findings from a Delphi study.
citation: Clau N, Tindall L, Sayal K, Holland J, Hewitt CE, Tiffin PA. (2026). Building consensus on the core clinical competencies and outcomes related to effective child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS) crisis team provision: findings from a Delphi study. BMJ Mental Health. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjment-2026-302719
title: Theory of Change-based logic model linking crisis team competencies to desired outcomes
description: The article integrates consensus findings into a Theory of Change informed logic model that "postulated how the desirable knowledge and skills related to both intermediate outputs and activities, and, ultimately the most valued outcomes." Outcomes were further categorised into 'activities', 'outputs' (process outcomes) and 'outcomes' (impacts) in accordance with the Theory of Change framework. description: The article demonstrates that employing a think-aloud design to cognitively validate questionnaire items with the target population surfaces ambiguities in terminology, scale formats, and question phrasing before full deployment. Students worked through the QVP aloud, and their interpretations prompted systematic revision of questions across both themes. The authors conclude that "Continued refinement of questionnaires can support the development of evidence-based learning didactics in an increasingly digital healthcare educational environment."

description: The article organizes swimming instruction around three mainstream pedagogical models: the traditional instructional pedagogic model (TIPM), teacher-centered with demonstration-imitation and low interaction; the understanding pedagogical model (UPM), problem-oriented with moderate autonomy and group discussion; and the cooperative learning pedagogic model (CLPM), built on "group cooperation-task-driven-mutual evaluation and mutual assistance" with heterogeneous four-person groups, role division, and emotional sharing. The framework holds that "The core differences among the three teaching modes lie in the interactive structure, students' autonomy and the intensity of emotional support", which serves as the study's theoretical basis for comparing psychological benefits.

title: Standardized three-phase assessment and reporting of surgical learning curves (competency, proficiency, mastery)
description: The authors recommend assessing surgical learning curves using three outcome-anchored phases: competency based on operative time, proficiency based on major complications (Clavien-Dindo ≥IIIa), and mastery based on textbook outcome. Prospectively maintained institutional databases
Outcome definitions: operative time, CD grade ≥IIIa complications, textbook outcome

target_learning_goals: acquisition of competency, proficiency, and mastery in robotic distal pancreatectomy
examples: The study applied the three-phase model to 1109 RDPs across 16 expert centers, identifying cutoffs at 46, 63, and 73 procedures.

citation: Allan, H. T., and M. O'Driscoll. (2026). Using Recontextualisation Theory to Understand Learning Across Multiple Sites in Simulation‐Based Nurse Education. Journal of Advanced Nursing 82, no. 5: 5513–5520. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.70163
title: Theory-practice split: learning across sites appears disintegrated because teaching assumes theory is applied to practice
description: Allan and Evans (2022) reframe the theory-practice gap as a theory-practice split, "continuously reproduced in everyday practice both in academic and clinical nursing". The split arises because teaching remains predicated on applying theory in or to practice, whereas learners actually rework or recontextualise knowledge for practice across settings — not a linear one-way process. Nurses are lifelong, agentic learners who rework knowledge in and through local practice. Many students find recontextualisation difficult and there are few resources to support it.
requirements: Nurse teachers, managers and leaders need to educate nurses to be active learners and co-producers of knowledge for practice
constraints: The split is premised on the belief that thinking and doing are different activities, threatening the learning ecology in a disintegrated environment
target_learning_goals: reducing the theory-practice split
valuing practice-produced knowledge
examples: The article reports that nurses adapt to changes in health care practices as they learn, redefining roles and building local knowledge, thereby reducing the theory-practice split.

Anonymous QR-code sign-in provided "a safe space for the students without the ability to identify individual pairs". The same ARS collected the multiple-choice retention data during the lectures.

title: Three levels of simulator validation: face, content and construct validity
description: The review organizes simulator validation into "different levels of validation of increasing value and complexity": face validity describes the realism of a simulator, content validity describes the relevance of the simulator content for the real task, and construct validity describes the extent to which groups with more experience perform better than groups with less real-life experience and how far training-session results reflect the trainee's actual skill. The review applies this framework to neonatal echocardiography simulators, reporting that face and content validity have been tested via standardized questionnaires and construct validity by expertise-group comparisons.

title: Three-Coordination training model for residency education
description: The Three-Coordination model is the article's organizing framework for residency training, coordinating three relationships: training bases with medical school education, theoretical learning with clinical practice, and technological empowerment with professional development. Its core component "established bidirectional mapping between theoretical knowledge and clinical application through a progressively challenging three-stage 'theory-virtual-practice' learning pathway." AI technologies (adaptive learning algorithms, NLP case generation, computer vision skill assessment, decision support) were embedded in the third coordination. title: Three-module simulation curriculum (HFS, SP, VR) in a respiratory medicine rotation
description: A three-module simulation sequence delivered during a one-week respiratory rotation for fifth-year medical students: HFS using Laerdal's SimMan for an acute respiratory distress scenario in groups of 2–3, SP-based one-on-one interviews with a standardized tuberculosis patient, and VR using Sim-X and Oculus Quest 2 for a sepsis scenario. The article states "The VR-based simulation utilized Sim-X and Oculus Quest 2," and each session was followed by a 30-minute group debriefing with instructor feedback.

A 30-minute group debriefing including instructor feedback after each simulation session.

Focused history-taking, physical examination, and patient-centered communication
Clinical decision-making and step-by-step clinical reasoning

citation: Guinat Marie, Vincent Jean-Louis. (2026). Better teaching in the intensive care unit: navigating a complex, multi-disciplinary learning environment. Critical Care. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13054-026-05845-w
title: Three learning zones model: comfort, learning/stretch, and panic zones bound optimal challenge
description: The article describes learning as occurring across three zones (Fig. 3): "comfort, a familiar, low-stress environment where learners engage in routine tasks with minimal effort and little learning or growth actually takes place"; a learning or stretch zone "where learning is challenging but manageable"; and a panic zone "where cognitive overload and overwhelming stress impair learning". Teachers should move learners beyond comfort without pushing them into panic, grounding cognitive-load management in ICU teaching.
requirements: Teachers must gauge task complexity against the learner's prior background and gradually expose learners to tasks consistent with their training level
constraints: The article states the boundaries between zones vary among individual learners and may differ within the same learner for different learning experiences
target_learners: ICU learners of all professions and training levels
target_learning_goals: Managing cognitive load so learning remains challenging but manageable
examples: Teaching leadership while managing an unstable polytrauma patient may suit expert learners, while for junior students this is better taught when managing a stable patient

citation: Si J. (2025). Eight practical strategies for designing case-based flipped learning to foster clinical reasoning in preclinical medical students. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586874
title: Structure case-based flipped learning across pre-class, in-class, and post-class phases with phase-specific activities
description: The article prescribes a lesson-level structure spanning three phases. Pre-class materials should be concise and focused (e.g. short online videos preferably under 10–15 min or targeted reading packages) explicitly connected to the cases, with comprehension-based quizzes at the start of class to ensure preparedness and identify misconceptions. In-class time is used for group case-based clinical reasoning with rubric-based assessment and formative checks. Post-class structured reflection, such as reflective journaling, consolidates learning, articulates diagnostic rationale, and fosters metacognitive awareness supporting transfer.
requirements: Pre-class materials must be cognitively manageable and linked to the in-class cases; in-class work needs rubric-based assessment and timely feedback; post-class reflection prompts must elicit key takeaways, unresolved questions, and reasoning behind initial hypotheses
constraints: Post-class structured reflection is described as essential yet often overlooked in medical education
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning development
Metacognitive awareness and transfer to future clinical contexts
examples: The article's appendices provide a reflective journal prompt and rubrics for clinical reasoning processes and reflective journal writing
