article_title: "From simulation to surgery: exploring variables influencing the translational impact of simulation-based education in neurosurgical competence".
citation: Roche Adam F., Kavanagh Dara O., Crimmins Darach, McGuire Barry B., O'Brien Donncha, Perin Alessandro, Houlihan Lena-Mary, Mohammad Wail, Ashpole Richard, Villanueva Pablo Javier, Kehoe Laura, Condron Claire M. (2025). From simulation to surgery: exploring variables influencing the translational impact of simulation-based education in neurosurgical competence. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07814-3
title: Three-step pathway for skill transfer from simulation to the operating room: cognitive load optimisation, fidelity calibration, predictive validity
description: The article proposes a "three-step pathway underpinning effective skill transfer" from simulation to the operating room: "cognitive load optimisation", then "fidelity calibration", then "predictive validity". Early in training, coached repetitive well-scaffolded tasks reduce intrinsic cognitive load; later, greater psychological and task fidelity maintains engagement and fosters germane load, underpinning confidence that simulation performance predicts operative competence.
requirements: Early-training simulation must be delivered as coached, repetitive, well-scaffolded tasks that reduce intrinsic cognitive load.
Fidelity must be calibrated to learner stage, with greater psychological and task fidelity for advanced residents.
constraints: The authors state the findings are context-specific, though several elements of the model may have wider applicability.
The article notes further research is needed to clarify SEE's specific impact on clinical performance, particularly in later stages of training.
target_learning_goals: skill transfer from simulation to operative practice
procedural fluency and technical competence
examples: The article reports that when fidelity was well matched to resident level, both residents and experts expressed greater confidence that simulation performance would translate to operative competence
key_sources: Roche Adam F., Kavanagh Dara O., Crimmins Darach, McGuire Barry B., O'Brien Donncha, Perin Alessandro, Houlihan Lena-Mary, Mohammad Wail, Ashpole Richard, Villanueva Pablo Javier, Kehoe Laura, Condron Claire M. (2025). From simulation to surgery: exploring variables influencing the translational impact of simulation-based education in neurosurgical competence. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07814-3

article_title: Effectiveness of the educational-operational intervention of the crisis management in earthquake simulation conditions in prehospital emergency personnel: a randomized controlled trial study.
citation: Farahmandnia Iman, Karimiankakolaki Zohreh. (2025). Effectiveness of the educational-operational intervention of the crisis management in earthquake simulation conditions in prehospital emergency personnel: a randomized controlled trial study. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-025-13376-3
title: Combined theory-plus-simulation maneuver pattern for crisis management training
description: A course-level design that pairs theoretical sessions with staged practical maneuvers of increasing complexity. The intervention type is described as "Combined intervention (educational-operational)" including "Theoretical training (training workshop based on the crisis management model)" and "Practical simulation (realistic earthquake scenarios with mannequins and actors)," followed by "Team exercise (coordination between personnel in crisis situations)." The simulation stages had "increasing complexity."
requirements: Realistic earthquake scenarios with mannequins and trained actors
Standard educational films and video debriefing
constraints: The authors note a "simulation-reality gap inherent in training exercises"
target_learning_goals: Decision-making under pressure, team coordination, and management of limited resources in disaster response
examples: The earthquake exercise distributed 5 mannequins (2 critical with active bleeding, 3 respiratory injuries) and 10 actors (3 fractures, 5 psychological injuries, 2 anxious companions)
key_sources: Farahmandnia Iman, Karimiankakolaki Zohreh. (2025). Effectiveness of the educational-operational intervention of the crisis management in earthquake simulation conditions in prehospital emergency personnel: a randomized controlled trial study. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-025-13376-3

article_title: Performance on classroom simulations enhances preservice teachers' motivation in teaching: A latent change perspective.
citation: Wang, H., Thompson‐Lee, S., & Klassen, R. M. (2025). Performance on classroom simulations enhances preservice teachers' motivation in teaching: A latent change perspective. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95(Suppl. 1), S239–S255. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12761
title: Three‐session online classroom simulation intervention with expert‐developed scenarios and tailored feedback
description: The intervention is an online classroom simulation programme consisting of "three 1‐h online sessions delivered over a 3‐week period of one semester", each with five video/text scenarios (15 total) depicting authentic teaching situations such as working with parents and managing disruptive students. Scenarios were built via a critical incidents approach from over 20 interviews with experienced teachers, animated and vetted by expert panels, and scored against a concordance panel's consensus key. Participants rated response options on a 4‐point appropriateness scale, received a match report and automatically tailored feedback after each session.
requirements: A scoring key established by a concordance panel of 20 experienced teachers, with disagreements resolved by discussion or dropping contested scenarios
Automatically generated feedback messages developed through year‐long workshops with experienced teachers and teacher educators
constraints: Content across the three sessions consists of 15 different scenarios reflecting general classroom challenges relevant to all teaching levels rather than level‐specific tasks
Administered as a programme 'hurdle' requirement, so no control group was available in the same setting
target_learners: Preservice teachers in a 4‐year undergraduate teacher education programme in Australia
target_learning_goals: Preparation for school placements; classroom decision‐making; teaching self‐efficacy, career intentions and person–vocation fit
examples: Participants completed three sessions with 1‐week intervals, each with five simulated classroom experiences lasting around 30–60 min, with four survey responses collected (one pre‐test, three post‐tests)
key_sources: Wang, H., Thompson‐Lee, S., & Klassen, R. M. (2025). Performance on classroom simulations enhances preservice teachers' motivation in teaching: A latent change perspective. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95(Suppl. 1), S239–S255. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12761

article_title: Students Don't Learn the Way They Think They Do in a Large, Active-Learning Genetics Course.
citation: Walck-Shannon, E. M., Barton, H. D., Rowell, S. F., Chalker, D. L., & Fink, A. (2025). Students Don't Learn the Way They Think They Do in a Large, Active-Learning Genetics Course. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.24-10-0251
title: Three cognitive-psychology-based problem-solving pedagogies for biology: prediction, faded worked examples, and tell-then-practice case studies
description: The article organizes problem-solving instruction into three pedagogies with distinct timing and theoretical grounding. Prediction activities use guided inquiry, including contrasting cases, before instruction, drawing on constructivism and desirable difficulties. Faded worked examples provide step-by-step expert solutions with progressively removed support after instruction, grounded in cognitive load theory. Tell-then-practice case studies apply recently learned concepts to real-world scenarios, grounded in constructivism and motivation through case framing.
requirements: Activities must be embedded in a course structure giving students repeated practice and feedback, as in the authors' flipped, high-structure design
constraints: The authors caution that worked examples are less potent as students gain expertise and are suited to near transfer rather than entirely novel problems
Occasionally the schedule required direct instruction of concepts prior to prediction exercises, deviating from the ideal sequence
target_learners: second-year undergraduate biology majors and pre-health students in a large-enrollment introductory course
target_learning_goals: disciplinary problem solving in genetics
conceptual understanding of genetics principles
examples: Genetic linkage contrasting cases with genes adjacent, nearby, or on separate chromosomes
A sparrow chromosomal inversion case study in which students classified inversions as paracentric or pericentric
A three-point testcross genetic mapping sequence moving from fully worked to faded to independent problems
key_sources: Walck-Shannon, E. M., Barton, H. D., Rowell, S. F., Chalker, D. L., & Fink, A. (2025). Students Don't Learn the Way They Think They Do in a Large, Active-Learning Genetics Course. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.24-10-0251

article_title: Training program on motivational interviewing for prison professionals.
citation: Martín-Coca A, Martín Herrero JA. (2025). Training program on motivational interviewing for prison professionals. Revista Española de Sanidad Penitenciaria. https://doi.org/10.18176/resp.00108
title: Three-phase motivational interviewing training program for prison professionals
description: A 25-hour training program delivered at Topas Prison in three consecutive phases, each combining face-to-face sessions with self-training activities. Phase 1 covers "Theoretical basics of MI*, intrinsic motivation and resolving ambivalence" (8 hours), Phase 2 covers advanced technical competencies and simulation of complex cases (8 hours), and Phase 3 covers constructive feedback, self-assessment and practical application (9 hours), with an evaluation moment after each phase.
requirements: Face-to-face sessions combined with self-training activities in each phase
Practical exercises reflecting day-to-day prison work situations
constraints: Delivered in a real prison setting where no random control group could be formed due to operational and logistical restrictions
target_learners: prison professionals in specialised inmate healthcare modules (psychologists, lawyers, educators, social workers, security personnel)
target_learning_goals: competency and adherence to motivational interviewing principles
reduction of practices incompatible with MI
examples: Each phase included specific activities to identify and correct incompatible practices as part of a continuous improvement process
key_sources: Martín-Coca A, Martín Herrero JA. (2025). Training program on motivational interviewing for prison professionals. Revista Española de Sanidad Penitenciaria. https://doi.org/10.18176/resp.00108

article_title: The effects of communication training on communication competence - a 360° evaluation.
citation: Zöll Lisa, Deschner James, Hollinderbäumer Anke, Nowak Thomas, Zajontz Tamara, Behling Lina, Fischbeck Sabine, Schmidt Uwe, Pfeiffer-Grötz Thekla J. (2025). The effects of communication training on communication competence – a 360° evaluation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07676-9
title: A three-level stage model of communication-skill complexity derived from the study's results
description: The article derives a stage model that classifies communicative learning objectives by complexity into three competence levels. The lowest level contains "simple instructions for action" that "can be learned without training"; the middle level contains skills that "can be improved through targeted training"; the highest level contains skills that "can only be learned through training", requiring "a deeper understanding, guided exercises and feedback". Relationship building and patients describing their own concerns are placed at the highest level, while involving patients in decisions and summarizing information are at the lowest.
requirements: The model was derived solely from the results of this study; the article states further research is needed to generalize the findings on complexity levels.
constraints: The stage model is based exclusively on available results in this single study and has not been generalized.
target_learning_goals: Dentist-patient communication skills, including conversation structure, nonverbal communication and relationship building
examples: Questions 1.2 and 1.5 (involving patients in decisions, summarizing information) were placed at the lowest level; questions 1.1 and 1.10 (relationship building, patients describing concerns) at the highest level, being significant only in the intervention group.
key_sources: Zöll Lisa, Deschner James, Hollinderbäumer Anke, Nowak Thomas, Zajontz Tamara, Behling Lina, Fischbeck Sabine, Schmidt Uwe, Pfeiffer-Grötz Thekla J. (2025). The effects of communication training on communication competence – a 360° evaluation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07676-9

article_title: How nurses' moral competence can be supported: Findings from international focus groups with professionals.
citation: Wiisak, J., Suhonen, R., Galazzi, A., Gastmans, C., Keogh, B., Papastavrou, E. et al. (2025). How nurses' moral competence can be supported: Findings from international focus groups with professionals. International Nursing Review, 72. https://doi.org/10.1111/inr.13080
title: Three-level framework for supporting nurses' moral competence: individual-relational, organisational and societal
description: The article organises support for nurses' moral competence into three nested levels: the individual nurse working in a relational context with colleagues, the organisation, and society. The results state that "support for nurses' moral competence can be located at individual‐relational, organisational, and societal levels", with three themes at the individual-relational level, two at the organisational level and two at the societal level. The framework is used to structure the study's findings and to argue that support must be integrated across levels rather than confined to one.
requirements: Support requires contribution from colleagues, leaders, organisations and society simultaneously, as the levels work integrated with each other.
constraints: Derived from focus group perceptions of 38 informants in six European countries in 2023; the article presents it as perceived support needs, not tested interventions.
target_learning_goals: moral competence
ethical decision-making
ethical reflection
examples: The study sorted seven themes into three individual-relational themes, two organisational themes and two societal themes (Table 2).
key_sources: Wiisak, J., Suhonen, R., Galazzi, A., Gastmans, C., Keogh, B., Papastavrou, E. et al. (2025). How nurses' moral competence can be supported: Findings from international focus groups with professionals. International Nursing Review, 72. https://doi.org/10.1111/inr.13080

article_title: Interdisciplinary medical education practices: building a case-driven interdisciplinary simulation system based on public datasets.
citation: Qiu Kangli, Zeng Tianshu, Xia Wenfang, Peng Miaomiao, Kong Wen. (2025). Interdisciplinary medical education practices: building a case-driven interdisciplinary simulation system based on public datasets. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07631-8
title: Three-stage dataset analysis workflow: differential/enrichment, survival, then machine-learning modeling
description: The system organizes practice into three sequential stages. As the article states, 'Stage I involves differential and enrichment analyses using the GEO datasets. Stage II conducts survival analysis utilizing the TCGA datasets. Stage III entails constructing and analyzing machine learning models for the diseases identified in the previous two stages.' Each stage is broken into numbered process steps with dynamically adjustable parameters (P-value, LogFC, enrichment thresholds), letting students compare algorithms such as DESeq2, edgeR, and limma.
requirements: Datasets with grouping information, survival status data, and clinical biochemical indicators; R and Python toolkits
constraints: General screening criterion for differentially expressed genes is an absolute log2FC greater than 1
target_learning_goals: standard process of disease-based data analysis from model algorithms to result presentation
examples: In the gout case, GSE160170 was analyzed with DESeq2, edgeR, and limma, and results were intersected so students could observe the effects of different methods
key_sources: Qiu Kangli, Zeng Tianshu, Xia Wenfang, Peng Miaomiao, Kong Wen. (2025). Interdisciplinary medical education practices: building a case-driven interdisciplinary simulation system based on public datasets. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07631-8

article_title: Designing a cultivation model for top-notch students in basic medicine: a Delphi method.
citation: Geng N, Qin Y, Wang F, Huang J. (2025). Designing a cultivation model for top-notch students in basic medicine: a Delphi method. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07347-9
title: Three-tier indicator structure (5 primary, 17 secondary, 63 tertiary indicators)
description: The structural backbone of the finalized cultivation model: a hierarchical indicator system with 5 primary, 17 secondary and 63 tertiary indicators. The article states: "A three-tier indicator structure was created to ensure vertical integration across different stages of the training process, optimizing the operational flow of top-notch student cultivation and maximizing quality." Each layer maps onto a distinct function — strategic direction, operational execution, and quality oversight — and indicators carry printed expert scores (means, SDs, full score frequencies, CVs) from the third Delphi round in Table 2.
requirements: Indicators must meet consensus thresholds (mean above 4, full score frequency over 50%, variation coefficient below 0.25) to be retained
constraints: The article notes the framework has been piloted in a limited number of universities and requires continuous updates to remain relevant to rapidly evolving fields
target_learning_goals: systematic program design and quality assurance for elite talent cultivation
examples: Table 2 prints third-round scores for every tertiary indicator, e.g. Comprehensive and Frontier Knowledge in Basic Medicine (mean 5.00, SD 0.00, full score frequency 1.00, CV 0.00)
key_sources: Geng N, Qin Y, Wang F, Huang J. (2025). Designing a cultivation model for top-notch students in basic medicine: a Delphi method. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07347-9

article_title: Development and effects of a chatbot education program for self-directed learning in nursing students.
citation: Han Jeong-won, Park Junhee, Lee Hanna. (2025). Development and effects of a chatbot education program for self-directed learning in nursing students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07316-2
title: Three-phase chatbot self-directed learning structure ending in case-based alarm scenarios
description: The chatbot program is organized into three phases: the first two deliver SDL content for knowledge acquisition through natural conversation, greetings, emoticons, support messages, photos, and videos, while "the third stage, structured as case-based learning, students can explore and learn about nursing care for situations in which alarms occur during mechanical ventilation." Three scenarios cover high-pressure, low-pressure, and high respiration alarm cases, with feedback regardless of response correctness.
requirements: Content structured from a prior literature analysis identifying mechanical ventilation learning content; preliminary survey with an ICU nurse and a nursing student informed interface adjustments
constraints: Scenarios are limited to the three alarm case types the authors built (high-pressure, low-pressure, high respiration)
target_learning_goals: mechanical ventilation nursing knowledge and alarm response decision-making
self-directed learning
examples: Students examine values and alarms displayed on the mechanical ventilation screen, click to identify the reasons behind the values, and confirm whether their answers are correct, receiving feedback either way
key_sources: Han Jeong-won, Park Junhee, Lee Hanna. (2025). Development and effects of a chatbot education program for self-directed learning in nursing students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07316-2

article_title: Simulation and comparison of objectively graded microsurgery steps by using a microscope and Symani robotic system by young professionals.
citation: Wieker H, Brandenburg N, Spille D, Wagner J, Weitkamp J-T, Wiltfang J, Spille J. (2025). Simulation and comparison of objectively graded microsurgery steps by using a microscope and Symani robotic system by young professionals. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-025-02490-3
title: Three-exercise microsurgery simulation protocol (needle grasp/place, needle threading, single-button anastomosis suture)
description: A simulation training setup comparing a dental surgical operating microscope with 8 × magnification against the Symani robotic system, in which students "looked at a screen with 3D glasses and controlled the 3 mm instruments using two joysticks and a foot pedal." It comprises three graded exercises simulating partial microsurgery steps: grasping and placing a 9.0 needle, threading the needle, and performing a single-button suture of an approximately 2 mm anastomosis in flexible, tear-prone rubber-like vessels. Operation time was the measured outcome, used to evaluate novice surgical skill.
requirements: A dental surgical operating microscope with microneedle holders and the Symani system with NanoWrist Needle Holder Suture Cut and Dilator microinstruments
Individual instructions and a brief familiarization period for participants before timed exercises
constraints: The article states the operation simulation cannot be accurately compared to real life, being carried out under optimal conditions with no blood, no patient movement, reduced noise, and little pressure
Failure criteria were not defined and time was unlimited
target_learners: medical students and young professionals with no prior surgical experience
target_learning_goals: basic microsurgical instrument handling
needle grasping and placement
suturing and knot-tying for anastomosis
examples: 40 students each performed all three exercises with both systems, with 20 randomized to start with the microscope and 20 with the Symani
key_sources: Wieker H, Brandenburg N, Spille D, Wagner J, Weitkamp J-T, Wiltfang J, Spille J. (2025). Simulation and comparison of objectively graded microsurgery steps by using a microscope and Symani robotic system by young professionals. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-025-02490-3

article_title: Cardiac Arrest: An Adult eCPR Simulation Case.
citation: Gelmann D, Giordano J, Gaillard J, Bryant C. (2025). Cardiac Arrest: An Adult eCPR Simulation Case. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11521
title: Three-team role structure for multidisciplinary eCPR simulation (airway, medical resuscitation, cannulation)
description: The simulation organizes participants into "three primary teams, each with specific personnel assigned to distinct roles to ensure a coordinated and effective resuscitation and cannulation process": an airway team (leader and assistant), a medical resuscitation team (medication nurse, recorder, two chest compressors, resuscitation leader), and a cannulation team (preparation assistant, cannulator, wire assistants). Roles are assigned by training background, with cannulator and wire assistant roles reserved for those who perform them clinically. Minimum staffing of three resuscitation and two cannulation participants is specified for limited enrollment.
requirements: At least three participants for medical resuscitation and two for cannulation when enrollment is limited; role assignment based on training background
constraints: Cannulator and wire assistant roles were performed by participants who assume these roles in real clinical scenarios (fellows and attendings)
target_learners: Multidisciplinary resuscitation teams including physicians, nurses, pharmacists, respiratory therapists, and advanced practice providers
target_learning_goals: Demonstrate quality team dynamics, including specifying roles and utilizing close-looped communication
examples: Participants rotated through all other roles in the scenario except cannulator and wire assistant
key_sources: Gelmann D, Giordano J, Gaillard J, Bryant C. (2025). Cardiac Arrest: An Adult eCPR Simulation Case. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11521

article_title: Effectiveness of blended learning to improve medical students' communication skills: a randomized, controlled trial.
citation: Gross Sebastian, Wunderlich Kurt, Arpagaus Armon, Becker Christoph, Gössi Flavio, Bissmann Benjamin, Zumbrunn Samuel K., Wilde Michael, Hunziker Sabina. (2025). Effectiveness of blended learning to improve medical students’ communication skills: a randomized, controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06938-w
title: Three-step online module pattern: animated theory videos, interactive video practice, gamified assessment
description: The online module addressed each of its five communication domains through a repeated three-step structure: the article states "Each domain was addressed though a three-step process" — theory acquisition via animated cartoon-style explanatory videos created with Canva, practice through video-based training with interactive videoclips of acted-out doctor-patient conversations whose course could be influenced by mouse click, and a gamified knowledge assessment with a multiple-choice quiz, a video annotation exercise, and a real-time leaderboard intended to foster motivation and friendly competition.
requirements: Animated explanatory videos, interactive videoclips, and gamified tasks delivered via the OpenOlat platform
A completion gating feature to ensure students fully watch the videos
constraints: Instructions to the video annotation task were reported by students as somewhat unclear, which the authors state might bias quantitative results
target_learning_goals: Understanding and application of patient-centered communication techniques (WEMS, NURSE) and communication structure
examples: In the trial, intervention students completed this three-step module for all five domains in about 90 minutes, then took the same knowledge assessment as controls
key_sources: Gross Sebastian, Wunderlich Kurt, Arpagaus Armon, Becker Christoph, Gössi Flavio, Bissmann Benjamin, Zumbrunn Samuel K., Wilde Michael, Hunziker Sabina. (2025). Effectiveness of blended learning to improve medical students’ communication skills: a randomized, controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06938-w

article_title: The impact of grade point average on medical students' perception of the learning environment: a multicenter cross-sectional study across 12 Chinese medical schools.
citation: Liu Yifan, Lyu Donghao, Xie Sujie, Yao Yuntao, Liu Jun, Lu Bingnan, Zhang Wei, Xian Shuyuan, Yan Jiale, Gong Meiqiong, Wu Xinru, Li Yuanan, Zhang Haoyu, Zhou Jiajie, Zhou Yibin, Lin Min, Yin Huabin, Wang Xiaonan, Wang Yue, Chen Wenfang, Zhang Chongyou, Du Erbin, Lin Qing, Huang Zongqiang, Xu Dayuan, Zhang Jie, Huang Runzhi, Ji Shizhao, Pan Xiuwu. (2025). The impact of grade point average on medical students' perception of the learning environment: a multicenter cross-sectional study across 12 Chinese medical schools. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06977-3
title: Three-category mechanism framework linking GPA rankings and MSLE perception
description: The article organises the factors connecting GPA rankings and students' perceptions of the MSLE into three categories: factors that influence both GPA ranking and MSLE perception (emotional stability, learning attitude and motivation, sleep quality, mental health); factors shaped by GPA ranking that in turn affect perception (academic pressure, peer interactions, self-efficacy); and learning-environment factors that affect GPA ranking (quality of teaching and mentorship, learning resources and facilities, curriculum structure and organization). The authors summarise these in a mechanism diagram (Fig. 6), stating they "illustrated the factors associated with higher GPA rankings that contributed to students' positive perceptions of the MSLE". It is an interpretive framework, not a tested model.
requirements: Interpretation rests on the cross-sectional correlational findings plus cited literature; it is not independently tested in the article.
constraints: The article states the cross-sectional design "only indicates correlation rather than causation", so the framework's directional arrows are hypotheses.
target_learners: Medical students in undergraduate medical education
target_learning_goals: Understanding and improving the medical school learning environment
Supporting students' academic performance and wellbeing
examples: The discussion enumerates emotional stability, learning attitudes and motivation, sleep quality, and mental health as factors influencing both GPA ranking and MSLE perception.
key_sources: Liu Yifan, Lyu Donghao, Xie Sujie, Yao Yuntao, Liu Jun, Lu Bingnan, Zhang Wei, Xian Shuyuan, Yan Jiale, Gong Meiqiong, Wu Xinru, Li Yuanan, Zhang Haoyu, Zhou Jiajie, Zhou Yibin, Lin Min, Yin Huabin, Wang Xiaonan, Wang Yue, Chen Wenfang, Zhang Chongyou, Du Erbin, Lin Qing, Huang Zongqiang, Xu Dayuan, Zhang Jie, Huang Runzhi, Ji Shizhao, Pan Xiuwu. (2025). The impact of grade point average on medical students' perception of the learning environment: a multicenter cross-sectional study across 12 Chinese medical schools. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06977-3

article_title: From novice to proficient: a longitudinal study of POCUS skill development through a hybrid certification program in the United Arab Emirates.
citation: Buhumaid R, Kilian P, Zidan MA, Salman H, AlSharhan R, Khansaheb H, Zary N. (2025). From novice to proficient: a longitudinal study of POCUS skill development through a hybrid certification program in the United Arab Emirates. BMC Med Educ. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07138-2
title: Ground hybrid clinical-skill program design in complementary educational theories (andragogy, constructive alignment, experiential learning)
description: The article grounds program design in three complementary educational theories: "Adult Learning Theory (Andragogy)", Constructive Alignment Theory, and Experiential Learning Theory. Adult Learning Theory informs flexible, practice-oriented scheduling; Constructive Alignment links learning outcomes, activities, and assessments; Experiential Learning shapes the cycle of practice, reflection, and refinement. The authors state the program's success supports the value of incorporating established educational theories into POCUS training design.
requirements: Assessment strategy directly linked to defined learning outcomes per application
Hands-on components with formative assessment and feedback
constraints: Recommendation is based on a single-cohort pilot program without a control group, so attribution to the theory-based design is limited
target_learners: Practicing physicians in postgraduate medical education
target_learning_goals: Procedural and diagnostic clinical skills such as point-of-care ultrasound
examples: The ADDIE instructional design model structured development, and Kirkpatrick's Training Evaluation Model guided program evaluation.
key_sources: Buhumaid R, Kilian P, Zidan MA, Salman H, AlSharhan R, Khansaheb H, Zary N. (2025). From novice to proficient: a longitudinal study of POCUS skill development through a hybrid certification program in the United Arab Emirates. BMC Med Educ. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07138-2

article_title: Case-Based Virtual Reality Simulation for Severe Pelvic Trauma Clinical Skill Training in Medical Students: Design and Pilot Study.
citation: Mogali Sreenivasulu Reddy, Yan Qi, Jiang Nan, Teng Peng, Xu Youran, Qian Kaoliang, Lu Ming, Hu Jun. (2025). Case-Based Virtual Reality Simulation for Severe Pelvic Trauma Clinical Skill Training in Medical Students: Design and Pilot Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/59850
title: Graded-severity case set: three pelvic trauma cases spanning mild fracture to severe hemorrhagic shock, each requiring different diagnostic and treatment strategies
description: The curriculum's core instructional pattern is a set of three initial cases ordered by trauma severity: "We developed 3 initial cases, each representing a different stage of trauma and treatment approach (Table 1)." Case 1 is a pelvic fracture treated with surgery; Case 2 adds mild hemorrhagic shock treated with antihemorrhagic shock therapy plus surgery; Case 3 adds severe hemorrhagic shock requiring CT of pelvis and abdomen. Learning paths follow a flowchart of correct and wrong diagnostic-treatment routes based on clinical treatment guidelines, serving as a framework for evaluating student performance.
requirements: Cases designed by basic and clinical medicine specialists drawing on a literature review, real patient cases, and the course syllabus, with learning paths based on clinical treatment guidelines
constraints: Cases were developed for severe pelvic trauma in orthopedic surgery education; the article does not claim generalizability beyond this domain
target_learning_goals: Progressive mastery of severe pelvic trauma diagnosis and treatment across increasing case severity
examples: The representative case involved a worker who fell from a high platform, sequentially evaluated in the emergency department, admitted to the intensive care unit, and taken to the operating room as his condition worsened
key_sources: Mogali Sreenivasulu Reddy, Yan Qi, Jiang Nan, Teng Peng, Xu Youran, Qian Kaoliang, Lu Ming, Hu Jun. (2025). Case-Based Virtual Reality Simulation for Severe Pelvic Trauma Clinical Skill Training in Medical Students: Design and Pilot Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/59850

article_title: Impact of a 3-year transformational change project in family violence clinical response: Qualitative evaluation of the depth and breadth of knowledge in hospital clinicians by training level.
citation: Troy K, Rushan C, Withiel TD, Felmingham KL, Fisher CA. (2025). Impact of a 3-year transformational change project in family violence clinical response: Qualitative evaluation of the depth and breadth of knowledge in hospital clinicians by training level. Women's Health, 21. https://doi.org/10.1177/17455057241305264
title: Thematic taxonomy of hospital clinicians' demonstrated family violence response knowledge across indicator, enquiry and disclosure domains
description: An inductive thematic taxonomy of hospital clinicians' demonstrated family violence knowledge, organised by the three survey text-box questions. For indicators, 'three main themes emerged from the clinician responses: Patient behaviours, Contextual factors and Lived experience of family violence'; asking about family violence yielded Laying the framework, Asking and Patient outcomes; and disclosure responses yielded Sensitive inquiry, Procedural response and Active response with patient.
requirements: Free-text survey responses that prompt clinicians to demonstrate their knowledge following a Yes or Somewhat forced-choice answer
constraints: Themes were derived inductively from one hospital's 2020 survey responses; the authors state meaning was interpreted from the data rather than excavated from it, so no data-saturation judgement was applied by design
target_learners: Hospital clinical staff (medical, nursing and allied health)
target_learning_goals: Knowledge of family violence indicators, sensitive enquiry skills and disclosure response practices
examples: The taxonomy underpinned comparisons across training levels, with the Red flags sub-theme for high-risk situations most evident in champion responses

Impact of a 3-year transformational change project in family violence clinical response: Qualitative evaluation of the depth and breadth of knowledge in hospital clinicians by training level. article_title: Consistency between inter-institutional panels using a three-level Angoff-standard setting in licensure tests of foreign-trained dentists in Sweden: A cohort study.
citation: Dalum Jesper, Paulsson Liselotte, Christidis Nikolaos, Andersson Franko Mikael, Karlgren Klas, Leanderson Charlotte, Sandborgh-Englund Gunilla. (2024). Consistency between inter-institutional panels using a three-level Angoff-standard setting in licensure tests of foreign-trained dentists in Sweden: A cohort study. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0313476
title: Simplified three-level Angoff standard-setting method (YES/NO/MAYBE with weights 1/0/.3, no consensus meetings)
description: A simplified modification of the Angoff standard-setting method in which panellists individually rate each test item 'YES', 'NO' or 'MAYBE' as to whether the minimally qualified but still acceptable candidate would answer correctly, weighted 1, 0 and .3 respectively, with total scores summed from weighted responses. In the Swedish re-certification examinations, "Training and consensus have been redacted, which serves to balance a manageable workload." The study used 10–12 panellists per test, within the recommended range of five to fifteen.
requirements: A panel of subject matter experts (here clinical teachers, 10–12 per test) rating each item individually
A blueprint of professional qualifications and disciplines from which test items are created
constraints: Skipping consensus meetings limits opportunities for in-depth discussions on item relevance and difficulty and may reduce support for new panellists
Concerns exist about reduced variability with only three rating levels; the original 1–100 Angoff may yield a more reliable outcome
target_learners: foreign-trained dentists undergoing re-certification licensure in Sweden
target_learning_goals: setting defensible pass marks for competency-based theoretical licensure examinations
examples: The reference panel rated three examinations (85–91 questions each) consecutively during 2019–2020; the external panel of ten novice Angoff raters rated the same items afterwards with written instructions only

article_title: Application of spaghetti knotting technology in single-hole laparoscopic suturing instructional program on the basis of multi-directional stitching technology: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Chen Ziqi, Zhu Sennan, Tao Jiayu, Chen Qiuyu, Du Wenzhuo, Sun Jindan, Yu Mengqi, Zhou Yi, Zhao Yu, Zhang Qiong. (2024). Application of spaghetti knotting technology in single-hole laparoscopic suturing instructional program on the basis of multi-directional stitching technology: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06266-5
title: Three-stage laparoscopic knotting training program: introduction with video demonstration, guided basic skill training, then independent consolidation practice
description: The teaching plan "consisted of three stages, with the first stage lasting one week, and the rest two stages lasting two weeks", with two 40-minute classes per week. Stage one introduces the surgery, suturing technology and the assigned knotting method with video demonstrations and ends with a pre-training assessment and NASA-TLX; stage two is instructor-guided basic skill training; stage three is "consolidation skill training mainly focusing on independent practice" ending in post-training assessment. Both groups shared one instructor and room at different times.
requirements: An experienced instructor, identical practice time across participants, and a simulator with a standardized suturing module
constraints: Studied with novice residents without prior laparoscopic surgery experience, to eliminate differences in past training volumes
target_learners: junior residents learning basic laparoscopic skills
target_learning_goals: laparoscopic suturing and knotting proficiency
examples: Both groups were taught by the same experienced instructor at different times in the same laparoscopic room, and all 40 participants completed the plan

article_title: Level of knowledge of nurses and healthcare technicians regarding soft skills: An exploratory study.
citation: Elkhalladi Jaouad, Sefrioui Amal, Fahssi Mohamed El, Tahiri Maroine. (2024). Level of knowledge of nurses and healthcare technicians regarding soft skills: An exploratory study. Revista da Escola de Enfermagem da USP. https://doi.org/10.1590/1980-220X-REEUSP-2024-0124en
title: Three-part closed-question questionnaire for assessing soft skills knowledge and priorities among nurses and healthcare technicians
description: The study's data collection tool is a questionnaire chosen for "a sufficiently distanced epistemological perspective and ensuring anonymous responses". It comprises three main parts — socio-demographic characteristics, knowledge of SS, and identification of the most important SS — with closed questions and opportunities for comments. It operationalises SS with a non-exhaustive list of 37 soft skills used in nursing and health techniques, and was preliminarily tested with six participants before 11 incomplete questionnaires were eliminated, leaving 350 for analysis.
requirements: Anonymous responses, closed questions with opportunities for comments, and preliminary testing with six participants before deployment.
constraints: The instrument was administered only to nurses and health technicians practising in the public sector of the Souss-Massa region.
target_learners: Nurses and health technicians (paramedical staff such as laboratory and radiology technicians)
target_learning_goals: Assessing practitioners' knowledge of soft skills and identifying the soft skills they consider most important for training
examples: Preliminary testing involved six participants, and 11 incomplete questionnaires were eliminated, leaving 350 for analysis.

article_title: Effectiveness of the application of small private online course combined with PBL model based on massive open online course in the teaching of neurology.
citation: Li Xiaoling, Li Fanju, Liu Wei, Xie Qinfang, Yuan Boyao, Wang Lijuan, Wang Manxia. (2024). Effectiveness of the application of small private online course combined with PBL model based on massive open online course in the teaching of neurology. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06460-5
title: Three-stage SPOC+PBL blended course structure: online preparation before class, PBL case discussion during class, online consolidation after class
description: The article's blended neurology course divides teaching into three stages. Before class, teachers release preview materials (PPT and flash GIFs of nervous system anatomy) on the Xuexitong platform so students "can watch videos repeatedly, post difficult questions online". During class, teachers use PBL with students as the main body: offline teaching of localization diagnosis methods, group discussion of cases with typical neurological signs, and online in-class exercises. After class, students complete online review of difficult parts and teachers post homework and extended reading. This structure reserves class time for detailed explanation and application rather than anatomy review.
requirements: Teachers must fully prepare online video content and publish online interactive test questions
An online teaching platform (Xuexitong) for releasing materials and collecting questions
Students need strong self-learning and problem-solving skills
constraints: The article states there is still a lack of unified syllabus to standardize online neuroanatomy teaching content, so preparation takes much time and effort
The study applied this structure to one chapter (Anatomy, Physiology, and Localization Diagnosis of Nervous System Lesions) over four class hours
target_learning_goals: neuroanatomy review and localization diagnosis of nervous system lesions
clinical reasoning and application of textbook knowledge to practical problems
examples: Teachers prepared cases with typical neurological signs; students were divided into groups to discuss and learn localization diagnosis, and completed in-class exercises online

article_title: Assessment IS learning: developing a student-centred approach for assessment in Higher Education.
citation: Rutherford S, Pritchard C, Francis N. (2024). Assessment IS learning: developing a student‐centred approach for assessment in Higher Education. FEBS Open Bio. https://doi.org/10.1002/2211-5463.13921
title: Three-stage educator-facilitated peer feedback: review a peer's work, replicate the process on one's own work, then build a change plan
description: Peer evaluation develops self-evaluation skills only when scaffolded. The review states that 'The process of peer evaluation and peer feedback needs to be a scaffolded process (illustrated in Fig. 5), whereby, initially, the peer assessor is guided through the evaluation process by the educator'. In the first stage the educator trains the peer assessor to appreciate and internalise required standards; the second stage, which the article calls the most important and often omitted, has the assessor replicate the evaluation on their own work; finally each student builds a change plan noting important points for the future. Evaluation can target exemplars, previous students' work (with permission), or GenAI output rather than a peer's work.
requirements: The educator needs to facilitate the surfacing of self-reflection; developing student feedback literacy is essential for self-feedback impact to be felt
constraints: Peer evaluation is often adopted sub-optimally, which students find disconcerting and disengaging; evaluating a colleague can be uncomfortable for students
target_learning_goals: self-evaluation, internalising standards, and scientific writing skills
examples: The authors use this pattern to teach scientific writing in Year 1: across five modules students write a set of figures or an introduction, methods, results or Discussion section, bring hardcopies to a facilitated peer feedback session guided through reviewing a peer's work then their own, note key learning points, and use these reflections in a final full scientific paper report
key_sources: Rutherford S, Pritchard C, Francis N. (2024). Assessment IS learning: developing a student‐centred approach for assessment in Higher Education. FEBS Open Bio. https://doi.org/10.1002/2211-5463.13921

article_title: Does an aptitude for surgery exist and can we predict it? An experimental study.
citation: Ruchay Zino, Julian Pape, Julia-Sophie Cordt, Carolina Kerres, Sebastian Siehl, Karina Jansone, Johannes Ackermann, Veronika Guenther, Liselotte Mettler, Leila Allahqoli, Nicolai Maass, Frauke Nees, Ibrahim Alkatout. (2024). Does an aptitude for surgery exist and can we predict it? An experimental study. International Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1097/JS9.0000000000001577
title: Three-factor latent-construct model of surgical aptitude: psychomotor skills, personality, and motivation
description: The article models surgical aptitude as three latent constructs — psychomotor skills, personality, and motivation — analyzed within a structural equation modeling framework. As the authors state, "These latent constructs cover three key factors of surgical aptitude, namely psychomotor skills, personality and motivation". Psychomotor skills were constituted by CANTAB variables (visual information processing, learning-based memory, spatial working memory, reaction time, motor response), personality by the five NEO-FFI traits, and motivation by fear of failure, challenge, probability of success, and interest. The model was applied separately to students and physicians, revealing different weightings by experience level.
requirements: Latent constructs measured via validated instruments (CANTAB, NEO-FFI, QCM) and SEM analysis software
constraints: The article notes the data stem from a cross-sectional design, and longitudinal approaches are needed to assess trajectories over the complete learning process
target_learning_goals: surgical training performance in minimally invasive surgery tasks

article_title: A case-controlled trial evaluating the summative performance of the 3-D skills Model.
citation: Robertson C., Noonan Z., Boyle J.G. (2024). A case-controlled trial evaluating the summative performance of the 3-D skills Model. BMC Medical Education 24:954. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05943-9
title: The 3-step deconstructed (3-D) skills model: a near-peer teaching model integrating Peyton's comprehension and self-practice steps around a formative OSCE
description: The 3-step deconstructed (3-D) skills model is a near-peer teaching model for psychomotor clinical examination skills, developed as a more focused alternative to Peyton's four-step approach. The article states it "integrates the comprehension and self-practice elements of Peyton’s model, structured around a formative OSCE assessment", delivered as three minutes of guided teaching per station. Its proposed mechanism is scaffolded learning supported by cognitive congruence.
requirements: Delivery by near-peer tutors trained in the model at a half-day training event
Embedding within a formative OSCE with additional guided time after each station
constraints: Developed and evaluated for clinical examination skills in undergraduate medicine
Uses about three minutes of guided teaching per station, more time-limited than Peyton's full four-step approach
target_learning_goals: clinical examination skills
summative OSCE performance
examples: Delivered at a voluntary formative OSCE with six examination stations, four weeks before the year three summative examinations

article_title: Enhancing cosmetic suturing skill acquisition in surgical residents through spaced learning training: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Yan Xinjian, Abudouresuli Adilijiang, Yuemaier Abudukeremu, Ge Yan, Shang Shiyao, Yang Jue, Zhang Liulu. (2024). Enhancing cosmetic suturing skill acquisition in surgical residents through spaced learning training: a randomized controlled trial. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2024.2363940
title: Three-theory account of the mechanisms by which spaced learning benefits clinical skill learning
description: The article names and substantively describes three candidate mechanisms for the spacing effect in skill learning. The processing defect hypothesis holds that "massed presentations cause less brain processing in learners, so memory is worse", whereas spaced learning increases processing volume. The neuroscientific mechanism holds that spacing improves long-term memory by increasing extraction and recovery of prior neural representations, supported by EEG evidence of spatiotemporal pattern similarity in the right prefrontal cortex and reduced neural repetition suppression. The metacognitive mechanism attributes part of the effect to adults' biased belief that concentrated learning is superior, a bias children lack.
requirements: Explains benefits of spaced relative to concentrated presentation schedules
constraints: These are theories about mechanism reported from prior literature, not tested within this trial's data
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention of complex procedural skills and knowledge
examples: The discussion cites EEG findings that stronger spatiotemporal pattern similarity after 543-727 ms predicted better memory and was more evident in spaced than concentrated learning.
key_sources: Yan Xinjian, Abudouresuli Adilijiang, Yuemaier Abudukeremu, Ge Yan, Shang Shiyao, Yang Jue, Zhang Liulu. (2024). article_title: Self and peer feedback engagement and receptivity among medical students with varied academic performance in the clinical skills laboratory.
citation: Abraham Reina and Singaram Veena S. (2024). Self and peer feedback engagement and receptivity among medical students with varied academic performance in the clinical skills laboratory. BMC Medical Education 24, Article 1065. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06084-9
title: Three-domain framework of feedback engagement: affective or interpersonal, orientational, and transformational
description: The article's thematic analysis grouped medical students' perceptions of self- and peer feedback into an organizing framework of three domains with seven sub-themes. The affective or interpersonal domain captures "how students perceive the purpose and value of feedback in relation to their self-assessment and peer interactions"; the orientational domain covers clarifying task requirements and feedback seeking behaviour; the transformational domain covers reflection and understanding, improved performance, and increased autonomy.
requirements: Derived from thematic analysis of focus group data from students with experience of formative logbook assessment feedback
constraints: Developed from a single undergraduate program at a single institution, drawing solely on medical students' perspectives rather than tutors
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in clinical skills training
target_learning_goals: feedback literacy
self-regulated learning
engagement with self- and peer feedback
examples: Focus groups of high, average and low performers were analysed into two sub-themes in the affective and orientational domains and three in the transformational domain

article_title: Beyond active learning: Using 3-Dimensional learning to create scientifically authentic, student-centered classrooms.
citation: Cooper M. M., Caballero M. D., Carmel J. H., Duffy E. M., Ebert-May D., Fata-Hartley C. L., Herrington D. G., Laverty J. T., Nelson P. C., Posey L. A., Stoltzfus J. R., Stowe R. L., Sweeder R. D., Tessmer S., Underwood S. M. (2024). Beyond active learning: Using 3-Dimensional learning to create scientifically authentic, student-centered classrooms. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0295887
title: Three-Dimensional Learning (3DL): practices, core ideas, and crosscutting concepts intertwined
description: 3DL is a framework for science learning originating in the National Academies' "A Framework for K-12 Science Education" that centers "constructing productive causal accounts for phenomena". It comprises three interconnected dimensions: Scientific and Engineering Practices, Disciplinary Core Ideas, and Crosscutting Concepts. The Framework emphasizes that "for meaningful learning, the three dimensions must be inextricably intertwined"; for example, modeling how energy is transferred within or between systems requires all three dimensions at once. The authors adapted the Framework for higher education, working with disciplinary experts to define discipline-appropriate Core Ideas, and use 3DL as a unifying framework tying together approaches such as POGIL, CUREs, and interactive simulations.
requirements: All three dimensions must be intentionally built into learning objectives, assessments, and classroom activities for meaningful learning.
constraints: The Framework's original Core Ideas were developed for interdisciplinary K-12 science and did not align with college-level introductory course organization or depth.
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory biology, chemistry, and physics gateway courses
target_learning_goals: using disciplinary knowledge to explain, model, and predict phenomena
engagement in Scientific and Engineering Practices
examples: A general chemistry class session on solutions in which students observed salt dissolution, then used the Core Ideas of Energy and Electrostatic and Bonding Interactions with the Crosscutting Concept of Systems and System Models to construct a model explaining the temperature change.
key_sources: Cooper M. M., Caballero M. D., Carmel J. H., Duffy E. M., Ebert-May D., Fata-Hartley C. L., Herrington D. G., Laverty J. T., Nelson P. C., Posey L. A., Stoltzfus J. R., Stowe R. article_title: Cost-effectiveness of virtual reality and wet laboratory cataract surgery simulation.
citation: Ng DS, Yip BHK, Young AL, Yip WWK, Lam NM, Li KK, Ko ST, Chan WH, Aryasit O, Sikder S, Ferris JD, Pang CP, Tham CC. (2023). Cost-effectiveness of virtual reality and wet laboratory cataract surgery simulation. Medicine 2023;102:40(e35067). https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000035067
title: Three-module progressive simulation curriculum: basic wet laboratory skills, wet laboratory phacoemulsification, then proficiency-based virtual reality training
description: The standardized curriculum consisted of 3 modules: a 6-hour supervised wet laboratory module on basic microsurgical skills (wound construction, viscoelastic use, instrument handling, wound closure, suture placement), a 6-hour wet laboratory module performing all phacoemulsification steps in synthetic model eyes, and a proficiency-based virtual reality module in which trainees practiced "for unlimited time until a score of 600 out of 700 was achieved" on validated Eyesi exercises. Randomization occurred only after module two.
requirements: All trainees must complete the first module before proceeding to the second module
constraints: The virtual reality simulator does not yet provide tactile feedback, which wet laboratory training enables
target_learners: novice ophthalmology residents with no prior microsurgical simulation or phacoemulsification experience
target_learning_goals: phacoemulsification surgical competency transferable to the operating theater
examples: Group A trainees spent a mean of 148.13 ± SD 57.60 minutes (range 84–312 minutes) completing the Eyesi proficiency requirement.

article_title: Realistic simulation in nursing education: Testing two scenario-based models.
citation: Martins, T., Santos, F., Lumini, M. J., Sousa, M. R., Peixoto, M. J., Freire, R. M., Salazar, B., Fernandes, C., & de Fátima Araújo, M. (2023). Realistic simulation in nursing education: Testing two scenario‐based models. Nursing Open, 10, 3326–3335. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.1585
title: Scenario template organizing patient and caregiver information by themes with infographic impairment indicators
description: A reusable scenario design pattern in which information is classified by topics for the patient (e.g. situation summary, self-care impairment, sociodemographic data, personal background) and the caregiver (e.g. availability to provide care, self-efficacy, affective relationship), supplemented by illustrative graphical elements. "The traffic light system was chosen to indicate the level of impairment": green for no impairment, yellow for moderate and red for severe, with three equal icons per concept for students who have difficulty distinguishing colours. The template adopts the ten domains of the self-care dependency evaluation form.
requirements: Intentional and systematic planning by the teaching team to identify and classify the information usually provided in scenarios
constraints: Developed for the specific topic of a person regaining independence and returning home after an acute event, with adaptation to other contexts proposed but not tested
target_learners: undergraduate nursing students in laboratory realistic simulation
target_learning_goals: recognizing focuses of attention to prioritize when formulating intervention plans and understanding patient and caregiver conditions
examples: Tables 1 and 2 present the matrices of scenario information on the person with self-care impairment and on the caregiver, each with type of information, rationale and example

article_title: Methodologies used by Nursing professionals in the production of educational videos: An integrative review.
citation: Barbosa RFM, Gonzaga AKLL, Jardim FA, Mendes KDS, Sawada NO. (2023). Methodologies used by Nursing professionals in the production of educational videos: An integrative review. Rev. Latino-Am. Enfermagem 2023;31:e3951. https://doi.org/10.1590/1518-8345.6690.3951
title: Three-stage model of educational video production: pre-production, production and post-production
description: The review organizes educational video (EV) production methodology into three sequential stages. As the review states, "the methodological stages used for the process to elaborate and make the videos include pre-production, production and post-production". Pre-production covers preparation and validation of a script and storyboard, production covers video recording and editing, and post-production covers evaluation of the video by the target audience. The review uses this model as its organizing axis for categorizing the 19 primary studies.
requirements: Each stage should be applied and/or described by the producers, including validation of the script and storyboard before production
constraints: The review notes that in 14 of 19 studies there was no use of a methodological framework to ensure rigor in conduction
target_learning_goals: Methodological rigor in producing and validating educational videos
examples: Studies in the sample such as Lopes et al. and Silva et al. applied the Fleming, Reynolds, Wallace (2009) framework across the three stages, while Razera et al. used the Falkembach (2005) framework with analysis, modeling, implementation, evaluation and distribution phases
key_sources: Barbosa RFM, Gonzaga AKLL, Jardim FA, Mendes KDS, Sawada NO. (2023). Methodologies used by Nursing professionals in the production of educational videos: An integrative review. Rev. Latino-Am. Enfermagem 2023;31:e3951. https://doi.org/10.1590/1518-8345.6690.3951
